docs.title: Partner readiness: agreeing terms with a device manufacturer — proposal
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-18 at 17d599d4e.

What this is: a proposal (part 3 of the overview, recommendations; how the overview is organised), for the Nightscout Foundation board, the maintainers of the ecosystem projects, and the community. Read after the quality system; leads to why organise. DRAFT PROPOSAL for discussion. Written 2026-10-16 against this repository at faafc57c. The facts it relies on are on the governance and evidence pages. It touches contracts, intellectual property, medical-device reporting, privacy and competition law. Each of those parts needs review by the foundation's counsel, and the reporting parts by a regulatory or quality professional, before any decision or negotiation rests on them (§10). Nothing here is decided.

Author's interests: the author maintains cgm-remote-monitor, founded a company that hosts Nightscout commercially, and could be a candidate for paid work under the related proposals. The collaboration rules §5 would apply to that company and to the author like anyone else.

docs.title: 1. The request
docs.text:
Prepare the ecosystem to make written agreements with pump and CGM manufacturers for access to their devices and data, starting with read-only access, and build the shared operations a manufacturer will ask about before it signs: one named accountable party per agreement, security response, and complaint and incident handling.

Today, access to most devices rests on protocols that volunteers worked out, and on the interoperability rights described in DIGITAL-RIGHTS. Those rights remain. Where a device accepts commands only from a client holding a credential the manufacturer issues, knowing the protocol is no longer enough: access then depends on an authorised relationship with the manufacturer. This page is about being ready for that relationship.

docs.title: What is at stake on each path
docs.text:
Encryption alone does not close a path. Tandem's t:slim X2 and Mobi pair with a code shown on the pump, and open implementations work with them (device-layer census; pumpX2 6fa9459). Dexcom G7 and Libre 3 also check the app: after the person's code or NFC scan, the sensor asks for a client credential, and the open implementations work by carrying a fixed one that the manufacturer did not issue to them, in their source or as a separate download (xdripswift c268542, Juggluco 75399d7, LibreLoop 150d2b1, read 2026-10-17). That access lasts while new sensors and firmware keep accepting it. A path closes when a device stops accepting every credential open software can present, or when the data is sealed so that the phone cannot read it.

path what it feeds what would close it what happens when it closes sensor to phone, over the device's own radio link the glucose input of an automated insulin delivery (AID) app; readers such as xDrip+ a sensor that stops accepting the client credential open apps present, or pairs only with an app the manufacturer has authenticated; readings encrypted end to end for the vendor's cloud, so the phone relays data it cannot read automation stops. In Loop, no new dose is recommended once the newest reading is more than 15 minutes old, and the temporary basal rates Loop sets last at most 30 minutes, after which the pump returns to its programmed schedule (LoopAlgorithm 7d016fb, inputDataRecencyInterval, tempBasalDuration). Other controllers: not verified here (§10) phone to pump, commands automated and manual dosing from the open app a pump that accepts commands only with a credential the manufacturer issues the pump keeps running its own programmed delivery; automation and dosing from the open app stop, and the person needs the manufacturer's own controller for that pump vendor cloud to a connector Nightscout sites, and the caregivers who follow them login, bot-defence or terms changes, or a cloud that admits only approved apps readings stop arriving at the site until a connector fix ships (evidence §5); remote following and alerts through the site stop. The loop on the phone is not affected device generations in supply which devices people can obtain today's accessible devices leaving sale or insurance coverage people move to newer devices, whose paths may be closed. No end-of-sale dates have been collected (§10) build and signing platform every self-built app signing and declaration policy (Apple, Google) the app stops running when its certificate or build expires (evidence §5)

How many people each closure would reach is not counted anywhere today (§6).

The paths are drawn as believed, today and emerging in 1·access-paths, with a ladder of how much each device makes an open app depend on its manufacturer. Device by device:

The cells that read "not checked", "not read" or "not collected" are the list of what to find out next (§10).

Keeping access has running costs, with or without an agreement. Without one, connectors follow each vendor-cloud change (evidence §5), the US copyright exemption for device data needs evidence at each three-yearly renewal (vendor note §3.4), and each new phone operating system needs app releases. With one, continued access depends on the terms in §4, which are the ecosystem's requests. Nothing in this repository yet shows what would lead a manufacturer to accept them.

docs.title: 2. Three tiers of access, and which to ask for first
docs.text:
The tiers are this page's terms for technical risk. They are not FDA classifications.

tier what the integration may do relative risk A — observe and export read glucose, device status, delivery history and alarms; export them. The agreement states the path (the device's own radio link, or the vendor's cloud) and the maximum delay lowest B — configure and coordinate limited, confirmed settings changes, with an audit trail and device-specific limits higher C — control insulin delivery authenticated dosing or delivery commands highest; needs device-specific validation and a regulatory pathway

Recommendation: ask for tier A first, and separately. Tier A is the data-rights agreement. It delivers the five rights in the data rights primer — access, export, share, delegate, audit — for one device line, and it does not wait on anyone obtaining permission for a closed loop. Tiers B and C can follow under the same framework, each as its own agreement.

What tier A protects depends on its path and delay. An AID app needs readings on the phone within minutes (Loop stops recommending at 15, §1). A tier A agreement for a delayed cloud feed, such as Dexcom's public API, which runs one hour behind in the US and three elsewhere (vendor note §1.2), secures display, export, sharing and research. It does not secure automated insulin delivery. For that, tier A has to cover real-time reads over the device's own link, and the pump side needs tier C.

The same relationship at each tier, drawn (idea·tiers):

docs.title: 3. What a manufacturer will need to see
docs.text:
A manufacturer weighs whether a relationship creates technical, security, legal, regulatory and business risk it can manage. These are the questions it is likely to ask, and the evidence that exists in the ecosystem today.

question evidence a manufacturer would expect what exists today Who is accountable? a legal entity, named officers, named technical and security contacts the foundation is a 501(c)(3) (governance §3); no named security contact for any project Is the software trustworthy? versioned specifications, independent review, reproducible test results tied to a release schemas, mappings and conformance assertions for the server API (programme §4); no device or connector repository publishes a per-release test report (evidence §1) Can a security problem be contained? a disclosure policy, a response plan, the ability to revoke a client's access none of the 20 repositories measured has a SECURITY policy of its own; private vulnerability reporting is on in 4 of them (governance §2) Will defects that reach users be handled? a complaint workflow, investigation records, an escalation route to the manufacturer a defect register for cgm-remote-monitor (backfix register); no complaint workflow in any project (§6) How are releases controlled? signed builds, recorded change review, a software bill of materials (SBOM), release provenance review rules differ by repository (governance §1); no SBOM or build-provenance record found in this repository's survey Is personal data protected? access controls, a privacy policy, retention rules, audit logs per site; no ecosystem privacy or retention policy Will the counterpart still be there? funding, insurance, succession, continuity and termination terms concentration measured in evidence §4; the rest is in what only the foundation can supply Who bears which liability? an allocation in the contract, stated intended uses, insurance matched to the role none What does the manufacturer gain? fewer unsupported integrations, structured reports of field failures, evidence about third-party use proposed in §6; not yet operating

Most rows in the last column say "none". That is the finding this page is built on: the engineering evidence is ahead of the operational evidence.

The proposition to a manufacturer changes with it. Not "allow our applications to connect to your devices", but: the ecosystem runs shared verification, security response and incident handling for independent applications, which lowers the cost and risk of supporting the third-party use that already happens, and shows what that use looks like.

docs.title: 4. What the ecosystem needs from an agreement
docs.text:
§3 is what the manufacturer needs from us. An agreement also has to secure what people with diabetes and the projects need from the manufacturer. These terms carry the data rights.

term why it matters Nonexclusive access any implementation that meets the published criteria may qualify; sponsorship or first arrival buys no right to exclude others (the principle of COLLABORATION-MODEL rule 2, "money and staff buy work, not control") Patient-directed and portable the person decides which tools and helpers receive their data, and can take it with them; delegation to caregivers and clinicians is included Notice before change a stated notice period for firmware, API, cloud and certificate changes that affect the integration, and test devices or a sandbox to try them Revocation by process a client's access is suspended or revoked under published grounds with notice and appeal, except an immediate suspension for an active security incident; revoking a credential must leave a person's devices in a defined safe state Freedom to publish results conformance and interoperability results can be published, so other implementers and users can see what works Stated costs and limits any fees, rate limits and support channels are written into the agreement, not set later

docs.title: 5. Terms of the agreement itself
docs.text: term what to settle Intellectual property and licences whether a protocol specification shared under a non-disclosure agreement can be implemented in source code published under the projects' licences (AGPL, GPL, MIT and BSD are all in use, governance §1); if not, which parts stay closed and who holds them. This is the term most likely to block an agreement. Regulatory roles who is the manufacturer for which function, and which claims each party may make Intended use and labelling what each tier's integration may say it does, and use of each party's name and marks Complaints in both directions what each party forwards to the other, within what time, and through which contact (§6) Data and jurisdiction which privacy regimes apply to the data each party handles, by region Termination and wind-down how people already using the integration keep working, or are moved safely, when an agreement ends Disputes, and competition how disagreements are resolved; a competition-law review of any exclusivity or selection criteria

docs.title: 6. Complaint, incident and support handling
docs.text:
Why it comes first. A manufacturer subject to FDA's quality-system rule must keep records of complaints about its device, and must report some events to FDA: certain deaths, serious injuries and malfunctions within 30 calendar days of becoming aware of them, and some within five work days (21 CFR Part 803). Reports that arise through third-party software are part of that duty. A partner with no channel to receive and forward them is a source of events the manufacturer cannot see. Expect any agreement to ask for one.

Three streams, one intake. Reports arrive today on Discord, Facebook, Zulip, Gitter and GitHub (governance §2). A shared intake can accept all of them, but triage separates three kinds:

stream example handling support how to set up a connector answered in the community's channels; no safety record complaint a stale glucose value shown as current; displayed delivery differs from the pump's record a record with an owner, investigation and disposition security vulnerability a flaw that exposes data or allows unauthorised commands under embargo until fixed; through private vulnerability reporting

The lifecycle of a complaint. Received → triaged for severity, safety, security and the devices involved → investigated (reproduce, logs, root cause, fix, test) → reviewed for referral to the responsible manufacturer, and for containment → closed with corrective action, a regression test, an answer to the reporter, and a place in the trend data. Each record keeps the time received, the software and device versions, the owner, the suspected safety effect, the investigation history, each referral decision, and the reason for closing. It also records when the party handling it is not the manufacturer of the device involved.

Intake is not legal responsibility. A shared intake coordinates investigation and routes reports to the party that is legally responsible. It does not take over a manufacturer's quality system, and it does not by itself give every project the duties of a manufacturer. Whether operating it creates any duty for the foundation is a question for counsel (§9, question 7). Anyone can also report a device problem directly to FDA through MedWatch.

What the records are for.

  • Across projects. A firmware change that breaks one CGM's link in Nightscout, AndroidAPS, Loop and xDrip+ appears as four unrelated reports in four channels. Shared intake can connect them, tell each project's maintainers, and give the manufacturer one reproducible report. That is the benefit a manufacturer gets from the arrangement (§3, last row).
  • Into the quality loop. A confirmed report becomes a replay vector or regression test in the shared kit of the quality-system proposal.
  • Into data-rights advocacy. Advocacy for access to device data — renewal comments in the Copyright Office's exemption proceedings, submissions to regulators, interoperability and right-to-repair work — is stronger with dated, counted cases than with accounts. The intake would record, for example, each time a device, app or cloud change cut a person off from their own data, how many people and projects it reached, and how long it lasted. The connectors have followed vendor-cloud changes since 2020 (evidence §5); today none of those cases is recorded in that form.

Privacy. Complaint records carry health data and reporters' identities. They are held with restricted access. Public trackers carry only de-identified summaries, links to the regression test, and the disposition. Published figures are aggregates with a minimum count, so that no person can be picked out.

docs.title: 7. Credentials for devices that require them
docs.text:
Where a device accepts only an authenticated, authorised client, the shared infrastructure needs:

requirement what provides it a recognised client enrolment of the developer or organisation, and of each release credentials issuance by an authorised party, protected storage, rotation, revocation permission boundaries separate authorisation for tiers A, B and C pairing documented enrolment, replacement, recovery and transfer of a device incident response the ability to suspend or revoke a compromised client audit a record of issuance and of security-sensitive actions continuity disaster recovery, a successor operator, support commitments patient autonomy access the person can direct, move and withdraw, wherever the device supports it

Three roles, kept apart. A registry of who participates, the authority that issues credentials, and the hosting of any application are different jobs with different exposure. The credential authority in particular needs an operator with its own contract, security controls, insurance and continuity plan (ECOSYSTEM-PROGRAMME §2b). Issuance has standing only under the manufacturer's authority; a way of distributing credentials without it does not supply revocation, accountability or a contract.

No single point of failure for therapy. A shared identity or credential service must not be able to stop someone's insulin delivery by being unreachable. Previously authorised, safely bounded local operation should continue without a connection. The permitted offline behaviour, the expiry rules and the safe states are defined and validated with each manufacturer. Drawn as three states of one credential (idea·credential-lifetime):

Separating request from effect. Identity answers who is asking; authorisation, whether they may; capability, whether this device and firmware can; and execution evidence, whether it happened. The last matches the split between requested and applied state that the hub-sync architecture already makes for state spans.

docs.title: 8. Order of work
docs.text:
Five pieces have the best ratio of effort to leverage, and four of them extend work that exists:

  1. A safety intake pilot (§6): one intake, the three streams, the record shape, an owner, and one drill run end to end. New.
  2. Cross-project compatibility tests: the conformance assertions and replay vectors in conformance/, extended to one device integration shared by two or more projects.
  3. A release-evidence baseline: the per-run record of the quality-system proposal, plus an SBOM.
  4. Common event schemas: the schemas in specs/, keeping requested and applied state apart.
  5. A readiness dossier: §3's table, kept current, with a link to the evidence for each row. It is what a manufacturer would be handed.

Security contacts and private vulnerability reporting for each project cost little and can start at once. An operating credential service comes last, after a contract with a manufacturer and funding for its operator.

docs.title: 9. Decisions requested
docs.text:
For the board:

  1. Whether to seek tier A agreements first and separately (§2).
  2. Whether to adopt the rule that the foundation may sponsor shared operations without operating them, and does not operate a credential authority itself (ECOSYSTEM-PROGRAMME §2b).
  3. Whether to fund a safety intake pilot, and who owns it.
  4. Who is the named accountable contact for a manufacturer conversation.

For the maintainers of the ecosystem projects:

  1. Whether each project would route complaints to a shared intake while keeping its own channels.
  2. Whether each project will publish a security contact and turn on private vulnerability reporting.

For counsel, and for regulatory and quality professionals:

  1. Whether operating a shared intake, or forwarding complaints, creates reporting or record-keeping duties for the foundation or for any project.
  2. How the terms in §4 and §5 are best written, and in particular how a specification shared in confidence can be reconciled with the projects' open-source licences.
  3. Whether any selection criteria or exclusivity in an agreement raise competition-law concerns.
  4. Which privacy regimes apply to complaint records (HIPAA only through covered-entity relationships; otherwise possibly the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule; GDPR for reporters in the EU; for reporters in Washington State, the My Health My Data Act, RCW 19.373, whose "regulated entity" is "any legal entity" doing business there or targeting its consumers, with no exclusion for non-profits, and which gives consent, access and deletion rights over consumer health data).

docs.title: 10. Points for reviewers to verify
docs.text:
• Regulatory references (§6). The Part 803 time limits and their conditions; the complaint-record requirements under the Quality Management System Regulation, effective 2026-02-02, which incorporates ISO 13485:2016 (complaint records at 21 CFR 820.35 and ISO 13485 clause 8.2.2). FDA reissued its cybersecurity guidance for device submissions in February 2026 to refer to the new regulation; confirm its current text before citing what it expects of software suppliers.
  • The measured rows of §3 were read from the governance and evidence pages, measured 2026-10-02. Re-measure before the table is given to anyone outside the ecosystem.
  • "No SBOM or build-provenance record" (§3) is from this repository's surveys, which did not search for one specifically. A targeted search should confirm it per project.
  • The tiers (§2) are a proposal. A manufacturer's own categories may differ, and the agreement should use whichever both parties can apply.
  • What happens when a path closes (§1). The Loop row was read from LoopAlgorithm 7d016fb, not run. AndroidAPS, Trio and iAPS should be read or run for the same case (stale glucose, lost pump link) before the table is given to anyone outside the ecosystem.
  • Device supply (§1). End-of-sale and coverage dates for the devices the open implementations support today (Omnipod Eros and DASH, the older Medtronic pumps, Dana, Dexcom G6) have not been collected.

cut branch behind dev conflicting paths 1 chore/retire-jsdom 362 12 2 chore/build-runtime-separation 362 19 3 chore/compose-mongodb6 362 22 4 chore/mime-exposure-review 362 36 5 chore/nightscout-modernization 238 27

docs.title: Status words: merged is not released
docs.text:
In the backfix register, neither fixed nor merged means an operator is safe. fixed means repaired on a branch that has not been merged. merged means merged into origin/dev and not released. released means in a tagged release operators run. 15.0.9 (RT-0) was released on 2026-10-21 (tag v15.0.9, master c6a0d8ed), so every entry merged before then is released 15.0.9. Merging to dev publishes a Docker Hub image; that is not a release. If a defect marked fixed or merged exists in 15.0.9, anyone running 15.0.9 still has it; anyone still on 15.0.8 also has every released 15.0.9 entry.

The size of that, from the register's §1 (the section whose defects reach existing operators), measured 2026-10-07 with node tools/queue/gates/register-exposure-legend.js: 120 defects (BF-12, invalid, BF-41, closed, and BF-71, closed as working as intended, excluded) — 27 open, 89 merged, 1 partly merged, 3 fixed (BF-52; BF-09 and BF-156 on unmerged branches). A few were introduced and repaired on dev before any release (BF-80, BF-106 and BF-142, as of 2026-09-26), so they never reached 15.0.8. The count moves when entries are filed or merged; re-run the gate before quoting it.

The register's open count is therefore not "the number of defects still shipping": it omits the 83 repaired-but-unreleased ones (81 merged, 1 partly merged, 1 fixed). The status column tracks work done, not operator exposure, which is why the queue carries ships_to_operators_today as a separate field.

Claimed state by parcel. Every cell is a claim about what the gates will say.

parcel not-started in-progress gate-not-met ready-to-push blocked in-flight-upstream merged-upstream released needs-decision done unsettled closed answered total phase0 3 18 1 22 release-train 8 2 1 22 15 2 1 4 55 register-open 29 3 1 1 5 2 55 58 5 5 164 tenancy 21 22 7 6 17 6 10 1 15 6 111 docs-truth 7 1 11 19 backfix2 2 2 platform 8 2 2 1 25 38

Three states here are not what a casual reader expects:

  • gate-not-met is a measured state, not an opinion. Work exists and a declared gate fails.
  • in-flight-upstream means handed to upstream reviewers and not ours to land.
  • merged-upstream means merged into dev and not released. It is deliberately not called done: nothing merged has reached an operator.

The queue also carries explicit no-gate: markers — a record that a property has no measurement built yet, with the reason. They are bookkeeping, not gaps in it; make queue-validate prints how many gate slots are in that state.

docs.title: The two constraints, neither of them engineering
docs.text:
1. Publication is a manual human act, on purpose. Agents prepare branches, commits and tags locally and stop. A human pushes, merges, tags and publishes. This is a standing rule. Pushing to cgm-remote-monitor's dev or master fires main.yml's docker-build job and publishes a Docker Hub image, so dev and master are publication events, not branches. A release is three separate human decisions: merge the code, push the tag, publish the package.

2. Review routes to the maintainer. The modernization commits have one author, so each cut needs a reviewer other than its author before it reaches dev.

Where the queue says each item's review has to come from:

the item is waiting for items share Maintainer 373 91% SECURITY reviewer 17 4% Maintainer + a second human 8 2% SAFETY reviewer 6 1% Unassigned 3 1% Whoever edits it next 3 1% Upstream reviewers 1 0% total 411

The SECURITY and SAFETY rows name a kind of reviewer. For #8754 (login security fixes and TRUST_PROXY, merged as 4f705217), the named reviewers were the maintainer and Andy. The other SECURITY and SAFETY rows still have no individual assigned. BFQ-72 (BF-72, an unauthenticated request that can occupy the database for minutes, live on 15.0.8 and dev) has a disposition decided by the maintainer. It is held outside this public repository because the defect is live on the shipping release (the disclosure rule, DOCUMENT-CONTROL §3.8).

If you are considering reviewing, REVIEWER-ONBOARDING.md is the read-this-first path, and reports/reviewer-packets/ has one bounded packet per item awaiting review.

docs.title: A quality system for the Nightscout ecosystem — proposal
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-18 at 17d599d4e.

What this is: a proposal (part 3 of the overview, recommendations; how the overview is organised), for the maintainers of the ecosystem projects, the Nightscout Foundation board, the companies that host or build on Nightscout, and the community. Read after working together; leads to partner readiness. DRAFT PROPOSAL for discussion, requiring review by the maintainers and by a quality-management professional before it is adopted. Where it touches vendor terms of use, device regulation or funding agreements, it also needs review by the foundation's counsel (§10). Written 2026-09-30 against this repository at df5e2ade and the stack census record of the same day; simulator and app-rig facts are from the device-simulators record of 2026-10-17; the lesson on parity tests in §4.1 is from the algorithm audition note of 2026-10-18 §3.5. Borrowing a practice from a quality standard is not a claim of conformity with it. Nothing here is decided.

Author's interests: the author maintains cgm-remote-monitor, founded a company that hosts Nightscout commercially, and could be a candidate for paid work under the sponsored-team proposal. The rules in COLLABORATION-MODEL §5 would apply to that company and to the author like anyone else.

docs.title: 1. The request
docs.text:
Adopt a small quality system shared across the whole ecosystem stack: from the radio link to a sensor or pump, through the controllers, connectors and servers, to the tools a person uses to see and move their own data. Size it the way SQLite sized its own, by keeping only the practices that "genuinely improve quality" (qmplan). Build it in stages, each useful alone (§5). And agree the requirements for success in public, with a method that records every objection and answers it (§8).

This page proposes what the system contains and how the requirements would be agreed. The ecosystem programme says where it sits; the collaboration rules say how organisations work together on it; the sponsored-team proposal says who could do the work that nobody is paid for today.

docs.title: 2. Why the whole stack
docs.text:
The census of 2026-09-30 (record; summarised with the other observations in evidence §1) measured 62 repositories (63 listed; a fork kept level with its upstream counts once), 56 of them active in the last year, with 219 human authors between them:

  • The same work is done many times, separately. 14 device protocols have 41 independent implementations, and for 10 of them no two implementations test against the same bytes. Six code bases log in to Dexcom Share and five to LibreLinkUp, and each meets a vendor change on its own schedule.
  • Evidence exists but is not kept as evidence. There are more than 35,000 test declarations across the stack, and simulators as good as faketandem, which since 2026-10-14 also holds its own Tandem codec to pumpX2's with 7,961 recorded cases. Since 2026-10-12 a Dexcom G7 sensor emulator (g7sim) and an Omnipod DASH pod simulator (LoopKit/pod) can serve one Loop build together in the iOS Simulator, with no radio. But only 14 repositories run their tests in CI, and no device or connector repository publishes a per-release test report.
  • Some checks exist nowhere. No fuzzing harnesses, no automated hardware-in-the-loop rigs, no shared fixtures for vendor clouds, no scheduled check that notices a vendor change before users do. The nearest to a rig is trio-test-harness, which builds Trio or Loop from a PR and drives it on the iOS Simulator or a phone with the apps' built-in device simulators, and reports per PR. No harness run yet configures a Nightscout or checks what an app uploads.

The ecosystem's purpose depends on every layer. People use these tools to keep their data portable and computable for their own benefit, and to hand that job to helpers and tools they choose. That holds only if the driver reads the sensor correctly, the connector still works after the vendor changed its login, and the server stores what the app sent. A quality system for one layer leaves the others unexamined.

docs.title: 3. What "enough" means: SQLite's plan, element by element
docs.text:
SQLite built its quality management plan by "going through the description of outputs in section 11 of DO-178B" (the avionics software standard) "and writing down those elements that seemed relevant". It keeps 100% MC/DC coverage for the core library because it is so widely deployed, and says full coverage is "probably not cost effective for a typical application" (testing). The transferable part is the method: take each element, keep it only where it pays. Sources for every SQLite row: histories annex §A.

element SQLite here today proposed for the ecosystem A plan short enough to read its test: "a competent developer can be assimilated into the development team quickly" DOCUMENT-CONTROL, DEFINITION-OF-DONE, REVIEWER-ONBOARDING, for this repository only this page, kept to what a new contributor to any project can act on Requirements are the documentation requirement text carries an ID hashed from the text; the build reports which tests cover which IDs schemas graded measured / declared / read-from-code (specs/); conformance assertions (conformance/) stable IDs on the normative statements of the shared API description and of each protocol's vector corpus, with a coverage report from the conformance suite (§4) A release checklist run by people about 200 items, "record when and by whom each validation step was performed"; items added "as new problems … are discovered" the work queue's gates and no-gate: reasons; the 15.0.9 integration record one checklist template per kind of component (driver, connector, server, app), each item naming who ran it and when (§4) A bug is fixed only with a test "not considered fixed until new test cases that would exhibit the bug have been added" the backfix register marks each defect reproduced or read-derived; What the layers share. Every layer needs the same three things: inputs described in one language-neutral format, a record of each run, and a way for every implementation to use the same inputs. That is what makes one person's test evidence reusable by the other projects.

docs.title: 4.1 The record every run leaves
docs.text:
A test run anywhere in the stack leaves one record with the same shape. Borrowed from design controls, where design inputs (requirements) lead to design outputs (the code), verification shows the outputs meet the inputs, and validation shows the product meets the user's need.

part contents identity component, version, commit, the digest of the artefact tested, and how the run reached it: through the call path the product uses, or only through a test harness inputs the requirement IDs covered; the vector-corpus or fixture version, and the source of its expected values; simulator scenarios; the configuration matrix (runtime, database, device, region) procedure the checklist item or gate; who ran it and when; automated or by hand outputs pass, fail and skip counts; the red control that shows the check can fail; logs, de-identified known gaps what was not covered and why (no device, no account in a region, no rig) status verified (checks against the requirements) or validated (checked in real use on a rig or with a person); never "safe"

Tests that pass against code the product never calls. In one independent implementation of the oref and Loop algorithms, parity tests passed against matching code that the app did not run; a live comparison against a running controller exposed a 2.30 U/hr disagreement in one recommendation. The same implementation's exported vectors carried its own outputs as the expected values, so they could detect a change in it but not an error (algorithm audition §3.5). Two parts of the record answer this: the identity says whether the run reached the artefact through the product's own call path, and the inputs name where each expected value came from.

The 15.0.9 records in this repository already carry most of these parts; the proposal is that every project can produce the same record with shared tooling. Rule 6 of the collaboration model applies: a record says what was checked, and says nothing about clinical safety or regulatory status.

docs.title: 5. Build it in stages
docs.text:
Zephyr, an open-source real-time operating system working toward safety certification, brings in its coding rules in stages: first published and "not enforced", then enforced on a small scope, then widened (Zephyr safety overview). The same pattern fits here, with each stage useful even if the next never happens:

  1. Publish. The vector-corpus format, the fixture format, the record template and the checklist templates. No project is asked to change anything. Volunteer-sized.
  2. Adopt where it is already half done. The projects that already share vectors or run simulators in CI: Omnipod (three implementations holding copied vectors, and LoopKit/pod), Tandem (pumpX2 and faketandem, which already check each other), Dexcom G7 (G7SensorKit next-dev and g7sim, which share known-answer cases), Medtronic 7xxG (PythonSake and JavaSake), and nightscout-connect with cgm-remote-monitor.
  3. Shared labs. A connector lab and a change canary for the vendor clouds; the conformance suite runnable against any server.
  4. The expensive pieces. New simulators, parser fuzzing across decoders, a hardware-in-the-loop rig, controller validation on real AID rigs.

Each project's maintainers decide whether and when their project takes part.

docs.title: 6. What it costs, and who could pay
docs.text:
The census record estimates the device and cloud layers at 167–388 person-weeks one-time (about 3–7.5 person-years), then 0.4–0.7 of a full-time engineer, plus 6–30 person-weeks a year of vendor changes (record §6). These are estimates with stated assumptions. They exclude maintainers' review time, counsel's time and the server layer, which the sponsored-team proposal sizes.

Much of stage 1 and 2 is volunteer-sized: a checklist template, the bug-to-test rule, and vectors extracted from tests that already exist. The rest is sustained work on fixed dates set by others, the kind the sponsored-team proposal describes. Some maintainer time is paid today: commercial Nightscout hosts pay for part of the time of maintainers who work for them, on terms each host sets, and those arrangements differ in scope, availability and the compliance obligations each host carries. No organisation pays for maintenance as shared ecosystem work, on published terms, with a public report. That shared arrangement is what this page and the sponsored-team proposal describe.

Funding routes found (sources: histories annex §C):

route fits caveat NLnet / NGI Zero small milestone grants for public deliverables; the only funder read that has funded health software (Goupile, 2024) its Commons Fund closed its final call on 2026-06-01; other programmes remain; a "clear European Dimension" is required, which a US 501(c)(3) would need to check Sovereign Tech Fund "open digital base technologies": the shared contract, conformance suite, protocol and connector libraries work over €50,000; "currently not looking for user-facing applications" Alpha-Omega security audits and security work on critical projects, in quarterly rounds security scope only companies that need assurance release evidence packaged for their own quality systems, fixes on the line they run (SQLite's model; collaboration rule 8) the evidence that decides a public release stays public a member-funded shared lab device and connector labs that hosts and app builders each run privately today, pooled (KernelCI's model) needs members; labs hold health data only when de-identified

docs.title: 7. Histories that map
docs.text: OpenSSL after Heartbleed, xz-utils, curl, Debian's paid long-term support and Dunc-Tank, the Open Home Foundation, KernelCI, ELISA and Zephyr, and Tidepool Loop are in PRECEDENTS: histories, each with what maps to this proposal; sources are in the histories annex §B. The two this proposal leans on most: OpenSSL turned money into a working project through named roles plus written policies, not money alone; and Debian's lesson from 2006 is never to let one person decide who is paid.

docs.title: 8.1 Methods other projects use
docs.text:
Sources: histories annex §D.

method where from how it would work here requirement records with published states Kubernetes KEPs (provisional, implementable, implemented, deferred, rejected, withdrawn, replaced), with approvers "distinct" from authors each requirement for the shared layers is a record with a state, approved by maintainers of the projects it affects who did not write it a champion who records dissent Python PEP 1: the champion is "responsible for building consensus … and documenting dissenting opinions" each record carries a dissent section; the volunteer-only view has a standing place there (§8.2) a final comment period Rust RFCs: ten calendar days, advertised widely; not "consensus amongst all participants" but no "strong consensus against" a ten-day window announced in every app community's channel before a requirement becomes implementable rough consensus IETF RFC 7282: "all issues are addressed, but not necessarily accommodated" the test for each requirement: every objection has a written answer; objections are answered, not counted goals with owners Rust project goals: "Goals cover a problem, not a solution"; "Nothing good happens without an owner"; reset every six months a six-monthly slate of ecosystem goals, each with a named owner (volunteer or paid) and the projects that support it; funders pay for a goal, not a solution a cap on any one employer Python PEP 13: "at most 2 members of the council can work for any single employer" no deciding group has a majority from one company or host

docs.title: 8.2 The volunteer-only view, stated fairly
docs.text:
Some people argue the ecosystem should have no paid maintainers. The strongest form of that view (histories annex §E):

  1. Independence. Whoever pays sets priorities, even without meaning to. In software next to dosing, a host's commercial priority could displace safety work.
  2. Fairness. Paying some people makes a two-class project and can demotivate the others; Debian's 2006 signers said so.
  3. Motivation is not bought. "Money alone will not fix a struggling infrastructure project" (Roads and Bridges), and some maintainers do not want pay.
  4. Money is fragile. A paid seat ends when its sponsor leaves; a volunteer project has no payroll to lose.
  5. Money brings noise. curl ended its bug bounty for that reason.
  6. The line between DIY and regulated. People build and run these tools themselves; paid development could blur that line.

Each of these protects something every stakeholder wants: independence, fairness, and a community that owns its tools. §8.1 asks that every objection get a written answer, so each has one here, drawn from the histories in §7 and the precedents:

  1. Independence. The risk is real, and the answer is structural rather than an absence of money: no payment decided by one person, paid people never approving their own work, and no deciding group with a majority from one employer (§8.3, rules 1, 4 and 5). Unpaid work is not free of outside priorities either; it goes to whatever its volunteers, or their employers, can fund.
  2. Fairness. Debian's objection came from a project of about 1,000 voting developers, and Debian later accepted paid long-term support run outside the project (§7). The census counted 219 human authors across 62 repositories in the last year, and cgm-remote-monitor had 11 to 18 a year from 2021 to 2025 (evidence §3). At that scale the question is less who is paid than whether the dated work in §6 gets done.
  3. Motivation is not bought. Agreed for the work people choose. Paid roles here cover the work that waits: review queues, releases, vendor changes, security response. A maintainer who does not want pay is never asked to take it; that is a reason not to require pay, not to prevent it for others.
  4. Money is fragile. So is volunteer time: cgm-remote-monitor's committers fell from 47 in 2019 to 11 in 2024 before its releases slowed (sponsored-team proposal §2). Fixed terms, several funding routes (§6) and public records that outlast any one person reduce both risks.
  5. Money brings noise. curl ended paying per report. Its lead is employed by a company that sells curl support (§7). Nothing here pays per report.
  6. The line between DIY and regulated. Tidepool Loop's clearance ran alongside the DIY project, each with its own label, and ELISA and Zephyr supply evidence while certification stays with the certifier (§7). The same releases can serve people who build their own tools and companies that use the evidence in their own quality systems; collaboration rule 6 keeps the labels apart.

docs.title: 8.3 Requirements both views could accept
docs.text:
Other projects reconciled the same tension with safeguards, each sourced in the annex. Together they make a set that a volunteer-only advocate and a proponent of paid maintenance could both accept:

  1. No payment is decided by one person.
  2. Paid work is a named role, service or goal, with public deliverables and an end date.
  3. Money is held and paid out by a body that does not hold merge rights.
  4. Paid people do not approve their own work.
  5. No deciding group has a majority from one employer or host.
  6. A public report every month.
  7. Each project's maintainers, paid or not, keep the merge decision; no payer gains it.
  8. Every proposal records its dissent, and every objection gets a written answer.

That gives the volunteer-only view a standing test that anyone can check in public. If a payer ever decides what merges, rule 7 has been broken; if paid people approve their own work, rule 4. If paid work goes unreported, rule 6 has been broken.

docs.title: 8.4 A first slate to discuss
docs.text:
These are candidate requirements for success, offered as the first records for the process in §8.1, not as decisions. Each is a standing commitment of someone's time on dates set by others, so each is read together with its cost (§6): adopting a requirement without funding it assigns the work to whoever volunteers.

id candidate requirement who it serves most evidence it would be measured by RQ-1 Alarms and data keep working through vendor cloud changes people with diabetes, caregivers days from a vendor change to a released fix, per connector RQ-2 The server is released on a published schedule, with security fixes on a stated horizon everyone, hosts most release dates against the schedule RQ-3 Every device protocol with two or more implementations has one shared vector set app projects, driver authors protocols with a corpus, and implementations loading it RQ-4 Every release of a shared component leaves a public record in the §4.1 shape reviewers, hosts, researchers records per release RQ-5 Data holders can run checks on their own data without sending it anywhere data holders, researchers probes available; studies run RQ-6 No single party controls the shared contract second servers, app projects the change-request record (collaboration rule 5) RQ-7 The rules in §8.3 hold volunteers, the foundation the monthly reports

docs.title: 9. Decisions requested
docs.text:
For the maintainers of each project:

  1. Whether the kit in §4 fits your layer, and which piece your project would try first.
  2. Whether your project would load a shared vector set or fixture set from its own tests, if one were published in a neutral repository.
  3. Whether the method in §8.1 is acceptable for requirements that touch more than one project.

For the foundation board:

  1. Whether the foundation hosts the neutral repository for the shared formats, corpora and records, and the requirement records of §8.
  2. Whether to adopt the rules in §8.3 for any paid work it funds or brokers.
  3. Which of the funding routes in §6 to pursue, and who writes the first application.

For the companies that host or build on Nightscout:

  1. Which records in the §4.1 shape your own quality processes would use, and what you would contribute toward the shared labs.

docs.title: 10. Points for reviewers to verify
docs.text:
For a quality-management professional:

  1. Whether the record in §4.1 is enough for a company to use as input to its own design controls, and what it must not be read as.
  2. Whether "verified" and "validated" are used consistently with the standards the reviewer works to.

For counsel:

  1. Whether a change canary that uses volunteers' own consenting accounts against vendor clouds is consistent with each vendor's terms of use (cloud annex §4.3).
  2. Whether shared vector corpora derived from device captures raise any issue under the exemptions in DIGITAL-RIGHTS, and what de-identification they need.
  3. Whether a US 501(c)(3) can meet NLnet's "European Dimension", and the terms of any grant in §6.

For everyone:

  1. The census figures are dated 2026-09-30; re-run the census before quoting them.
  2. The effort figures are estimates; check them against maintainers' own experience.
  3. The histories in §7 were read 2026-09-30; the annex §F lists what could not be verified.

docs.title: Reviewer onboarding — read this first
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-06 at 773c8bc59.

What this is: a guide (contributor-facing). Read after the overview; leads to the mission. Written for somebody who has never seen this repository and is considering reviewing work in it. Prose revised 2026-10-03 against cgm-remote-monitor official/dev 1ad03e29 and official/master 92d08342 (tag 15.0.8).

Thank you for looking. What you would be taking on, so you can decide quickly:

The modernization work reached chore/nightscout-modernization through 100 child pull requests from one author. Before any of it reaches dev, each cut needs a reviewer other than its author. That is the review you would be doing; the gates and evidence documents are there to keep each review bounded.

docs.title: What you are looking at, and what it is not
docs.text:
Nightscout is open-source software that people run themselves to see their own or a family member's glucose data. The Nightscout Foundation stewards it; it does not manufacture devices or prescribe therapy. Users build and run these tools themselves, which means a defect here reaches somebody's kitchen table, not a support queue.

That shapes what review means here. In most codebases the bad outcome is a crash. Here the bad outcome is a read that is silently wrong — a number that renders plausibly and is not the number in the database, or an alarm that does not fire. A crash is loud. These are not. So a change that "passes the suite" is the failure mode to design against, not the evidence to relax on.

Two repositories, and they have different rules. This repository (rag-nightscout-ecosystem-alignment) holds tooling, documentation, evidence and QC harnesses. The shipping application is cgm-remote-monitor, and it stays pristine — findings are written up here and referenced from there, never pasted into its code comments. Harnesses here require() the shipping module by path so the two cannot drift.

docs.title: The reading path — about an hour
docs.text:
Five documents, in this order. Each row says what that document is authoritative for, which matters because several documents discuss the same facts and only one of them owns each.

# read ~ authoritative for 1 PROGRAMME-STATUS.md 5 min the three horizons, and which constraint is actually binding 2 queue/README.md 10 min how work state is recorded, and why state is a claim rather than a fact 3 ../30-design/remedial/nightscout-backfix-register.md — §3 and §4 first, then skim §1 20 min defect facts and BF- ids. Nothing else may contradict it 4 ../30-design/remedial/phase0-pr-sequencing-2026-09-15.md 15 min which branches are coupled, and what order they can land in 5 the packet for whichever PR you take, in reports/reviewer-packets/ 10 min that one change: what it does, what the evidence proves, what it does not prove

If you only read two, read 1 and 3.

Then, by horizon, when you need it:

  • Modernization — ../30-design/modernization/semver-and-release-versioning-policy-2026-09-15.md
  • Multitenancy — ../30-design/tenancy/nightscout-multitenancy-execution-plan-2026-09-14.md (decisions D1–D21)
  • Research and measurements — ../60-research/{remedial,modernization,tenancy}/, filed by horizon

docs.title: Five conventions you need, or the documents will read wrong
docs.text:
1. A claim is not a measurement. queue/work-queue.yaml carries state: for each item. That field is only a claim about what the gates will say. make queue-status runs them. The runner prints CLAIM DIVERGES when they disagree. queue/QUEUE.md is generated so that nobody can quietly edit a status into the human-readable view.

2. no-gate: is bookkeeping, not a gap in it. Every queue item's gate is either a runnable command or an explicit no-gate: marker carrying a reason. There is no third option, and validation rejects a manifest where the gate list is empty — because a missing gate that renders as blank looks exactly like a passing one.

3. A check that has never failed is not yet evidence. Before a gate counts, the thing it tests gets broken to confirm the gate notices. Two ways a gate goes vacuous: the corpus never exercises the property, or the code never distinguishes the branches. And a green ablation has two opposite meanings — the check may be vacuous, or the break may not have broken anything. Always confirm the break landed before concluding anything about the test.

4. Read-derived and reproduced are different grades of claim. Register entries are marked as one or the other. Across Phase 0, every claim that failed when run was read-derived, and two prescribed fixes would have made things worse. Treat any "the fix is X" as a hypothesis until somebody runs it; if you are reviewing a fix, that is the thing to be suspicious of.

5. Neither fixed nor merged means released. In the register, fixed means repaired on a branch that has not been merged; merged means merged into origin/dev and not released; released means in a tagged release operators run. No programme fix is released: official/master is 523 commits behind dev (2026-10-02) and the shipping tag is 15.0.8. The register's open count is therefore not "the defects still shipping": of the 109 defects in the register's §1 (2026-10-02), 26 are open, 81 merged, 1 partly merged and 1 fixed on a branch. See PROGRAMME-STATUS.md.

docs.title: Picking something to review
docs.text:
Four entry points, easiest first:

  1. An open pull request. NEEDS-A-HUMAN.md lists them with a one-line description, and reports/reviewer-packets/ has a bounded packet for each item awaiting review. Every 15.0.9 pull request is merged into dev, and none is released; the largest is #8758 (records keep their own _id across API v1, v3 and the websocket, a change to core data paths), and a review of its evidence is still useful after the fact. The connector's fixes are released as nightscout-connect 0.1.0 (2026-09-24), which dev pins exactly (#8762).
  2. A security or safety item. #8754 (login security fixes and TRUST_PROXY) is merged into dev but not released; a second pair of eyes on its evidence is still welcome. Among safety items, BFQ-92 (a page with no glucose reading presents no server alarm, including device alarms) has no fix yet.
  3. The release. RT-0, 15.0.9, was released on 2026-10-21: release PR #8598 merged as master c6a0d8ed (100 first-parent merges, dev 4bca2ac2), tag v15.0.9. How it was released and what is left are in ROADMAP §1, its contents are in contents.md, and how the candidate was tested is in the 15.0.9 integration record.
  4. An unsettled item. BFQ-09, A7A-7 — it is not yet established that these are defects at all. Settling one either way is a complete, self-contained contribution.

docs.title: What good review looks like here
docs.text:
• Check what the gate does not prove. Every packet has a section for this. A gate can pass for the wrong reason.
  • Stop and report a mismatch; never reach for the nearest thing that works. Many real defects here surfaced that way — a dropped RegExp that widened a live query, a synthesised acknowledged, a missing non-upserting replace, an inverted $exists. In each case a workaround would have kept the suite green.
  • Call out changed test expectations loudly. If a change edits what a test expects, that needs a stated reason, in the diff, where a reviewer will see it.
  • Say when you are not sure. "I could not tell whether this is right" is a useful review outcome and is recorded as such.

docs.title: Two rules that are not negotiable
docs.text:
• Never push, merge, tag or publish. Prepare work locally and stop. Pushing to dev or master builds and publishes a Docker image — those branches are publication events, not branches. A human makes that call deliberately.
  • Treat any user-submitted data as sensitive health data. CGM traces, Nightscout exports, crash and device logs. Do not reproduce names, emails or other identifiers in issues, comments, commits or documentation.

docs.title: Getting set up
docs.text:
make bootstrap        # clone the external repositories into externals/ (git-ignored)
make queue-status     # run every static + unit gate — this is the measurement
make queue-check      # what CI runs
make queue-vacuity    # ask every gate whether it could actually fail
make views-check      # confirm the generated tables in docs/00-overview are current

If you are reviewing a branch, give yourself your own git worktree and your own test database. Worktrees share a MongoDB instance and concurrent runs destroy each other's data.

npm run test:unit is not the whole suite and is not database-free. It resolves to 44 of 159 test files, and without MongoDB it fails six. CI runs all 159. If a packet tells you to run a specific test, run that one rather than assuming the local script covers it.

docs.title: Questions, and who to ask
docs.text:
Open an issue in this repository, or comment on the pull request you are reviewing. If something in these documents contradicts something else, say so: contradictions are tracked as defects in the docs-truth parcel, because readers act on the section they read. The standard these documents are held to is DEFINITION-OF-DONE.md.

Generated from queue/work-queue.yaml by tools/queue/emit_views.py. Manifest measured_at 2026-09-27, against cgm-remote-monitor-official 7000eb18 and this repository at 18cdcce0. Every state above is a claim about what the gates will say — make queue-status is the measurement.

What this is: a map of the work ahead (contributor-facing). Read after programme status; leads to work waiting on a person. Prepared for the Nightscout project; proposed for Nightscout Foundation stewardship. This page gives the order of the work ahead. It records no decisions itself. The decisions live in these places, and this page links to them:

what where it is decided the release train and each release's number versioning policy §8.3 tenancy decisions D1–D23 tenancy decisions reference defect facts, and what ships to operators today backfix register each item's state, gate and blockers queue/work-queue.yaml; make queue-status measures it

For where things stand, see PROGRAMME-STATUS. For which decisions are waiting on a person, see NEEDS-A-HUMAN. How to read the order tables. An item's wave comes from the blockers it is still waiting on. An item waiting on nothing that is still open is wave 1. The states shown are claims about what the gates will say, not measurements.

docs.title: 3. Multitenant
docs.text:
Self-hosted single-tenant Nightscout stays first-class permanently (D1, D4). Multitenant is an additional deployment target.

The multitenant delivery roadmap owns milestone acceptance criteria; the batching plan §5 owns the current completion sequence. Start with the tenancy reading guide. Use the delivery dashboard for bounded accepted evidence and remaining gates, and the next-generation platform map for architecture dependencies and parallel lanes. docs.title: 4. Remedial: fix what ships
docs.text: The remedial work is not a sequence. It is prioritized by what reaches operators today: the operator-exposure table on PROGRAMME-STATUS lists the queue items for defects that are present on 15.0.8. A fix reaches operators only in a release, so each merged fix joins the next step on the release train.

docs.title: 5. Proposals
docs.text:
These are proposals for discussion with other projects and maintainers. None is scheduled in the queue.

Cross-project adoption (hub and spoke). This is a proposal to the controller projects (AAPS, Loop, Trio) and to Nightscout as the hub. Each phase is useful even if the next never happens:

  1. A schema for controller settings documents in the existing v3 settings collection.
  2. Two one-symbol fixes, one in Nocturne and one in NightscoutKit, that stop dosing records being discarded.
  3. A catalogue of controller registrations shipped with the hub.
  4. A read-only sync contract.
  5. Therapy effects, then batched writes, then decomposition.

Nothing in it requires a Loop protocol change. Detail and evidence: adoption roadmap.

Product direction after the modernization baseline. This is a discussion between the maintainers. It proposes these work packages once the modernization branch is accepted:

  • bringing the connector's source in-tree;
  • extracting the report statistics into a tested module and exposing them through a documented API;
  • a first Svelte report (Daily Stats), also usable as a standard Web Component;
  • PDF export for sharing with a clinician;
  • vendor test fixtures shared across projects.

Library and implementation choices are open. Detail: modernization review and proposed next steps.

A shared quality kit for the whole stack. A proposal to every project: vector corpora for device protocols, simulators, fixture suites and a change canary for vendor clouds, a conformance suite any server can run, and one record shape for every test run, built in four stages. It also proposes how requirements that touch several projects are agreed. Detail: quality-system proposal, measured by the stack census.

docs.title: 6. What bounds all of it
docs.text:
Review capacity, not engineering. Most queue items route to the maintainer, and the SECURITY and SAFETY review rows do not name a person. The current split is on PROGRAMME-STATUS. Onboarding for reviewers is in REVIEWER-ONBOARDING.
