client constraint Loop (NightscoutKit) needs exactly 200 and a reply array as long as the batch; a shorter array or a whole-batch 400 makes it resend the batch on every trigger Trio any non-2xx stops its upload pipeline for up to 24 h xDrip+ entries stay queued (up to 7 days); treatment PUT failures drop later items in the pass AndroidAPS v3: treatments, entries, food a 400 drops the record and moves on; any other 4xx blocks that kind's queue AndroidAPS v3: profile, devicestatus any non-2xx blocks the queue all no client reads a refused member or a Warning header

docs.title: 4.2 Message text
docs.text:
text constraint "Bad or missing utcOffset field" AndroidAPS string-matches it and resends with utcOffset: 0; a new rule must not produce it "cannot be modified by the client" AndroidAPS string-matches it and marks the record as never uploadable. Reuse it only when "permanent, don't retry" is intended, as the BF-170 PATCH _id decision does any reply containing "Not" on the v1 socket AndroidAPS 3.4.2.6's v1 socket client reconnects on it (session f4's lane report, 2026-10-25; not re-checked for this note)

The draft's unit test checks every rule message against the first two (design note §3.2).

docs.title: 4.3 Relaying writers
docs.text: Some writers re-send content that is already stored: oref0, tconnectsync, nightscout-connect's Nightscout source, the Nightscout profile editor, and AndroidAPS 3.4.2.6. Refusing a value that a working site may already hold can wedge them: the same stored content is refused on every pass. tconnectsync exits after 45 minutes of failures. (Session f4's lane reports, 2026-10-25; not re-checked for this note.)

docs.title: 4.4 Value types sent today
docs.text: oref0 sends timeAsSeconds and value as strings (lane report, 2026-10-25). A type rule must not cover those fields.

docs.title: 4.5 Status codes
docs.text: Prefer a status clients already handle (400 for a refused item; the D2 200 for a mixed v1 batch). Never answer a client error with a 5xx.

docs.title: 5. Adding a new check
docs.text:
step question if yes 1 Is it a structural invariant (class a: true for every client, e.g. a range is ordered, a timed record has a time)? candidate for the shared module 2 Is it controller policy (class b: a range or vocabulary one controller chose)? stays client-side; Nightscout may surface a declared range (design note §3.5) but does not refuse on it 3 Is it time sanity (class c: a reading dated ahead of the server clock)? flag only (log, read-side flag); do not refuse 4 For class a: can the value already be stored on a working site? follow the staged ladder: log → notify → opt-in refuse → refuse by default in a major (as decided for BF-67/86 on 2026-10-13, and for WRITE_VALIDATION D1) 5 For class a: the value could not be stored without the site already failing refusing directly is acceptable

Worked example (a maintainer decision of 2026-10-25): refuse a value the server could never have loaded; tolerate on read a value a working site may hold. Then check §4: the status and message the refusal produces, and whether a relaying writer re-sends the value.

docs.title: 6. Open items for maintainers
docs.text: item question queue batch-policy alignment move today's whole-batch field-type refusal to the D2 policy, or keep it whole-batch WRITE-CONTRACT, MOD-WRITE-VALIDATION read-side flag flag stored records that break a rule on API v3 reads (R1), report them (R2) MOD-WRITE-VALIDATION-READ units canonicalisation N1 (spelling) or N2 (mg/dL plus original), and the conversion constant MOD-UNITS-CANONICAL socket coverage opt-in validation on the socket's add and update paths (design note §3.1 lists it as the next step) MOD-WRITE-VALIDATION filtered /storage broadcast BF-164 plan C, decided 2026-10-25: filtered broadcast after checks cover every path; filter and path-naming details open; /storage stays v3-only until then, and afterwards only records that pass the type checks are announced BFQ-164

docs.title: Platform contracts: the index to six layers and eight specifications
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-06 at 773c8bc59.

Contributor-facing. Living index, current at main 010e1661 (2026-10-18). Terms are defined in the platform glossary.

This page maps the work on how controllers (Loop, Trio, AndroidAPS and others) and hubs (cgm-remote-monitor, Nocturne) agree on what records are, who wrote them, and how they move. The aim has three parts:

  • Full audit fidelity. Every stored record says what it is, which copy of which controller wrote it, under which definition, and whether it was requested, applied, mapped or projected.
  • Controller-owned definitions, secured. A controller declares its own typed definitions. The hub accepts them per element, binds them to the credential that wrote them, and never lets one controller redefine another's data.
  • Cost-effective sync. Fewer requests per cycle with typed records, REST for writes and catch-up, a socket for live delivery, and versioned definitions so a new release does not need a full re-sync.

The material is organised in six layers. A lower layer never depends on a higher one.

layer question it answers depends on L0 Identity Which record, definition, instance or subject is this? — L1 Records What typed observations exist, and how are today's documents decomposed into them? L0 L2 Definitions and instances Who declared what a record means, and which running copy wrote it? L0, L1 L3 State and intent What was requested, what was applied, what is active now, and why did it end? L1, L2 L4 Change and sync How are writes matched, re-sent, ordered and delivered over REST and the socket? L0–L3 L5 Authority Who may register, write, route a command or act for someone else? L0, L2

Audit fidelity is not a separate layer. Each layer's section below lists what it records for audit.

Status words used here and in every specification's header. Evidenced: measured or read from source in the corpus or controller code. Decided: the maintainer decided it, recorded in the execution plan. Proposed: written as a rule for the maintainer to decide. Specified: a contract with synthetic conformance cases and a reference decision function in tools/nsschema/, which checks the cases but is not a hub. Implemented: a hub serves it. On 2026-10-18 the L2, L3 and L5 contracts are specified and not implemented; the first hub implementation is HUB-REG-CRM.

docs.title: The specification set
docs.text:
Eight specifications and a glossary, one file each under spec/. Each answers one question a reader brings, and each has its own rules, conformance cases and gate.

file question layer rules status queue glossary what does this term mean, and where is it specified? all — written — identity which record, definition, instance or subject is this, and when is a write a re-send? L0 I1–I9 written SPEC-ID records what typed observations and settings snapshots exist, and how do today's documents decompose into them? L1 R1–R9 written SPEC-RECORDS registration how does a controller declare what its data means, and how does a hub accept it and attribute what is written? L2 G1–G5, Q1–Q4 written SPEC-REGISTRATION state and intent what was requested, applied and active, who started it, and why did it end? L3 S1–S12 written SPEC-STATE-INTENT commands how does a request or a proposal reach a controller, and how does its outcome come back? L3, L5 CM1–CM32 written SPEC-REG-COMMANDS plans how is a plan proposed, approved in parts, held by the controller and mirrored by the hub? L3, L5 PN1–PN18 written SPEC-PLANS sync-transport how are writes matched, ordered and delivered over REST and the socket, and at what cost? L4 T1–T15 written SPEC-SYNC-TRANSPORT authority who may register, write, own, route or act for someone else? L5 AU1–AU6, DR1–DR7 written SPEC-AUTHORITY

Why these boundaries. Each boundary falls where the reader, the rate of change or the review differs:

  • identity changes rarely and every other specification uses it;
  • records change with the observation catalogue and the corpus;
  • registration changes with hub releases, and is read by both controller and hub authors;
  • state and intent changes with controller releases and their vocabularies;
  • commands carry the safety review of anything that reaches a controller;
  • sync-transport changes with performance work;
  • authority changes with the tenancy and authentication decisions.

Why not more. The grammar stays in registration: declaring an element and accepting it are read together, and the meaning table is what decides version-conflict. Version-scoped quirks stay there because they are declarations and recorded mappings. The effect and motivation model stays in state and intent while it is a proposal.

Why not fewer. Commands are kept apart from state and intent, because the request, proposal and acknowledgement lifecycle has its own cases and review, and from authority, which says who may rather than what happens. Authority is kept apart from registration so that binding, the owner's actions and delegation are read in one place.

Each file should stay readable in a sitting. Registration is the largest; command routing has moved from its §9 to commands §2.

How they are kept.

  1. One home per rule. Other specifications link to it by section and never restate it. Decisions stay in the execution plan; defects stay in the backfix register.
  2. Stable rule ids. A changed rule keeps its id; a removed id is not reused.
  3. One skeleton. Each file has the same parts, in order:
  4. a header: audience, the commit it is current at, its layer, its decisions and its queue item;
  5. files, rules, the sections, compatibility and open items;
  6. its conformance cases.
  7. Current rules only. History is in git. A section moved out of a dated document leaves its heading, a pointer, and a link to its text at the commit it was taken from.
  8. Generated, gated, one commit. Case and declaration tables are generated (python3 -m tools.nsschema.spec_cases <layer>). node tools/queue/gates/platform-spec.js <layer> checks a specification's cases, links and wording. A rule change lands with its schema and case changes in one commit.

docs.title: Who owns each layer
docs.text:
Each layer changes with a different group's work, so each has a natural owner. Status at main 0b0d150f, 2026-10-18:

layer changes with natural owner engaged today L0 identity rarely; every layer uses it hub and controller maintainers together the Loop developers shared an identifier proposal on 2026-10-17, close to D20 rule 5; the reply is drafted, not sent L1 records the observation catalogue and the site corpus hub maintainers, with research users specified in this repository L2 definitions and instances controller releases each controller team, for its own data proposals to the controllers not started (queue) L3 state and intent, commands, plans controller releases; carries the safety review controller teams, with caregiver-app teams specified in this repository; implemented in no hub or controller L4 change and sync performance work hub implementers (cgm-remote-monitor, Nocturne) proposal to Nocturne not started L5 authority tenancy and authentication decisions hub operators, with the foundation's oversight role decided in part (D7, D13–D19; D17 row 2 open) in the execution plan

L2 and L3 describe what controllers send and do, and today they are written here, not by the controller teams. They become the controllers' own when those teams review the parts that describe their data and hold a route to change them. Why the cut follows the teams is read in the Conway's Law case study §6.

docs.title: L0 Identity
docs.text: Spec spec/identity.md: rules I1–I9, contract ids, match order per collection, the proposed identifier format, open decisions, today's cgm-remote-monitor behaviour, 20 cases Drawn from hub-sync §3.7 rules 5–8; write contract §2.2, §3 and §6.1; hub-sync §3.6 Evidence identifier conventions (living draft: decisions of 2026-10-18 and one URL-form template per record kind and source); identifier format (UUID not required; constraints C1–C7); identifier duplicates; Loop identifier ask Schemas, cases specs/sync/registration-submit.schema.json (write.ids, matchedBy); specs/quirks/; 29 cases in specs/sync/conformance/quirks/ Decisions D20 Open ID-FORMAT-DECISION, ID-CLIENT-OID-DECISION, ID-V3-IMMUTABLE-DECISION (needs decision); ID-SIMPLE-MATCH, ID-VALIDATE, ID-FIRST-MATCH, ID-V1-LOOKUP, ID-UNIQUE-INDEX (blocked) Audit every write reply returns identifier and _id and says which one matched; an assigned ObjectId's time is the hub's receipt time, never the record's time Status specified (SPEC-ID); the v1 identifier match for entries and devicestatus is queued for cgm-remote-monitor after 15.0.9

docs.title: L1 Records
docs.text: Spec spec/records.md: rules R1–R9, the generated catalogue with evidence grades, decomposition measured, the settings snapshot and completeness, sensitivity labels, 10 checks. Drawn from specs/sync/primitives.yaml (the observation catalogue, graded measured, declared or proposed); D11 (devicestatus is decomposed, not given columns); hub-sync §3.3 Evidence typed schema evidence; primitive coverage; devicestatus and profile fidelity; extensibility models; quirks registry; glucose units at the profile boundary (a profile's values in its labelled units; one conversion at the accessor, proposed; BF-172 to BF-174) Schemas specs/nsschema/*.model.json (today's collections); specs/sync/controller-settings.schema.json; specs/sync/sensitivity.yaml (the two-axis sensitivity label) Open devicestatus and profile decomposition coverage is unmeasured (hub-sync §7) Audit the composite document is kept beside its decomposed records, so "what did the device send" stays answerable Status evidenced (SPEC-RECORDS); treatment routing measured at 99.86% by eventType alone; devicestatus and profile decomposition not measured

docs.title: L2 Definitions and instances
docs.text: Spec spec/registration.md: the grammar, the capability document, the product resource and fallback, definitions, instances, channels and roles, labels, typed writes, read selection, projected views, retention, binding and the owner, version-scoped quirks, open choices, 186 cases Evidence controller descriptions (the well-known tier); intent and workflow landscape §8–§9 (what a registration must declare); control-plane reconciliation (the kind/instance split of the earlier draft in cgm-remote-monitor docs/proposals, which these specifications are proposed to supersede) Schemas, cases specs/sync/controller-state-model.schema.json, hub-capabilities.schema.json, registration-submit.schema.json, controller-instance.schema.json; generated registrations in specs/sync/registrations/; 54 cases in specs/sync/conformance/, 103 in conformance/instances/ API surface API v4: which parts to share with Nocturne, and which listener serves each (snapshot, 2026-10-26): every proposed v4 operation by listener and status, Nocturne's v4 surface at 89dcaf1dd split by group, and the open decisions; the operations are described in specs/openapi/proposed/nightscout-v4.yaml Decisions D18 and its addendum; D19 Open SPEC-REG-MODES, SPEC-REG-MIGRATE; implementation HUB-REG-CRM, HUB-REG-CRM-SEAM, HUB-REG-CRM-ADMIN; adoption HUB-REG-NOCTURNE, PROPOSAL-REG-CONTROLLERS; §3.7's choices 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 12 await the maintainer Audit every typed record carries its instance, its definition id and its role's provenance; projected documents carry projectedFrom; records are attributed to the registration and its bound credential, never to a namespace string Status specified (SPEC-REGISTRATION)

docs.title: L3 State and intent
docs.text: Spec spec/state-intent.md: rules S1–S12 and A1–A12 (composition reported by the controller, kinds, slots, states, end reasons, the wire carrier, requested and applied, initiators, definitions, acceptance, the controller's command contract), the declared kinds (generated), composition per controller, effect and motivation (proposed), what is active at a time, 59 cases; channels from slots are registration §9 Evidence intent and workflow landscape (per-controller matrix, end encodings, how each hub decides what is active, command lifecycles); effects and versioning (effect separated from motivation); authority model Schemas specs/sync/controller-state-model.schema.json (stateSpans, composition, commands); specs/sync/shared-slots.yaml; specs/sync/therapy-effect.schema.json; specs/sync/effect-remapping.yaml Open the active-state choices (state and intent §6.3); undeclared vocabularies for PROPOSAL-REG-CONTROLLERS; LAB-TRIO-INTENT Audit requested and applied are recorded separately; each span records its end reason and initiator in the controller's own vocabulary; composition is recorded as the controller reports it, never computed by the hub Status specified for declarations (SPEC-STATE-INTENT) and, as a proposal with ten choices to confirm, for what is active at a time (rules A1–A12, SPEC-ACTIVE-STATE), where LAB-HUB-ACTIVE-STATE measured cgm-remote-monitor and Nocturne disagreeing

docs.title: L4 Change and sync
docs.text: Spec spec/sync-transport.md: rules T1–T15 (the write step, re-send outcomes, server write times, the change event; the measured cost; the sync read and write, the merged cursor, one opaque cursor, the low watermark, the socket as fast path; typed records on the socket; definitions and versions), 13 cases. Drawn from the write contract §2–§3 and §6.1, hub-sync §3.2 and the replay-fidelity proposal §1 Evidence make schema-sync-cost on 2026-10-18: endpoints each client's code declares, read from source (AndroidAPS 7e1d537d49 26, three never called; Loop 7; Trio 5), not calls per cycle (sync-transport §3); the write contract's measured matrix; lib/server/srv-dates.js on dev fade2299 Open WRITE-CONTRACT, WC-STEP-PATCH, ID-BATCH-RESULTS (blocked); BF-164 (which writes reach the socket); the choices in sync-transport §8; the in-flight window under single Audit one change event per write call; a matched re-send stores no second copy and is answered with the stored ids; each mapping the hub applies is recorded as quirksApplied Status the write path is decided and specified (T1–T4; T3 merged on dev); the sync read, cursor and socket rules are proposed and specified with 13 cases (SPEC-SYNC-TRANSPORT); typed socket delivery and versions are proposed without cases

docs.title: L5 Authority
docs.text: Spec spec/authority.md: principals and credentials (AU1–AU6), the binding and credential kind, the owner's actions, the authorisation of registrations and namespaces, who may receive a command, delegation as requirements DR1–DR7 with what is decided around it, what is recorded for audit, 70 cases Evidence agent trust boundaries (develop, interpret and act; a proposal lifecycle, proposed and not specified); configuration and delegation §5 (what a delegation design must provide); control-plane reconciliation; authority model Decisions D13–D17 (credential root, listeners, auth plane; D17 row 2 open) Open the choices in commands §9; delegation (authority §7); D17 row 2; the owner choices in authority §9 Audit the owner's listing shows every product's binding, credential kind and binding event, every instance's roles and liveness, and every overlap Status specified for registration, owners and command destinations (SPEC-AUTHORITY); the command record, outcomes and proposals are proposed in commands (SPEC-REG-COMMANDS); delegation is not specified

docs.title: Ideas borrowed from Kubernetes
docs.text:
Several parts of this design take what Kubernetes does well for declared, typed resources, and apply it to controllers that share a hub:

idea in Kubernetes here one object shape apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec every registration and definition has the same four members (registration §3) declared spec, reported status spec is what is wanted, status what is observed a definition declares what a controller's data means; the owner's listing reports what the hub granted, refused and saw overlap (registration §7–§9); a command record separates the request from its state (commands §4) reconciliation a controller drives observed state toward its spec the controller reconciles; each instance renewal re-evaluates every claim, and the hub records what it observes (registration §8–§9) leases coordination.k8s.io Lease for liveness and leadership instances hold leases; a lapsed holder loses its roles and is never a command destination (registration §8) labels and selectors key-value labels, selected by queries instance labels and read selection (registration §10, §12) typed extension resources CustomResourceDefinitions, versioned, with conversion controller-owned definitions with namespaced extensions, version-scoped quirks and projected views for older readers (registration §7, §13, §16) admission requests are checked and refused with a reason before they are stored each element is accepted or refused with a reason code, and nothing is rewritten (registration §5)

What the hub does with these is narrower than a Kubernetes control plane: it schedules nothing and acts on no therapy. It records, routes and refuses; the controller decides and enacts (D18).

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
For someone new to the series: this page, then the glossary, then intent and workflow landscape §2 and §9 for why the contract exists, then the eight specifications in layer order:

  1. identity (L0): every other specification uses its ids;
  2. records (L1): the typed observations a hub stores;
  3. registration (L2): how a controller declares what those records mean, the largest file;
  4. state and intent (L3): requested, applied and active state;
  5. commands (L3, L5): requests and proposals that reach a controller;
  6. plans (L3, L5): recurring intents approved once and held by the controller;
  7. sync-transport (L4): how all of the above moves;
  8. authority (L5): who may do each of the above.

Across the eight, control loops is an STPA analysis: it draws the loops the specifications set up, lists each unsafe control action with the rule that prevents it, and names the gaps the specifications now carry as open. Compatibility says, for every app the corpus holds and every layer, what the app does today and what it sees from a hub that implements the specifications without the app changing.

Two guides walk a controller developer through the specifications step by step, each step naming its rule and the conformance case that shows it: add a setting in your next release and bring a new controller onto a hub. Their hub-side companion, implementing registration in cgm-remote-monitor, tells a hub contributor where each slice goes in the code, in what order, and how it is checked.

docs.title: Controller descriptions: Nightscout describes the controllers it already recognises — proposal
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-06 at 773c8bc59.

What this is: a proposal (contributor-facing). Read after the hub-and-spoke sync sketch; leads to the replay-fidelity changes and the registration specification. Snapshot, written 2026-09-11. Current: the only statement of the controller-description proposal. Status: proposed to the named projects; the proposal to the controller projects is PROPOSAL-REG-CONTROLLERS. Corrected in place 2026-10-18: §4 says what the proposal is and which ideas it takes from Kubernetes, mapped to D18–D20 as specified. Its §5 decomposesTo mechanism is the direction adopted for devicestatus storage by D11 — execution plan §1. Measurements are over the 11-site corpus (snapshots 2026-04-01 and 2026-04-26). §2.2 was added 2026-09-27, checked against Nocturne 42275c81. One page of proposal, then a worked example, then the evidence.

Phase 1 is a file a controller never has to call. Descriptions are fetched, advisory and generated from measurement; a controller writes as it does today. The controller-owned tier that D18 adds takes several ideas from Kubernetes, credited in §4.

docs.title: 0. What this series is for
docs.text:
The work has three motivations, and every measurement in the series serves one of them:

Motivation Why it is not optional Where the evidence is a Unify typed representations of data. One place says what a field means, what type it holds, and which controller writes it Today every reader re-derives it and they disagree. 56 of 166 devicestatus paths are dropped by a typed consumer because the shape was never written down Typed schemas, Primitive coverage, specs/sync/primitives.yaml b Provide ways to extend it. A controller can ship a feature nobody else has without negotiating with the ecosystem first The current answer is "invent an eventType and hope". The quirks registry is the archaeology of that answer Extensibility models §1, §5 c Offer full data fidelity — replay and observability. What a controller decided, on what inputs, in what state, is recoverable afterwards Replay completeness is 20% for Loop, 50% for the oref0 family. A real consumer reads settings from screenshots because there is nowhere else devicestatus and profile fidelity §3, Hub-and-spoke sync §4.2, specs/conformance/observability-profile.yaml

Motivation (c) has a change list. Concrete changes for replay fidelity names them: eight more keys in a settings block Loop already writes takes it from 20% to 65% recorded and 100% recorded-or-derivable; one input-vector object takes the oref0 family from 50% to 78% and 100%. Neither needs a new API version, and the same document shows why adding typed resources need not cost a single extra request.

These pull against each other, and the controller description is the artifact that resolves the tension. Unification (a) pushes toward one fixed schema; extensibility (b) pushes toward letting each controller differ; fidelity (c) fails if either wins outright — a schema too fixed drops the vendor subtrees, and a schema too open cannot say what is missing. A description is the third option: the shape stays per-controller, and the fact of it is unified. That is also how (c) becomes measurable at all, because "Loop does not publish automaticBolusApplicationFactor" is only sayable once something enumerates what Loop publishes.

And the practical outcome, which is the point of the whole exercise: a controller keeps innovating on the features unique to it, while every controller gets a sync and observability floor for free. Being described earns the floor with no controller change (§3); publishing a description of your own is how you go above it. Nothing in this series asks a controller to give up what makes it different — it asks that the difference be written down where other software can read it.

docs.title: 1. The problem, in one paragraph
docs.text:
Nightscout already knows what kind of controller wrote a document — it has to, because Loop's devicestatus and Trio's look nothing alike. But that knowledge lives nowhere: it is re-derived, differently, by every reader. So the same divergence is rediscovered over and over, and the parts nobody writes down get silently dropped. Three measured consequences:

Measured devicestatus paths a typed consumer silently drops 56 of 166 — including Loop's automatic dose recommendation, on 10 of 11 sites Loop dosing inputs recorded in Nightscout 4 of 20. Eight are absent, including the factor that scales every automatic dose Temporary effects that record what they did, not just why 2,466 of 2,865 — the other 399 carry a label and no effect at all

None of this is a bug in any project. It is the cost of the shape being tacit.

Drawn 2026-10-17: the loop whose record this proposal is about, common to Loop, Trio and AndroidAPS, read from their source (the technical loops note §1 compares them). What the controller reports to the hub is the right-hand, dotted edge.

docs.title: 2. The proposal
docs.text:
Write the description down, in the hub, on the controller's behalf.

graph LR
  subgraph TODAY["Today — every reader re-derives it"]
    D1[devicestatus] --> R1[Nightscout UI<br/>guesses]
    D1 --> R2[Nocturne<br/>guesses differently]
    D1 --> R3[a report tool<br/>guesses again]
    R2 -.->|56 paths dropped| X1[lost]
  end
  subgraph PROPOSED["Proposed — written down once"]
    D2[devicestatus] --> REG[["controller description<br/>shipped with Nightscout"]]
    REG --> S1[Nightscout UI]
    REG --> S2[Nocturne]
    REG --> S3[a report tool]
  end
  style REG fill:#d4edda,stroke:#2c7a3f,color:#111
  style X1 fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#a12b2b,color:#111

A controller description is a static file that says: here is how to recognise this controller's documents, here is what it writes, here is which dosing inputs it publishes and which it does not.

Nightscout ships these files, and serves them. A controller that never changes anything still gets described correctly, because the descriptions are generated from measurements of what controllers actually write — not from what they promise.

docs.title: 2.1 Serving the catalogue: .well-known
docs.text:
Shipping the files only helps software that vendors this repository. Serving them helps everything that can make an HTTP request:

GET /.well-known/nightscout/controllers          → the catalogue index
GET /.well-known/nightscout/controllers/loop      → one description

Static JSON or YAML, cacheable, no authentication — a description of a controller product contains nothing about a person, which is what makes it servable at all (specs/sync/sensitivity.yaml carries the type-level sensitivity annotation that says so).

This is a small change with a disproportionate effect on motivation (a), because it moves the unification from this repository to the deployment:

Reader Today With a served catalogue Nightscout's own UI re-derives the shape inline reads its own catalogue Nocturne re-derives it differently — 56 paths dropped reads the same file A report or replay tool vendors this repo, or reverse-engineers four codebases one GET, no dependency on this repo oref-digital-twin vision model over screenshots discovers which settings should exist, then reads them A follower app guesses from the device string structural discriminator, published The site operator — can see what their own site believes it is talking to

It also gives the operator-declared posture a runtime home: a site configured with ENABLE=loop (see the roadmap §2.2) serves the Loop description as its declared expectation, and a controller that disagrees overrides it by publishing its own. The precedence is the same three-way order in both places — controller-published, then operator-declared, then structurally inferred.

It is discovery. The endpoint is optional: a hub that does not serve it behaves exactly as it does today, and a client that cannot fetch it falls back to what it does today.

docs.title: 2.2 Two halves: who a controller is, and what its data means
docs.text:
A server needs two things from a controller. It needs to know who the controller is and what it may touch. It also needs to know what the controller's documents mean. Today each server has at most one of the two, and never the same one.

half what it answers Nocturne (42275c81) cgm-remote-monitor (dev 295f1177) registration who is writing, and with what permission RFC 7591 dynamic client registration keyed on a reverse-DNS software_id, with OAuth scopes; a bundled directory of 13 known apps (src/Core/Nocturne.Core.Models/Authorization/KnownOAuthClients.cs), for example org.loopkit.loop, org.nightscout.trio and info.nightscout.androidaps, each with typical scopes such as GlucoseReadWrite and TreatmentsReadWrite none. An operator creates a subject with roles in the admin UI and gives its token to the app (lib/authorization/storage.js) description what the documents mean: how to recognise them, which paths they carry, which dosing inputs they publish none a controller can supply. Each algorithm's handling is compiled into the server: IAidDetectionStrategy implementations (ApsSnapshotStrategy, TbrBasedStrategy, NoAidStrategy) and the V4 decomposers none served. This proposal's descriptions exist in this repository only (specs/sync/registrations/{loop,trio,androidaps}.yaml)

The proposal: join the halves on one identifier. Add the software_id Nocturne already uses to each description:

metadata:
  vendor: LoopKit
  product: Loop
  softwareId: org.loopkit.loop   # proposed; the same reverse-DNS id as the known-app directory

Note, 2026-10-26: metadata.softwareId is now in the grammar as proposed (maintainer, 2026-10-26), in Nocturne's software_id form for compatibility: specs/sync/controller-state-model.schema.json and registration §5.1.

Then one identifier connects both:

step registration half description half a known controller the known-app directory has its software_id and scopes the served catalogue (§2.1) has its description under the same id a new controller registers itself with its software_id and the scopes it asks for optionally publishes its description under that id (§3, "one POST, once per release") a reader learns who wrote a document learns what the document means, from the id the write carried

What this keeps from phase 1 (§4). Registration stays wherever a server already requires it, and nowhere else. On cgm-remote-monitor, a controller still writes with a token and never has to call anything. The description stays advisory: fetched, not called; describing, not gating. A controller with no description is treated as it is today.

Why this matters for agents. This is design reasoning, not a measurement. Take a software agent that takes part in the system, for example one acting for a person or caregiver. It needs both halves:

  • Registration says what it may read and write, as narrowly as scopes allow.
  • Description says what its writes mean and which data it depends on that does not arrive through the server (out-of-band data, such as a phone's own sensor readings or a prediction it computed). A reader can then tell a delegated agent's records from a controller's, and can see what the agent relied on.

The authority questions this raises are in the authority specification; the control-plane supersession map names the rule that carries each part of the earlier draft. No lab has yet run a synthetic controller or agent through both halves. That would be the first measurement.

What it proposes to each project:

  • Nocturne: let a known-app entry, or a registration, point to a description by software_id, and read the description where its detection strategies and decomposers now hard-code the shape.
  • cgm-remote-monitor: serve the catalogue (§2.1) keyed by the same id. If it ever adds app registration, use the same software_id.
  • Both: agree on the identifier scheme, including how a build-specific id maps to the stable one. Nocturne already does this for Trio, whose iOS bundle id carries the developer team; its directory uses the stable org.nightscout.trio.

docs.title: 3. What changes, for whom
docs.text:
graph TD
  A["A controller's document arrives"] --> B{"Does Nightscout<br/>ship a description<br/>that matches?"}
  B -->|yes| C["Use it.<br/><b>Controller changed nothing.</b><br/>Loop lives here, permanently"]
  B -->|no| D{"Did the controller<br/>send its own?"}
  D -->|yes| E["Use that.<br/>One POST, once per release"]
  D -->|no| F["Treat as today:<br/>store it, describe nothing.<br/><b>Nothing breaks</b>"]
  style C fill:#d4edda,stroke:#2c7a3f,color:#111
  style F fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#a1791b,color:#111
Actor What they do When Loop nothing, ever — Trio, AAPS, a new controller optionally POST a description to correct or extend the shipped one once per release, if they want Nightscout ship the files; read them where it already guesses phase 1 A report or replay tool read one file instead of reverse-engineering four codebases immediately

The default path requires no controller change at all. That is not a concession to get adoption — it is forced by the evidence: Loop has made 24 commits in six months, none touching Nightscout, and is 9 of 11 sites in the corpus. A proposal Loop must act on is a proposal that does not happen.

docs.title: 4. What the proposal is, and what it takes from Kubernetes
docs.text:
Earlier text: §4 at 85c645c8.

Phase 1, the well-known tier. A controller description is a file per controller product, generated from measurement, shipped with the hub, reviewed in a pull request and served at a .well-known path. It is advisory: readers fetch it, and it describes documents that already exist. A controller writes with a token as it does today and calls nothing first; a hub that serves no description, and a reader that cannot fetch one, behave as they do today. The closest everyday analogy is a browser's list of known user agents served at a .well-known path: a description of something that already exists, which the thing described may correct.

The controller-owned tier (D18). A controller that wants typed support for its own features submits a registration, and the hub derives typed API from it. Several ideas in that tier come from what Kubernetes does well for declared, typed resources:

idea in Kubernetes here typed extension resources CustomResourceDefinitions add typed kinds, each versioned, to the API a registration declares typed kinds, extensions, settings and inputs; each kind and extension is versioned on its own, and readers ignore members they do not know (G1, G4, registration §3); definitions are content-addressed, so releases and builds coexist (§7) spec and status spec is what is wanted, status what is observed a controller declares where it records what was requested and where it reports what it applied, as separate carriers (state and intent S7); a registration's response reports what the hub accepted, element by element (registration §5.3) reconciliation a controller drives observed state toward its spec the controller reconciles, toward what it was asked, and reports the result; the hub observes and records what each instance reports, including composition, which it never computes (S1; D18: the hub is responsible for observability, the controller for syncing and reconciling) leases a coordination.k8s.io Lease for liveness and leadership each running copy is an instance holding a lease it renews; a lapsed instance holds no roles and is never a command destination (registration §8) labels and selectors key-value labels, chosen by selectors instance labels, with dev.nightscout/purpose, dev.nightscout/build and dev.nightscout/migration-group reserved (§10); a view with a label selector reads only matching instances (§12) admission requests are checked, in order, before anything is stored a submission passes ordered checks (authorisation, preconditions, the registration as a whole, then each element) and each element is accepted or refused with a reason (§5.2); a refused typed write goes to its carrier in today's shape (§6, §11) discovery the API server lists its groups, versions and resources GET /.well-known/nightscout/sync, the capability document: grammar versions, the members the hub interprets, limits, the well-known catalogue and where to submit (§4) owner and binding RoleBindings tie permissions to subjects; owner references tie dependents to an owner a registration is bound to the credential subject that wrote it, and an instance to the subject that created it (authority §3); the tenant's owner can block, release or transfer (authority §4); records keep their instance and definition ids, and a definition stays while records reference it (registration §14) object identity metadata.name and uid a product is (vendor, product); instance ids are random UUIDs the controller supplies; a record carries its own identifier and the hub's _id (identity §2, D20)

Where the design differs, and what it does instead. The hub schedules nothing and computes no dosing state. It records what controllers report, routes a command to the instance that holds the role (commands, proposed), and refuses what its checks refuse; the controller decides, enacts and validates (D18). Version-scoped quirks record how stored documents from a given controller version deviate, and the mapping the hub applies to each (D20, registration §16).

docs.title: 5. Worked example
docs.text:
The whole of phase 1 for Loop, which involves no change to Loop.

Step 1 — the description Nightscout ships (abbreviated; the generated file is specs/sync/registrations/loop.yaml):

apiVersion: nightscout.dev/sync/v1
kind: ControllerStateModel
metadata:
  vendor: LoopKit
  product: Loop
  algorithmFamily: loop
spec:
  documents:
    - collection: devicestatus
      discriminator: {path: loop, test: is-object}   # structural, not the device string
      decomposesTo: [ApsSnapshot, PumpSnapshot, UploaderSnapshot]
  replayInputs:
    - {input: maxBolus,  status: recorded, path: loopSettings.maximumBolus}
    - {input: automaticBolusApplicationFactor, status: absent, path: null}

That last line is the point. status: absent with path: null is how the file says "Loop has this value and does not publish it." It is not a complaint; it is the thing that makes "can this dose be reproduced?" a question with an answer.

Step 2 — what a tool can now do, without reading any controller source:

import yaml
reg = yaml.safe_load(open("specs/sync/registrations/loop.yaml"))
absent = [i["input"] for i in reg["spec"]["replayInputs"] if i["status"] == "absent"]
print(f"Loop replay is missing {len(absent)} inputs: {absent[:3]} ...")
# Loop replay is missing 8 inputs: ['automaticBolusApplicationFactor',
#   'carbAbsorptionModel', 'gradualTransitionsThreshold'] ...

Today the same answer takes reading AlgorithmInput.swift, LoopStatus.swift and a corpus of documents. oref-digital-twin currently gets settings out of screenshots, with a vision model, because there is nowhere to read them from.

Step 2a — the same thing over HTTP, for a reader that does not vendor this repository:

GET https://<site>/.well-known/nightscout/controllers/loop

Same document, no checkout, no authentication, cacheable. This is what makes Nocturne and a report tool able to agree without either depending on the other.

Step 3 — a controller that wants to correct it posts the same document to the hub. One request, per release, optional. The served catalogue then reflects the correction, so every other reader of that site picks it up without coordinating with anyone.

docs.title: 6. Impact, measured
docs.text: Today With descriptions A reader learning a controller's shape read 4 codebases read 1 file Loop's dose recommendation reaching a typed consumer dropped, 10 of 11 sites described, so droppable only on purpose "Which dosing inputs can I not replay?" unanswerable without source 8, named, per controller A new controller's on-ramp improvise an eventType, hope a file to copy Two readers agreeing on a controller's shape vendor the same repo, or diverge fetch the same URL Sync request floor for a described controller 1,440–5,760 requests/day, per controller's own design the batched contract's 576, earned by being described A controller's unique feature negotiate, or be silently dropped declared in its own description; readers can choose to handle it Cost to Loop — zero Cost to Nightscout — read a file it can already generate; optionally serve it

docs.title: 7. If you only do one thing
docs.text:
Phase 1 is not this proposal. It is smaller, and it needs neither descriptions nor new endpoints:

Agree a schema for the settings collection — which cgm-remote-monitor already enables in v3 — so controllers can publish the settings that determine dosing.

That closes the complaint physicians actually make, and the roadmap sequences it first for that reason. Controller descriptions are phase 3, and are worth doing because they make phase 1 checkable — a description states which settings a controller publishes, so "it publishes none" stops being invisible.

docs.title: 8. Evidence and caveats
docs.text:
Every number above is reproducible from this repository:

Claim Command Output 56 of 166 devicestatus paths dropped make schema-nocturne reports/schema-census/nocturne-coverage.json Loop records 4 of 20 dosing inputs make schema-dosing reports/schema-census/dosing-inputs.json 2,466 of 2,865 effects separable make schema-effects reports/schema-census/effects.json The shipped descriptions make schema-sync-model specs/sync/registrations/

Caveats that matter to this proposal specifically:

  • The corpus is Loop-dominant — 9 of 11 sites — and contains no AAPS closed-loop site at all. Every AAPS statement is read from its source, not observed.
  • The descriptions are generated from one corpus and today's source. A wrong shipped description is worse than none, which is why they are versioned, derived from measurement rather than assertion, and why a controller must always be able to disown one.
  • Every phase that names a project is a proposal to that project; the packet for the controller projects is PROPOSAL-REG-CONTROLLERS.

docs.title: 9. Where to read more
docs.text: If you want Read Why the schemas were wrong, with measurements Typed schemas What devicestatus loses and why replay fails devicestatus and profile fidelity Effects versus motivations, and privacy Effects and versioning The sync contract, if descriptions are adopted Hub-and-spoke sync Who should do what, in what order Adoption roadmap Whether the primitives are actually evidenced Primitive coverage The earlier draft of all of this, in cgm-remote-monitor's docs/proposals/ cgm-remote-monitor/docs/proposals/ — agent-control-plane-rfc.md, bridge-rules.md, conflict-resolution.md, integration-questionnaire.md. See hub-and-spoke sync §5.2 Which specification rule is proposed to supersede each part of that earlier draft The earlier control-plane draft and the specifications proposed to supersede it — objects and rules mapped to spec rules, with the corpus findings each rule carries The concrete changes that raise replay fidelity, per project Replay fidelity changes — five changes, measured before and after

docs.title: Replay fidelity: the concrete changes, per project — proposal
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-09-11. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

What this is: a proposal (contributor-facing). Read after the controller-descriptions proposal; leads to the sync-transport specification. Snapshot, written 2026-09-11. Current: the only statement of the replay-fidelity change list. Change A (§1) is carried, with its cursor rule, as rules T5–T7 of the sync-transport specification. Status: proposed to each named project; each change is independent of the others. Measurements are over the 11-site corpus (snapshots 2026-04-01 and 2026-04-26) and the source trees as of 2026-09-11. It is a change list rather than an analysis. Decisions it touches: execution plan §1.

Two things this document refuses to concede. That sync has to be inefficient, and that fidelity has to be traded against it. §1 shows the request count should be O(1) in the number of resources, which is a small change to code that is already generic. Once it is, every typed resource that improves replay costs zero additional requests, and the rest of this document is just a list of what to record.

docs.title: TL;DR — five changes, measured
docs.text:
# Change Who Measured effect A Collection-agnostic delta read + one batch write cgm-remote-monitor AAPS 20 → 2 requests/cycle, and adding N typed collections costs 0 — the count stops mattering B Eight more keys in loopSettings, which Loop already writes on 200 of 202 profile documents Loop Loop replay 20% → 65% recorded; 55% → 100% recorded-or-derivable C Emit the determine-basal input vector alongside its output Trio / AAPS / oref0 oref0 replay 50% → 78% recorded; 72% → 100% recorded-or-derivable D Exempt cursor-paginated reads from the range cap cgm-remote-monitor Backfill and catch-up stop being indistinguishable from abuse E Read openaps.iob.lastTemp instead of assuming no temp basal oref-digital-twin One of the two inputs its own docstring calls unrecoverable is already published, on 73,891 documents

Change B is the headline and it is smaller than anyone has been assuming. Every one of Loop's eight absent dosing inputs is configuration, and Loop already publishes a configuration block — loopSettings, on 200 of 202 profile documents across 10 sites, carrying eight keys today. The ask is eight more keys in a dictionary it already serialises. Not a new resource, not a new endpoint, not a new API version.

And a finding about this repository's own artifact: the conformance profile this work published passes on 27 of 28 obligations at every in-scope site, while replay completeness is 20%. A profile that passes everywhere while the thing it exists to protect is broken is not measuring the right thing. §7.

docs.title: 1. Sync cost should be O(1) in the number of resources
1.1 Why the current cost is structural, not necessary
docs.text:
v3's delta machinery is per collection: GET /api/v3/{collection}/history/{from}. A client that syncs six collections makes six delta calls, plus GET /lastModified, plus a POST per collection it writes. The measured result is the one that should have been the clue:

AAPS — the only client using v3 as designed — has the worst fan-out, 20 distinct endpoints per cycle, an upper bound of 5,760 requests/day. Loop and Trio, which ignore v3 entirely, are cheaper by accident.

Cursor-based sync solved what changed. It never addressed how many round trips, and the per-collection shape means every resource added to the model is a new request in the loop. That is the reason a fidelity proposal reads as a cost proposal. It does not have to.

docs.title: 1.2 The change, concretely
docs.text:
Two endpoints, both built from code that is already generic.

GET  /api/v3/history/{lastModified}?collections=&limit=
     → { srvDate, cursor, complete, collections: { treatments: [...],
         entries: [...], devicestatus: [...], ... } }

POST /api/v3/batch
     → [ { collection, doc }, ... ]   idempotent per document

Why this is a small change and not a rewrite:

Piece needed Already exists Where Iterate every collection with a per-collection permission check yes — collectionsAsync does exactly this loop with security.checkPermission(auth, 'api:' + col.colName + ':read') lib/api3/specific/lastModified.js A delta query generic in the collection yes — history(opCtx, fieldsProjector) reads opCtx.col and does srvModified > from, sorted ascending, with a limit lib/api3/generic/history/operation.js A registry of live collections yes — app.set('collections', cols) lib/api3/generic/setup.js Per-document create with dedup yes — the create operation each collection already mounts lib/api3/generic/create/

The new endpoint is lastModified.js's loop with findMany in place of getLastModified. It is not a new storage layer, a new index, or a new identity model.

docs.title: 1.3 The one detail that must not be got wrong
docs.text:
A merged cursor is only safe if it is the minimum over truncated collections. With a per-collection page limit, treatments may return 500 rows ending at srvModified = T1 while entries drains completely to T2 > T1. Advancing the global cursor to max() silently skips every treatment between T1 and T2 — a data-loss bug that would look like flaky sync.

The rule:

cursor   = min( last srvModified returned, over collections that hit the limit )
           or srvDate, if no collection hit its limit
complete = no collection hit its limit

A client loops while complete is false. This is the whole of the correctness argument, and it is worth stating in the endpoint's own documentation because it is the kind of thing a second implementation gets wrong.

docs.title: 1.4 What it does to the numbers
docs.text:
Same model as reports/schema-census/sync-cost.json — a source-derived upper bound on distinct endpoint calls per 5-minute cycle, not a packet capture.

Endpoints/cycle Requests/day Cost of adding 10 typed collections AndroidAPS today (v3, per-collection) 20 5,760 +2,880/day Loop today (v1) 7 2,016 n/a — no delta at all With history/{from} + batch 2 576 0

That last column is the point of this section. Under the current shape, every typed resource that improves replay makes sync worse. Under this one, it does not. The argument that the control-plane RFC's typed collections are too expensive dissolves — it was an artifact of the sync primitive, not of the collections.

docs.title: 1.5 What this does not claim
docs.text:
• Payload size is untested. Request count and byte count are different costs and this trades one for the other. A cycle with nothing to report should return an empty envelope cheaply; one catching up after an outage will be large, which is exactly why complete and the page limit exist.
  • v1 is untouched. Loop and Trio are on v1 and this gives them a reason to move that is not "v3 exists", which has not worked for several years.
  • Nothing is retired. Per-collection history keeps working.

docs.title: 2. What replay actually needs, and who has to change
docs.text:
specs/nsschema/dosing-input-sources.yaml maps each algorithm's declared dosing inputs to where, if anywhere, Nightscout records them. 60 inputs, all 60 verdicts confirmed against the corpus.

Declared Recorded Derivable Partial Absent Loop 20 4 (20%) 7 1 8 oref0 family 40 20 (50%) 9 3 8

The structural finding that decides the whole proposal:

All eight of Loop's absent inputs are configuration. Seven of oref0's eight are runtime state the algorithm holds in hand at decision time.

Two different gaps, two different fixes, neither of which is "design a new API". §3 and §4.

A note on the third column that must travel with every number here: a derivable input is recomputed from stored history, which yields a value and not necessarily the value the controller used — it saw a different window, with different de-duplication and different noise handling. A replay built on derived inputs tests the replayer as much as the algorithm. The two columns should never be collapsed.

docs.title: 3. Change B — eight more keys in a dictionary Loop already writes
3.1 The channel exists and is in use
docs.text:
Measured Profile documents carrying loopSettings 200 of 202, across 10 of 11 sites Therapy keys it already carries dosingEnabled, dosingStrategy, maximumBasalRatePerHour, maximumBolus, minimumBGGuard, overridePresets[], preMealTargetRange, scheduleOverride — eight of them, plus two identity keys handled in §3.4 Conformance obligation OBS-PROF-004 — "the dosing safety limits in force" met on 10 of 10 sites, via this block

Loop is already publishing a settings snapshot. It is simply missing the eight values that scale the dose.

docs.title: 3.2 The eight
docs.text:
Input What it changes Why a default is not good enough automaticBolusApplicationFactor The fraction of a recommended bolus actually delivered — scales every automatic dose Defaults to 0.4 and is user-adjustable. A replay that assumes 0.4 is replaying the default, not the user maxActiveInsulinMultiplier Loop's IOB ceiling, as a multiple of maxBolus Defaults to 2. It is the safety limit that determines when dosing stops carbAbsorptionModel Piecewise-linear vs nonlinear carb absorption Changes the carb effect curve, and so the dose recommendationInsulinModel Which insulin activity curve the recommendation uses insulinType on a treatment names the product, which is not the same thing useIntegralRetrospectiveCorrection Integral RC is a materially different correction behaviour A user-facing toggle; two users with identical profiles dose differently includePositiveVelocityAndRC Whether positive velocity and RC enter the forecast — useMidAbsorptionISF Whether ISF is re-evaluated mid-absorption — gradualTransitionsThreshold Dose transition smoothing —

Plus one clarification rather than an addition: recommendationType is partial today — dosingStrategy distinguishes automaticBolus from tempBasalOnly, which covers the common case but is not the full set. A mapping note in the controller description resolves it without a code change.

docs.title: 3.3 What it buys
docs.text: Loop replay completeness Now After Recorded 4/20 — 20% 13/20 — 65% Recorded or derivable 11/20 — 55% 20/20 — 100%

docs.title: 3.4 Hub-side cost, and one safety condition
docs.text:
cgm-remote-monitor needs nothing new to accept these — they are keys in a profile document it already stores. What it should add is a published schema so the block stops being tacit, which is Phase 1 of the roadmap and needs no new endpoint.

The safety condition. loopSettings already carries deviceToken and bundleIdentifier — push-notification identity, on 200 documents. Any settings schema, catalogue entry, or conformance report derived from this block must carry the type-level sensitivity annotation (specs/sync/sensitivity.yaml) and must never propagate those two fields into a served catalogue, a shared report, or an issue. A settings resource that leaks a device token is worse than no settings resource.

docs.title: 4. Change C — oref0: emit the input vector, not just the output
4.1 What is missing is not configuration
docs.text:
Seven of the eight absent oref0 inputs are values determine-basal computes or receives on the way in and then discards:

Input What it is mealData.mealCOB Carbs on board as the meal-assist path saw them mealData.slopeFromMaxDeviation Unannounced-meal detection state mealData.slopeFromMinDeviation ditto flatBGsDetected Whether the glucose series was flat enough to suppress dosing microBolusAllowed Whether SMB was permitted on this run iob.bolusSnooze Bolus snooze at decision time iob.iobWithZeroTemp.bolussnooze ditto, zero-temp projection

Plus one that is configuration and is the most-cited gap in the series:

| profile.maxIob | The IOB safety limit. Recorded by no oref0 derivative anywhere in the corpus. oref-digital-twin lists it in REQUIRED_SETTINGS and must assume it |

microBolusAllowed is the clearest illustration of why "inferable" is not "recorded": you can infer it after the fact from whether an SMB was enacted — but only when one was. A cycle where SMB was allowed and not used is indistinguishable from one where it was forbidden.

docs.title: 4.2 Where it goes
docs.text: Alongside the decision, in the document already being written: openaps.suggested.inputs (or a sibling key — the name matters less than that it is one object containing the vector the algorithm was called with). No new collection, no new endpoint, no API version change. oref0 has these values in scope at the moment it writes suggested.

docs.title: 4.3 What it buys
docs.text: oref0 replay completeness Now After Recorded 20/40 — 50% 31/40 — 78% Recorded or derivable 29/40 — 72% 40/40 — 100%

docs.title: 4.4 The caveat that governs every oref0 number here
docs.text: All openaps.* frequencies in this document come from one site. The corpus has no AAPS closed-loop site at all. Every AAPS-specific statement is read from source, not observed, and is marked so. Trio and AAPS both discriminate on openaps and are not distinguishable from each other at the top level — a limit in this work, not only in anyone else's.

docs.title: 5. Change D — bounded reads must stay possible
docs.text:
docs/proposals/api-query-normalization.md caps devicestatus at 100 documents and a 7-day range for anonymous callers, 5× for admin. The problem it documents is real: count=999999 and unbounded devicestatus fetches are listed as common.

But the cap is expressed in the wrong unit for three legitimate readers:

  • a replay tool walking a history,
  • a decomposition migration reading everything once,
  • a cursor client catching up after an outage — indistinguishable from an abusive caller by request shape alone.

The change: cursor-paginated reads are exempt from the range cap and bounded by page size instead. A cursor already guarantees forward progress and bounded work per request, which is the property the cap exists to enforce. §1.3's complete flag is what makes the client loop rather than ask for everything.

This is the same argument the sync design makes from the other side: a query profile fixed in advance is what lets a bounded query be safe without being small.

docs.title: 6. Change E — the cheapest fidelity gain, and it needs nobody's permission
docs.text:
oref-digital-twin/replay/inputs.py opens with:

Two inputs cannot be recovered faithfully from devicestatus alone and are approximated: currenttemp — the temp basal running at decision time (assumed none); insulin activity — the IOB curve's instantaneous activity (assumed 0), which degrades bgi/eventualBG.

Both halves are out of date (measured 2026-09-11), in different directions.

Docstring says Actually insulin activity assumed 0 Already fixed in its own code — _iob_data_from_cycle reads openaps.iob.activity when present and flags activity_known currenttemp assumed none Published, and not read. openaps.iob.lastTemp carries rate, duration, started_at and date on 73,891 documents. Our own dosing map classifies currentTemp.rate and currentTemp.duration as recorded, and OBS-OREF-006 already checks for the path

So the replay tool still substitutes {"duration": 0, "rate": 0} for a value that is sitting in the document it is already parsing. That is a few lines in one consumer, and it improves fidelity for every oref0 site immediately.

This pair is therefore not evidence of unrecoverable inputs. The category of finding stands — a serious replay tool works around gaps Nightscout leaves (it reads settings from screenshots) — and max_iob, which is recorded nowhere, is the correct illustration of an unrecoverable input.

docs.title: 7. The conformance profile passes while replay is at 20%
docs.text:
specs/conformance/observability-profile.yaml defines 28 obligations across seven roles. Measured across all 11 sites:

Obligations met at every in-scope site 27 of 28 The only exception OBS-CGM-005, signal quality — MAY level, met at 1 of 11 sites Loop-specific obligations OBS-LOOP-001…006 all met, 10 of 10 sites oref0-specific OBS-OREF-001…007 all met, 1 of 1 site

A profile that passes everywhere, while the thing it exists to protect sits at 20% completeness, is measuring presence rather than sufficiency. It asks "is IOB written down" and not "is enough written down to reproduce the dose".

The change: derive the profile's obligations from the dosing-input map rather than from hand-picked paths. Concretely, add one obligation per declared input with status: recorded, at SHOULD, per algorithm family — which makes the profile fail today, on purpose, at exactly the eight-plus-eight places §3 and §4 name. A conformance report is only useful if passing it means something.

This is a change to our artifact, not anyone else's, and it should land before the profile is quoted at a maintainer.

docs.title: 8. Cost, per project
docs.text:
Project What is asked Size Loop Eight more keys in the loopSettings block it already writes on 200 of 202 profile documents Serialisation only. No new call, no new endpoint, no schema negotiation Trio / AAPS One object alongside openaps.suggested carrying the input vector; publish maxIob Serialisation of values already in scope at the call site cgm-remote-monitor One collection-agnostic history endpoint and one batch write (§1); a published settings schema (§3.4); a cursor exemption in query limits (§5) The two endpoints reuse lastModified.js's loop and history/operation.js's query. No storage or identity change oref-digital-twin Read openaps.iob.lastTemp; refresh a stale docstring A few lines This repository Rebuild the conformance profile from the dosing-input map so it can fail (§7) Generator change

Nothing in this list requires a new API version, and nothing requires any two projects to move together. Each change is useful alone, so each project can take its row independently, in any order.

docs.title: 9. Evidence
docs.text: Claim Command Output 60 dosing inputs, per-algorithm status make schema-dosing reports/schema-census/dosing-inputs.json loopSettings on 200 of 202 profile documents make schema-profile reports/schema-census/profile.census.json openaps.iob.lastTemp on 73,891 documents make schema-devicestatus reports/schema-census/devicestatus.census.json 27 of 28 obligations met everywhere make schema-observability reports/schema-census/observability.json Endpoint counts and the batched comparison make schema-sync-cost reports/schema-census/sync-cost.json

docs.title: 10. What is not measured
docs.text:
• Payload size under a merged envelope. §1.5.
  • Whether a decomposed set round-trips into a document a legacy client accepts.
  • Anything about AAPS from data. No AAPS closed-loop site in the corpus; all openaps.* figures are single-site.
  • Whether the eight Loop settings are accessible at the point Loop serialises loopSettings. They are all LoopSettings/therapy-settings values, so this is likely; it is read-derived (from source), not measured.
  • Cursor behaviour under concurrent writers. Two controllers plus a care-portal user writing to one site is the normal case, and srvModified ordering under that load is unexamined — here and upstream.

docs.title: Agents in the ecosystem: develop, interpret, act
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-10-18. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

What this is: a map (contributor-facing). Read after the authority specification; leads to auditioning a dosing algorithm. Snapshot — describes 2026-10-18. Status: current; a map of what exists and what is missing for each of develop, interpret and act. The proposal lifecycle in §4.3 is proposed, not specified. Also 2026-10-18: §1 adds the drawing 1·agents (the three domains as paths from an agent to the ecosystem); §4.3 adds a figure of the command lifecycle replayed from the commands specification's conformance cases (tools/diagrams). Repository facts are read at this repository's 5a9a49cc; facts about other repositories and publications were checked 2026-10-18 through the GitHub API or the publisher's page, and each names its commit or date. Every claim is read-derived (from source or documents) unless marked measured. Current decisions: execution plan §1.

The question. Software agents built on language models now touch this ecosystem in three different ways: they write and change the code of apps and servers, they read a person's data and explain it, and they could propose or start a therapy change. Each needs a different assurance, and most of what each needs is already written down here or in cgm-remote-monitor's docs/proposals, in separate places. This page puts them side by side and names what is missing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text: Domain What the agent does What exists What does not exist Develop writes or changes code each controller project's own contribution rules; review and test work measured in the evidence; simulator asks drafted (§2) signed builds, an SBOM or a build-provenance record in any project surveyed Interpret reads data and explains it one read role; seven requirements for delegated reads; at least seven MCP servers and two agent tools that read a Nightscout site (§3) scoped, purpose-bound or audited reads; a hub whose "what is active now" both hubs agree on Act proposes or starts a therapy change the earlier draft's agent issuer, suggest scope and DelegationGrant, proposed to be superseded by the authority and commands specifications; D19 instances, roles and command routing, specified (§4) any path of its own for an agent; an implemented proposal record, approval bound to the exact change, or command API (proposed in the commands specification)

docs.title: 1. Three domains
docs.text:
Develop Interpret Act What the agent touches source code of a controller, hub, uploader or follower app a person's glucose, treatment, device and settings records a controller's inputs: an override, temporary target, carbs, a bolus, a mode, a setting What goes wrong a defect ships to people who dose from or display the software a wrong state read as right, a stale value read as current, a summary that misstates the data, data sent where the person did not expect a change enacted that nobody approved, on stale state, or by an actor nobody can identify afterwards Assurance it needs review by people who own the code, tests and simulators, release control minimal and scoped read access, deterministic computation, a hub state that is right, a record of what was read an authority grant, approval bound to the exact change, the controller's own validation and enactment, an outcome record Who decides each project's maintainers the person whose data it is, and whoever operates the site the person, and the controller that owns the pump (D18)

1·agents. Dashed boxes and lines are proposed (commands specification §4–§7); the controller's validation and enactment exist today (D18). Source: tools/structure-diagrams/inputs/1-agents.yaml, drawn from §1–§4 of this page. Read-derived.

One tool can sit on two rows. An interpretation that ends in a recommended settings change is at the edge between Interpret and Act, and its regulatory status is a question for counsel (§6).

docs.title: 2. Develop
docs.text:
The controller projects own their contribution rules; this repository points at them. Checked 2026-10-18 through the GitHub API at each repository's default or development branch.

Project What its contribution rules say about AI-generated code Where LoopWorkspace "We do not accept pull requests that are largely AI-generated or submitted without careful engineering judgment, testing, and alignment with Loop's existing patterns." No pull-request template CONTRIBUTING.md, last changed ae75603c (2026-07-06) Trio the same sentence, naming Trio. No pull-request template CONTRIBUTING.md, last changed 74b94426 (2026-04-15) AndroidAPS "AI-generated pull requests are not welcome"; AI analysis goes into an issue and the maintainers write the fix CONTRIBUTING.md on dev, last changed 1b583b8f8d (2026-10-04); not on master (85b5e89c29, 2024-11-24) cgm-remote-monitor no rule on AI-generated contributions CONTRIBUTING.md on dev, last changed 20e5ad2a (2026-09-06) Nocturne no CONTRIBUTING.md; AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md at the root give instructions to coding agents AGENTS.md last changed 49d61d177 (2026-09-27)

What the rules are about, and how the projects use agents themselves. The rules govern who verifies and owns a change, not whether a tool was used. AndroidAPS gives its reason: "Verifying and reviewing AI-generated code reliably takes maintainers more time than the AI took to produce it, and unverified code is a risk we cannot accept". LoopWorkspace's and Trio's rules say "Do not submit AI-heavy or 'vibe-coded' pull requests; we welcome thoughtful use of tooling, but contributions need to be intentionally designed." Each project's own development uses coding agents (measured 2026-10-18 over each branch's latest 300 commits through the GitHub commits API, counting commits whose message names a coding agent, nearly all as a Co-Authored-By trailer; a lower bound, since attribution is optional):

Branch Commits read (dates) Naming a coding agent Agent instructions in the tree AndroidAPS dev 300 (2026-10-07 to 2026-10-16) 6 (Claude, Copilot) CLAUDE.md, 28 KB, 28 commits since 2026-01-10 Trio dev 300 (2026-09-11 to 2026-10-18) 28 (Claude) none at the root Loop next-dev 300 (2025-10-07 to 2026-10-17) 1 (Claude, 2026-04-23) none at the root LoopKit next-dev 300 (2025-08-22 to 2026-10-18) 1 (Claude, 2026-04-23) none at the root

Beside these, in one commercial controller's private repository, 3,441 of 6,055 commits (57%) carry a Copilot co-author trailer (measured 2026-10-18 by counting trailers in its history; the repository is private, so the count cannot be re-run from here), and its automated task loop's only gate is that the test suite passes (read-derived from its source, 2026-10-18).

What exists in this repository.

Item Where Status Which steps still need a person, where much of the 2026 cgm-remote-monitor engineering was done with AI coding agents under a maintainer's direction evidence §4; sponsored-team proposal §3; accountability thresholds §5 observation and proposal Asks to the simulator and test-rig projects, drafted to be sent in the sender's own words because of the rules above upstream asks: device simulators drafted; nothing sent Signed builds, recorded change review, an SBOM and release provenance, as evidence a manufacturer would expect partner readiness §3, §8 item 3 requirement in a draft; none found in this repository's survey A record every test run leaves quality-system proposal §4.1 proposed

What does not exist. A rule shared across projects for agent-written changes; a way for a reviewer to see, per change, which parts an agent wrote; signed builds, an SBOM or a build-provenance record in any project surveyed.

docs.title: 3.1 Read access today
docs.text:
Item Where Status The read role is one bit: readable is *:*:read, every collection, every field, all time cgm-remote-monitor lib/authorization/storage.js:235 at dev fade2299; configuration and delegation §5.3 shipping Seven requirements for a delegated reader: scoped reads enforced in storage, bounded queries, purpose and expiry, answers rather than data, read audit, revocation that is real, minimization at the boundary configuration and delegation §5.4 requirements, stated 2026-09-10; the read role above is still one bit A worked delegation grant with constraints, purpose and expiry authority model proposed, not implemented Tools that read a site for an agent: MCP servers, an agent skill, an AI platform evidence §7.1 third-party; the list lives there

Requirement 6 bears hardest on agents: once a model has read raw data, revoking the grant does not un-read it, and the data has also gone to whoever runs the model. Where the model runs is a property of the agent's host, not of the tool that fetched the data: a tool that keeps its database local still returns its output into the conversation, which goes to the model provider when the model is a hosted service. Lumose (repository GlycemicGPT) states this choice in its README; the evidence table records which tools do. A plain-language page for people connecting such a tool to their own site is giving an AI tool access to your Nightscout data.

docs.title: 3.2 MCP is an adapter
docs.text: The Model Context Protocol, at its current revision 2026-07-28, lets a server offer resources (context and data), prompts (templated messages) and tools (functions the model may call), over stdio or Streamable HTTP. The revision describes stateless, self-contained requests, and says the protocol cannot enforce its security principles itself: hosts must obtain the user's consent before invoking a tool. An MCP server for Nightscout is therefore an adapter over the API it calls, not a new source of state or authority: a local copy it keeps is a copy, and it holds whatever credential it is given and reads or writes what that credential allows. The servers surveyed differ on exactly that point — which credential they accept and whether they expose write tools (evidence §7.1). The statistics API proposal specifies an MCP resource provider over a documented statistics API (REQ-STATS-005, proposal).

docs.title: 3.3 Compute first, then explain
docs.text:
An explanation is only as right as the numbers under it. Two layers come before the model:

  1. The hub's state. The two hubs do not always report the same thing as active. Measured by tools/lab/hub-active-state on synthetic records, running each hub's storage and active-state code directly rather than over HTTP (cgm-remote-monitor fade2299, Nocturne 42275c812; intent landscape §5):
  2. Temporary Override Cancel: the hubs agree — in both, the override runs its full duration.
  3. A temporary target followed by a cancel: the latest span agrees (it is Nocturne's Cancelled span); Active-state and list reads disagree until the target's own end, and the open Cancelled span stays in Nocturne's list reads afterwards.
  4. A Loop devicestatus override: cgm-remote-monitor reads duration as seconds, Nocturne as minutes, so a 30-minute override is active at +40 and +120 minutes in Nocturne only.
  5. Also disagreeing: the profile after a timed switch ends, AAPS timeshift units, and out-of-order backfill of two open overrides.

An agent that asks either hub "which override is active?" gets the hub's answer, not the controller's. 2. Deterministic computation. Time in range, GMI, variability and patterns are arithmetic; a tool that computes them in code and hands the model the result can be tested, and one that asks the model to compute them cannot. Several MCP servers in the evidence table compute aggregates server-side; one documents checking them against Nightscout's own report.

docs.title: 4.1 What exists
docs.text: Item Where Status Six things entity CRUD cannot carry, including the initiator (P5) and the command lifecycle (P6) intent landscape §2 read-derived from Loop, Trio, iAPS, AAPS source A hub sees acceptance on no command path except AAPS dev's, whose signed requests and correlated acknowledgements go through NS settings; elsewhere success shows as the resulting entity and failure as free text, or not at all intent landscape §6; remote commands; remote bolus read-derived An automated agent has no path of its own: it holds a caregiver's credential and is indistinguishable from that caregiver (path H) technical loops §3 read-derived issuerType: human \| controller \| agent; scopes read, suggest (override.suggest # Can propose, human must approve), activate, deliver, admin; DelegationGrant {grantId, grantedBy, grantedTo, scopes, constraints {maxOverrideDuration, allowedOverrideTypes, requireConfirmation, expiresAt}, grantedAt, revokedAt}; append-only audit docs/proposals/agent-control-plane-rfc.md, part of the earlier draft in cgm-remote-monitor's docs/proposals (draft v1.0, January 2026; read at official b5ddd662) proposal, not implemented; proposed to be superseded (§4.2) D19 instances with leases, roles source / command-sink / {value: other, controllerTerm} ("any other role, such as an agent's"), required provenance device or simulated, a device command-sink only for the product's bound subject or by the owner's transfer (grantedBy), and routing that refuses rather than guesses (no-command-destination, 409 ambiguous-command-destination) registration specification §8–§9 Specified, not implemented: no hub serves any of this An earlier controller registration protocol controller registration protocol proposal draft v2, 2026-01-17

docs.title: 4.2 The earlier draft and the rules proposed to supersede it
docs.text:
The authority and commands specifications are proposed to supersede the agent parts of the earlier draft in cgm-remote-monitor's docs/proposals; the control-plane supersession map covers the rest of it.

earlier draft proposed to be superseded by agent as an issuer type state and intent S8: an agent initiator is {value: other, controllerTerm}; registration §9: an agent's role is an other role a hub lists suggest scope ("can propose, human must approve") commands CM11–CM14: a proposal needs api:proposals:create and a granted propose role; an approval names the payload hash and needs api:commands:create; a readable credential can do neither DelegationGrant: who granted, to whom, scopes, constraints, expiry, revocation authority §7, DR1–DR7: requirements; the grant's shape is open (authority §9 item 6) append-only audit with issuer and authority authority §8; commands CM1: a command is recorded before it is sent conflict rules: override composition inside the hub, "Human > Agent > Controller" state and intent S1: the controller composes; the hub records the result (D18)
