The same draft's integration questionnaire has a default answer per controller, read from source, in integration questionnaire defaults.

An agent as initiator (maintainer, 2026-10-18). No agent value is added to any initiator vocabulary; an agent initiator is written {value: other, controllerTerm} (state and intent S8), as an agent's role is (registration §9). No controller records an agent as initiator today. The registrations are built for needs that are latent but measured and demonstrated — in the corpus, in controller source and in the labs — not only for what apps send now; the open form lets a controller, simulator or lab record an agent initiator today, and a shared value can be named once the corpus or a lab shows one in use. Recorded in the execution plan (row 17).

docs.title: 4.3 What a proposal lifecycle would add — proposed, not specified
docs.text:
Nothing in this subsection is specified or decided. It states what exists nowhere above, so that the item that specifies commands can take it or leave it.

propose → validate → (evaluate) → approve | reject → command → outcome
Step Who What it would carry propose an agent instance holding a propose role ({value: other, controllerTerm}) the exact change; the controller instance it is for (D19 instanceId and definitionId); the state it was based on; an expiry; the SHA-256 of the payload's RFC 8785 canonical JSON, the rule D19 already uses for definition ids and etags validate the controller (D18) its own checks, as today on every remote path (technical loops §3.3); a proposal the controller would refuse goes no further evaluate optional; any checker a risk check may request human review; it never grants authority. A probabilistic check — a classifier or a second model — is evidence for the approver, not a decision approve or reject a subject that may send the command itself; when an agent proposed, not the subject that proposed it (commands CM14) an approval names the payload hash, so it binds to that exact change and no other; an expired proposal cannot be approved command the hub routes to the live device command-sink, as specified in registration §9 the approved payload and its hash; the controller checks the hash before enacting outcome the controller accepted or refused, applied effect (P3), correlated to the proposal

Three constraints carry over unchanged. Validation and enactment stay the controller's (D18). Read access never confers a propose or act role: a readable credential, or an MCP server holding one, cannot be promoted to either. And the hub routes and records; it does not decide whether a change is safe. For comparison, OWASP's LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency recommends minimum extensions, minimum permissions, and human approval of high-impact actions.

"The state it was based on" has no home yet. What D19 versions is the registration: the product's etag and the instance's etag cover the declaration, the binding and the granted roles (registration specification §5.4 and §8). Neither covers the controller's therapy state — which override is active, which profile, what is on board — so neither tells an approver that the state the agent read is still the state the controller holds.

What one prototype shows. A commercial controller prototype implemented the client side of the agent control-plane RFC of that earlier draft: sources including agent, delegation grants with auto-approve types, and an audit log held in memory. Its approval records only the reviewer, the time and a note against the proposal id — no payload hash and no state — and its remote-command "success" means the HTTP request succeeded, with no acknowledgement or outcome (read-derived from its source, 2026-10-18; not reproduced here). That is evidence for the binding requirement above and for its open question: an approval that names neither the payload nor the state does not bind to either, and an HTTP status says nothing about what the controller did.

Where it is specified. The command record, outcomes, proposals and approvals are proposed in the commands specification §4–§7 (SPEC-REG-COMMANDS; the proposal record was folded in by the maintainer on 2026-10-18), with cases for an approval bound to one payload hash, an expired proposal, and a proposal from a credential with no propose role. Its CM15 takes the open question above: an approval is refused when the hub's state version differs from the proposal's, which still says nothing about the controller's own state. What controllers do with outstanding commands, enacting each once (CM21), and plans confirmed in advance are in the command queue and planning design note.

The lifecycle as the commands specification proposes it, from five synthetic conformance cases, call by call. An approval names the payload hash and creates one command with the proposal's payload (CM13, CM14, CM1); the controller fetches it and recomputes the hash before enacting (CM10). An approval after the proposal's expiry is refused 409 proposal-expired (CM13). A received payload whose hash differs is refused hash-mismatch, and the hub records the report as a mismatch (CM10, CM7, CM8). A command fetched before its expiry reads unconfirmed after it, and the controller's late report replaces that state (CM3, CM9). A cancel after hand-over is a request: 202 cancelRequested, carried by the next fetch, refused by the controller with reason cancelled (CM25, CM21). Proposed (commands specification §4–§7); replies from each case's expected block (specs/sync/conformance/commands/), replayed by the reference tools/nsschema/commands.py. Generated by make diagrams-svg.

docs.title: 5. Evaluating an algorithm before it acts
docs.text:
An agent that proposes a change, and a developer who changes an algorithm, both need to know what the algorithm does with the inputs it gets.

  • Cross-implementation equivalence. ADR-005 fixes the adapter protocol for comparing oref0 in JavaScript, Swift and Kotlin, and Loop, on identical inputs; the vectors and assertions are under conformance/.
  • Shadow comparison. The cross-validation log (A10, 2025-03-30) records Trio's shadow mode, which logs JavaScript and Swift outputs for the same inputs; at Trio e41c9db37 the Swift port is the running algorithm (intent landscape §1).
  • Replay is bounded by what was recorded. Of the dosing inputs each algorithm declares, 20% are recorded for Loop and 50% for the oref0 family (55% and 72% counting inputs derivable from history), as of 2026-09-11 (hub-sync §4.2). Loop's input set is read from its source; oref0's is the union of inputs across 385 replay vector files (specs/nsschema/dosing-input-sources.yaml), which hold 308 distinct inputs, 22 of them synthetic (measured 2026-10-18, algorithm audition §2.1). A derived input is a value, not necessarily the one the controller used, so a replay on derived inputs tests the replayer as much as the algorithm. The change list that would raise the figures is replay-fidelity changes.

Comparing algorithms on the same recorded inputs in shadow, what an independent implementation's shadow runner and replay work show, and what an audition harness would need without ever granting control, are in auditioning a dosing algorithm.

docs.title: 6. Regulatory boundary
docs.text:
Facts, and questions for counsel; no conclusion is drawn here.

  • FDA's guidance Clinical Decision Support Software was issued January 29, 2026, superseding the issue of January 6, 2026 (nonbinding recommendations). It states: "Software functions that support or provide recommendations to patients or caregivers – not HCPs – meet the definition of a device", and that FDA intends to be consistent with its existing digital-health policies for them.
  • The programme's question for counsel is §9 item 11: whether a report that proposes settings changes is clinical decision support under device regulation, and what clinical review it needs. The same question arises for an agent that explains data to a person with diabetes or a caregiver and ends with a suggestion.
  • Regulatory roles, intended use and complaint handling in any agreement with a manufacturer are in partner readiness §5 and §6.

Questions for counsel: whether an MCP server or agent skill that only reads and summarises is in scope of the guidance when its user is a patient or caregiver; whether a server that exposes a treatment-write tool changes that; and who, among the server's author, the host's provider and the person running it, would be the manufacturer of such a function.

docs.title: 7. Not measured, not decided
docs.text:
• No agent, MCP server or skill was run against a site for this page; the tool facts are from READMEs and source read.
  • Whether any controller project would accept an agent as a command sender at all, under any grant.
  • How an agent instance is scoped, limited and revoked: no decision covers it (authority §9 item 6; process models).
  • A shared initiator list (§4.2).
  • A therapy-state version a proposal could bind to (§4.3): the hub's state version is proposed in commands CM15; it versions the hub's record, not the controller's state.
  • Read audit, purpose limitation and real revocation for a delegated reader (§3.1).
  • The delegation grant's shape, storage and checks (authority §9 item 6).
  • Whether outstanding commands on a channel are shown to an approver or included in what the state version check compares (commands §9 item 7).

docs.title: Auditioning a dosing algorithm: same inputs, shadow only
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-10-18. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

What this is: a research note (contributor-facing). Read after agents in the ecosystem; leads to the controller-descriptions proposal. Snapshot — describes 2026-10-18. Status: current. The harness in §4 is proposed, not specified; no decision rests on this note. Repository facts are read at this repository's ef29293a; counts marked measured were taken that day with the command or method named beside them. Facts about an independent implementation (§3) are read-derived from its source and documents, 2026-10-18; not reproduced here. Current decisions: execution plan §1.

The question. Can a dosing algorithm be compared with others on the same recorded inputs, in shadow — computing what it would do, with no path to the pump — and what would the ecosystem need for that comparison to be trustworthy? "Auditioning" here means exactly that: an algorithm is heard, never given control.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text: What exists What does not exist Same inputs, several implementations the ADR-005 adapter protocol and its vectors (§2.1); a shadow mode in Trio's Swift port work and in an independent implementation (§2.2, §3.2) an input snapshot per run that can be replayed exactly after a divergence Knowing which algorithm ran D19 content-addressed definitions — for a controller's data model (§1.2) an identity for an algorithm, its implementation version and settings schema Knowing what the run lacked replay completeness per controller: 20% Loop, 50% oref0 recorded (§2.3) completeness shown per run An independent reference captured controller outputs in the public vectors (§2.1) a stated reference implementation per family Keeping it out of control D18: the controller validates and enacts a recorded decision, outside any harness, that moves an algorithm from shadow to control

docs.title: 1.1 Definition, instance, authority
docs.text:
Object What it is What it carries Algorithm definition what the algorithm is identity; implementation version; the settings it takes (a schema); the inputs it requires; its output contract (decision, predictions, intermediate values) Execution instance one running copy of a definition its version as built; its configuration (the settings values); where it runs; the provenance of its inputs and outputs Execution authority what the instance may do with its result replay only (offline, on stored inputs), shadow (live inputs, result stored and never enacted), or authorised control (the result reaches a pump)

The three vary independently. One definition can run as a dosing instance on one phone and as a shadow instance on another; one instance can be moved from shadow to control without any change to its code. An audition is about the first two; it must never change the third (§4.6).

docs.title: 1.2 What D19 covers, and what it does not
docs.text:
D19 (execution plan §2.6.2; specified in registration specification §7–§9, not implemented) has the same three-way split, for controllers:

Algorithm object Nearest D19 element Fit definition a definition: a ControllerStateModel registration, its id the SHA-256 of its RFC 8785 canonical JSON partial. The document describes the controller's data model — documents, intent kinds, composition, commands, replayInputs, settings, extensions (hub-sync §3.1). Its only algorithm members are metadata.algorithmFamily (oref0, loop or other) and metadata.versionRange, a free-text string (specs/sync/controller-state-model.schema.json). It has no algorithm identity, no implementation version, no per-algorithm settings schema and no output contract required inputs replayInputs, each with a status and a path (a null path declares an input the controller has and does not publish) close, per controller, not per algorithm execution instance an instance: a random id, a definitionId, roles, labels, a lease the shape fits; nothing in it names which algorithm the copy is running provenance per role, closed: device or simulated gap. A shadow result computed from a real person's live inputs is neither: its inputs are device data and its output was never enacted. No provenance or role says "computed, not enacted" authority roles: source, command-sink, {value: other, controllerTerm}; a device command-sink only for the product's bound subject or by the owner's transfer routing only. Roles say who may receive a hub-originated command. They do not say which algorithm's output a controller enacts; that stays inside the controller (D18)

So D19 registers a controller and the copies of it that connect, and says what data each copy writes and receives. It does not register the algorithms inside a controller. A controller that holds several algorithms registers once; which of them produced a decision is not visible to the hub. The content-addressed id is the part an algorithm registry would reuse unchanged (§4.2).

docs.title: 2.1 The adapter protocol and its vectors
docs.text:
ADR-005 (accepted 2025-03-30) fixes a JSON-over-stdio protocol: each implementation runs in its own process behind a thin adapter that reads {mode, algorithm, input}, runs the algorithm and writes a standard output; a manifest.json per adapter declares its capabilities, invocation, modes and tolerances. Contracts are in tools/test-harness/contracts/. Measured 2026-10-18 (ls tools/test-harness/adapters): four adapters carry a manifest — oref0 in JavaScript, AndroidAPS in JavaScript, AndroidAPS in Kotlin, and one Swift oref0 port. There is no Loop adapter, and the conformance README lists the Loop runner as not implemented.

The vectors. specs/nsschema/dosing-input-sources.yaml takes the oref0 input set as the union of input.* paths across "the 385 replay vectors in conformance/". Measured 2026-10-18 by loading every JSON file under conformance/ with an input member:

Directory Files Expected output kept from Notes conformance/vectors/ 85 AndroidAPS's own result at capture (originalOutput), all 85 AndroidAPS replay fixtures conformance/loop/vectors/ 200 Loop's own devicestatus prediction (groundTruth.source: loop-devicestatus), all 200 Loop data replayed through the oref0 harness; they describe oref0's input shape, not Loop's one adapter's end-to-end oref0 set 100 originalOutput on 99 its manifest counts 78 captured from AndroidAPS fixtures, 1 from an OpenAPS example and 22 synthetic; 77 have the same input as a file in conformance/vectors/

385 files therefore hold 308 distinct inputs, 22 of them synthetic. The union of input paths, and so the oref0 completeness figure below, is unaffected by the duplicates. Every non-synthetic expected output in this corpus comes from the original controller at capture, which is what makes it a reference (§3.5).

docs.title: 2.2 A shadow run on record
docs.text: The cross-validation log (A10, 2025-03-30) records Trio's port of oref0 to Swift and its shadow mode, which logs the JavaScript and Swift outputs for the same inputs and compares them; its exit criterion for the first phase was "no inconsistencies on 200k+ inputs". At Trio e41c9db37 the Swift port is the running algorithm (intent landscape §1). That is an audition inside one project, of one port against its original, with the original's output as the reference.

docs.title: 2.3 Replay completeness is bounded by what was recorded
docs.text:
From dosing-input-sources.yaml (last changed 2cad3225, 2026-09-10), counted 2026-10-18:

Declared inputs Recorded Derivable Partial Absent Recorded Recorded or derivable Loop 20 4 7 1 8 20% 55% oref0 family 40 20 9 3 8 50% 72%

Loop's input set is source-derived: read from AlgorithmInput in LoopAlgorithm, because no vector set here carries Loop's native inputs. oref0's is capture-derived: the union of input paths across the vectors above. The figures are published in hub-sync §4.2, and the change list that would raise them is replay-fidelity changes. A derived input is a value, not necessarily the one the controller used, so a replay on derived inputs tests the replayer as much as the algorithm.

docs.title: 2.4 Inputs come from the controller's records, not from a hub's answer
docs.text: The two hubs do not always agree on what is active. Measured by tools/lab/hub-active-state on synthetic records (summarised in agents in the ecosystem §3.3): a Loop devicestatus override's duration is read as seconds by one hub and minutes by the other; a temporary target followed by a cancel disagrees on Active-state reads; the profile after a timed switch, AAPS timeshift units and out-of-order backfill of two open overrides also disagree. A harness that asked a hub "which override was active?" would audition each algorithm on the hub's answer, not on what the controller held. Replay inputs have to be read from the controller's own records of what it used.

docs.title: 3. What an independent implementation shows
docs.text: Every fact in this section is read-derived from the source and documents of an independent Swift implementation of the oref and Loop algorithms, built for a commercial controller, 2026-10-18; not reproduced here. It is described by role only. No figure from it other than those below is cited, because its other parity and error figures are not backed by a run anyone here can repeat.

docs.title: 3.1 Several algorithms behind one interface
docs.text: It registers several algorithms behind one interface: each has a name, a free-text version string, declared capabilities, a source-family tag, a calculate step and an input check. One is active at a time; selection is by capability. The version is free text, not tied to content, so two builds that compute differently can report the same version. That is the gap D19's content-addressed definitions close for controllers (§1.2), and the one §4.2 would close for algorithms.

docs.title: 3.2 A shadow runner
docs.text:
It runs several algorithms on the same inputs, stores each result as never enacted, and reports how often they agree and diverge. Two limits follow from how it stores a run:

  • A divergence cannot be replayed. Each stored run keeps glucose, IOB and COB as numbers. It keeps no hash and no copy of the full inputs, so a divergence found afterwards cannot be re-run on exactly what produced it.
  • IOB and COB are not compared. Inputs arrive with IOB and COB already computed, so two algorithms that compute IOB differently are compared on one shared IOB, not on their own.

docs.title: 3.3 Inputs it found Nightscout does not carry
docs.text:
Its replay work found these independently. Compared with dosing-input-sources.yaml at ef29293a:

Input it needed In dosing-input-sources.yaml? the nominal temp-basal duration — Nightscout stores the duration after a later temp basal superseded it listed without the distinction. currentTemp.duration is recorded from openaps.iob.lastTemp.duration; Loop's doses is derivable from treatments' duration. Neither entry says whether the stored value is the nominal or the superseded duration pending insulin (requested, not yet confirmed delivered) not listed the pump's own dose log, rather than the uploaded treatments, because of upload gaps and races not listed. Loop's doses is derivable from treatments; upload gaps and races are not noted the profile's time zone not listed. No entry names a time zone the active temp basal at a decision, which needs the previous devicestatus, and its real duration, which needs the next not listed as a dependency. currentTemp is read from the same devicestatus's lastTemp

Four of the five are therefore new to this repository's input map, and the fifth is listed without the distinction that decides its value.

docs.title: 3.4 One measured comparison, and what it is not
docs.text: It compared its IOB with the IOB Loop itself reported: mean IOB error +0.51% over 14 samples in one hour, 3 of 14 within ±1%. This measures outputs — one computed value against the controller's own — and is a different measure from the 20% / 50% figures of §2.3, which measure input coverage. Fourteen samples from one hour of one person's data is not a validation.

docs.title: 3.5 Two lessons
docs.text:
• Parity against code the product never called. Its parity tests passed against matching code that the product did not run; a live comparison against a running controller exposed a 2.30 U/hr disagreement in one recommendation. A parity suite needs an end-to-end gate that proves the code it tested is the code that runs: the same artefact, reached through the same call path the product uses.
  • Expected values from the port are not a reference. Its exported test vectors carry the port's own outputs as the expected values, so they can detect a change in the port but not an error in it. A reference must come from the original implementation — a run of JavaScript oref0, or the upstream LoopAlgorithm package — or from captured controller output, as the public vectors of §2.1 do.

docs.title: 4. What an audition harness would need — proposed, not specified
docs.text: Nothing in this section is specified or decided.

docs.title: 4.1 One input snapshot per run, content-hashed
docs.text: Each run starts from one canonical input snapshot: every input the algorithm reads, in one document, identified by sha256: and the SHA-256 of its RFC 8785 canonical JSON — the rule D19 uses for definition ids and etags. Every result names the snapshot hash, so any divergence can be re-run on exactly its inputs (§3.2). Two algorithms that compute IOB or COB themselves get the raw history, not one shared derived value.

docs.title: 4.2 The algorithm definition and its settings
docs.text: Each run names a content-addressed algorithm definition (identity, implementation version, settings schema, required inputs, output contract; §1.1) and the settings values it ran with, hashed the same way. A free-text version is kept as a label, never as the identity (§3.1). Whether such definitions live in D19's store, as a new element or a new resource, is open.

docs.title: 4.3 A reference per family
docs.text:
Family Reference implementation How expected outputs are produced oref0 JavaScript determine-basal (oref0) run on the snapshot; or the controller's own output captured at the time (originalOutput) Loop the upstream LoopAlgorithm package run on the snapshot; or Loop's devicestatus output captured at the time

A port's own outputs are never the reference (§3.5).

docs.title: 4.4 Completeness shown per run
docs.text: Each run shows, per input in dosing-input-sources.yaml, whether it was recorded, derived or absent in that snapshot, and the result is labelled with it. A run on derived inputs is reported as such, never merged into a single agreement rate with runs on recorded ones.

docs.title: 4.5 Disagreement reports and fault injection
docs.text: A disagreement report names the snapshot, both definitions and settings, both outputs and the first intermediate value that differs (ADR-005's comparison granularity: predictions, eventual glucose, IOB arrays). The harness also runs the same snapshot with faults, as the labs already do for the hub: missing data; out-of-order arrival, as in the hub-active-state backfill cases and the connector soak's backdated records; and duplicates and re-sends, as in the v3-identifier-immutable lab.

docs.title: 4.6 No audition result is promoted to control
docs.text:
The harness has no path to a pump and no way to change which algorithm a controller enacts. Execution authority is a separate, recorded decision outside it. Under D18 the controller validates and enacts (execution plan §2.6.1), and a proposed change reaches it only through a lifecycle such as agents in the ecosystem §4.3: propose, validate, approve against the exact payload, command, outcome. An audition result is evidence for that decision, never the decision.

A registry is not enough to swap algorithms. Changing the algorithm without replacing the whole app also requires separating the algorithm's semantics from the pump and sensor safety responsibilities around it: maximum basal and bolus enforcement, suspend handling, delivery confirmation and the pump's own dose history. Today some of these limits are algorithm inputs (profile.maxIob and profile.maxBasal in oref0's set) and the rest sit in each controller's pump and sensor code; registering algorithms behind one interface (§3.1) moves neither.

docs.title: 5. Not measured, not decided
docs.text:
• No audition harness exists here; §4 is a list of requirements.
  • No independent-implementation fact in §3 was reproduced; none of its code was run.
  • Whether an algorithm definition belongs in D19 (a new element or resource) or elsewhere (§4.2).
  • A provenance or role for a computed, never-enacted result (§1.2).
  • Whether Nightscout stores nominal or superseded temp-basal durations on each upload path, and whether the four unlisted inputs of §3.3 should enter dosing-input-sources.yaml.
  • A Loop adapter under ADR-005, and Loop's native inputs captured in any vector set.
  • Fault-injection cases for algorithms; the labs linked in §4.5 exercise the hub, not an algorithm.
  • Who decides that an auditioned algorithm may control a pump, and how that decision is recorded.

docs.title: Command journeys: plans, confirmations and moment commands for one pump with many orchestrators
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-10-18. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

What this is: a journey map (contributor-facing). Read after the command queue and planning note, whose use cases and §5 decisions it walks step by step; the needs it finds are specified in commands (CM1–CM25) and plans (PN1–PN18). Snapshot — describes 2026-10-18. Status: proposed.

Each journey follows the format of the 15.0.9 journey map: who is involved, then numbered steps. Each step names its level (policy, confirmation, moment or algorithm, as in the note's §3), then Do (what happens), Working (what correct looks like), Watch for (the failure a tester or reviewer looks for) and Contributor (the rules that apply, the existing conformance case under specs/sync/conformance/, the unsafe control actions from the control-loop analysis, and what is not specified, with the open item or decision it needs). Claims about a named controller are read-derived, as in the note.

The journeys follow the maintainer's decisions of 2026-10-18 (note §5): a controller enacts each commandId at most once; plans run on the controller and the hub keeps a read-only mirror; a plan or proposal may require named reviews before approval; the person may withdraw or cancel any item on their own therapy; followers read the queue; an adjustment is a new proposal, and an approval may accept a plan in parts, naming the elements it accepts. Two dose checks apply: the hub refuses a proposal's approval when a dose or carb record reached it after the proposal was made (CM22), and the controller refuses at enactment by its own rule (CM23); Part 3 shows which serves each journey.

docs.title: Words used here
docs.text: word meaning queue item a proposal, a plan or a command on one tenant's channel, with its state plan a recurring intent with its trigger, conditions, bounds and end date, approved once and held and run by the controller (note §3) element one separately acceptable part of a plan, such as an eating-soon target or a meal entry occurrence one run of a plan, such as Tuesday's lunch confirmation a small command against one occurrence, sent hours ahead and bounded by the plan mirror the hub's read-only copy of a plan and its occurrences, written from the controller's reports since check comparing what changed (doses, carbs, intents, the definition) since an item was made hub refuses the hub refuses a proposal's approval when a dose or carb record reached it after the proposal was made (CM22); it does not apply to a plan (PN7) controller decides the controller refuses a dose or carbs at enactment by its own rule (CM23), at each plan occurrence too (PN10); the outstanding list shows doses and carbs since (CM24)

docs.title: The people
docs.text: role does who, in these journeys proposer drafts an item (CM11, CM12) an agent with calendar, location or activity access; a clinician; a caregiver; the person evaluator or reviewer attaches evidence (CM16); a required reviewer must do so before a plan's approval (PN6) a risk-check agent, a second agent, a caregiver, a clinician approver turns an item into a command or an active plan (CM13, CM14) the person, or a delegate under a grant (authority §7) the person may approve, adjust (by a new proposal), withdraw or cancel any item on their own therapy (CM14, CM25), skip an occurrence or end a plan (PN14, PN16) the person with diabetes, or a parent for a young child enactor the singleton controller holding the channel's command-sink; validates, enacts once, reports the AID app on the person's phone (authority §6) follower reads the queue, the mirror and outcomes (CM24, PN11); never acts a partner, a school nurse with read access, a watch app

docs.title: PL1. A weekday lunch, planned from the calendar and location
docs.text:
proposer reviewer approver the person enactor a planning agent a risk-check agent; a caregiver the person approves in parts; may skip any day the controller 
sequenceDiagram
  accTitle: PL1, a weekday lunch planned from the calendar and location
  accDescr: A planning agent drafts a plan with an eating-soon element and a meal element. A risk-check agent and a caregiver review it. The person accepts the eating-soon element and declines the meal, preferring to bolus at the table. The controller holds the plan and the hub mirrors it. Each morning the agent confirms the day from the calendar and location; on a day the meeting runs over the person skips it; otherwise the controller starts eating soon after its own checks and reports it.
  participant G as Planning agent
  participant R as Reviewers
  participant P as Person
  participant H as Hub (mirror)
  participant C as Controller
  G->>H: plan: eating soon + meal, weekdays, end date (PL1.1)
  R->>H: risk check, caregiver review (PL1.2)
  P->>H: accept eating soon, decline meal (PL1.3)
  H->>C: the accepted plan (PL1.4)
  C->>H: holds it, mirror active
  G->>H: morning: lunch on the calendar, usual place (PL1.5)
  H->>C: confirmation for today
  alt meeting runs over
    P->>H: skip today (PL1.6)
    H->>C: skip, confirmation cancelled
  else lunch happens
    Note over C: own checks (PL1.7)
    C->>H: eating soon ran
  end

PL1.1 · policy · The agent drafts the plan. - Do: the agent sees the usual lunch at the usual time and place over past weeks and proposes a plan with two elements: an eating-soon target before lunch, and the usual lunch carbs with their meal bolus; weekdays only, each occurrence needing a confirmation that morning, with an end date. - Working: the queue shows one open plan proposal: its elements, trigger, bounds, end date, the proposing agent and its expiry, and an evaluation saying in words why (no calendar entries). - Watch for: calendar titles or places in the proposal or evaluation; a plan with no end date. - Contributor: CM11, CM12 (propose-with-permission-and-role, propose-without-role), CM16, authority DR7; UCA-PROP-001, UCA-PROP-004. The plan object: plans PN1–PN4 (plan-proposed-and-approved, plan-ends-missing); a plan proposal stays open up to plans.maxProposalSeconds, not CM3's commands.maxExpirySeconds (PN1, plan-proposal-open-past-command-expiry). Not specified: the trigger grammar (plans §9 item 3) and the grammar of an element's content (commands §9 item 3).

PL1.2 · policy · Required reviews. - Do: the plan names two required reviews: a risk-check agent and a caregiver. Each attaches an evaluation. - Working: an approval before both are attached is refused 409 review-required; each review shows who made it, and a review by the proposer does not count. - Watch for: an approval accepted with a required review missing; a review that changes the proposal's state. - Contributor: CM16 (evaluation-does-not-change-proposal, evaluate-without-read); plans PN6 (approve-review-missing, approve-review-by-proposer-not-counted): the proposer names them in requiredReviews (PN1), and a plan accepting an R3 or higher element needs at least one; UCA-PROP-011. Not specified: whether a second agent run by the same person or operator counts (plans §9 item 7).

PL1.3 · policy · The person accepts part of it. - Do: the person accepts the eating-soon element and declines the meal element, preferring to bolus at the table. - Working: the approval names the element accepted and the hash it binds to; the declined element is recorded as declined; one plan, with one element, reaches the controller. - Watch for: the declined element reaching the controller; an approval refused because the person's intents changed between drafting and approval (an unrelated override). - Contributor: plans PN5, PN7, PN8 (approve-one-of-two-elements, approve-element-hash-mismatch): the approval names each accepted element by id and hash, the rest are recorded as declined, and the command carries the accepted elements under one hash; PN6 and CM14 (approve-own-agent-plan-refused); a plan's basedOn is per channel, so a change on a channel no accepted element acts on does not stale it (PN7, approve-plan-unrelated-channel-changed, approve-plan-state-changed); UCA-PROP-003, UCA-PROP-006. Not specified: approver signatures over the accepted elements (plans §9 item 5).

PL1.4 · policy · The controller takes the plan; the hub mirrors it. - Do: the approval becomes one command; the controller validates the plan against its own limits, holds it and reports succeeded. - Working: the command reads succeeded; the mirror moves from approved to active on that report and shows the accepted and declined elements; a redelivered copy of the command is not stored twice. - Watch for: the mirror showing the proposal's content rather than what the controller holds; the plan stored again after two fetches before its report. - Contributor: CM1, CM7–CM10, CM18, CM21 (enact-identical-payload-succeeds, enact-hash-mismatch-refused, enact-refetched-once); plans PN8, PN9, PN11 (plan-held-active, plan-refused-by-controller, plan-command-expires-at-ends): the hub keeps the mirror and moves the controller's states only on the controller's reports; UCA-CMD-006, UCA-PROP-008. Not specified: the plan channel a product declares (plans §9 item 6).

PL1.5 · confirmation · The morning confirmation. - Do: at a set hour the agent reads today's calendar and location and confirms today's occurrence, with an evaluation of one line ("lunch on the calendar, at the usual place"). - Working: a confirmation command for this occurrence, expiring at the occurrence's time, appears in the queue; the mirror shows the occurrence as confirmed. - Watch for: a confirmation carrying anything outside the plan's bounds; a confirmation for a plan that was ended; an agent able to send commands outside plans. - Contributor: CM3, CM12; plans PN12 (confirm-by-proposer, confirm-by-other-subject, confirm-too-early, confirm-after-role-lost): the approved plan is its proposer's grant to confirm from its proposing instance without a further approval, and a confirmation never releases a dose by itself; UCA-AUTH-002, UCA-AUTH-003.

PL1.6 · moment · The lunch is cancelled. - Do: the meeting runs over; the person skips today's occurrence from the phone or the hub. - Working: the occurrence reads skip-requested; its confirmation is cancelled if not handed over, and a cancel request if it was; the controller reports skipped, or ran if it had already run; tomorrow's occurrence is untouched. - Watch for: a skip that ends the whole plan; a skip read as done before the controller reports. - Contributor: CM2, CM3; plans PN14 (skip-by-person, skip-cancels-pending-confirmation, skip-then-controller-reports-skipped), cancelling as CM25 does; UCA-CMD-015, FB-CMD-001.

PL1.7 · algorithm · The occurrence runs. - Do: at the planned time the controller starts the eating-soon target, after its own checks of what was dosed and eaten since the confirmation. - Working: the hub shows the target active, with initiator {value: other, controllerTerm} naming the plan, and the mirror links the occurrence to its intent. - Watch for: the target shown as applied when only requested; the target started twice. - Contributor: S8, S10, A2, A3, A10, A12 (active-state/requested-and-applied); FB-STATE-004, UCA-CMD-010; PN10, PN17; the controller's ran report carries the identity of the intent that shows it (PN11, plan-report-occurrence-ran). Not specified: a field on the intent naming its plan and occurrence; no open item in commands §9 or plans §9 carries it.

docs.title: PL2. Exercise from the calendar
docs.text:
proposer reviewer approver the person enactor a planning agent none required the person may cancel any session the controller

PL2.1 · policy · Plan proposed and approved whole. The agent proposes a temporary target before calendar entries marked as exercise, confirmed by location or activity; the person approves. Working: one active plan in the mirror; a target the controller announces ahead reads scheduled, not active (S4). Contributor: CM11–CM14, PN1–PN5, PN7 (plan-proposed-and-approved), S4. Precedent: AndroidAPS automation triggers on time, location and activity and can start a temporary target (note §3). Not specified: conditions on calendar, location or activity in the trigger (plans §9 item 3).

PL2.2 · confirmation · Confirmed by activity. - Do: the agent sees the person arrive at the gym and confirms the occurrence. - Working: the confirmation is within the plan's bounds and expires at the occurrence's time; the evaluation says "at the usual place", not where. - Watch for: location data in the queue; a confirmation arriving after the session ended. - Contributor: CM3, CM16, DR7; PN12 (confirm-by-proposer): a confirmation at or after the occurrence's time is 409 occurrence-passed; UCA-CMD-003.

PL2.3 · confirmation · The session does not happen. The entry stays on the calendar; the person stays home; no confirmation is sent. Working: the occurrence ends unconfirmed and nothing is enacted, and the controller reports the occurrence missed. Watch for: an occurrence run without a required confirmation. Contributor: HAZ-1; PN10, PN11. Not specified: how a plan states that an occurrence runs only when confirmed, part of the trigger grammar (plans §9 item 3).

PL2.4 · algorithm · Two intents at once. - Do: the target starts while an override the person set is active. - Working: the hub reports both, with their initiators; the controller's combined result, if it publishes one, is the only composed value shown. - Watch for: the hub computing a combined target, or ending one intent with the other. - Contributor: S1, S3, A1, A9 (active-state/exclusive-overlap-reported); FB-STATE-003.

docs.title: PL3. A caregiver's week of school overrides
docs.text:
proposer reviewer approver the person enactor a parent a school nurse (follower, may evaluate) the second parent a teenager, may cancel the controller

PL3.1 · policy · A week planned on Sunday. - Do: a parent proposes five occurrences of a preset override around the timetable's sports lessons, referring to the preset by its controller id. - Working: the proposal records the destination's definitionId; the nurse can read it. - Watch for: a preset referred to by a name the controller can rename. - Contributor: CM11, PN1, S9 (idField, referencedBy); UCA-PROP-008. The nurse reads the proposal with api:proposals:read (CM11), and the outstanding list and the mirror with any of CM24's read permissions (PN11, plan-read-with-proposals-read, plan-read-without-permission).

PL3.2 · policy · The other parent approves. - Do: the second parent approves. The proposing parent may also approve a plan they made from their own app (CM14); a plan with an R3 or higher element still needs a review from another subject first (PN6). - Working: one approval, one command, the plan held by the controller and mirrored. - Watch for: two approvals at once creating two plans. - Contributor: CM13, CM14 (approve-own-proposal-by-person, approve-approved-proposal; self-approval-refused applies to an agent's proposal), PN5, PN6 (approve-r4-without-any-review); UCA-PROP-009, UCA-PROP-013. Not specified: that the change from open to approved is atomic under concurrent approvals (commands §9 item 7).

PL3.3 · policy · Wednesday changes. A school trip moves Wednesday's lesson; the parent proposes an adjusted plan, a new proposal. Working: once approved it replaces the held plan, and the mirror shows which plan is current. Watch for: both plans running on Wednesday. Contributor: decision 4; S3 supersedes, A7; PN16 ends the held plan. Not specified: an adjusted plan replacing one the controller holds, and several plans active on one channel (plans §9 item 10).

PL3.4 · algorithm · The controller was updated midweek. - Do: the app updates and renews under a new definition in which the preset changed. - Working: the controller refuses Thursday's occurrence with a reason the hub records, and the parents see it. - Watch for: the occurrence enacted under the changed preset with no notice. - Contributor: CM8, S12, registration §8; UCA-PROP-008. A plan approved after a renewal under a new definition is refused 409 definition-changed (PN7, approve-plan-definition-changed); a renewal after the approval does not affect it (approve-plan-definition-unchanged), so the controller's check at the occurrence catches this (PN10) and it reports the occurrence refused with its reason (PN11). For a moment proposal the definition at approval is open (commands §9 item 7).

docs.title: PL4. A sensitivity plan for illness or a cycle phase, with an end date
docs.text:
proposer reviewer approver the person enactor a planning agent a named human reviewer (a clinician or caregiver) the person may end it early the controller

docs.title: What the journeys cannot show without a controller implementation
docs.text:
• whether a controller holds, runs and reports a plan, and the end reason of an unconfirmed or refused occurrence;
  • whether enact once survives a restart on each controller;
  • what a cancel after hand-over achieves;
  • the since checks a controller makes at enactment, and how often they refuse;
  • a preview before approval, outside AndroidAPS's client control;
  • whether the mirror stays in step with what the controller holds.

docs.title: Command queue and planning: outstanding commands, enacting once, and plans confirmed in advance
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-10-18. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

What this is: a design note (contributor-facing). Read after commands and the control-loop analysis; it prepares the maintainer's choices for commands §9 item 7 and the use cases that drive them. Snapshot — describes 2026-10-18. Status: proposed; the maintainer's answers of 2026-10-18 are in §5; nothing here is in a specification yet. Every claim about a controller is read-derived from source at the release named; nothing was run.

The question. The control-loop analysis found that the command contract has no list of outstanding commands, no cancel, no rule that a controller enacts a command once, and no check for doses since a proposal was made. The maintainer framed the answer as a queue with transparency and operations for managing workflows and intents, asked what controllers do today, and asked for use cases. The use cases that matter most are planned ones: an agent with access to calendar, location and activity confirms a repeated meal at a repeated time hours or days ahead, so the person manages a policy instead of pressing buttons in the moment.

docs.title: 1. What controllers do today about duplicate commands
docs.text:
Read at Loop v3.14.9 (NightscoutService 2cef4896), Trio v1.0.2 (0b29cd53), AndroidAPS 4.0.0-rc1 (d5e7f5bd) and the unreleased Remote Commands 2 controller on a fork (gestrich/NightscoutService 5bc54fac).

controller and command how a duplicate is stopped survives a restart Loop bolus, carbs the one-time password is single use, stored in the Keychain, valid about 60 s yes; a refused duplicate still writes an error Note Loop override, cancel a list of seen sent-at values, in memory, never pruned; none without sent-at no; a replay after a restart starts the override again from now Loop Remote Commands 2 (fork) a stored set of handled record _ids, marked before enacting, on push and fetch yes; never pruned, and a duplicate is written back as Error Trio bolus refused when boluses since the command's own timestamp reach 20 % of the request yes (stored pump events) Trio meal refused when newer carbs exist yes; misses a back-dated or future-scheduled meal Trio temp target, override, cancels nothing; dev adds a command_id that is echoed, not checked — AndroidAPS client control (4.0 prereleases) a per-client counter that must strictly increase, stored, advanced before dispatch; a dose is prepared, then committed once yes

The same command does arrive twice today: a force-killed Loop received one bolus twice (Loop

docs.title: 2174, refused by the password check), and Trio fixed doubled carbs from push redelivery or a
docs.text:
resend in v1.0.2 (#1346, #1348). AndroidAPS already receives each client-control command by socket and by polling, the situation CM18 creates.

What follows. No released controller keys de-duplication on an id the hub assigns. A rule that a controller enacts each commandId once, remembered until the command expires, matches the newest designs (AndroidAPS client control, Remote Commands 2) and is small work for the rest: Loop stores the override list it already keeps; Trio keeps a seen set on the command_id its dev branch already parses; AndroidAPS needs nothing when its signed envelope rides through the hub unread (CM10). A caregiver's manual resend is a new command and is not caught by this rule; on the hub side that is CM4's requestId, and it is why the outstanding list (§2) matters.

docs.title: 2. The queue the specifications already imply
docs.text:
Commands §4–§7 already define most of a queue, per tenant and per channel:

  • Objects. Proposals (open, then approved, rejected, withdrawn or expired), evaluations attached to them, commands (from pending to an outcome) and outcome reports.
  • Operations specified. Send (with requestId re-send), propose, evaluate, approve (bound to a payload hash and a state version), reject, withdraw, fetch, push, report, expire.
  • Who sees what. The sender and approver see a command's state; proposals are read with api:proposals:read or api:commands:create; the destination fetches only its own.

Operations to add, each named as a gap in commands §9:

operation what it does why list outstanding every proposal and command on a channel that is not final, returned with each send and approval and on its own a second command or approval in the upload lag (UCA-CMD-001, UCA-PROP-007) cancel pending → cancelled, final, nothing handed over; after hand-over, a request the controller may refuse a meal not eaten (UCA-CMD-015) enact once the controller rule in §1 delivery is at least once (UCA-CMD-006) limit open proposals per proposing instance and channel flooding (UCA-PROP-002)

List outstanding, cancel and enact once are now specified as CM24, CM25 and CM21; the proposal limit is still open.

Not added: reordering (no precedent; a pump's command queue is the controller's own) and superseding one command by another (supersession is a property of intents, S3 and A7, and a superseding override is a new command).

docs.title: 3. Planning: a level above the moment
docs.text:
The person, the algorithm, caregivers and agents all act on one pump; STPA calls this several controllers of one process, and the control-loop analysis gives the controller the only arbiter's seat (§3). The planned use cases add a level above the moment, as hierarchical control structures in STPA do:

level horizon who acts by policy days to weeks the person, a caregiver, a clinician, an agent that proposes a plan: a recurring intent with its conditions and bounds, approved once confirmation hours an agent reading calendar, location and history; the person confirming, adjusting or skipping one occurrence of a plan moment minutes the person, a caregiver a command, as today algorithm five minutes the controller its own loop, within the active intents

One enactor, many orchestrators. At every level the one instance holding the channel's command sink (Loop or Trio on the person's phone) is the only thing that acts on the pump. Around one plan or one proposal, several parties may work: agents that draft it or check it against other data, human reviewers, a delegate who may approve it, and the person, who may approve, adjust or withdraw it. The queue item is the shared record they work on, and each party's part is a role on it:

role does specified as proposer drafts the item CM11, CM12 evaluator attaches evidence: a risk check, a second agent's view, a reviewer's note CM16 approver turns it into a command or an active plan; the person, or a delegate under a grant CM13, CM14; the grant is open (authority §7) the person may also adjust, withdraw or cancel it, whoever proposed it not specified enactor the singleton controller: validates and enacts, reports the outcome CM7–CM10, D18

The specifications have the proposer, evaluator, approver and enactor. What they do not have yet: an item that changes as parties work on it (an adjustment is today a new proposal), a review that must happen before approval (an evaluation is optional evidence), and the person's standing to withdraw or cancel any item on their own therapy.

A precedent already on a controller. AndroidAPS's automation plugin (dev 7e1d537d49) triggers on recurring time, location, Wi-Fi network, steps and heart rate, and its actions include starting a temporary target, a profile percentage and scenes; it has no bolus or carb action. The plan lives and runs on the controller, which is where D18 puts enactment.

Where a plan runs. Two shapes fit the specifications differently:

  • On the controller (recommended). A plan is a controller-owned definition: a recurring intent kind with its trigger and bounds, declared in the controller's registration. A plan made off the phone reaches the controller as a proposal (CM11) whose payload is the plan; once approved, the controller holds it, runs it, and reports each occurrence as an intent with its initiator. A confirmation an agent sends hours ahead is a command against that plan's occurrence, small and bounded by the plan. The hub records and routes; it schedules nothing, as the platform index says.
  • On the hub. The hub stores the plan and issues commands when its conditions hold. Simpler for controllers, but the hub would decide when therapy changes, which D18 rules out, and it would need the calendar and location data, which then sits on a server.

Out-of-band data stays with the agent. Calendar, location and activity are identifying data. An agent that reads them sends the hub its proposal or confirmation and, as an evaluation (CM16), only what the approver needs to see ("lunch on the calendar, at the usual place"), not the data. That is the minimisation delegation requires (authority DR7).

Checks move with the level. A plan is checked when it is approved: its definition, its bounds, who may approve it. An occurrence is checked when it is confirmed and when it is enacted: what is active, and what was dosed and eaten since; the controller does the last check, because only it knows its state at that moment.

outstanding moment A2 agent proposes a correction bolus doses and carbs since; a controller preview (prepare, then commit) moment A3 agent proposes too often proposal limit any U1 the controller's own automation a scheduled override, a shortcut the controller's own window algorithm U2 another client's treatment a careportal temporary target a controller downloads nothing today (UCA-SYNC-DL-001) moment F1 follower watches commands, proposals and plans without acting nothing; What the table says about the dose check: the moment-level cases need doses and carbs since, and two controllers already do it themselves (Trio's 20 % rule, AndroidAPS's prepare and commit); the policy cases need intents and definition at approval and leave doses to the controller when the plan runs. A hub-side "refuse if dosed since" check helps only the moment-level proposals (A1, A2, P1), and is limited there by the upload lag.

docs.title: 5. Decided and open
docs.text:
The maintainer's answers, 2026-10-18:

  1. Enact once: adopt the controller rule of §1, with the hub's commandId carried to the controller; specified as CM21.
  2. Plans run on the controller, and the hub mirrors them. The controller holds and runs an approved plan; the hub keeps a read-only copy of the plan and of each occurrence, so followers and reviewers see the policy as well as the moments.
  3. Several orchestrators on one item: a plan or proposal can require named evaluations (a risk check, a human reviewer) before it can be approved; the person can always withdraw or cancel any item on their own therapy, whoever proposed it; followers can read the queue (proposals, plans and commands) without acting on it.
  4. Revision: an adjustment is a new proposal. A plan may be accepted in parts: the approver accepts some of its elements and not others, and the approval names what it accepted.
  5. Next: write PL1–PL5 and the moment cases as journeys, now in command journeys, in the format of the 15.0.9 journey map, with the rules and cases each step needs.

Answered later the same day: the self-approval refusal applies to agents only, and the person may withdraw any proposal (CM14); the hub refuses an approval when doses or carbs arrived since the proposal (CM22), and the controller checks doses since before it enacts (CM23). A plan accepted in parts binds as the partial acceptance prototype recommends: the approval names each accepted element by id and hash, the command carries one hash of the subset, and approver signatures come next. A bounded standing bolus is acceptable with predetermined withdrawal criteria and mitigations (a reduced portion with eating soon, or an approval within the 12 hours before), drafted as FL1 of evidence-weighted approval, which drafts what approval a plan needs by risk and by evidence for clinical review.

The plan object, its approval in parts, the controller's hold, the hub's mirror and the occurrence operations are specified in plans (PN1–PN16).

Still open:

  • Out-of-band data: agents keep it; the hub receives proposals, confirmations and minimised evaluations only.

docs.title: Effect link: how a command's outcome names the record that shows its effect
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-10-18. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

Contributor-facing. Research note, 2026-10-18. Prototype for the maintainer's decision on commands CM7: how the outcome report of an enacted command links to the record that shows the effect. Read after the commands specification §5 and the partial acceptance prototype, whose shape this note follows: a small executable model per option, one set of scenarios run against each, the measured results, and an assessment. Snapshot — describes 2026-10-18. Status: proposed.

The question. CM7 says a report on an enacted command carries "the identity of the record that shows the effect" (identity). It does not say where that identity lives, who writes it, or what happens when the record is lost and re-sent, ended by a new record, changed by a second command, or arrives after the report. The maintainer judged the answer unclear, asked for prototypes, and noted that the work of building and maintaining the link may weigh as much as what a person or follower sees.

docs.title: 1. What was built
docs.text:
file what it is tools/nsschema/prototypes/effect_link.py one controller and one hub per option, the write step's re-send matching, the 24 scenarios, the measures, and the generator for the tables in §3 and §4 tools/nsschema/prototypes/test_effect_link.py the expected links per scenario and option, four invariants, two weakenings that must be caught, and a check that the tables in this note equal the model's

The tables between BEGIN GENERATED markers are written by python3 -m nsschema.prototypes.effect_link --write (run from tools/); --check and test_note_tables_are_current fail when they differ from the model.

What the model holds. A hub stores records through one write step: a re-send matches on identifier, else on the time and kind among records without one (identity I5 and §3); a match merges (sync transport T2); a delete is soft. The hub records each command, accepts one final report (CM9), and the controller keeps CM21's decided ids. Ground truth is kept beside the model: each step that makes a record says which command caused it, or that it was a local action on the phone. The link functions read only what the hub stores. Routing, tenants, expiry and payload hashes are left out: they do not differ between the options. Every record is synthetic; the kinds stand for the carrier a controller writes.

The options.

the controller sends the hub stores and links prior art B0 today, inferred nothing nothing; a reader links a succeeded command to the earliest unclaimed record of each kind it asked for, within a window after it was made what a follower does today when it watches for a record to appear E1 effect[] on the report the report lists the identity of each record showing the effect, in identity I4's form (collection, identifier, else _id) the list as reported, unverified, like the reported hash; resolved to stored records when read Trio dev's reply to a direct sender carries command_id and meal_id; for an edit, meal_id is the new carb entry E2 commandId on the record each effect record carries the commandId links by the field; keeps a stored value on merge and replace and refuses a different one the drafted DeliveryObservation.relatedRequestId; Loop's override record carries the sender's remoteAddress E3 both both the union; a pair one source gives and the other, able to speak, does not, is flagged and never resolved by the hub — E4 a reconciliation record a record of its own kind, one per command (its identifier derived from the commandId), naming the effect identities stores it through the write step like any record, so it can be re-sent and amended after the report is final the drafted Reconciliation {requestId, observationId, outcome}

The drafts named above are the cgm-remote-monitor docs/proposals/ files this repository wrote earlier; the platform specifications are proposed to supersede them.

Decided for the prototype.

  • E1 lists the effect on any report whose command wrote a record, including failed: CM7 as written lists it only "when enacted", which would leave the carbs of a part-enacted meal unlinked (meal-part-enacted).
  • E2 has one commandId per record. A second command that changes the record (a remote cancel) cannot add its own; the controller keeps the first.
  • A conforming controller under E1 and E4 keeps each command's effect list with CM21's decided id across a restart; restart-effects-not-kept shows one that does not.
  • The hub does not follow an instance across records (state and intent A2): E1 does not learn that a re-posted override is the same instance as the record its report named.

docs.title: 4. Cost
docs.text:
E1 E2 E3 E4 schemas or carriers touched 1 13 14 1 hub fields and indexes 2 2 4 2 new invariants 1 3 5 3 controller must keep or write 2 2 4 2 conformance cases 7 18 27 8

Counted from lists in effect_link.COSTS; each item is named there.

  • E1 adds one member to one message, the outcome report. Nothing changes in any record kind, so adding a command kind later adds nothing here. The hub stores the list and keeps an index from identity to command for "was this dose remote?". The controller keeps each command's effect identities with CM21's decided id until its report is accepted, and needs an identifier on each effect record, or the _id from the write reply. Seven cases.
  • E2 touches every carrier a command can reach: 12 carriers across treatments, profile and settings as commands §3 and §8 read them (bolus, carbs, Loop's and Trio's overrides, temporary targets, profile switch, running mode, temp basal, extended bolus, therapy events, AndroidAPS scenes, Loop's loop mode), plus a well-known field. Each needs the field in its schema, in each controller's uploader for that kind, in the projection to typed records, and a case. The hub gains three invariants, one of which (kept on replace, refused when changed) is a new exception to T2's merge and to API v1 and v3 PUT. Every app that round-trips a record (an editor, a downloader that re-uploads) must keep the field or rely on that exception. Eighteen cases.
  • E3 is E1 and E2 together, plus the flag rule. Twenty-seven cases.
  • E4 adds one record kind, an authorisation check on a record write (only the destination's subject, as CM7 checks a report), and a second place where an outcome is stated beside the command's state. Eight cases.

With older apps (compatibility, verdicts in §2 there). Every controller's L3 command row is opt-in today: no released controller reports to a hub. Under E1 and E4, nothing a non-participating app sends or reads changes. Under E2 an older reader ignores the field, but an older editor or a client that rebuilds a record from its own model sends a body without it: on merge it survives (T2), on PUT only by E2's new rule. A record copied to another hub carries a commandId that names no command there, which a reader on that hub must not take as remote without the command. Under every option an older follower sees what it sees today: the records, unlinked.
