docs.title: 5. Effect and motivation (proposed)
docs.text:
specs/sync/therapy-effect.schema.json is a draft that separates a temporary effect from why it was asked for, so that a projection which withholds the motivation is a field selection rather than a redaction. It is not adopted as a decision; the effects and versioning analysis is its evidence. A TherapyEffect is a span (startTimestamp, endTimestamp or null while running, an id, a correlationId linking the decisions taken under it, a structural source, and supersededById when a later effect replaces it) with:

  • effect: insulinNeedsScaleFactor, basalScaleFactor, sensitivityScaleFactor, carbRatioScaleFactor, targetRange, timeShiftSeconds, smbAllowed, maxSmbMinutes, suspendDelivery. Absent means unchanged; a factor of 1.0 is not the same as absent.
  • motivation: an optional closed classification, an optional label in the person's own words, and decidedBy.
  • disclosure: effect-only, effect+classification or full, chosen by the person whose data it is.
  • provenance: the remapping rule from specs/sync/effect-remapping.yaml and whether it was lossy.

disclosure controls what a record states, not what an observer could infer from it: a recurring effect is itself a signal. The remapping is lossy for Trio's override, whose wire document carries a preset name and no effect.

docs.title: 6. What is active at a time
docs.text: How a hub answers "what was active at time t" from the records a controller wrote and the kinds it declared. Proposed, for the maintainer to confirm (§6.3, ten choices): specified with synthetic cases and a reference function (tools/nsschema/active_state.py), not implemented by any hub. The hub reports instances and which are active; it never combines them (S1).

docs.title: 6.1 Rules
docs.text:
# rule A1 Per product and kind. Instances are derived per (vendor, product) and kind, from that product's records only. Instances of two products are both reported, even on one shared slot; neither ends the other. A2 Identity makes an instance. A record belongs to a kind's requested layer by its wire carrier (collection, eventType, discriminator) and, when the kind declares a requested carrier, by that carrier too. Records whose wire.identity fields are equal are one instance; its content is the last live write the hub received for that identity. Two records with equal identity at the same instant are one instance, never two. A3 Start is the record's own time. An instance starts at its record's timeField (created_at when none is declared), never at the time in its _id or the time the hub received it (identity I3). A4 End from the declared duration. An instance ends at its start plus durationField in durationUnit. A record carrying the indefinite sentinel, or no duration, is open-ended. A5 End encodings. An amendment that shortens an instance (amend-duration, repost-same-created_at, or delete-and-repost under one identity) ends it early, with end reason cancelled; one that runs its duration ends expired. Under zero-duration-record, a zero-duration record ends the latest-starting instance of the kind and product that started strictly before it and is active at its time, with cancelled, and is not an instance itself; an instance starting at the marker's own time is not ended. The end reason describes an instance once it has ended; an amendment that shortens an instance is read as an early end, and an edit that only shortens it reads the same. A6 Deletion. A delete removes the write it names: by _id, as a delete by id carries no other field, or by identity. A soft delete (a write with isValid: false) removes its identity. An instance with no live write left is listed as ended deletedBeforeStart, and is never active and ends nothing, when the delete was received before its start; otherwise it is not reported, as a deleted document is not today. A re-post received before the delete of the record it replaces still amends the instance. A7 Supersession by start. Under supersedes, an instance ends at the start of the next instance of the same kind and product that starts after it and before its end, with superseded. Order is by start, never by arrival, so a backfilled earlier instance is ended by the later one whichever arrived first. Two instances that start at the same instant: the one whose last write was received later supersedes. A8 Overlay. Under overlay, a timed instance applies over an open-ended one without ending it; the open-ended one is not active while the timed one is, and is active again when it ends. A9 Overlap is reported, not resolved. For a kind that is exclusiveWithinSlot and declares neither supersedes nor overlay, overlapping instances are all reported active, each marked overlap. A10 Requested and applied are separate layers. Wire records matching the requested carrier give the requested layer (A2); applied records give the applied layer. Each applied record is in effect from its timeField until its own end or the next applied record of the same carrier and product, whichever is first; a record whose activeField is false ends what the earlier one put in effect. An applied carrier sampled per cycle (devicestatus) gives an applied layer only when it declares activeField; without one its values are the controller's composed result (S1) and name no intent, so no instance is reported from them. A request with no applied record is reported as requested only. A11 Units are declared, never assumed. A duration is read only in its declared durationUnit. A kind whose carrier has a duration and no unit yields no instances and is reported unreadable; the other kinds still answer. A field's unit is reported from its typed path, and a path with no unit carries none. A12 A state version. A product's state version at a time is sha256: over the RFC 8785 canonical JSON of its active rows with each instance's content. It changes when an instance starts, ends or is amended, including an amendment that changes only what the instance says. It versions the hub's record of what the controller reported, not the controller's own state: an approval bound to it is checked by the hub (commands CM15), and only the controller's own validation checks its own state (D18). A13 Sampled state. A kind whose endedEncoding is sampled-state has no instance records: each record carries the current value, which holds from the record's time until the next record of the kind and product. The value reported is the first declared path's.

The rules drawn. Each panel draws one conformance case's records and its expected answer, not an application of the rule; tools/diagrams/active_state_rules.py generates them from the cases (make diagrams-svg; make diagrams-svg-check fails when one is stale).

docs.title: 6.2 What decides each measured disagreement
docs.text:
LAB-HUB-ACTIVE-STATE measured cgm-remote-monitor and Nocturne disagreeing on one synthetic record set (landscape §5). The lab ran each hub's storage and active-state code directly, Nocturne on SQLite, not either hub's HTTP write path. The rules give one answer for each; it is not always either hub's.

disagreement (measured) rule and declaration case against the hubs a temporary target followed by a cancel: cgm-remote-monitor truncates the target; Nocturne records the cancel as an open span of its own A5, for a kind declaring zero-duration-record active-state/zero-duration-ends-instance cgm-remote-monitor's answer Loop's devicestatus override duration: seconds in cgm-remote-monitor, minutes in Nocturne A3, A10, A11; Loop's applied carrier declares override.timestamp, override.active and seconds (NightscoutService StoredDosingDecision.swift:118-136) active-state/applied-duration-in-declared-unit cgm-remote-monitor's answer a timed profile switch after a permanent one: cgm-remote-monitor falls back to the permanent profile; Nocturne has none after expiry A4, A7, A8; AndroidAPS's profile switch declares duration 0 as permanent, overlay and supersedes (AndroidAPS AppRepository.kt:408-415, ProfileSwitchDao.kt:37) active-state/permanent-profile-switch-returns cgm-remote-monitor's answer AndroidAPS timeshift: milliseconds in cgm-remote-monitor, hours in Nocturne A11; the profile switch declares {path: timeshift, unit: milliseconds} active-state/field-unit-from-declaration cgm-remote-monitor's answer two temporary targets at the same millisecond: cgm-remote-monitor keeps the first; Nocturne stores both A2 for equal identity (the last received write); A7 for different identities active-state/equal-identity-same-instant neither: cgm-remote-monitor keeps the first write, the rules the last (§6.3 choice 1) an earlier open override backfilled after a later one: Nocturne leaves two open spans A7 active-state/backfill-supersedes-by-start cgm-remote-monitor's list answer

Both hubs ignore a stored Temporary Override Cancel (measured), so they agree; that careportal does not store one is read-derived. The writers that end with a zero-duration record (careportal, nightguard, iAPS) have no registration, so A5 applies to them once one declares zero-duration-record. AndroidAPS's running mode reads its duration from originalDuration in milliseconds, 0 when permanent, because its wire duration is 0 for loop modes and a 10-year placeholder for an open-ended loop-disabled mode (RunningModeExtension.kt:25-97), and it is resolved like the profile switch (AppRepository.kt:451-458).

docs.title: 6.3 Choices for the maintainer to confirm
docs.text:
1. The last received write is an instance's content (A2), so a late, stale re-send of an older version would win. The alternative, the latest by the record's own time, needs a time that changes on amendment, which no carrier declares.
  2. A record deleted after its start is not reported (A6), rather than listed as cancelled.
  3. Two instances starting at the same instant: the later received supersedes (A7).
  4. Overlay is checked before supersession, so a timed instance never ends an open-ended one of an overlay kind (A8).
  5. An applied record holds until the next one or its own end, with no staleness limit (A10): a controller that stops uploading leaves its last applied record in effect until that record ends, or indefinitely if it is open-ended.
  6. A carrier with a duration and no unit is not read (A11), rather than read in a default unit.
  7. The state version covers content (A12), so any amendment of an active instance changes it.
  8. A zero-duration record ends only an instance already running (A5). A zero-duration record written to cancel a target scheduled for later (careportal, nightguard and iAPS cancel before start this way) does not cancel it, because nothing on the record says which future instance it names.
  9. An amendment that shortens an instance is read as an early end (cancelled, A5), so an edit from 60 to 45 minutes made before the 45th minute reads the same as a cancel.
  10. Per-cycle values that name no intent give no applied instance (A10), so Trio's and iAPS's applied state is reported as composed values only.

docs.title: 8. Open
docs.text:
• The active-state choices (§6.3), for the maintainer to confirm.
  • Undeclared vocabularies (§3): for PROPOSAL-REG-CONTROLLERS to confirm with each controller's authors.
  • Effect and motivation (§5): proposed, not adopted.
  • Treatments a controller downloads and acts on (S10 treatment-download), found by the control-loop analysis: unlike a command, such an entry has no expiry, no destination, no outcome and no record that a controller acted on it (UCA-SYNC-DL-001); an edit or delete after the controller acted changes the record and not what was enacted (UCA-SYNC-DL-003).
  • Not measured: anything about AndroidAPS from data (no AndroidAPS closed-loop site in the corpus); whether shipping AndroidAPS sites turn on the NsClientAccept* preferences; Trio's preset name join; the order in which a Trio override factor and a temporary target's sensitivityRatio multiply; either hub's HTTP write path and Nocturne on PostgreSQL; xDrip+ remote and follower paths; the NightscoutKit fork LoopCaregiver uses; behaviour that depends on app lifecycle.

docs.title: L4 Sync transport: how writes are matched, ordered and delivered over REST and the socket, and at what cost
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-06 at 773c8bc59.

Contributor-facing. Living specification, current at main df621fa7 (2026-10-18). Layer L4 of the platform index; terms are in the glossary; how a re-send is matched is in the identity specification §3. Decisions: the write contract's §6.1 (2026-10-12) and D6 (the change feed under multi). Queue: SPEC-SYNC-TRANSPORT.

Specification 7 of 8 in the reading order; after the layers whose records it moves, before authority. Expect the decided write path (T1–T4), each client's declared sync endpoints, the proposed read, cursor and socket rules (T5–T16), and the conformance cases.

How writes are applied, ordered and delivered, over REST and the socket, and what a client pays to stay in sync. Status: the write path is decided, except re-sends of devicestatus (T2), and T3 is on dev; §3 is evidenced; §4–§6 are proposed, and §4 is specified with cases. §2 is the write path, with each rule's status; §3 is what each client's sync code can call, read from its source; §4–§6 are proposed and specified with cases where a rule can be checked by one.

docs.title: 1. Files
docs.text: file what it is write contract the measured write matrix, the write step and the re-send rule this page states as rules tools/nsschema/sync_cost.py make schema-sync-cost: distinct endpoints each client's sync path can call, from its own source tools/nsschema/sync_cursor.py reference decision function for the cursor rules (§4); it checks the cases and is not a hub specs/sync/conformance/sync-transport/ 13 synthetic cases (§9)

docs.title: 2. The write path
docs.text:
# rule status T1 One write step. Every path that writes (API v1, API v3, the socket, in-process callers such as nightscout-connect) writes through one step, which decides per item, in order: the _id form, the target (identity §3), the outcome (inserted, merged, replaced, unchanged, deleted, not-found, refused), the server dates, the storage write, and then one change event for the call. Each item is answered with its outcome and both ids (identity I4). specified (WRITE-CONTRACT, blocked) T2 Re-send outcomes. For treatments, entries, profile, food and activity, a re-send that matches a stored record merges into it; an explicit update (v1 PUT, v3 PUT) replaces. A null in an update removes the field (JSON Merge Patch, RFC 7386, recursive, arrays replaced whole) on a merge on match, on an API v3 PATCH and on the socket's dbUpdate, which follows PATCH; never on a replace (v1 or v3 PUT) or on any create, which store a null as sent. On API v1 it runs after prepareData; dbUpdateUnset stays (identity §3). An identical re-send keeps each path's behaviour today: rewritten on API v1, v3 and in-process, answered unchanged on the socket. For devicestatus, a re-send whose identifier is already stored writes nothing (no merge, no new record, no srvModified change) and is answered with the stored _id, on API v1 and v3 (decided 2026-10-26); a re-send with the same created_at and device is a retry only when its body is identical, answered unchanged; a differing body is a new record. The socket keeps its ±2 s similar-treatment match as an explicit option. activity gets server dates and soft delete like the other collections. The step ships first with today's behaviour pinned (a patch), then these changes (a minor). decided 2026-10-12; devicestatus reopened the same day, because Loop writes distinct statuses that share created_at and device; the null rule and its scope decided 2026-10-26, for 16.0.0 (write contract Q1b) T3 Server write times. srvModified and srvCreated are the server's, in milliseconds since the epoch, set on every write to a collection API v3 serves, by any path; a value a client sends is replaced. Within one process every srvModified is unique and never goes backwards, even when the clock does, and boot restores the clock from stored records before any writer starts. A hard delete leaves no srvModified, so history does not show it; a soft delete does. merged on dev (lib/server/srv-dates.js, lib/api3/generic/create/insert.js:27 at fade2299, read) T4 The change event. One event per write call: the collection, the operation, the stored documents (or the removed ids), the largest srvModified among its records, and the origin. Under TENANCY_MODE=multi the event is read from the replication slot (D6), so every field but runtime and origin is derived from the committed row; how the slot reader groups one call's rows into one event is not specified. specified (write contract §2.4)

The write step, per item, as T1 orders it:

flowchart LR
  accTitle: The one write step
  accDescr: A write from API v1, API v3, the socket or an in-process caller goes through one step. Per item it reads the _id form, finds the target by the collection's match order, decides the outcome, sets the server's write times, and stores the item; each item is answered with its outcome and both ids. After the call, one change event goes to the socket, and the history read finds the same records by their server time.
  src([API v1, API v3, socket,\nin-process caller]) --> id[_id form\nidentity I2]
  id --> target{target, by the\nmatch order\nidentity §3}
  target -- matched --> merge[merged, replaced\nor unchanged, T2]
  target -- none --> ins[inserted]
  target -- refused --> ref[refused]
  merge --> dates[server times\nsrvModified, srvCreated, T3]
  ins --> dates
  dates --> store[(storage write)]
  store --> reply[each item answered:\noutcome and both ids, I4]
  ref --> reply
  store --> event[one change event\nper call, T4]
  event --> sock[socket subscribers, T10, T11]
  store --> hist[history read by\nserver time, T5, T6]
  classDef stop fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b42318,color:#1a1a1a
  class ref stop

docs.title: 3. What each client's sync code can call
docs.text:
make schema-sync-cost, run 2026-10-18, counts the distinct endpoints each client's Nightscout code declares, read from its source. It is not a count of calls per cycle: some endpoints are called only on first load or on a user action, and AndroidAPS declares three that nothing outside its SDK calls (createSettings, patchSettings, getSettingsModifiedSince, read 2026-10-18). The units differ: AndroidAPS is counted by method and path, Loop and Trio by path alone, so their reads and writes to one path count once.

client (source read) API endpoints declared watermark delta read AndroidAPS 7e1d537d49 (dev; core/nssdk/.../NightscoutApi.kt) v3 26 yes per collection Loop: NightscoutKit 4ec9fd12a1 v1 7 (one an authentication check) no no Trio 0b29cd5341 v1 5 no no

What this shows is the shape, not a price: API v3 gives a client one delta read per collection, so the client that uses v3 as designed reads each collection separately, and every typed collection added to the model adds a read. T5 and T7 make one read and one write per cycle whatever the number of collections. Request counts and payload sizes on the wire are not measured.

docs.title: 4. The sync read and write (proposed)
docs.text: # rule T5 One read across collections. GET /api/v3/history/{cursor}?collections=&limit= answers {cursor, complete, collections: {name: [records]}} for every collection the credential may read (each checked as api:<collection>:read); a collection it may not read is left out. Per-collection history stays. T6 The merged cursor. A page returns records with srvModified above the cursor and at or below the low watermark (T9), up to a limit per collection, and never ends inside a group of records that share one srvModified. The cursor returned is the smallest last srvModified among the collections that were truncated, or the low watermark when none was; complete is true only when no collection was truncated. A client reads again from the returned cursor while complete is false. A record can come back twice across pages; the client keeps one (T10). T7 One write across collections. POST /api/v3/batch takes [{collection, doc}] and answers each item as T1 does; a batch is idempotent per record. T8 One opaque cursor. The sync cursor is opaque to clients. Under single it is a srvModified watermark; under multi it is the replication slot's position (D6), which is commit-ordered. An event cursor, if one is added, is the same cursor. T9 A low watermark. Over the collections the reader may read, the low watermark is one less than the smallest srvModified taken by a write not yet visible, or the largest value taken when none is in flight. A value is released when its write becomes visible or fails. No page returns a record above it and no cursor passes it, so a slow write is never skipped and a page cannot loop. The same rule applies to the per-collection history read. Under single the hub tracks the values it has taken and not yet stored; under multi the slot's position gives this. Computing it over readable collections only keeps a reader from learning when collections it cannot read were written. T10 The socket is the fast path; history is the record. A socket event delivers a record; it never moves the client's history cursor. The client reads history from the cursor its last history read returned: after a reconnect, and from time to time while connected, so a write that produced no event (T12), or one in a collection it did not subscribe to, still arrives. A record version received both ways is kept once, by identifier (or _id) and srvModified; an update is a new version.

docs.title: 5. Typed records on the socket (proposed)
docs.text: # rule T11 Subscribe by what the credential may read. A client subscribes by product and channel (registration §9); the hub delivers events for typed records the credential may read. Each event carries the typed record, both ids (identity I4), its definition id, its instance and the role's provenance, and the T10 cursor. Where an element's carrierView is served (registration §13), subscribers to the carrier's collection receive the projected document. T12 Which writes reach the socket is open. Today only API v3 writes reach the API v3 storage socket; writes through v1, the v1 socket and in-process callers do not (BF-164, reproduced on dev 43289dde and 15.0.8). Whether broadcasting them would help or harm AndroidAPS, which uses the socket by default and stops polling after its first load (read), is a question to its authors before a rule is set. T10 holds either way: a client that misses an event reads it from history. T16 The socket carries the fetch-now signal. A controller instance subscribes to its own signals on the existing listener with its own credential, naming its instanceId; a subscription naming an instance that is not the credential's own is refused, as a fetch is (commands CM18). The hub sends the signal (commands CM27) to that subscription only, as an event that carries nothing, and only inside a request bound to the command's tenant (CM19). It is not a record: it carries no record, ids or cursor, and the controller answers it with a fetch. T10's rule holds for it: the fetch, not the signal, is what delivers.

docs.title: 6. Definitions and versions (proposed)
docs.text: # rule T13 Stored records keep their definition. A typed record keeps the definitionId it was written under. The hub never converts a stored record to another version without a lossless mapping the definition declares (registration G4); a reader chooses the version it shows (registration §12). T14 A page carries the definitions it needs. A sync read includes, under definitions, each definition referenced by a returned record, so a client can read a record written under a definition it has not seen. T15 Moving records to a new version is the controller's. A controller that wants stored records under a new version sends them again under the new definition with the same identifier; the re-send matches the stored record (identity I7) and replaces its content and definitionId. The hub records the change like any other write.

docs.title: 7. Compatibility
docs.text:
older hub newer hub older client today's per-collection reads and writes unchanged: per-collection history, v1 and the v1 socket stay newer client no history envelope: it reads per collection, as AndroidAPS does today one read and one write per cycle (T5, T7), with the socket for latency (T10)

Nothing is retired. The capability document member that would say a hub serves T5 and T7 is open (§8).

docs.title: 8. Open
docs.text:
1. Choices for the maintainer: the T5 and T7 paths; whether a typed re-send under a new definition replaces or merges (T15); whether a page carries definitions inline (T14) or only their ids; a capability member for the sync envelope; how often a connected client reads history (T10). Letting socket events move the cursor would save those reads, but only once every write to a subscribed collection produces an event (T12), with each event naming the cursor before it so a client can tell it missed none.
  2. The in-flight window today. srv-dates.js takes a value just before the write, and the per-collection history read returns the largest srvModified it found as its ETag and Last-Modified (lib/api3/generic/history/operation.js:45-50 at fade2299, read). A slow write can therefore become visible after a reader has passed its value, for every API v3 client today. T9 closes this once the hub tracks the values it has taken. How often it happens is not measured.
  3. Several writers on one site. T3's uniqueness and T9's tracking hold within one process. A second process, or a writer that goes to the database directly, can produce equal or out-of-order values; T6 keeps equal values on one page, and multi (T8) orders by commit, but single with more than one writer is not covered.
  4. BF-164 (T12). A socket event's permission check (T11) has no case (UCA-SYNC-SERVE-006 in the control-loop analysis).
  5. The write step (WRITE-CONTRACT, WC-STEP-PATCH, ID-BATCH-RESULTS) is blocked behind the storage seam refresh.
  6. Not measured: payload size; real request counts; srvModified order under several writers on one site; the replication-slot path (T4.1 in the execution plan).
  7. The v1 socket's events under multi. On the seam branch the load cycle's dataUpdate and the /alarm events reach no tenant (commands §3); LoopFollow slows its polling while connected, and AndroidAPS 3.4.x listens for them (compatibility §5). Whether a hub under multi sends them inside a bound request, as CM19 does for fetch-now signals, is not specified.

docs.title: 9. Conformance cases
docs.text:
13 cases under specs/sync/conformance/sync-transport/, checked by tools/nsschema/test_sync_cursor.py, whose expectations are written by hand. Each is a timeline of writes, each taking its srvModified at one step and becoming visible at the same or a later one (or failing), and the client's history reads and socket events. The typed socket (§5) and versions (§6) are proposed without cases.

case shows expected control sync-transport/duplicate-delivery-is-one-record A record version received by event and by history is kept once rules T10 sync-transport/equal-values-at-page-boundary A page never ends inside a group of records with the same srvModified rules T6 sync-transport/failed-write-released A write that fails releases its value, and the cursor moves on rules T9 in-flight-write-not-skipped sync-transport/in-flight-write-not-skipped Nothing above a write still in flight is returned, so the cursor cannot pass it rules T9 no-write-in-flight sync-transport/merged-cursor-min-over-truncated A page truncated in one collection holds the cursor at that collection's last value rules T6 single-page-complete sync-transport/no-write-in-flight With nothing in flight the page reaches the latest value rules T9 sync-transport/nothing-new A read with nothing newer returns no records and keeps the cursor rules T6 sync-transport/single-page-complete With a large enough limit one page is complete rules T6 sync-transport/socket-resume-after-disconnect After a disconnect the client reads history from its last history cursor rules T10 sync-transport/truncated-above-watermark-no-stall Records above the low watermark wait for the next read, so a truncated page cannot loop rules T6, T9 in-flight-write-not-skipped sync-transport/unreadable-collection-omitted A collection the credential cannot read is left out and does not move its cursor rules T5, T9 sync-transport/update-is-a-new-version An update to a record already received is received again, as a new version rules T10 duplicate-delivery-is-one-record sync-transport/write-without-event-not-lost A write that produced no event is still read, because events never move the cursor rules T10, T12 socket-resume-after-disconnect

docs.title: Nightscout 16.x: questions for controller and uploader authors
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-25 at 38cbdb9a9.

What this is: an outreach draft for the authors of AndroidAPS, Loop, Trio, xDrip+ and xDrip4iOS. It is contributor-facing. Read it after the architecture review, whose next step 6 it carries out. Status: draft, not yet sent; for maintainer review (2026-10-25). Facts are as of cgm-remote-monitor dev 428b20b7. The client behaviour comes from the cited studies; most of it was read from source, not run. Each project's maintainers decide what, if anything, to do. The private AndroidAPS report and the public AndroidAPS issue from 2026-10-25 cover two of these topics in more depth for AndroidAPS.

Hello AndroidAPS, Loop, Trio, xDrip+ and xDrip4iOS maintainers,

Nightscout 16.0.0 is a major release focused on robustness. We'd like to agree a few contracts with you before we change any default. Nothing below changes how your app works today: each change starts off by default or log-only, and moves only on a dated, announced plan.

We found that most recent Nightscout defects come from a few shared causes:

  • Nightscout accepts the same data through four doors (API v1, API v3, the websocket and in-process callers), and each door applies its own rules.
  • Readers trust whatever got stored.
  • Each app validates in its own way.
  • When Nightscout refuses something, most apps can't tell.

The architecture review has the evidence.

There are two parts to our plan:

  • Near term (16.x), for apps as they are today. One shared write path inside Nightscout, with one set of checks, one reply shape and one change event per write.
  • Longer term, opt-in per app release: controller registration.
  • Your app publishes typed definitions of its records: field types, units and ranges.
  • Nightscout validates your typed writes against your declaration, and never imposes another app's rules.
  • Typed writes come with a defined refusal protocol: a refusal is visible to the app, and the record is never silently dropped.
  • Registration is specified, not built yet.

The questions below shape both parts. Short answers are fine, and so is "we need to look".

docs.title: 1. Write replies and retries
docs.text:
We plan one reply shape for every write:

  • Each item comes back with its stored _id, its identifier, and which of the two matched.
  • A re-send that matches a stored record is answered with that record's ids, and no second copy is stored.
  • Status codes stay as clients already handle them, and a client error is never answered with a 5xx.

We read your upload code to see how each app reacts when Nightscout refuses part of a batch. Most rows are read from source, not run; see the study.

App What it needs from a batch reply If one item is refused inside a 200 If the whole batch gets a 4xx Loop (NightscoutKit) exactly 200, with one object per item sent the item is recorded as uploaded, with id "NA" the batch is resent on every trigger Trio any 2xx; the body isn't read the item is treated as uploaded the pipeline retries for up to 24 h xDrip+ any 2xx entries are treated as uploaded entries stay queued for up to 7 days xDrip4iOS any 2xx; treatments are matched by content the item stays pending and is resent for readings, the cursor waits for up to 7 days AndroidAPS (API v3, one record per request) 201 or 200 n/a on a 400, the record is dropped and the cursor moves on; on any other 4xx, that kind's queue waits

Our draft batch reply is opt-in, behind WRITE_VALIDATION=reject:

  • The reply is 200, with one object per item, in order.
  • A refused item has no _id, and has a refused: {status, message, rules} member.
  • If every item is refused, the reply is 400.

Questions:

  • Is that shape safe for your app? Would you read refused, so that a refusal can reach the person instead of being lost?
  • Does your app depend on an exact status (Loop: exactly 200), or on the reply's length?
  • AndroidAPS: is the difference between 400 (drop) and other 4xx (hold) intentional? Which should Nightscout use for "this record can never be accepted"?

docs.title: 2. Who validates what
docs.text:
We propose that Nightscout checks the structure of what it stores, and leaves policy to you.

Today API v3 checks only identifier, date, utcOffset and app. Most protection therefore lives in your apps, and each app does it differently:

  • AndroidAPS drops records at about 24 points.
  • Trio clamps temp targets to 80–200 mg/dL.
  • Loop reads only two units spellings.
Kind of check Example Who would enforce it Structural: true for every app targets are finite numbers, bottom ≤ top, units come from a known set, duration ≥ 0, a timed record has a time Nightscout, on every write path, opt-in first (off → log → reject) Policy: your app's own limits AndroidAPS's 72–180 mg/dL temp targets, Trio's 80–200 clamp, the maximum bolus your app. With registration you can declare these; Nightscout shows them, but never enforces them on another app's records Time sanity a reading dated ahead of the server clock Nightscout flags it, and never refuses it

With registration, your app declares each field's type, unit and range in its own typed definition, and Nightscout validates your typed writes against that declaration. Records from apps that haven't registered keep today's shapes, and get only the structural checks above. See the write-validation design.

Questions:

  • Which of your ingestion checks would you want Nightscout to enforce at write time, for every path?
  • For your users, is a record that Nightscout refuses or flags better than one your app drops quietly?
  • Would you publish your ranges and units in a registration, if Nightscout served them to other apps and to followers?

docs.title: 3. Records already stored
docs.text:
Sites hold years of records written by many app versions, so stricter checks can't assume clean data. We propose:

  • normalise on write from now on;
  • tolerate older shapes on read;
  • flag a record that doesn't meet the contract, rather than hide it.

A stored record must never stop Nightscout itself.

Two effects matter to you:

  • Apps that re-send what they read. oref0, tconnectsync, nightscout-connect's Nightscout source, the profile editor and AndroidAPS 3.4.2.6 copy stored content back to Nightscout. Refusing a value that a working site may already hold would make those uploads fail repeatedly. For such values, Nightscout therefore logs and flags first, and refuses only in a later major, after operators have been told.
  • Shapes your app can't read. Some stored records fail to decode in some apps. Two examples: a timestamp that some uploaders send as text, and fractional durations. A flag on read could let your app skip one record instead of a whole page.

Questions:

  • If API v3 marked a nonconforming record with a flag on read, what would your app do with it: skip it, show it, or warn?
  • Does your app re-send records it downloaded? If so, which fields does it copy without retyping?

docs.title: 4. Delivery and cursors
docs.text:
We'd like to write down what an app may assume when it syncs from Nightscout. Today nothing states it, and the gaps cost records.

The API v3 /storage socket announces only writes made through API v3. In our lab, an app that sets its history cursor from each pushed event can permanently miss careportal, API v1 and connector records. See the lab; its client behaviour is modelled from AndroidAPS source.

The proposed contract, from the sync-transport spec:

  1. History is the record. srvModified is set by Nightscout, never by the client, and only moves forward.
  2. A socket event is a hint to read history. It never moves the client's cursor past records it hasn't fetched yet.
  3. Writes from other paths are announced on /storage only once Nightscout checks every write path, and only records that pass those checks are announced. Until then, /storage stays as it is today.

Questions:

  • Does this contract match how your app syncs, or would it need a change?
  • Which apps besides AndroidAPS subscribe to /storage?
  • Would it help if each event carried the cursor position before it, so that an app can detect a gap?

docs.title: 5. Units and identity
docs.text:
Units. Apps spell and convert units differently, so one app can misread a record another app wrote. With registration, units are declared per field and never assumed. Until then, records in today's shapes need a common convention.

App mmol/L spelling it reads Conversion it uses AndroidAPS exactly mmol; anything else is read as mg/dL 18 Loop (NightscoutKit) exactly mmol/L, alongside mg/dL to confirm Trio reads no units on a temp target to confirm Nightscout several three constants in use: 18, 18.016 and 18.01559

Identity. Nightscout follows a two-id rule:

  • identifier is the record id your app assigns. It is stable across retries and devices, compared exactly, and not required to be a UUID.
  • _id is the storage key Nightscout assigns.
  • Every write reply will return both.
  • Planned for 16.0.0 (PR #8845): API v3 refuses a client-supplied _id with a 400 that asks for identifier instead. We found no app that sends one.
  • Next, Nightscout plans to match re-sends on identifier first, so an app needs no cache of server ids.

Questions:

  • Which units spellings should Nightscout accept and store, and which constant should it use?
  • Loop: does the simple contract we discussed still hold with identifier-first matching?
  • xDrip+ and xDrip4iOS: today, entries uploaded with your own _id have it moved to identifier. Would identifier-first matching change how you de-duplicate?

docs.title: Questions by project, and where to reply
docs.text:
Not every question applies to every app. The table shows where your answer matters most.

Topic AndroidAPS Loop Trio xDrip+ / xDrip4iOS 1. Reply shape and retries yes yes, especially yes yes 2. Validation and declaring ranges yes yes yes — 3. Flags on stored records; re-sending yes yes yes — 4. Delivery and cursors yes, first — — if you use /storage 5. Units spelling and constant yes yes yes — 5. Identity and matching yes yes, especially yes yes Registration: would you adopt it, and what would you need first? yes yes yes yes

Reply wherever suits you: here, in your own tracker, or in a call. We'll collect the answers in one public place, and link it back to each of you before anything changes by default.

Thank you, The Nightscout maintainers

docs.title: Upstream ask (draft): AndroidAPS NSClientV3, bound or handle a 410 reply
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-30 at c20ee8bb3.

Contributor-facing outreach draft, 2026-10-30, prepared by session -4f from the AndroidAPS code (read, not run). Not sent. Companion to the questions for controller and uploader authors.

To: AndroidAPS maintainers (nightscout/AndroidAPS), NSClientV3 plugin From: Nightscout cgm-remote-monitor maintainers Status: draft for the upstream-asks list, not filed Pins: AndroidAPS 7e1d537d49, unchanged on origin/dev 325e562380; cgm-remote-monitor dev ca1652d6

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: When Nightscout's API v3 answers an NSClientV3 upload with 410 Gone, NSClientV3 stops uploading that collection and retries the same record without limit. API v3 answers 410 when a client updates a record that is soft-deleted on the server. We ask that NSClientV3 bound or handle 410, the way it already bounds 404.

docs.title: What happens today
docs.text:
• What 410 means: API v3 answers PATCH/PUT /api/v3/{collection}/{identifier} with 410 when the stored record is soft-deleted (isValid: false). This is documented API v3 behaviour, and Nightscout 16.0.0 keeps it.
  • How NSClientV3 handles each status: dbOperation* in plugins/sync/src/commonMain/kotlin/app/aaps/plugins/sync/nsclientV3/NSClientV3Plugin.kt (e.g. treatments, :1012-1030) branches on the status:
  • 200, 201 and 400 advance the cursor. 400 is logged as FAIL and dropped.
  • 404 retries an UPDATE up to maxUpdateRetries, then gives up (retryUpdateLater, :720-730).
  • Any other status, 410 included, takes else -> return config.isEnabled(IGNORE_NS_V3_ERRORS). With that option off (the default), the call returns false, the collection's sync cursor does not advance, and the next round sends the same update again. Nothing bounds it.
  • Where else: the same else branch appears in the profile store, device status, entries, calibrations and food paths (:761-763, :786-788 and the matching blocks below them).

docs.title: How a record reaches that state
docs.text:
1. A record deleted on the server while AndroidAPS still holds it as valid. A caregiver or the user deletes a treatment in Nightscout's web UI, or another uploader deletes it. The AndroidAPS row is still valid locally. The next local change to it (a temp target ended, a temp basal or extended bolus closed, a profile switch updated) is sent as a PATCH and answered 410. This can happen with today's released servers.
  2. A re-entry that matches a deleted record. This is the case we weighed for 16.0.0.
  3. AndroidAPS treatments carry no device, so the identifier API v3 computes is undefined_<date>_<eventType>.
  4. A carb entry deleted and re-entered at the same minute through the time picker (seconds set to zero, EventTimePickers.kt) gets the identifier of the deleted record.
  5. If the server keeps that record deleted, any later update to the new row is answered 410.
  6. For this reason, Nightscout 16.0.0 keeps reviving a deleted treatment on such a re-create. Bounding 410 in NSClientV3 would let a future version stop reviving it.

docs.title: Effect on the user
docs.text: Uploads for that collection stop until the user notices and acts. For treatments, that means boluses, carbs, temp basals and temp targets stop reaching Nightscout. Followers, caregivers and reports then see stale data. The phone keeps looping, so this does not affect dosing on the phone. It does affect everyone who relies on Nightscout to see what happened.

docs.title: What we ask
docs.text:
Any of the following, in order of preference:

  1. Treat 410 on an UPDATE as final for that record. Log it, mark the local row as synced or as deleted on the server (as the download path already does for isValid: false), and advance the cursor.
  2. Bound it like 404: route 410 through retryUpdateLater, so the cursor advances after maxUpdateRetries.
  3. At minimum, show the user a notification naming the stuck record, so the stall is visible.

Optionally: on 410, read the record (GET /api/v3/{collection}/{identifier}) and copy isValid: false into the local row, matching SyncNs*Transaction.

docs.title: What Nightscout does in 16.0.0
docs.text:
• API v3 PATCH/PUT of a soft-deleted record keeps answering 410.
  • A v3 create that matches a deleted treatment keeps reviving it, as it does today (decided 2026-10-30, because of this stall).
  • For entries, profile, food and settings, a re-create that matches a deleted record is acknowledged (200 with the stored identifier), and the record stays deleted. AndroidAPS handles that reply as it handles today's (stores nightscoutId, marks the row synced). It never updates these records after creating them, except glucose values; see "For AndroidAPS to verify".
  • We would like to treat treatments the same way once NSClientV3 bounds or handles 410.

docs.title: For AndroidAPS to verify
docs.text:
• Whether a glucose value can be PATCHed while it is valid. Our reading says no, which is why entries can stay deleted in 16.0.0:
  • an invalidated glucose value is sent as a v3 DELETE, which answers 404 for an already-deleted record, and NSClientV3 counts that as success (NSAndroidClientImpl.kt:228-231);
  • UpdateGlucoseValueTransaction has no non-test caller;
  • a change that only adds an NS id is not uploaded (DataSyncSelectorV3.kt:471). Please confirm no other path updates a valid glucose value.
  • That getByNSId returns the older, already-invalid row first when two local rows share a nightscoutId.
  • Whether a bolus and a carb entry can be stored with the same timestamp. They would then share a computed identifier, independent of deletes.

docs.title: Compatibility notes (draft): re-sent treatments and profiles in Nightscout 16.0.0, every path
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-31 at f8369156f.

Contributor-facing outreach draft, 2026-10-31, from the maintainer's decisions of that day (decisions, "Slice 6, socket treatments" and "Slice 6, socket profiles"). Not sent. Companion to the questions for controller and uploader authors and the tconnectsync note. Behaviour described here is decided and being built in the identity work (cgm-remote-monitor draft PR #8879, slice 6); it is not on dev yet.

To: maintainers of apps that upload treatments or profiles to Nightscout, over API v1, API v3 or the websocket (AndroidAPS, including 3.4.2.x's older Nightscout client; Loop; Trio; xDrip+; xDrip4iOS; tconnectsync; nightscout-connect)

docs.title: What changes in 16.0.0
docs.text:
Nightscout 16.0.0 matches a re-sent record to the stored one by its identifier first, on every write path (API v1, API v3, the websocket and in-process). The rules below are the same whichever path your app uses.

  1. Treatments: a re-send replaces the stored treatment. When a treatment you send carries the identifier of one already stored, the stored record is replaced by what you sent, not merged with it. A field you leave out is gone from the stored record. This is how API v1 already behaved; 16.0.0 makes the websocket and API v3 the same. Reason: apps re-send whole records and show a cleared field by leaving it out (for example, an ended override). Under a merge, the old field stayed, and caregivers' charts showed an ended override as still running.
  2. What to check: if your app sends a partial treatment as an update, send the whole record instead.

  3. A consequence: a field someone added to your app's treatment in the Nightscout careportal is lost when your app re-sends that treatment, as it already is over API v1.

  4. Profiles: a create with a different startDate is a new profile. When a profile you create carries the identifier of a stored profile but a different startDate, Nightscout stores it as a new profile without that identifier, and logs a warning (with no values). With the same startDate, it is a re-send, and the stored profile is updated (its store replaced whole). This keeps profile history as it is today.

  5. What to check: when you add a profile by copying the current one, delete identifier as well as _id, so the new profile is new by design and no warning is logged.

  6. Known to copy the identifier today (read from source): tconnectsync (tconnectsync/sync/update_profiles.py:208-215) and oref0 (bin/oref0-upload-profile.js:110-111 and :246-271). Both keep working; each added profile is stored as a new profile, with a warning on the server.

  7. Every other collection merges on match (device status, entries, food, activity), as decided on 2026-10-29. A null in a merge removes that field.

docs.title: What we ask
docs.text:
• Tell us if your app relies on a socket treatment re-send being merged into the stored record.
  • Tell us if your app sends a profile create that is meant to update an existing profile while changing its startDate.

Short answers are fine, and so is "we need to look".

docs.title: What happens
docs.text: In its default add mode, tconnectsync adds a profile by deep-copying the site's current profile (GET /api/v1/profile/current), deleting _id, setting a new startDate, created_at and enteredBy, and POSTing the copy to /api/v1/profile. When the current profile was created over API v3, it carries the server-computed identifier, and the copy keeps it. Measured: each add then stores another record holding the same identifier (2 records, then 3); the source record is unchanged.

docs.title: What Nightscout 16.0.0 does
docs.text: Nightscout 16.0.0 matches re-sent records on identifier, and adds a unique index on it. So that profile history is kept, a profile create that matches a stored profile by identifier but carries a different startDate is stored as a new profile without the copied identifier, with a server-side warning (maintainer decision, 2026-10-30, for API v1 and in-process; extended to the websocket 2026-10-31; see the compatibility notes). tconnectsync keeps working unchanged.

docs.title: What we ask
docs.text: When copying a profile to add a new one, delete identifier as well as _id, so each added profile is a new record by design and no warning is logged.

docs.title: What this is
docs.text: The Loop developers shared a proposal on 2026-10-17: Client-supplied identifiers for Nightscout, based on 15.0.8. It is a private page shared with the maintainer and is not linked from here. Our draft reply is reply.body.md, ready to paste as GitHub or Zulip markdown. It links the published pages on the project site.

docs.title: The simple contract
docs.text:
What the reply proposes, and what Nightscout supports today except where the reply's table says otherwise:

  1. _id is a MongoDB ObjectId (24 hex) or absent. A client may create its own ObjectId and send it over API v1; API v3 refuses a client _id with 400 from 16.0.0 (BF-170, identity I2). Other values are not valid; UUID_HANDLING (default on) moves any non-24-hex string _id to identifier on treatments and entries, as a compatibility rule.
  2. If _id is absent, the client sends identifier, an opaque string compared exactly, not necessarily a UUID: the record's semantic identity (this reading, this pump event, this carb entry), so two uploads of one real thing carry one value. URL syntax, from the identifier conventions table: a source scheme for readings and pump events (manufacturer as scheme, model first: dexcom://g7/<serial>/<offset>), an app scheme for records made in the app (loop://carbs/<uuid>) (maintainer, 2026-10-18). 1-256 characters from A-Za-z0-9._~:/-, percent-encoded as one segment in API v3 paths (a raw / is 404; measured 2026-10-18, identifier format §3.4), not exactly 24 hex, no placeholders (invalid, undefined, null, NaN); a UUID is needed only for today's v1 by-_id routes (queue ID-FORMAT-DECISION, ID-CONVENTIONS). The server assigns _id. One identifier names one record.
  3. If neither is sent, the collection's time key applies (entries sysTime + type, treatments created_at + eventType). identifier becomes mandatory at a future version boundary and for registered controller instances; until then legacy paths keep this fallback (maintainer, 2026-10-18; queue ID-ABSENT-DECISION).

Tie-break (maintainer, 2026-10-18; queue ID-CLIENT-OID-DECISION): when a write carries both and they point at different records, identifier decides, as in D20 rule 5 and v1 treatments today (identifier present drops _id, server/treatments.js:356-362 @15.0.8). An earlier draft proposed _id-first; it was reversed to keep today's behaviour. Every write reply returns both ids (rule 5).

The one server change it needs, v1 entries and device status matching on identifier, is queue item ID-SIMPLE-MATCH; it ships with BF-169 after 15.0.9 (maintainer, 2026-10-17; see 15.0.9 decisions).

docs.title: The proposal, summarised
docs.text:
The ask. An uploader gives each record a stable identifier taken from the data's source. The server puts a unique index on it and upserts on it, in every collection and both API versions. Records without one keep today's rules.

  • identifier is an opaque client string with a published length limit; a sparse unique index in entries, treatments and device status.
  • If present, upsert on it and keep the stored _id. If absent, today's rules. Additive.
  • v1 GET, PUT and DELETE by identifier. API v3 treats a client's value as authoritative and computes one only when none is sent.
  • Clients derive it from the source: sensor serial + sensor time (for example g7:<serial>:<seconds since activation>, so a phone and a watch agree), the pump's event id, or a UUID made once for a manual entry.
  • Loop would send its syncIdentifier as identifier on all three collections.
  • Questions: (Q1) a new identifier at an existing sysTime + type: keep both or merge, perhaps merge only when the stored row has none; (Q2) per-record batch results; (Q3) is insert-only device status intentional, and should an identifier make re-sends idempotent.

docs.title: How the reply argues
docs.text:
Rewritten 2026-10-17 around the simple contract, at the maintainer's direction that the simple model is generally workable; the previous, longer version is in git history at dd6febcc.

  1. Agrees with the ask; most of it works; the confusion is largely the swagger sentence (BF-169).
  2. The three rules and the tie-break, with D20 rule 5's "every write reply returns both" quoted.
  3. A table of what works today and the one gap (v1 entries and device status store identifier but do not match on it).
  4. The watch-and-phone case: four options; recommends a source-derived identifier, with an agreed timestamp as an interim that needs no server change. FHIR and HealthKit precedents.
  5. Cautions for Loop starting today; what we will do (the one server change and BF-169, after 15.0.9); the deferred questions as a short list.

docs.title: Reply.body
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-29 at f3a1d540d.

Re: client-supplied identifiers for Nightscout

Thank you for writing this up. We agree with the core of the ask, and most of what Loop needs already works. The one gap we found, v1 entries and device status ignoring identifier on a re-send, is closed for 16.0.0. Much of the earlier confusion came from our API documentation, not the design: API v3's swagger said "The client should not create the identifier", but the server keeps one a client sends. That sentence is removed for 16.0.0 (BF-169).

Code references are to cgm-remote-monitor 15.0.9 (c6a0d8ed, released 2026-10-21) and dev at 7abe1cf6, which becomes 16.0.0 (in development, not released). Behaviour marked measured is from our record identity lab of 2026-10-27, which runs both versions side by side.

docs.title: The contract, in three rules
docs.text:
1. _id is a MongoDB ObjectId (24 hex characters) or absent. A client that keeps a local cache may create its own ObjectId and send it over API v1. (Over API v3, send identifier instead: from 16.0.0 API v3 refuses a body _id with HTTP 400, and 15.0.9 and earlier store it as sent, so a 24-hex value becomes a string there; measured.) ObjectIds are designed to be made by clients without coordination (a timestamp, a random part and a counter). Other values in _id are not valid. For compatibility, UUID_HANDLING (on by default) moves any string _id that is not 24 hex characters to identifier on treatments and entries, and the server assigns the ObjectId.
  2. If _id is absent, send identifier: an opaque string, compared exactly as sent. It does not have to be a UUID. The server assigns _id. One identifier names one record in each collection.
  3. If neither is sent, the server falls back to the collection's time key: entries sysTime + type, treatments created_at + eventType. This fallback stays. Sending identifier is recommended for every app. It will be required for controllers that register with Nightscout, a registration interface we are building, which apps opt into.

Tie-break: if a write carries both and they point at different records, identifier decides. That is what v1 treatments do today (they drop _id when identifier is present), what rule 5 of our design decision D20 says, and what your proposal implies, since identifier is the key clients own. Rule 5 also says what every write reply should carry:

Two ids, one rule. … Every write reply returns both. (D20 rule 5)

Returning both means a client never needs a cache of server ids to edit or delete what it sent.

What an identifier is. It names the real thing a record describes: this CGM reading, this pump event, this carb entry. Two uploads of the same thing should carry the same value, whichever app sends it. The server treats it as opaque and keeps one record per identifier in each collection; clients compute the values from a published conventions table, one row per record kind. Values are written in URL syntax. Readings and pump events take the manufacturer as the scheme and the model as the first segment, so every app that reads one sensor produces the same value: for a G7 reading, dexcom://g7/<serial>/<sensor offset>. Records made in the app take the app's scheme, with the kind as the first segment: loop://carbs/<uuid>, loop://tempbasal/<syncIdentifier>, loop://override/<uuid>. The kind segment also keeps values unique across collections, which the server does not check. Would that work for Loop?

What an identifier may contain (proposed). 1 to 256 characters from A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ ~ : / -, and under MongoDB's index key limit. In API v3 paths (/api/v3/{collection}/{identifier}), send it percent-encoded as one path segment (/ as %2F, : as %3A): that works for GET, PATCH, PUT and DELETE, while a raw / is 404 (measured 2026-10-18 on 15.0.8 and the 15.0.9 candidate, identifier format §3.4). No %, ?, # or space. Not exactly 24 hex characters, which both APIs read as an _id. Never a placeholder such as invalid, undefined, null or NaN: once identifiers are matched, every reading sharing one would overwrite the last. A UUID (v4 for a record made on one device, or v5 of a source-derived key) is needed only for today's v1 by-_id routes (find[_id]=, DELETE /api/v1/treatments/:id), which recognise UUID-shaped values only. API v3 and find[identifier]= take any string (identifier format).

docs.title: What works, by version
docs.text:
path 15.0.9 16.0.0 (dev) v1 treatments, identifier matched first, the reply carries the stored _id (since 15.0.7, #8421) the same; a treatment matched by time (no ids) is now also answered with its _id (BF-165), measured API v3, every collection, identifier a client value is kept and re-sends match on it the same v1 entries, identifier stored, not matched: a re-send at another time is a second record, measured matched: one record, updated (#8859), measured v1 device status, identifier stored, not matched: two records, measured matched: a re-send writes nothing and is answered with the stored _id (#8859), measured client ObjectId _id, v1 treatments, entries and device status: a re-send is matched, measured the same; a re-sent profile _id is answered 200 instead of 500, measured

A merge on a match follows RFC 7386 from 16.0.0: a field sent as null is removed from the stored record, and a field left out is kept. A PUT replaces the record.

docs.title: Your watch-and-phone case
docs.text:
Neither id alone solves two devices uploading one reading: both must arrive at the same key.

option server change 1. one uploader at a time (today's workaround) none 2. both devices agree on the timestamp: the phone adopts the watch's activation estimate for the loaned period none: v1 entries already merge on sysTime + type. The match is exact, so the times must be identical to the millisecond. device need not match: it is not part of the v1 key (over API v3 it would, because the server computes identifier from device + date). The later upload's fields overwrite the stored ones, so device becomes the phone's 3. a source-derived identifier, dexcom://g7/<serial>/<seconds> none from 16.0.0: v1 entries match on identifier. The inputs must come from the sensor: the real serial and the sensor's own seconds counter 4. server-side fuzzy time matching avoid: it can merge readings from two real sensors

We recommend (3), with (2) as an interim that works on any version. Today's G7 syncIdentifier would not serve (3) as it stands. It embeds each device's own activation estimate, as fractional hours, and the BLE name DXCMxx rather than the serial, and it falls back to "invalid" (G7SensorKit dd91f46, G7CGMManager.swift:511-517). Hashing it into a UUIDv5 would not help, because the input already differs between devices.

For a G7, an identifier both devices can compute is dexcom://g7/<serial>/<seconds>. <serial> is the sensor serial from the transmitter-version (0x4A) reply, which G7SensorKit next-dev reads. <seconds> is the sensor's seconds-since-activation counter for the reading: messageTimestamp − age for a live reading, the record's timestamp for backfill. Every G7 implementation we read (G7SensorKit, xDrip+, xDrip4iOS, Juggluco, DiaBLE) treats that counter as the sensor's own session clock, and backfill uses the same clock. We have not yet seen a capture with two displays on one sensor, so we would confirm with one before relying on it (identifier format §7). G6 (<transmitterID> <timestamp>, as dexcom://g6/<transmitterID>/<timestamp>) and Libre 3 (<serial>-<lifeCount>, as abbott://libre3/<serial>/<lifeCount>) already key on a sensor-side counter; Loop's Libre 2 key uses the phone's clock.

Precedents: FHIR keeps the server id apart from the business identifier, and its conditional create answers 200 with the existing record when the identifier already matches (Aidbox). HealthKit pairs a sync identifier with a sync version, so a newer version of a sample replaces the stored one (Apple's pages word the comparison slightly differently).

docs.title: Cautions for Loop starting today
docs.text:
• Each identifier must name exactly one record. In our corpus, 13 of 255,811 Loop syncIdentifier values are on 2 to 4 treatments, for example a Suspend Pump and a Temp Basal pair (identifier duplicates §2.2). Sent as identifier to 15.0.7 or later, the second would replace the first. A kind segment (loop://suspend/…, loop://tempbasal/…) keeps such a pair apart.
  • On 15.0.9 and earlier, entries and device status do not match on identifier. A re-send with the same identifier is stored twice there; from 16.0.0 it is matched (lab).
  • Older servers store the field and ignore it.
  • A carb edit can be lost. Loop 3.14.9 sends a carb edit as a v1 PUT by the record's _id, which it caches for 24 hours. If the _id is no longer cached, the edit is not sent at all, and nothing tells the user. The server can take the edit by identifier instead: API v3 PATCH or PUT /api/v3/treatments/{identifier} today, and a v1 re-send with the same identifier (merged on match). Would Loop send edits that way?

docs.title: Six cases: what should Nightscout do?
docs.text:
To make the contract unambiguous, we would like your answer for each case. "Our default" is what our decisions so far give, chosen to keep today's clients working.

# case 15.0.9 / 16.0.0 today (measured) our default your answer 1 The watch uploads a G7 reading. Later the phone uploads the same reading: same identifier, other device, time 1.5 s later v1 entries: two records on 15.0.9, one (updated) on 16.0.0. API v3: 400 on both one record, updated with the later upload's fields (merge on match) 2 Loop re-sends a record that changed after its first upload, same identity: a dose whose final amount differs, or an override ended early (Loop 3.14.9 does both by POST; a carb edit is a PUT, below) v1 treatments: updated. API v3: 400 if the date, device or event type changed updated (merge), kept as the default; an explicit PUT replaces. A switch, a site setting or a per-client rule, may later select keep-first or refuse for clients that opt in 3 Loop re-sends an identical record after a timeout 16.0.0: matched, and the reply carries the stored _id, on v1 entries, treatments and device status and on API v3. 15.0.9: device status stored again, and a treatment matched by time is answered without _id success, and the reply carries the stored _id and identifier 4 A record is deleted, then the same identifier arrives again v1 (hard delete): stored again as a new record. API v3 (soft delete): a POST brings it back, a PUT is 410; on 16.0.0 an API v3 device status stays deleted the re-send is acknowledged (a success reply naming the stored record, so the app stops retrying) and the record stays deleted (decided 2026-10-27; not built yet) 5 An app sends no identifier each collection's time key the time key stays; identifier is recommended for every app and required for registered controller instances 6 One write carries an _id and an identifier that name different stored records v1 treatments: identifier wins, _id is dropped identifier wins, as today (the tie-break above)

For case 1, if you would rather Nightscout keep the first upload unchanged, or refuse the second, please say so and what the phone should do next. An error reply makes NightscoutKit treat the batch as failed. For case 4, would Loop treat a success reply for a deleted record as final?

docs.title: What we have done, and what is next
docs.text:
Done for 16.0.0, on dev now: v1 entries and device status match on identifier (#8859), the swagger correction (BF-169) and API v3's refusal of a body _id (#8845). Next: case 4's re-send after delete, results per record in a batch, and a unique index on identifier per collection, each after your answers. Later, and only if needed: identifier length and character checks (a warning first).

Details and evidence are in our notes on your proposal.

Where would you like to continue?
