An eventual probe would implement entries/treatments under the same conformance corpus, first local SQLite and then a trusted cell boundary. Preserve existing lab work; do not migrate the app runtime or select celld operational guarantees through this hypothetical. No SQLite implementation or performance acceptance is claimed.

docs.title: Claimed public names, the alias registry and the deploy companion: scope split and line of sight
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-11-09. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

Contributor-facing decision-preparation note, 2026-11-09, read-derived. Anchors: alignment main 9029fb6dd; cgm-remote-monitor draft #8898 candidate ed2ced00; nightscout-roles-gateway 90840ace; nightscout-gateway-www 67cbe466. No service was run for this note. It proposes a scope split between cgm-remote-monitor, a sibling deployment repository and hoster-private adapters, and an ordered path to a running staging rehearsal. The sibling repository exists as a local scaffold at ~/src/nightscout-deploy (also reachable as externals/work/nightscout-deploy in this workspace); it has no remote yet, so the GitHub links in its README resolve only after the maintainer publishes it. Nothing here is adopted until it is a row in release decisions; the public-name contract and the production critical path keep their canonical roles.

docs.title: 1. The model to carry forward: a claimed public name
docs.text:
The roles gateway already separates the three things the public-name contract asks for, in a schema that ran unmodified against current Kratos in the Ory proof §5. Read at 90840ace:

roles-gateway concept (table / column) what it is tenancy vocabulary it maps to registered_sites.expected_name (unique) the host label a person claims and may publish permanent public alias, owner-chosen registered_sites.upstream_origin where the edge sends an admitted request private internal name (a resolution label in the shared cohort, not a URL) registered_sites.owner_ref the identity-provider subject who owns the claim tenant owner, current OIDC subject reserved_expected_names, reserved_upstream_origin names nobody may claim, with a reason and source project floor plus operator list nightscout_authenticity_records proof that the claimant controls the upstream, checked out of band implied by provisioning in multitenant; needed only when fronting an independent site registered_sites.is_enabled, require_identities, exempt_matching_api_secret per-site policy switches alias policy binding: anonymous allowed, human login required, native device credential path (D17) group_definitions, group_inclusion_specs, connection_policies, scheduled_policies, joined_groups who is in a group, what a group may do, when the group/schedule policy the public-name contract defers to a bounded decision warden route GET/HEAD /warden/v1/active/backend/for/:expected_name one auth_request decision returning x-upstream-origin and an exchanged token the edge decision point; in the cohort the decision moves inside the admitted application

What the model adds beyond the gateway: a stable tenant ID that none of these tables has (expected_name is the primary handle throughout), and an explicit alias kind with a lifetime. Two kinds are enough for the first production scope:

  • claimed: permanent, owner-chosen, checked against the reserved list, safe to publish; knowing it confers nothing, current policy decides.
  • ephemeral: issued by the operator or by an operator's adapter, rotatable or expiring, bound to the same tenant; expiry changes reachability, never ownership, and the name carries no capability (the public-name contract already says so).

The public contract covers kinds, lifetimes, policy binding, versioned reassignment and cache invalidation. How an operator mints, distributes or brands ephemeral names is an adapter behind that contract, which is what keeps a hoster's own issuance scheme out of the public repositories without leaving a hole in the model.

Default names, built in (direction given in discussion, 2026-11-09). Every tenant gets a generated label at provisioning: DNS-safe, lowercase, fixed length, drawn from a CSPRNG, starting with two letters so it is never confused with a number or an identifier, and checked against the reserved list. The label is the tenant's internal resolution name and, under the deployment's base domain, its default permanent primary alias. That is the whole built-in: a deployment with no issuer and no owner claims still has one working, unguessable name per tenant. The precedent is the per-site runner's own internal naming, which the maintainer found desirable in operation.

Everything beyond the default is policy a hoster supplies behind core's contract: an alias issuer for ephemeral or additional stable names, and an alias policy that decides whether an owner may claim or choose a name (pattern, length, reserved list, cooling-off on release). An owner claim goes through the owner API under that policy; on rename the previous label stays as a stable secondary alias until the owner releases it, so configured uploaders keep working; no timer is involved.

What does not carry forward, from what the port measured and what the tables hold:

  • registered_sites.api_secret and nightscout_secrets.api_secret hold a site's root credential in clear, because the gateway verifies authenticity and brokers tokens with it. In the cohort the tenant's root lives in the secrets component, and owner authority treats legacy hashes as bearer credentials. The registry stores no credential.
  • upstream_origin as a URL. A shared cohort has no per-tenant origin; resolution ends at a stable tenant ID inside the admitted application (D10, D13, D14).
  • The runtime: restify on Node 24 fails at require, the lockfile needs --legacy-peer-deps, the per-site Hydra client path needs reconfiguration (Ory proof §5). The schema vocabulary, the decision chain's cases including its own cross-site denial, and the WWW journeys (what I own, why I have access, what I consent to, how I leave) are the inheritance. The code is reference, not a dependency.

docs.title: 2. Scope split: core, sibling repository, hoster-private
docs.text:
The rule: core owns anything that defines authority or identity; the sibling owns anything that varies by hoster or vendor; a hoster owns only adapters behind published interfaces.

concern cgm-remote-monitor sibling deploy repository (working name nightscout-deploy) hoster-private Private names: stable tenant ID and internal resolution name owns: migration under the project's runner, operator API on the private plane consumes snapshots — Public aliases: host, kind, lifetime, policy binding, reserved names owns the record and the decision: the same migration, the operator API, and a read-only resolution endpoint on the private plane returning tenant ID, policy and a snapshot version the auth_request facade that calls that endpoint and caches it, for edges that resolve before proxying; a reference issuer for ephemeral aliases a replacement facade or issuer behind the same endpoint Resolver owns lib/tenant-resolution; adds a snapshot-source interface (the README already says "construct a new resolver to replace the mapping") registry-backed snapshot source, cache, invalidation signal — Edge owns the trust predicate contract (peer list) and the fast unknown-host refusal in the app reference nginx, auth_request adapter for edges that need one, trust-record template, spoof/conflict/outage probes TLS termination, DNS, certificates Alias policy: anonymous vs human-required vs device path owns the binding and the decision point on every exposed path — — Group and schedule policy later, after the bounded decision the public-name contract requires later: the WWW journeys as an adapter over the headless owner API — Ephemeral alias issuance the kind, lifetime and reassignment rules a reference issuer for the Compose and Kubernetes bindings a hoster's own issuer and distribution Human identity generic OIDC adapter, conformance cases provider configuration profiles (Authentik reference, Kratos fallback); no login UI the provider deployment Owner self-service one thin page over the headless owner API — branding, support links Operator lifecycle headless operator API and lifecycle library (exists at ed2ced00) CLI, console (read-mostly first), runbooks billing, ticketing Secrets component contract and the Vault Transit reference provider cloud key-service providers, service-login adapters, conformance kit key custody Deployment the deployment-plan schema and the role table plan renderer; Compose, Kubernetes and DIY single-tenant bindings; targets registry with owner and expiry per vendor derived image with installed providers Observability readiness and admission endpoints shaped for fleet polling Grafana mixin, alert rules, runbook skeletons paging

Why the alias record is core even though an edge may resolve it first (answered in discussion with the maintainer, 2026-11-09): the application must refuse an unknown host and apply the alias policy on every exposed path, sockets included, so it needs the alias record inside its own authority. The resolver already accepts X-Resolved-Tenant only as a consistency check against its own map. An edge that resolves is therefore a cache in front of core's record, and the sibling ships the demo facade for it; a hoster can swap the facade without touching authority. Deployments with a plain edge (Compose, DIY) use the same record in direct-alias mode and need no facade.

Two placement rules from operating experience, stated as mechanisms:

  1. Config names a registered provider; it never names a module path. A module path in config is code execution for anyone who can write config and it hides the supply chain from the image digest. Providers are installed at image build and registered by name; core refuses unknown names.
  2. The trusted-peer predicate is configuration, not a provider. It is the one place where a wrong adapter silently widens trust.

docs.title: 3. Line of sight to a staging rehearsal
docs.text:
Waves show dependency, not dates. Each wave names the gate that ends it. "Rehearsal" means a synthetic export of a few tenants loaded into the Compose binding on a clean host, served through a TLS edge with a written trust record, and restored once, with nothing real in it.

wave core sibling gate 0 (in flight) ed2 one-host reference accepted; shared OIDC/owner source accepted natively; Vault service login behind the existing seam — M6 acceptance families for identity and secrets 1 registry migration, operator API, snapshot export; resolver snapshot source; unknown-host refusal before tenant context; reserved-name floor repository created; plan schema extracted from deploy/multitenant/config.js; resolver and secrets conformance kits with red controls registry CRUD plus alias rename, reassignment and revocation measured on PostgreSQL; a stale snapshot refuses, a fresh one serves 2 full Mongo→PostgreSQL loader for the admitted collections (CAP-02); operator CLI verbs over the headless API Compose binding consumes deploy/multitenant at a pinned commit; edge reference with probes; trust-record template; targets registry empty but checked loader round-trip on synthetic exports with populated identity and order fidelity; CLI provision/suspend/export/delete/bind-alias against the Compose binding 3 — staging rehearsal on Compose: TLS edge, provider over HTTPS, Vault service login, backup and restore of the assembled tree, upgrade and rollback the deployment admission probes pass against the live edge and Vault; one restore rehearsed 4 thin owner page Kubernetes binding (one Pod per cohort, private socket volume, no-overlap update); console read-mostly; first two DIY single-tenant targets with expiry dates binding equivalence table in the public-name contract 5 group/schedule policy after its decision packet WWW journeys over the owner API; connector sync tooling; observability mixin policy evidence list in the public-name contract

Priority between the three columns: core first where it defines authority (waves 1 and 2 are mostly core), the sibling where it lowers the cost of running a deployment (waves 3 and 4), and hoster-private work only as adapters once the interface they sit behind exists.

docs.title: 4. Questions for the maintainer, one topic each
docs.text:
Items marked answered in discussion were settled with the maintainer on 2026-11-09 and await their row in release decisions; the rest are open.

  1. Where deploy/multitenant lives during 16.0.0. Answered in discussion: re-running acceptance to move a directory is process drag, so the move is not gated on it. Move the tree into the sibling now with its history (git subtree split), record the source commit, and make the sibling's check a byte-identity comparison of the moved tree against that pinned core commit plus the existing demo.sh smoke. Core keeps a one-paragraph pointer. The ed2 evidence keeps its attribution because the files it cites are unchanged, only relocated.
  2. Registry authority. Answered in discussion: private names are core schema. Public aliases are also a core record with a read-only private resolution endpoint; the sibling ships the auth_request facade over it and a hoster may replace the facade. Mechanism in §2.
  3. Default alias kind and label length. Answered in discussion: a simple built-in default (§1). The generated label's length is provisional at 10 characters (two letters plus eight from a 32-symbol lowercase alphabet, about 40 bits) and is to be measured against collision at the intended tenant counts and against typing and reading comfort before it is fixed. Uploaders, followers and controllers are configured with one hostname and do not rotate it, so a tenant needs exactly one permanent primary alias. Whether that name is owner-chosen or operator-generated (unguessable) is a separate axis from its lifetime. Ephemeral aliases are additive and never the only alias; reassignment inherits nothing. Recommendation: default one permanent primary alias per tenant, generated unless claimed; ephemeral aliases opt-in per tenant under operator policy.
  4. Reserved names as a project floor. A built-in list (well-known, api, admin, www and the like) plus an operator list, in the D22 style. Recommendation: yes.
  5. Roles gateway reuse. Port or re-implement. Recommendation: re-implement the decision chain over core's resolver and current authority, carry the schema vocabulary and the gateway's test cases, credit the design; the measured port cost is the runtime and dependency graph.
  6. Strong identity for single and multitenant, and the gateway's disposition. Direction given in discussion: both profiles should have strong human identity, and uploaders may move toward zero trust over the long term. The adopted generic OIDC adapter already runs in single under ENABLE=oidc, so fronting an independent site with an external gateway is not needed for human identity; the gateway is archived as reference once the decision chain and the group and schedule vocabulary are carried into core. For uploaders, D17's permanent native credential path stays; a later contract can add per-device enrolment through the owner API, with short-lived or attested device tokens and the legacy secret as the compatibility path. That is a core identity contract; the sibling would hold enrolment tooling only. No change to D17 is proposed here.
  7. Retiring sole maintenance of the roles gateway while OIDC lands in both profiles. Feasible, and the order matters more than the effort. Conditions: (i) the gateway serves no production users; the maintainer's operator reports a staging-only deployment; (ii) the generic OIDC adapter is accepted natively in single and multitenant, which is wave 0; (iii) a minimal membership record exists in core, a person bound to a tenant with a role and revocable on the next operation, so the question the gateway answered, who may act on this site, has a home. The identity plan (MT-IDENTITY-PLAN) already names tenant access grants. Groups and schedules stay deferred to their bounded decision; nothing in retirement depends on them. Steps: archive the repository with a pointer to the alignment note, keep its test cases as the source of the resolver and OIDC conformance kits, and port the WWW journeys later as a sibling adapter over the owner API. For single, answered in discussion: an OIDC subject becomes a Nightscout subject by explicit binding by the site admin, with an invitation flow later; no auto-provisioning on first login. In addition, when OIDC is enabled an environment variable may name the one subject that binds to the site's admin at boot, so a fresh site can be claimed without a console; the mechanism and its refusal rules (unset, malformed, already bound) need a small decision row of their own.
  8. Repository home and licence for the sibling. Answered in discussion: the nightscout organisation, as nightscout-deploy. Licence recommendation: AGPL-3.0-only, matching cgm-remote-monitor and nightscout-connect and required anyway by the imported Compose tree, with the provider and plan interface contracts published as a small separate MIT package (the roles gateway's licence) so a hosting operator's private providers are not derivative works. The workspace lockfile carries the intended URL; bootstrap reports a failed clone until the repository is published, and the local scaffold stands in meanwhile.

Draft for maintainer review. Decisions taken go into decisions.md as rows; the queue and the public-name contract move only after the row exists.

docs.title: Counters, compatibility and tenant restore options
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-10 at 4917b2d4a.

Living contributor-facing design analysis, 2026-11-07. Read-derived from the published f0fac99a application unless a linked experiment says reproduced. Release decisions own the adopted experiment direction and conditional preview pause allowance. This analysis adopts no schema, new cursor format or runtime admission.

2026-11-10: the restore census now also refuses a connected non-participant whose identity can write the insertion-order or write-clock tables; read-only identities stay exempt, and only the restore of the tenant being restored refuses. In the current design only api writes those counters.

docs.title: Two independent mechanisms
docs.text:
The transactional tenant history clock has one tenant_write_clock row per tenant. It coordinates admitted writes through commit so a reader cannot advance past a still-uncommitted earlier history watermark. Existing numeric timestamp cursors remain compatible. Cross-tenant total ordering is not required.

insertion_ordinal is a separate PostgreSQL table identity used to emulate existing natural-order reads. A shared table's sequence supplies values for all its tenants, although readers remain tenant-bound. It is not the history clock, public record _id, or a clinical timestamp. Source anchors on f0fac99a: migrations/candidates/postgres-write-clock-v1.json:8, migrations/candidates/postgres-entries-v1.json:38, lib/storage/postgres-entries-read.js:105.

The engineering concern is giving implicit storage ordering application meaning. MongoDB defines natural order as physical RecordId order, with replica/sharding qualifications. Existing client compatibility must be measured before changing this inherited behavior; matching historical behavior must not silently invent a stronger universal guarantee.

docs.title: Comparison with other systems
docs.text:
Kubernetes resource versions support change tracking, consistent list/watch and optimistic update concurrency. etcd revisions order modifying operations/transactions. This is a useful analogy for the tenant history clock, not a reason to require cross-tenant ordering or add etcd here. Unique sequence allocation alone cannot establish commit-order visibility.

Restore has similar problems in etcd: an old snapshot can move revisions backward relative to clients' caches. Its documented revision bump/compaction procedure forces stale watches to rebuild. Our restore must likewise address stored checkpoints, history floors and derived caches; inserting rows is only one step.

MongoDB change-stream resume tokens and PostgreSQL WAL/logical decoding provide other durable positions, with retention/replay/failover obligations. These move ordering into a database/feed protocol; they do not eliminate the need for an ordering/recovery contract or automatically preserve legacy cursors.

docs.title: Options before a shared pause
docs.text:
Option Benefit Cost / explicit limitation Preserve the live allocator Smallest first experiment: restore original A ordinals without resetting shared state; B may continue. Must prove future allocations cover the artifact, source/sequence identity and supported cache state; A still needs exclusive restore authority. Higher-floor artifacts refuse. Recreate internal ordinals in original relative order Potentially avoids sequence-floor maintenance using normal allocation; public IDs remain stable. Proposal only. Requires a consumer census proving exact ordinal values have no external/checkpoint meaning, faithful relative ordering across all relevant domains, and review of artifact-fidelity changes. Tenant-local insertion allocation Removes cross-tenant insertion-counter maintenance; can reuse the existing tenant transaction fence while keeping ordinal and history meanings distinct. Schema/migration/write-path work; same-tenant contention and all-writer coverage need proof. New tenant data generation plus atomic routing switch Stage/verify A separately and retain old generation for rollback; B remains current. Requires routing-generation support, cache/session fencing and stale-writer refusal. Current global namespace mapping does not provide this automatically. Explicit domain sorting plus stable tie-breaker Can remove insertion-order state where no consumer actually requires it. Client-visible ordering, ties, retries and replacement behavior require measured compatibility and an explicit change contract. Narrow A suspension with ordinary transaction rollback Limits interruption to the tenant being restored. Must exclude every admitted A writer and stale serving/cache state; a clock-row lock alone misses lower-port callers.

The read-derived f0fac99a consumer census finds the physical value used for ORDER BY insertion_ordinal ASC while queries return only id_kind, doc (lib/storage/postgres-entries-read.js:102-113). The common natural-order path also serves selected entries/food and socket treatments/devicestatus/profile. No ordinal foreign-key or checkpoint consumer was found in lib//migrations/. Generic lifecycle artifacts do retain and hash the original physical ordinal. Consequently, regenerating it is a proposed logical tenant restore contract, not a repair to the existing exact physical backup oracle. Whole-deployment physical restore keeps its separate fidelity contract.

A logical prototype must sort captured rows explicitly by BigInt ordinal; export array order is not an ordering contract. Preserve public IDs and typed clinical values. The later adopted forward history correction policy supersedes exact history-timestamp copying for same-ID logical restore: retain the live issued floor, advertise changed/restored values and deletions above it, and publish effects only after the actual restore commit. Exact raw metadata remains the physical-backup contract. Admit exact positive noncycling CACHE 1 behavior first; larger allocator caches and stale writer sessions require independent ordering proof.

These alternatives reduce shared interruption, not the need to coordinate writes to the very state being replaced. A transparent online restore would additionally need a declared merge/replay/conflict policy for writes arriving during restore.

docs.title: Conditional pause and safe recovery
docs.text:
A preview shared write pause is allowed only if needed and explicitly bounded. Define admission/exclusion, drain, transaction boundaries, interruption recovery, verification and reopening. A watchdog deadline cannot make partial recovery safe or promise a deterministic completion time. Failure must retain a known safe state; reopening requires positive verification. Restoring A must not roll B's committed state back. A service restart and a rollback of durable data are different operations.

Keep the tenant-local history clock while measuring allocator-preserving restore. Investigate concrete natural-order consumers before adding another counter or requiring a shared pause. Future versioned cursors and restore generations are incremental architecture options, not prerequisites silently added to the preview.

docs.title: Fault isolation and the selected next step
docs.text:
The maintainer selected per-tenant insertion semantics and a tenant-local state prototype. Cross-tenant ordering is not required; same-deployment restore must preserve other tenants' current state. The global counter concern is shared mutable state under faulty or malicious behavior, not an observed requirement for cross-tenant ordinal values.

Ordinary atomic sequence allocation and privileged sequence maintenance have different authority. PostgreSQL nextval requires USAGE or UPDATE; setval requires UPDATE. Aborted transactions can leave gaps, which do not by themselves break relative order. The sequence contract does not turn the allocator into a global application transaction lock held until every writer commits. Avoid all-tenant read/modify/write counter code.

A faulty actor with privileged sequence mutation can affect tenants sharing that sequence. Per-tenant allocation reduces this state coupling, but does not protect against a compromised database administrator or a worker authorized across tenants, or isolate shared CPU/pools. Complete admission must verify actual privileges; table RLS alone does not bound sequence setters. The f0 serving-readiness survey has not established a complete sequence-privilege check across all roles. The new planner's own role check does not fill that broader boundary.

The narrower compatibility finding is in the native consumer proof: renumbering while preserving order retains the selected full profile; reversing order selects a different duplicate-match profile. Explicit date-sorted entries are unchanged. Source tracing reaches the released AndroidAPS NSClient v1 profile upload/ack path, but no Android binary was executed. No observed client requires cross-tenant ordinal numbers or exact private ordinal values.

docs.title: Minimal tenant-local state prototype
docs.text:
Use a counter row per tenant in each existing ordered collection namespace, with forced RLS and an invoker INSERT trigger. Keep history timestamps separate. Migration preserves existing ordinal values and seeds each tenant floor; ordinary inserts increment only their tenant's row transactionally. Explicit operator restoration preserves original ordinal values while advancing only the restored tenant floor. Updates cannot change ordinal/tenant identity. Serving column INSERT excludes the private ordinal; operator restore has separate rights.

This trades an extra small relation/trigger and per-tenant transaction lock for removing cross-tenant allocator state and restore counter-maintenance machinery. It is an operational simplification, not a claim of fewer SQL statements or of Byzantine tolerance against a trusted all-tenant worker/DBA. Shared pools/CPU remain. No new service, per-tenant native sequence or SECURITY DEFINER is needed.

The first prototype is explicit standalone SQL, not a runnable catalogue/default selection. Current migration validation rejects LOCK, SET and DO statement forms; runner-compatible transaction/precondition integration remains explicit work. Do not hide those controls in an unreviewed migration function to make validation pass. Lifecycle inventories, role grants, read-only trigger/counter readiness, old/new upgrade/rollback and final client/cursor/cache acceptance also remain. A normal one-time schema DDL lock is distinct from a recurring shared restore pause.

The native tenant-local proof now establishes all-five populated conversion and A restore/B preservation under restricted roles, entries A-lock/B-progress and the real profile first-match result. It also demonstrates that direct own-floor corruption can damage A ordering while B remains exact; it is not Byzantine tolerance of privileged multi-tenant workers. Migration-runner, readiness and lifecycle integration remain open.

docs.title: Deployment scenarios and rig testing
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-10 at 4917b2d4a.

Contributor-facing living runbook. Deployment structure and commands are read-derived from cgm-remote-monitor 151de0248a1e4301c85b5c638185eec3ca8c38e6, with the nginx edge-network correction in 4935aa77049c66793669a7be940e40ed6ba5b386, inspected 2026-11-07. Executed results retain their own source in the linked records. The accepted cold Compose measurement records the later ed2 implementation, including its Host-preserving demo sender. Architecture/evidence grooming: 2026-11-08; no new runtime campaign was run. This document implements the documentation scope of MT-DOC-DEPLOY; current claims live in the work queue and delivery dashboard.

docs.title: Choose the experiment
docs.text:
Scenario Purpose Boundary Existing single-tenant installation Compatibility baseline for a selected rig/client Existing MongoDB deployment and client configuration; nightscout single remains the default. One-host synthetic Compose preview Exercise separate services, browser/API/socket paths and tenant-local restore Fixed participants, private Unix sockets, direct PostgreSQL and locally generated credentials. Cold functional acceptance passed on ed2; real-client, capacity and production admission have separate gates. Headless client lab Compare pinned clients against the admitted API surface Follow the binary client lab; its evidence does not establish every mobile device or every new source head. Physical mobile or pump/CGM rig Verify the chosen client, network path, upload/history and reconnect behavior A separately recorded experiment using synthetic input. Device execution is not implied by source-pattern replay. Multi-host, orchestrated replicas or failover Explore later deployment design Proposed topology: the current private socket roster is a one-host contract, not distributed discovery or HA.

The application Compose guide owns runnable packaging instructions at the ed2 reference. The Compose tree lives in the sibling repository nightscout-deploy and is its home from the next #8898 batch on; core then keeps only the fixture its own tests boot. The commands below describe the ed2 reference as accepted; run current packaging from nightscout-deploy. The service-process decision owns the deployment requirement. Compose is implemented; a Jsonnet generator is an optional way to produce configuration, not another runtime component or a selected prerequisite.

The binding and public-name contract maps ordinary Kubernetes resources onto these logical roles without assuming multi-host membership or a particular Ingress controller. Its candidate resource layout and access-policy extensions need their own acceptance.

docs.title: Deployment choices and fault domains
docs.text:
Tenancy, storage, execution and placement answer different questions. The adopted profiles are resident single on MongoDB and explicit multitenant roles on PostgreSQL/RLS. Storage ports make other combinations researchable; they do not admit a new supported deployment. The comparison below is read-derived architecture analysis; executed acceptance is linked separately.

Axis Current supported/reference choice What changing it requires Tenant scope One site for single; bound tenant context for multitenant roles Authorization, configuration, caches, history and lifecycle must all preserve the chosen scope. Datastore MongoDB for single; PostgreSQL/RLS in the multitenant preview Backend conformance, isolation, migrations, backup/recovery and operational acceptance; a new adapter alone does not qualify a server. Computation Resident single-site runtime; request-local API frames plus independent multitenant evaluator/realtime projections The separate nonresident-single prototype and reusable derived-result proposal need their own admission. Process/container Existing combined single-site server; separate API, realtime, evaluator and tenant-admin preview processes Role authority, private communication, operation lifetime and recovery must work across the actual processes. A container is packaging, not a tenant boundary. Host/replicas One-host fixed-cohort multitenant reference Fixed-roster API replicas need endpoint trust, instance-complete drain/invalidation and recovery acceptance; they do not replicate evaluator production. Multi-host/HA additionally needs partition/failover acceptance and explicit producer ownership where work is partitioned. See the scaling plan. Deployment model Scope of a failure Evidence and decision use Independent single-site servers A server process failure affects its site. Shared database/host/ingress still couple whichever sites use them. Existing compatibility baseline; inspect the operator's actual infrastructure before calling sites independent. One-host multitenant reference Tenant authority/history/restore are scoped; role processes, PostgreSQL, Vault, ingress and host remain shared. Actual cold UI/socket/restore and tenant-local restart proofs inform one-host composition and protocol design. They do not establish HA or capacity. Per-tenant database/process/host cells Isolation depends on what each cell actually owns; a shared controller, identity provider or ingress can still couple cells. An architectural alternative, with no admission from the current RLS/cohort proof. Define and test cell provisioning, migration, credentials, recovery and cross-cell operations first. Replicated or multi-host roles New partitions, split ownership, delayed messages and failover can affect tenants across hosts. Fixed-roster API scaling is planned separately from multi-host/HA. Platform inventory and stable worker identities can supply placement/assignment; actual operation lifetime, invalidation and disjoint producer ownership remain application contracts.

The distinction matters during failures:

Fault Boundary established by the reference Shared or unmeasured consequence A's restore, uncertain DATA commit or unresolved operation A remains unavailable where required; tested B traffic and fresh shared-role startup continue. This is cooperative tenant-operation isolation, not a bound on all database locks, pool use or tenant load. A role process exits Separate roles can be restarted; incarnation checks prevent a replacement participant satisfying an old restore pin. Tenants using that role lose its service; automatic failover and recovery-time bounds are unmeasured. PostgreSQL, shared schema/privileges or pool fails Unsafe shared readiness refuses rather than serving through it. Shared tenants/roles depend on that infrastructure; RLS isolates rows, not database uptime or resource exhaustion. Vault or credential service becomes unavailable Current-authority and secret-dependent paths retain their refusal rules. Do not infer that every operation fails or survives identically; production service login, key recovery and dependency-outage acceptance remain separate. nginx or the host fails No redundant public path or host is accepted in this reference. Public reachability or all local roles can be lost together. Independently authorized direct SQL bypasses the cohort A current-session census can detect and refuse known unexpected actors. The adopted application ownership contract excludes independent direct writers. Stronger fencing would be needed only to support that additional writer model; it is not a prerequisite for the supported cooperative topology.

These boundaries explain why tenant-local restore can be useful before a production topology is qualified. The accepted experiment narrows the recovery mechanism; production admission additionally needs the intended edge/service identity, credential custody/renewal, lifecycle/key recovery, workloads and operating limits, monitoring and operator recovery procedures. See the architecture evidence guide for which results support current decisions.

For aligned top-to-bottom zones and explicit communication planes, use the current and proposed grid topology plates. The compact flowchart below retains the accepted reference's connection summary.

docs.title: One-host reference topology
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Rig["Synthetic rig / API client"] --> Edge["nginx: one published origin"]
  Browser["Existing browser"] --> Edge
  Edge -->|"pages and assets"| UI["UI process"]
  Edge -->|"/api"| API["REST APIs process<br/>admitted v1 / v2 / v3 adapters"]
  Edge -->|"/socket.io"| RT["Realtime process"]
  RT -->|"private API socket"| API
  Eval["Evaluator process"] -->|"private alarm socket"| RT
  API --> PG["PostgreSQL"]
  RT --> PG
  Eval --> PG
  Admin["Tenant-admin process"] --> PG
  API --> Vault["Vault Transit over TLS"]
  Bootstrap["One-shot bootstrap"] --> Vault
  Bootstrap --> PG
  Operator["Private maintenance operator"] --> PG
  Operator -->|"private participant control sockets"| API
  Operator --> RT
  Operator --> Eval
  Operator --> Admin

The accepted cold measurement exercises this topology as a one-host synthetic reference. UI and nginx receive no database credentials. PostgreSQL, Vault, tenant-admin and maintenance endpoints have no public port in this reference. The UI renders the shipping templates/assets; API and realtime decide data authority. See the communication architecture for the two distinct record-frame and evaluator-output paths.

The Compose file declares internal service ports: API 1337, realtime 1339, UI 1340 and tenant-admin 1341. Only nginx's 8080 is published, by default at 127.0.0.1:18080. The nginx route map preserves the public Host for configured tenant resolution and strips selector headers. Public tenant-management/operator routes are refused. The preview's public origin is HTTP; Vault's internal connection uses the generated CA and TLS. An external TLS ingress requires its own declared trust configuration and test.

nginx alone attaches to both the internal backend network and the edge bridge. The edge bridge permits host publication; every application, database, Vault and maintenance service stays on the internal backend network. The accepted cold measurement reproduces reachable UI/API/socket paths and A restore with B committing work; it retains exact source/image and independent cleanup attribution.

docs.title: Prepare a disposable synthetic instance
docs.text:
Use an isolated application checkout, Docker Engine with Compose v2, Node.js and OpenSSL. The reference requires the host uid/gid to match the image's 1000:1000 account. Check the selected source and clean tracked build inputs before preparing. The wrapper uses a fixed Compose project name. A second checkout alone does not isolate its containers and volumes from that project: reserve it for one experiment, or use a separate Docker context. Another project requires explicit Compose invocations with its own project name rather than the unchanged wrapper. Preparation records that commit, generates private state and refuses an existing state directory or deployment .env. Build uses a Git archive and lockfile; runtime commands refuse an image whose recorded source differs.

From that application's root:

cd deploy/multitenant
./demo.sh prepare
docker compose --project-name nightscout-multitenant-demo --env-file .env -f compose.yaml pull postgres vault nginx
node check-compose.js
./demo.sh build
./demo.sh bootstrap
./demo.sh up
./demo.sh status

On a fresh host, the explicit pull fetches the digest-pinned public dependency images. Startup uses --pull never; bootstrap does not start nginx, so it cannot be relied on to fetch that image.

These are the inspected source's commands, not commands executed by this documentation change. check-compose.js checks structural boundaries; it does not perform the browser, restore or rig experiment. Bootstrap deliberately prepares schemas, grants, Vault and synthetic tenant configuration. Runtime readiness checks do not migrate or repair a partially provisioned deployment. up invokes bootstrap's supported restart/unseal handling before starting roles; unknown existing state must refuse rather than be adopted.

For the already configured lab interface, choose this instead of the default preparation, before any state or .env exists:

./demo.sh prepare --bind 169.254.1.1 --port 18080

Preparation accepts only loopback or that existing address. It does not create an interface, route or firewall rule. A mobile device's loopback addresses the device itself; reaching this host requires an explicitly arranged lab route and name resolution. The reference does not establish remote reachability merely by selecting a bind.

docs.title: Connect clients without changing their protocol
docs.text:
Resolve the generated synthetic tenant aliases to the chosen ingress address. Use the alias in the client's configured URL, including the selected port; substituting the bare IP loses Host-based tenant selection. Check a known tenant, an unknown alias and the other tenant's credentials before a longer experiment. Container loopback belongs to that container, not to the host or another service.

Take credentials only from the generated private operator material. Do not print it into a lab report, shell history or captured request URL. A legacy subject credential must use the shipping authorization exchange before API3 Bearer use; the resulting DATA JWT is the Bearer credential. Existing clients using their supported tenant-local API secret or token flow retain that flow. A public login page does not supply management membership or implement the separate optional OIDC/session capability.

For each selected client, record the client build, server source/image, tenant alias and transport shape without recording credentials. Use the same synthetic records for single-tenant and multitenant runs. Check upload acknowledgement, addressed read, history cursor advancement, deletion handling and reconnect. For a browser/socket consumer, verify an actual new frame contains the uploaded record; a connected socket alone proves no data delivery. Public API identifiers and internal storage identifiers need not be identical.

The pinned client lab owns supported headless client execution. Android emulator and physical-device runs remain separately attributed; promotion decisions define their milestone scope. Avoid replacing a real client execution with a handwritten request and describing the result as that client's acceptance.

docs.title: Restore and failure scenarios
docs.text:
Run the synthetic restore demonstration only in its prepared disposable instance:

./demo.sh demo

The demo implementation captures A, changes A, restores A using the real lifecycle/controller, writes B during the held A operation and checks forward history correction/deletion. The restore-history decision owns client convergence semantics. B's preexisting state must remain unchanged; its explicitly authored new writes are expected differences.

Experiment Observe Required failure behavior Ordinary A restore A's clinical values/public identity and relative ordering; normal forward history updates and deletions; B read/write progress No global pause or indiscriminate rewind of current authority/consumer state. Interruption before activation Durable claim, audit, unfinished operations and actual data outcome Keep A unavailable; no blind replay, timeout-based reopening or orphan clearance. Activation acknowledgement lost Actual persisted phase and the recorded uncertain result Activation may already have committed after its prerequisites succeeded; inspect the outcome rather than assuming suspension or blindly repeating activation. Shared-role restart with A suspended Fresh API/realtime/evaluator processes actually serving B; A refused with no stale output; A protected state unchanged Deferred A initialization cannot bypass shared schema/permission checks or silently reactivate A. The c23 native matrix reproduces the bounded shared-role restart criterion; the ed2 cold record supplies the separate packaged ordinary-restore proof. Missing/restarted participant Changed incarnation, missing acknowledgement or unresolved operation Old restore pins cannot activate using replacement processes. Database/Vault/shared-host outage Which shared dependency failed and what each tenant can still do Tenant-local restore does not promise tenant-local infrastructure failures or HA.

The startup-admission decision and application recovery contract own restart behavior. Process/control liveness and each tenant's readiness are different observations. Realtime /health retains strict aggregate readiness; Compose probes TCP, private sockets and participant status instead.

docs.title: Credential and recovery boundaries
docs.text:
Each service mounts its own private configuration. Bootstrap alone receives initial database/Vault material; runtime roles must not reuse that administrator. The credential inventory owns generated capabilities. Fixed private sockets require the common numeric uid, 0700 directories and 0600 endpoints. No dynamic membership is inferred.

Restore excludes A's cooperating service operations. Private database ingress and custody of serving credentials are deployment requirements. A census of current PostgreSQL sessions can refuse unknown actors; it cannot prevent a new independently authorized raw SQL client from bypassing the protocol. A stronger database/authentication fence is separate work, not a requirement to combine API and realtime into one process. Direct PostgreSQL is required; transaction-pooling proxies and multihost coordination are outside this reference.

The preview provides no automatic orphan clearance or supported suspended-restore resume command. Operator-verified recovery remains separate work; the native refusal and restart evidence does not establish a recovery-time bound.

The lab Vault credentials expire after 24 hours and restart does not renew them. The generated CA expires after 30 days. Preserve verification and prepare a fresh synthetic instance when appropriate; do not disable TLS checks. Vault sealing, key custody and production Vault connectivity (a Vault Agent sidecar, maintained in nightscout-deploy) remain governed by the adopted trust contracts.

docs.title: Stop, retain and report
docs.text:
./demo.sh stop
./demo.sh down

Both commands retain named data volumes and private state. down removes the Compose services/network; it does not erase database/Vault volumes. Record the exact project and owned resources before any separately authorized destruction. Do not remove sockets from running participants or use whole-cohort restart as a substitute for investigating an uncertain restore.

A useful report contains the exact source/image/client versions, named scenario, synthetic workload, observed HTTP/frame/history outcomes, fault and restoration control, and verification that owned processes/sockets/containers are released. Separate elapsed observations from a recovery guarantee. Keep raw credentials, private identities and record payloads out of committed evidence.

The c23 native matrix reproduces the separate-role restore and shared-role restart criteria, including B progress while A remains unavailable, with independent physical closure. Its fixed trusted cooperative cohort and private credential/ingress boundary remain load-bearing. The earlier b029 record retains its own narrower scope. The current acceptance family keeps their source-specific verdicts separate. The ed2 cold record adds actual UI/socket and ordinary restore/history/B-continuity acceptance. The ed2 pinned-client record adds actual cgmsim/oref0 execution with matching stored outcomes and independent physical closure. The final ed2 regression passed all seven nonbrowser tiers. Other clients and rigs, capacity, HA, production recovery and M6 retain their own admission criteria. The release contents own the latest executed acceptance and remaining blockers.

docs.title: Deployment bindings, public names and load behavior
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-12 at e0765ac4a.

Living contributor-facing deployment contract and decision-preparation guide, reconciled 2026-11-12 against release decisions at alignment 8ae6f4a3729548de0c88cc0ee5b3c0aede9aba61. Mechanisms below are read-derived; this edit runs no cluster or provider. Release contents and named reports own implementation, qualification and publication; the queue owns claimed state. Resource profiles, sharing schedules and fleet arrangements are proposals unless adopted in their canonical decision home.

A deployment binding translates application contracts into processes, addresses, credentials, placement and lifecycle actions. It reuses the same roles across supported topology choices; it cannot create missing ownership, migration or failover behavior through configuration. Start with runtime topology for role contracts and scale envelopes, then production sequencing for qualification and admission. Existing platform scheduling/discovery primitives are inputs, not application services to reimplement.

docs.title: Portability is distinct from distributed application ownership
docs.text:
The target is a deployment contract with Compose and Kubernetes bindings. Kubernetes may schedule and expose one bounded application cohort without introducing multiple active producers or dynamic restore membership. It does not need a particular Ingress controller, service mesh, discovery service or operator. An ordinary public address/load balancer can lead to the deployment's nginx or other trusted HTTP edge. A Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer is one binding when the platform supports it; an external load balancer to an available service endpoint is another. The actual peer/source-address and TLS behavior must be measured, rather than inferred from the YAML. See Kubernetes Services.

flowchart LR
  N["Permanent or ephemeral public name"] --> IP["Public address or load balancer"]
  IP --> Edge["Trusted HTTP edge: TLS, host and access policy"]
  Edge --> Registry["Alias binding and current policy"]
  Registry --> Tenant["Private internal name / stable tenant ID"]
  Tenant --> C["Fixed application cohort"]
  C --> PG["PostgreSQL: authoritative tenant and operation state"]
  C --> V["Vault: protected keys and recoverable secrets"]
  O["Explicit operator provisioning / migration"] --> PG
  O --> V

The diagram describes logical responsibilities, not a selected process count or a new mandatory per-request network hop. The registry/policy lookup may be a current-authority component inside an admitted application. DNS locates an edge; it supplies neither tenant authority nor permission to see data.

docs.title: What a Kubernetes binding must preserve
docs.text:
The colocated reference uses a fixed participant roster and private Unix control sockets. A normal TCP Service does not transport a filesystem socket. A colocated binding can place role containers in one Pod with a private shared socket volume. Independent role placement instead requires the selected private network binding and direct participant inventory. A complete-cohort Pod is not an independently replicated workload: its replica count cannot replace per-role ownership rules. Multi-container Pods can share an emptyDir volume. The volume can hold IPC endpoints; durable operations, tenant identity, keys and recovery evidence must survive Pod replacement elsewhere. Their durable homes remain the database and admitted secret/artifact stores.

Responsibility Candidate ordinary-resource binding Acceptance that makes it equivalent Public reachability A Service/public-address adapter leads to the selected nginx/edge. No particular Ingress API is required. Actual TLS, Host, forwarded-client identity, socket upgrades and trusted-peer behavior; unknown/conflicting names refuse. Public DATA ingress cannot bypass separately authenticated owner controls or reach private operator/database controls. Fixed application cohort Separate containers/processes with the same explicit roster and private IPC; one-Pod placement is an initial candidate. Effective UID/socket permissions, actual participants and incarnations, drains/invalidation acknowledgements, A restore and B continuity; individual container restart and whole-Pod replacement retain uncertainty/refusal semantics. Non-secret configuration Versioned ConfigMaps and image/config identity, rendered from deployment inputs. Effective role/catalogue/tenant binding matches the declared generation; drift and partial rollout refuse where required. Image/config identity is evidence of intended inputs, not producer exclusion. Credential delivery Narrow per-role Secret mounts or an admitted secret-delivery adapter; Vault retains the adopted cryptographic role. Each workload can use only its declared credentials; service login/renewal/rotation and failure behavior pass. Kubernetes Secret storage/RBAC and workload creation authority enter the deployment trust record. Secret objects alone do not satisfy Vault custody or renewal. Explicit provisioning/migrations Operator-executed command or controlled Job, separate from ordinary serving startup. Idempotency/partial-failure recovery, effective grants/RLS, supported catalogue and read-only startup checks; retries or a Job completion flag cannot erase uncertain results. Datastore and recovery artifacts Declared external services or admitted persistent storage; separate ownership from disposable compute. Actual backend identity/direct-connection contract, backup/key fidelity and recovery under restart/replacement. A Service address or PVC existence alone is insufficient. Health and replacement Separate shared-process liveness from tenant admission; declare readiness/termination/update policy. A suspended tenant does not cause a restart loop or block healthy-tenant startup. Delayed termination, overlapping replacement and dependency recovery preserve authority, durable operations and client results.

A replica count of one is desired placement, not proof of unique execution. Kubernetes Deployments default to rolling updates, which can overlap old and new Pods. A binding can use a controlled update without overlap. It must still prove safe replacement and retain application and database safeguards. Control-plane state alone does not prove an old actor has stopped. Refer to Deployment strategies. Splitting the same roster across Pods or nodes requires a qualified transport, membership and lifetime binding; merely adding Services does not close that gap.

Kubernetes Secret guidance explains storage encryption and access controls. The production trust record must cover those controls as well as the existing database/Vault/edge boundary.

A role box is not a mandatory service deployment. The logical REST/worker placement map permits data, authorization and owner REST modules with separate audiences. Background connectors, evaluation and privileged maintenance have their own responsibilities. The admission review distinguishes generic participant gating from owning the restoration workflow.

docs.title: Configurable transports and independently scaled API
docs.text:
REST APIs (v1/v2/v3) are one stateless request-serving component with internal version-specific adapters. A Compose service or Kubernetes Deployment runs instances of that component; replica count and placement do not split API versions. Each replica serves the same configured admitted route set. See the component contract for transient-state, maintenance and owner-audience boundaries.

Read-derived mechanism assessment: there is no architectural requirement that the request-serving API have a single replica or share a host with realtime. The current cohort specification already permits explicitly declared API replicas as separate participants. The API implementation acquires fresh request frames and exposes invalidation of local startup/readiness state. Stateless request handling keeps durable authority outside the process. Local state can be reconstructed. Each instance still has connections, caches, in-flight responses and restore obligations.

The shared transport implements service schemas and named clients over UDS or explicit TCP/HTTP endpoints. The original implementation record and joined acceptance retain their tested scope; current deployment qualification is recorded separately in release contents.

Bindings render the adopted serve.internal listener. Each role process has one private listener. Its default is a Unix socket. Network exposure uses explicit NS_SERVE_INTERNAL_HOST/_PORT settings. Callers use peer addresses such as NS_API_INTERNAL_URL. A dial service name may differ from the bind interface. Public/management listeners remain separate. Code selects the contract modules; configuration cannot move them between authority planes. The binding's termination grace must exceed the listener's graceful-shutdown deadline.

The current adapter supports http:, not direct https:. The deployment owns network reachability and any selected standard TLS proxy/mesh boundary; contract and version headers are not credentials or proof of process identity. No new bearer credential protocol is required. Preserve UDS ownership/inode protections, exact operation registration, schemas, deadlines, cancellation, no redirects or silent fallback, and current tenant/client authority across either binding. Internal peers require coordinated upgrade for the mandatory service/version headers. A proposed endpoint string or generic HTTPS URL is not a shipping option.

The calls have different addressing semantics:

Call / component Appropriate destination What changes with replicas Realtime to API authorization/mutation A trusted service endpoint may select any equivalently configured, admitted API replica. Each request still resolves the tenant and checks current authority, RLS and operation lifetime. No inherent affinity to one API is needed for these request-scoped calls; joined concurrency/compatibility acceptance remains required. Restore controller to each participant A separately addressable instance endpoint under the selected deployment access boundary, with pinned actual boot incarnation. The controller must reach every relevant instance for status/drain/invalidation. A single load-balanced endpoint cannot stand in for the complete roster: repeated calls could reach the same replica while missing another. Evaluator notification to realtime A destination whose receipt/fanout contract reaches the intended connected viewers. Load-balancing one handoff to one realtime replica does not broadcast it to sockets on other replicas. Qualify fanout or explicit delivery ownership and durable retry/deduplication. Browser to realtime A connection-owning realtime instance. Socket connections, rooms and local projections are retained state. Current polling plus WebSocket compatibility needs session affinity for polling, and correct cross-instance delivery. A generic URL alone does not solve that. See Socket.IO multiple-node guidance.

Start API scale-out with an explicit fixed roster if desired. Prove concurrent requests on different APIs and current revocation and configuration checks. Test response drain, all-replica invalidation and replica replacement. Check foreign-tenant refusal and unchanged mutation replies. Database pool/connection limits and load tests must account for the aggregate across replicas. Ordinary API replication does not inherently need the evaluator's single-producer ownership protocol. Dynamic joins and removals need admission and drain rules serialized with maintenance. These can use the existing authoritative database. They do not inherently require a new consensus or discovery product.

Preserve deadlines, cancellation, byte bounds and actual acknowledgement semantics across both transports. An ambiguous mutation response must not cause a new transparent retry: the current forwarder returns no acknowledgement rather than fabricating success. Network/partition tests add cases to prove; they do not make API scale-out theoretically invalid. Evaluator scheduling/notification production and realtime fanout retain their own independent ownership questions.

The inspected node-multienv source provides narrower prior art. Its redirector listener passes configured listen values through and handles a filesystem socket. Its backend selection constructs a remote URL. This source reading does not establish one uniformly interchangeable Unix/HTTP/HTTPS client abstraction across that project. That historical source assessment supplies no transport-parity or replica runtime measurement; later evidence retains its own scope.

docs.title: Jsonnet and node-multienv integration boundary
docs.text:
A declarative binding takes a deployment identifier, role set and image/configuration generation. Inputs also specify tenant resolution, edge placement, resource limits and secret references. It should render resources and an inspectable inventory, never embed live credentials or clinical data. Keep public name/access-policy records separate from internal service-discovery endpoints.

The reviewed node-multienv prior art can inform renderer inputs, reconciliation, resource ownership and provisioned vs serving states. It does not make an existing per-site resource schema the required shape for shared multitenant roles. A binding must render deterministically and expose the same logical endpoints. Test cold start, restart, restore, current authority and cleanup on its actual topology. Renderer implementation and Kubernetes runtime equivalence have separate evidence. Use release records for delivered bindings; this contract does not select a new operator dependency or infer actual-cluster acceptance from rendered resources.

docs.title: Experiment rigs and deployment recipes
docs.text:
An experiment isolates a question on pinned inputs. A deployment recipe specifies a complete supported installation. The runtime scale envelopes keep small-group efficiency, operator density and fleet growth distinct.

Artifact Must state What it can establish Diagnostic or stress rig Exact source/image/instrument, role counts, resources, workload, changed axis, scope and stop condition A bounded correctness finding or measured bottleneck; no deployment recommendation follows from a stress-only pass. Qualified deployment recipe Actual placement and trust, total application/dependency resources, workload mix and retention, admission limits, failure/recovery behavior, upgrade/rollback and cost basis An operator can select and operate the named profile within its accepted envelope. Fleet design proposal Bounded group/database responsibilities, stable tenant placement, routing/control authority and migration/recovery boundaries An explicit design decision to evaluate; not implemented cross-database mobility or a claim that one database supports the fleet.

Resource accounting includes aggregate per-role pools, all replicas' retained state, storage/index/WAL/backup growth, load generators and platform overhead. Node count and Pod density alone are not cost or redundancy measurements. A consolidation comparison uses matched workload and surviving capacity after the declared failure, with private operator baselines labelled assumptions until reproduced. Generic synthetic scenarios suffice; private service facts are not needed in public configuration examples.

A recipe lists which configurations are supported and which upgrades require coordinated replacement. Protocol versions, schemas and actual role incarnations must agree. A service endpoint or Kubernetes readiness response does not prove every replica has initialized every relevant tenant. Ready/drain preconditions may precede a steady-serving or continuity window whose declared oracle requires zero refusals; warm refusals during that window remain failures. Intentionally cold/startup/refusal experiments keep their separately declared expected outcomes. Preserve exact evidence when reusing a completed component in a new profile, and qualify the changed composition instead of rerunning unrelated proofs.

docs.title: Public name, tenant identity and access policy
docs.text:
Identity or binding Lifetime and meaning Required boundary Stable tenant ID Durable authority/data identity RLS, credentials, grants, history and lifecycle bind here; a public rename never transfers them. Private internal name Operator-controlled resolution label bound to the stable tenant Discovery or routing metadata is trusted only through the admitted deployment boundary. It is not a public authentication credential. Permanent public alias A long-lived address intended to be safe to publish, including on social media Knowing the address confers no additional authority. Explicit current access policy determines anonymous/authenticated behavior; revocation or suspension applies without needing to hide or rename the URL. Ephemeral public alias A rotatable or expiring address bound to the same tenant Expiry/rotation changes reachability, not ownership. It is not an authorization capability unless a separate reviewed capability-link contract is adopted. Alias policy binding Which current policy applies to this public entrypoint Binding changes are versioned/audited and may narrow access; another alias or direct backend route must not bypass the intended policy. Reassignment cannot inherit the old tenant's memberships, grants or caches.

The existing resolution contract already separates disposable aliases, durable internal names and stable IDs. The public-name policy requirement extends the design questions beyond simple host lookup. Its persistence/update/API contract still needs implementation and acceptance; this document selects no table schema or policy engine.

docs.title: Authenticated sharing and group policies
docs.text:
Strong OIDC login identifies a person. Current membership and the permitted Nightscout grant determine what that person may do. Anonymous access is a separate explicit policy choice; neither a permanent alias nor a successful OIDC login silently grants tenant data or management authority.

A proposed policy surface needs these distinct controls:

  • Require human authentication for selected public browser journeys, or allow only the explicitly configured anonymous permissions under project/operator floors. A blocked journey must not fall back to a broader anonymous policy.
  • Bind authenticated groups to explicit allowed operations and any operator ceiling, with current membership, grant and session/key state on protected use. Merely having permission does not establish delegation authority.
  • Preserve the permanent native device/headless credential path from D17. Its route/audience policy is explicit; it does not gain human-management authority, and a browser policy change cannot accidentally remove supported device access.
  • Apply the selected policy across pages, API routes, socket subscription/write and protected delivery, reconnects and relevant cache keys. UI-only login is insufficient; direct backend access cannot bypass the public policy boundary.
  • For optional schedules, specify timezone/DST, boundary/clock behavior, group overlap/precedence and ongoing-stream rechecks. Specify whether access is the intersection of grants and schedule constraints, or an explicit alternate grant; do not let an implementation choose that policy silently.

The roles gateway and WWW journeys are prior art for these controls. Current OIDC/owner authority remains the base contract. Alias-bound group/policy behavior and schedule precedence need a bounded decision packet before claiming the feature. Ordinary production identity acceptance does not imply these richer sharing policies are already implemented.

Use synthetic anonymous, allowed and blocked users to test a policy. Include overlapping groups, revocation, issuer outage and exact schedule boundaries. Test alias rotation and reassignment, cached and reconnected sockets, and independent stored effects. Exercise every exposed path. OIDC-provider outage follows the adopted bounded-existing-access rule with current local authority still available. If current alias/group/schedule authority cannot be established, refuse the protected operation; never expand permissions. The first production scope must state which of these public-name features it offers and qualify those features before publication of user data. The clarification adds a target capability, not an unmeasured M6 promotion or an implicit waiver of existing preview decisions.

docs.title: Load-bearing metrics and emergent failure experiments
docs.text:
The measurement unit is a workload and shared dependency, not a uniform tenant. Use aggregate metrics and synthetic fixtures; exclude identifiers, credentials, public aliases and clinical values from metric labels and captured logs.

Trigger Observe Evidence / proposed mitigation to evaluate Many tenants/processes start or reconnect together Work arrival/concurrency, pool acquisition wait, connection churn, CPU/event-loop lag, memory, error/retry rate and evaluator/data freshness Burst and recovery campaigns with a quiet comparison. Evaluate bounded concurrency, retry backoff/jitter and staged admission; prove healthy-tenant progress and absence of duplicate effects. Timers, polling or token renewals align Per-interval scheduled vs actual work, queue age, lag tails, Vault/identity request rate and renewal failures Compare synchronized and staggered workloads. Any jitter must preserve expiry/freshness; never extend credential validity or silently skip safety-relevant work. One hot tenant, large history or public-name traffic spike Per-workload resource cost, shared pool/lock waits, cache churn, rejected/admitted work and latency/freshness for other tenants Independently verify isolation and state while evaluating budgets, bounded queues and load shedding. Unknown names/unauthenticated bursts must not allocate unbounded tenant contexts or expensive work. Dependency outage and return Retry amplification, outstanding work, recovery drain time, ambiguous commits and restored service freshness Test outage plus recovery, including a prolonged one. Evaluate capped retries/backlog and gradual resumption; report when operator recovery is required. Configuration/watch/reconcile or rollout churn Queue depth, reconcile/watch frequency, API calls, desired/observed generation, overlapping actors and replacement time Test partial rollout and repeated changes. Evaluate idempotency, coalescing/debouncing and paced rollout while preserving the fixed-cohort recovery protocol. Group/schedule policy changes affect many active viewers Authorization query/load, protected-delivery delay, current-policy version and refusal rate Test simultaneous boundary/revocation and reconnect. Any policy cache needs scoped identity, valid lifetime and current-authority guarantees; a wider TTL is not a correctness-neutral optimization.

Agree thresholds and supported workloads before using them as pass criteria. Thundering-herd avoidance is an experiment with before/after outcomes, not an assumption that jitter, Kubernetes or an extra load balancer solves the problem. These experiments feed the production operating-envelope gate.

docs.title: Derived output ownership: evaluator, realtime and HTTP
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-11-07. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

Contributor-facing decision preparation, 2026-11-07. Read-derived source review, not a reproduced defect or an adopted serving change. Homes: ARCH-DERIVED-FRAME for calculation/output contracts; MT-RUNTIME-PLAN for ownership and delivery. The seams plan owns the existing shared-code direction. This note defines its output-publication follow-up, without changing single-tenant behavior or enabling a service.

docs.title: Source anchors and observed boundaries
docs.text:
Inspected application 9298d79305e941fcfd36effa594e0e0bccf79994; alignment base 6114cfecf5a6bc4bdcefb161a04a7ded45d3af0d. References below are application paths at that source, not a claim about a later integrated head.

Coordinator read-derived recheck against published f0fac99a and local prototype 6a245c09 found the six referenced calculation/input modules byte-identical to 9298d793. The prototype changes operation lifetimes in runtime wrappers, not those calculation bodies; it selects no evaluated-result publication service.

Consumer Source and operation Output and effects Evaluator lib/data/tenant-projection-evaluator.js acquires a durable projection, materializes properties and calls views.evaluateCycle; lib/data/views/index.js:282 returns one calculation pass Properties plus requested/emitted notification results. Latest evaluated output is process-local; notification consumer state/outbox are separate durable boundaries. Realtime lib/server/realtime/projection.js:17 reconciles its own projection, :26 loads a tenant snapshot, :29 builds dataWithRecentStatuses() Browser data frame and recovered rows/checkpoint. It does not call evaluateCycle or derived-frame; independent input acquisition is not a duplicate full alarm cycle. Derived HTTP lib/server/tenant-app/snapshot.js loads request inputs; derived-frame.js runs selected plugin property setters Properties computed for a request, without notification/connector phases. Property-setter errors propagate; the code explicitly distinguishes this from evaluator error policy.

lib/data/ddata.js:128 shows that the realtime data frame contains admitted records/statuses, not the evaluator's entire property result. Replacing it with properties alone would change the client contract. Independently recovered projections can also have different checkpoints and evaluation instants. No same-revision guarantee follows from using common calculation code.

docs.title: Assessment and recommended direction
docs.text:
There is overlapping acquisition/transformation and property computation between some paths, but source inspection does not reproduce a performance defect or a clinical disagreement. The architecture risk is unclear result identity and freshness/failure policy, or accidental re-execution of effects when sharing a calculation. Retain consumer-specific wire shaping and authorization.

Recommended next boundary: define an immutable, versioned evaluated-result contract and compare it with request-local calculation before selecting a shared materialization service. Keep calculation code shared where semantics agree. Publishing reusable results is a separate architecture change from sharing code: it adds producer availability, result freshness, restart and ownership dependencies. Transport may be a database-backed materialization, authenticated request API or durable publication; none is selected here. Wake-ups alone are not stored results.

Candidate identity must include tenant, input checkpoint/projection identity, settings and plugin/calculation versions, input-bound/frame policy, evaluation instant, producer generation and output revision. A checkpoint alone does not identify time-derived results or establish an atomic all-domain revision. Publication must describe completeness, freshness/expiry and calculation errors. Normal notification effects remain separate from reusable read data. Consumers still apply current authority and endpoint-specific field/secret filtering.

docs.title: Ordered work and ownership
docs.text:
The bounded characterization now records actual f0 evaluator/realtime/API comparisons, instrumented costs, semantic controls and physical closure. It supports scoped reuse, not a publication-service decision or distributed admission.

  1. ARCH-DERIVED-FRAME owner: characterize overlap. Compare actual evaluator, realtime data frame and HTTP properties with identical synthetic inputs, settings and explicit instants. Inventory which calculations execute, and measure CPU, query volume, retained memory, result size and observable values. Do not infer duplicate cost from a shared function name.
  2. Same owner: prepare publication decision. State per-endpoint freshness, completeness/error and evaluation-time requirements; identify reusable results versus raw rows/consumer wire shaping. Compare request-local calculation with a versioned materialized result, including producer outage behavior. Keep historical/on-demand views and current time-driven alarm work explicit.
  3. MT-RUNTIME-PLAN owner: define publication ownership if selected. Specify tenant/partition assignments, fencing, handoff, durable output recovery, settings invalidation and retry boundaries. Existing local runtime generation checks do not fence another process. Deployment versus StatefulSet does not implement this contract.
  4. Integration owner: join only the selected bounded implementation. Verify journey-map equivalence over API reads, socket frames, writes, reconnect, alarm acknowledgement and restart. Preserve single-tenant behavior, current authority, no-egress reads and existing protocol limitations. Run broader acceptance on the coherent joined candidate, not after each preparation step.

Required semantic controls: cross-tenant result substitution; stale settings or plugin version; incorrect calculation; a time tick incorrectly reusing a result identified only by data checkpoint; partial-input success; obsolete-owner publication; producer failure after input commit but before output publication; hard deletion missing from a reused frame; accidental notification/connector egress from a read; and restored ordinary journeys after each break. Explicitly test refused versus stale-labeled versus synchronous-refresh behavior once chosen. Duplicate external delivery must not be described as exactly-once.

Publication implementation, transport selection, operating budgets and policy adoption remain UNMEASURED. Existing recorded functional runtime evidence is not invalidated by this follow-up; it does not establish these additional publication guarantees.

docs.title: Durable event delivery contract for multitenant consumers
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-11-06. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

Contributor-facing design contract, 2026-11-06, design direction adopted by the maintainer. Batch B7 of the integration batching plan; queue home MT-RUNTIME-PLAN (in-progress, no runnable gate yet). It reconciles D-EVENT's in-process commit event with D6's change-feed design and the transactional tenant clock, and names the entry bar before any distributed evaluator or realtime wiring. It promotes no milestone, selects no provider, admits nothing to a release candidate, and infers no consistency stronger than what the cited records reproduced.

Anchor Read from tool output at the time of writing Alignment main 18a9a5420c062aeb6cfe195d0fc0d5fd096509e2 CRM cumulative head (codex/serial-integration-20261106) 35903069b46974cfbaddd8dce00c994fb2562bc3; every file:line below is read at this commit unless it names another Tenant clock lane heads cited through their reports product 3e76b270, lower-port fixture 887c4aad, HTTP fixed-recovery head 3532c1a4 with repair 11770146
