Every claim is labelled reproduced (with the record that ran it) or read-derived (from source or a design page). Designs borrowed by name: the D6 slot-plus-NOTIFY-plus-poll pattern (execution plan, measured in T4.1), the transactional tenant commit clock (clock proof plan and its two reports), and the independent evaluator's retained-cycle policy (R50, R55, seams plan).

docs.title: 0. Premise, as read
docs.text:
• D-EVENT (maintainer, 2026-10-31; decisions.md D-EVENT question 1 row) names one in-process event per write(intent), carrying the step's items[]; delivery between processes is deferred to the multitenant roles; a timer serves time-driven alarms only, never catch-up on writes; writers that bypass Nightscout are unsupported. Read-derived.
  • The event as built at 35903069 is storage-intent-committed (lib/storage/write-intent.js:4635), documented at :4622-4634 as "INTERNAL: nothing in lib/ listens". Read-derived.
  • D6 (execution plan §1, row D6): change feed = replication slot (spine) + NOTIFY (latency) + bounded aggregate poll (backstop), NOTIFY emitted by the slot reader, never by a trigger. T4.1 (same plan, Phase 4) reproduced 200/200 rows delivered after a stopped reader returned, 0 on re-consume, and a 0.000000% notification-queue gauge with reader-emitted NOTIFY against 0.019073% from a trigger.
  • The roadmap §4 names this reconciliation as a design task, and its MT-RUNTIME-PLAN packet asks for durable checkpoint ownership, commit coupling, ordering, duplicates, hard and soft deletes, configuration invalidation and restart boundaries, with executable controls, before one producer/consumer recovery slice.
  • The seams plan "Shared frame join and multitenant recovery" says a local EventEmitter and a cell lease cannot establish these guarantees, and that provider selection stays open.

The event payload at the anchored source carries no tenant or stamp. B2 has since joined the clock locally; the R56 report owns that measured baseline. The original source references below remain anchored to the table above; they are not line references into the joined source.

docs.title: 1. Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning in this contract logical intent event the record of one resolved write(intent): collection, source, op, per-record _id, identifier, outcome and problems, counts, collapsed flag (write-intent.js:4656-4678). It names records; it carries no document contents and no filter (D-EVENT question 3) commit stamp the per-tenant monotone value the transactional tenant clock allocates inside the data transaction and holds through COMMIT; persisted on the committed rows as the server-owned modification field. The ordering fence of the clock proof plan checkpoint one consumer's durable position for one tenant: the highest stamp whose complete equal-stamp cohort that consumer has processed. A database row owned by the consumer, never process memory consumer a process that derives state from committed writes: the evaluator role (plugins, notifications), the realtime role (socket fan-out), a cache, a view materializer. Each has its own checkpoint per tenant tenant-local evaluator the consumer that runs the plugin and notification cycle for one tenant from that tenant's rows under its own tenant binding, retaining one cycle per tenant (R50's policy) backstop the bounded aggregate poll of D6: a periodic per-tenant read of rows with stamp above the checkpoint, which finds what a lost NOTIFY did not announce timer the time-driven trigger (bootevent.js:526 tick today) that evaluates alarms whose condition is elapsed time, not a new row

docs.title: 2. The spine: what is durable and what is not
docs.text:
Thing Durable Basis the committed rows of a tenant, with their server-owned dates and (under the clock) their commit stamp yes: this is the spine lower-port proof: rollback leaves "data and durable floor unchanged" and "no queued logical event escapes" (reproduced, tenant-commit-clock-lower-proof) the tenant clock floor row yes: readiness refuses a missing or stale floor before binding (reproduced, lower-port and HTTP fixed-recovery reports) the in-process storage-intent-committed event no: built and emitted only while a listener is attached (write-intent.js:4682); an observer failure is logged and the write stays committed (:4686); nothing in lib/ listens read-derived the PostgreSQL ports' post-commit emission no: withCommitEvents emits after connection.transaction() resolves (postgres-intent-common.js:42-48), which has verified COMMIT (postgres-connection.js:59-62); a crash between those two lines loses the emission and keeps the rows read-derived; "a failed mutating transaction publishes nothing" is reproduced by the port corpus (lib/storage/PORT-CONTRACT.md:141-146) the settle emission for a resolved no-op no, and it is not a spine event at all: it opens no transaction and proves no physical write (PORT-CONTRACT.md:120-124, postgres-intent-common.js:49-53) read-derived NOTIFY no: latency only (D6); a wedged consumer does not fill the queue when the reader emits it (T4.1, reproduced 2026-09-15) a replication slot's unacknowledged WAL durable while the slot exists; retention horizon is deferred (§9) T4.1 pinned 234.5 KB for 200 rows across a stop (reproduced)

Rules.

  1. The spine is the committed rows plus their stamp. A consumer that has the rows and its checkpoint needs no event to be correct; events only make it faster. This is the D6 shape and the D-EVENT scope decision read together.
  2. A consumer's position is a per-tenant checkpoint stamp owned by the consumer and stored in the database, under that tenant's binding, never in process memory. Two consumers never share a checkpoint row; the evaluator and realtime roles advance independently.
  3. The logical intent event must carry the tenant and the commit stamp of the write it describes before it is an interprocess message. At 35903069 it carries neither (write-intent.js:4676-4677); D-EVENT question 3 already reserved "later the tenant". A consumer that receives an event without a stamp treats it as a wake-up only and reads from its checkpoint. Current joined implementation: after-COMMIT callbacks receive the final transaction floor; stamp is null for unclocked, no-allocation and settle events. R71 owns the physical component proof and R72 owns comprehensive integration and the explicit nullable single-site settle assertions. The following initial allocation-time prototype is historical. Built on lane codex/event-payload-20261106 (head 4b5edf02, three commits over 65bb8456, unpushed): withCommitEvents.write captures the tenant from the bound scope and the stamp from a new connection.currentStamp() on the clock decorator when the nested write resolves; settle, Mongo and clock-off carry null. Unit 9 passing, controls red for a null stamp (7 / 2) and a remembered tenant (6 / 3), focused clock run 28 / 1 / 0; the Mongo-gated case is UNMEASURED. The figures are the lane's own (HANDOFF-event-payload-20261106.md), not re-run here.
  4. Commit coupling: the stamp is allocated inside the data transaction and held to COMMIT (clock proof plan "Proposed invariant"; postgres-write-clock.js:52 per the HTTP report, read-derived at the clock head); publication happens strictly after the transaction resolves, never inside it, and never from a database trigger (D6).

docs.title: 3. Ordering and duplicates
docs.text:
Delivery is at-least-once. Every consumer is idempotent on (tenant, stamp, collection, identity), where identity is the stored _id with its typed form kept distinct from a same-spelling string (write-intent.js:4640-4642 keys them apart; the port corpus preserves typed forms in delete records, PORT-CONTRACT.md:125).

Guarantee Holds Basis Two writes for one tenant that both commit receive distinct, increasing stamps, and an exclusive cursor taken after the higher one commits includes the lower one yes, under the clock, for the schedules run: lock wait observed while the lower write is held, no early visibility, ordered rows after release reproduced, lower-port "transaction clock fence"; HTTP "same-tenant concurrent writers" (1793991708168 → 1793991708169) The same, without the clock no: an authored detached counter commits distinct stamps yet the lower, later-committing row becomes invisible behind an already-observed higher exclusive cursor reproduced as the alternative-design control, lower-port report Parallel REST reads of two collections share one database revision no reproduced, R49 "parallel reads do not provide a common database revision" Every row has a unique stamp no: two identifier-absent typed twins marked by one mutation share a stamp; a sorted LIMIT 1 read followed by an exclusive cursor omits the tied second row reproduced, lower-port "existing bulk tie characterization" (that cohort and schedule, not every interface) Stamps across the two write paths (v3 identifier writes and legacy filter writes) are one sequence yes under the clock for the exercised plan: after an intervening committed v3 cursor, two distinct preplanned legacy targets receive later authoritative stamps reproduced, lower-port "earlier legacy plan"; raw import and mixed enabled/disabled writers are outside the captures Equal wall clocks in separate API workers give distinct stamps yes reproduced, HTTP report (1793991706986 → ...987 → ...988)

Rules that follow.

  1. Equal-stamp cohorts are the unit of progress. A consumer records checkpoint s only after it has read every row with stamp s. A page cut by a limit inside a cohort records the previous stamp, not s. The cursor is stamp > checkpoint, ordered by stamp then identity, and the page size is larger than the largest bulk write the writer admits (the step's resolve cap, RESOLVE_CAP, bounds the named records in one event; the bulk soft-delete case is the reason this rule exists).
  2. Duplicates are expected, not errors. A replayed row with (tenant, stamp, collection, identity) at or below the checkpoint is a no-op. A replayed row above it is processed once.
  3. Ordering is per tenant only. No cross-tenant order is promised or needed; tenant B progresses while tenant A's writers wait on A's clock row (reproduced, lower-port "cross-tenant progress" on a shared pool of four; HTTP report, same observation).
  4. No cross-collection snapshot. A consumer that reads entries and treatments in two statements may see a later treatment with an earlier entries cohort (R49). The evaluator's answer is the retained-cycle policy (§7), not a snapshot; a stronger policy needs its own implementation and test (seams plan).
  5. Without the clock the contract is not satisfiable by cursor replay. On a backend or configuration without the commit-coupled stamp (single-tenant MongoDB under D4, which opens no transaction on a standalone server, seam interface §9.1; or PostgreSQL with the opt-in clock off), the in-process bus stays the mechanism and this contract does not apply. That is the D-EVENT scope decision, not a gap.

docs.title: 4. Deletes
docs.text:
Kind Status under the contract Basis soft delete (the v3 default and every path that marks a record invalid) an ordinary write: the row stays, its stamp advances, and a consumer that replays it removes the record from its view. A bulk soft delete is one event with many records (or collapsed above the cap) and one cohort that may share a stamp (§3 rule 1) read-derived from the step; the tie case reproduced in the lower-port report hard delete through the intent path (v3 prune/autoPrune, write-intent.js:4606-4613; permanent delete) outside the spine. The event names the removed ids, but no durable row carries a stamp afterwards, so replay cannot reconstruct it. Strict replay cannot recover absence. The adopted full current-state snapshot backstop below handles absence separately; tombstones remain deferred (§9) read-derived stamped-spine limit; separate native characterization and the adopted reconciliation direction are linked in §11 raw writers that bypass write(intent) (a direct MongoDB upload, an independent SQL client) outside the contract, by decision: writers that go straight to the database are unsupported and xDrip+'s MongoDB upload is deprecated (D-EVENT question 1 row, decisions.md). R50's fixture used exactly such raw writes to show they "emit no process event" (reproduced); under the clock they also carry no stamp allocated by the fence

A consumer never infers a hard delete from a missing event. Strict stamped replay retains the limits above. The later bounded snapshot reconciliation decision selects full admitted current-identity/absence reconciliation in a consistent tenant snapshot, independent of floor movement. An arbitrary recent-time window is not sufficient. It preserves existing hard deletes and unstamped activity behavior; explicit row/byte refusal is required. Cadence/capacity and implementation acceptance remain unmeasured; every-transition history remains separate.

docs.title: 5. Configuration and grant invalidation
docs.text:
Decision: re-read per cycle, not an event. Current authority is checked per operation from a tenant-bound snapshot taken for that operation, and the evaluator binds each cycle to the settings version it read at the start of the cycle.

Why this and not an invalidation event:

  • R48 reproduced that the shipping data-access path consumes one tenant-bound SQL snapshot "for every permission and current-name attribution in the operation", with no retained cross-request permission cache; its controls show the failure mode of the alternative exactly: "reusing an earlier snapshot makes committed grant removal's next GET answer 200 instead of 403". Revocation-as-event would reintroduce that cache and make its correctness depend on at-least-once delivery, the property this contract exists to make tolerable rather than load-bearing.
  • A grant revocation and a settings change are per-tenant configuration rows under D15 and D22; they are not writes to a data collection and do not pass through write(intent), so they have no logical intent event to ride on today. Whether configuration rows also appear on the feed is deferred (§9); a consumer never relies on it.
  • R51 keyed its settings differential to actual settings rows and refused on stale state (reproduced, 12/0 with three semantic controls). Reading the settings version at cycle start costs one indexed read per cycle, the same order as the T4.1 payload decision ("a consumer told only 'tenant T changed' reads under its own tenant binding").

Consequences: a revoked grant stops delivery to the affected socket at the next operation that checks authority, and the realtime role performs that check per fan-out cycle, not per connection lifetime (the execution plan already notes that a tenant suspended mid-session is not re-checked after the handshake under the current socket; that is the behaviour this rule replaces for the multitenant roles). A settings change takes effect at the next cycle; retained state keyed to the old version is discarded (§7).

docs.title: 6. Restart and catch-up
docs.text:
Situation What happens Covered by consumer starts, or restarts after a crash reads its checkpoint for each tenant it serves, replays stamp > checkpoint in cohort order, records the new checkpoint after each complete cohort, then subscribes to NOTIFY replay from the spine crash after COMMIT, before the emission (postgres-intent-common.js:46-47) the rows and stamp are durable; the emission is lost; replay finds the rows replay, never the publish crash inside the transaction nothing is visible, floor unchanged, no event escapes; the writer gets a sanitized 503 and the same worker continues reproduced: lower-port "actual rollback"; HTTP fixed-recovery operator-abort case (STORAGE_UNAVAILABLE, then GET 200 and POST 201 from the same worker) lost NOTIFY the bounded aggregate poll reads stamp > checkpoint on its interval and finds the cohort backstop (D6) slot reader stopped and restarted rows written meanwhile are delivered once on return; the slot is acknowledged only after the batch's notifications commit reproduced, T4.1 (200/200, 0 on re-consume), on the 2026-09-15 reader time passes with no writes (stale data, missed readings, pump age) the timer evaluates time-driven alarms from the retained cycle timer; it reads no new rows and advances no checkpoint a writer's process is killed mid-transaction while holding the fence the backend stays active until the lock holder is released; the survivor advances the floor by one; this is not a rapid-recovery bound reproduced characterization, HTTP report "Node SIGKILL" row; the bound is UNMEASURED

The rule the roadmap states is kept verbatim in effect: the timer may drive time-based alarms; it never silently repairs lost write events. A consumer that finds its checkpoint missing starts from the floor the operator provisioned, and says so in its health report; it does not invent one.

docs.title: 7. Evaluator and notification state
docs.text:
R73 owns current functional M5 acceptance. The historical source inventory below remains anchored to the earlier source in §0; it is not a current code inventory.

The later tenant-wide suppression decision settles first-preview ack/snooze effects: shared within the tenant for the alarm group/level, original absolute expiry retained through restart, and no extension from repeats during the active window. Preserve the existing default duration and level-2-to-level-1 effect. Per-user/device suppression is separate. Storage shape and historical retention are engineering/operational work; the unchanged client protocol supplies no durable request identity for indefinite post-expiry deduplication. R73 records bounded persistence, crash/retry and cross-tenant acceptance. Live provider/device delivery and operating/retention budgets remain separate.

Historical state locations at 35903069, read-derived:

State Home today Scope today alarm levels and lastEmitTime per group; the per-cycle requests = { notifies, snoozes } lib/notifications.js:23-74, reset by initRequests each cycle one process-global ctx.notifications ack and snooze notifications.ack at lib/notifications.js:166-184 deletes lastEmitTime; requestSnooze at :118-127 same object; the web client's ack arrives over the socket. Under D23 (adopted and amended 2026-11-06) the socket protocol is unchanged: realtime forwards every socket write and the alarm ack, with the socket's own authorization, to an internal write endpoint on api, which runs the write step with the socket source label and writes the tenant-keyed ack row that the evaluator consumes from the feed; the result is relayed into the socket acknowledgement, and a failed forward is no acknowledgement the data the cycle evaluates ctx.ddata (lib/data/ddata.js), loaded by lib/data/dataloader.js from ddata.lastUpdated; the cycle runs on data-loaded → plugins → data-processed → socket dataUpdate (lib/server/bootevent.js:514-551, lib/server/websocket.js:122,159) one process, one site the write-driven trigger data-received from the socket write paths (websocket.js:285,538,598,...) and the timer tick (bootevent.js:526) in-process bus private, bounded acquisition that leaves the caller's ddata untouched lib/data/views/index.js:121-219 and lib/server/tenant-app/snapshot.js:15-75 (per the seams plan's inventory, R49 reproduced the caller-cache-untouched control) per call the retained cycle (last successful properties and timestamp, kept on a failed cycle, refreshed by the next real trigger) lib/server/nonresident.js on the #8891 profile branch (2ee8b493), not at 35903069 one process, one site; R50 and R55 reproduced the retention and recovery controls the evaluator role lib/server/serve/roles.js:27-29: a summary ("change feed, plugins and notifications; no listener") and no start does not exist as code

No "memory-ignore" marker exists in lib/, docs/ or tests/ of the CRM tree or in this repository's documents; the term in the brief has no source behind it and is not used here.

Contract for the multitenant roles, borrowing R50's retained-cycle policy and the seams plan's identity rule:

  1. Evaluator and notification state is keyed by (tenant, settings version, plugin set) with a bounded lifetime; a key change discards the retained cycle rather than carrying it across versions. There is no process-global mutable clinical frame.
  2. A failed clinical cycle retains the prior successful result and timestamp and creates no new ordinary/alarm notification request; the next real trigger recovers (R50, R55 frame-retention control: null replacing the kept properties is the red). Independently committed, authorized ACK/snooze controls under D23 remain effective and may produce a control-clear while acquisition fails. That control effect does not mark the clinical cycle successful.
  3. Ack and snooze are per tenant writes. D23 names their writer: the client acks on the /alarm socket as today, realtime forwards the ack, like every other socket write, unchanged to api's internal write endpoint, and api persists a tenant-keyed ack row that the evaluator reads from the feed like any other committed row, so an ack survives a consumer restart by replay and realtime holds no storage write authority. A forward that fails yields no acknowledgement, so the client's existing no-ack retry applies. The roadmap keeps "owner ack/snooze and actual notification delivery" on their separate gates, so the row's shape and historical retention remain implementation/operational work; the later decision above settles suppression scope, original expiry and active-window repeats.
  4. The retained cycle's inputs are the tenant's rows at or below the consumer's checkpoint; the evaluation instant is recorded with the cycle and is not a database revision (R49).

docs.title: Durable notification request handoff
docs.text:
The maintainer adopted durable requests and retries for the explicit multitenant preview after reviewing actual-component/synthetic- provider ambiguity evidence on 57d54963. That evidence models lost process-local state through component recreation; it is not a measured process crash, live provider acceptance or device delivery. The decision selects the responsibility for retry; joined implementation acceptance remains separate.

  1. Persist tenant-bound accepted request intent and a stable logical request identity before dispatch. Retry that identity after restart or an ambiguous provider result. Input checkpoint/floor alone is not an identity: time-only evaluation and unstamped changes can produce distinct evaluated outputs.
  2. Persisted intent, send attempt, adapter acceptance/receipt and device delivery are distinct facts. A lost response after external acceptance can lead to a repeated notification. Clinical-record write identity prevents neither that ambiguity nor the repeated external effect. No exactly-once delivery is claimed.
  3. Preserve existing normal alarm/snooze/repeat-window behavior and tenant-wide suppression/original expiry. Current authority, configuration identity and suppression must govern dispatch/retry; a queued request cannot bypass them. Failed clinical cycles enqueue no new ordinary/alarm request. Independently committed, authorized ACK/snooze controls may enqueue a control-clear; their effects are distinct from clinical-cycle success. Shutdown fences late dispatch/publication.
  4. Preserve the single-tenant path and existing client/wire shapes. New durable preview recovery is not evidence of equivalent external failure behavior: retrying an uncertain send can repeat an alert. Reuse shared seams only with explicit default/single compatibility verification.
  5. Joined M5 acceptance exercises actual notification consumers with controlled adapters: ordinary alarm, snooze, active repeat window, restart, ambiguous acceptance, failed cycle, foreign tenant/configuration and shutdown. Verify stable retry identity and persisted state independently. Actual selected provider/device delivery retains its own gate. Uploader corpus passes cannot substitute for notification-consumer evidence. Select actual browser alarm presentation/ack consumers and existing notification cache contracts, with controlled Pushover/Maker-compatible sinks where admitted. Run joined restricted-PG/process-death, lost-completion and same-identity retry controls, including snooze/config changes before retry and D23 ack/no-ack stored outcomes. Pinned mobile socket-pattern replay is not execution of those mobile binaries; neither proves live provider/device delivery.

Request storage/state-machine layout and a controlled synthetic sink are implementation choices within these effects. Provider selection, retry timing, queue retention and capacity need their own measurements/contracts; no numeric budget or live egress is authorized by this decision.

docs.title: 8. Entry bar before any implementation
docs.text:
The roadmap asks for executable controls before one producer/consumer recovery slice. Each row names the predicted green and the exact red symptom; a control that goes red for a setup reason is not evidence (clock proof plan). The rows below retain the original predicted controls. docs.title: 9. What this contract does not decide
docs.text:
For the current decision queue, use the M5/M6 decision list. The later snapshot-reconciliation choice in §11 settles the initial current-state absence backstop; the historical spine limitations below do not reopen that choice.

Question Status provider: logical replication slot with wal2json-style decoding versus poll-only versus change streams deferred, research continuing. D6 selected the slot as spine on T4.1's 2026-09-15 measurement; the seams plan reopens provider selection; nothing here closes it. The contract is written so that the slot, a poll, or both satisfy it, because the spine is the rows and the stamp, not the transport multi-node consumers: leasing a tenant to one evaluator, failover, split-brain deferred. The seams plan says a cell lease cannot by itself establish these guarantees; the single-machine separate-role reference deployment is the adopted first proof (clock proof plan) retention horizon: how far behind a checkpoint may fall before replay is refused; slot WAL retention UNMEASURED. T4.1 measured one stop of 200 rows performance budgets: contention, fresh-ingestion latency, lock-held work, evaluator cost per tenant UNMEASURED; the clock reports say so in the same words, and the benchmark is opt-in and pending whether configuration and grant rows appear on the feed deferred; §5 makes consumers correct without it tombstones for hard deletes deferred; §4 keeps hard deletes outside the spine the storage shape and retention of per-tenant ack/snooze rows separate gate per the roadmap; the writer is settled by D23 (api, via the realtime forward) which floor the event carries when an outer transaction allocates more stamps after a nested write resolved: the write's own floor (as built, at most the final floor) or the transaction's final floor (readable from the clock state in the after-commit callback) decided, maintainer, 2026-11-06: the transaction's final floor. The event names the cohort that committed together, read from the clock state in the after-commit callback; built on codex/event-payload-20261106 at e7baff74a8da0035a2ff473ecadf09123abbdeb7: the clock hands each after-commit publish the final floor, a nested-allocation test asserts it (unit 134 / 33 / 0; the stamp-null control 7 / 3 with "the event carries the final floor, not the floor at resolve", restored 10), and the Mongo-gated d-event suite ran on MongoDB 8.0.34 at 103 / 0 / 0. Either choice keeps §3 ordering; the final floor makes the event's stamp equal the cohort's stamp anything about single-tenant MongoDB out of scope; D4 and the D-EVENT scope decision keep the in-process bus there M5/M6 promotion, RC admission, default enablement no; this is a design acceptance input for batch B7, nothing more

docs.title: 10. Decisions this contract makes
docs.text:
For the reviewer's convenience, the decisions above in one list, each one a sentence the entry bar in §8 can falsify:

  1. The spine is committed rows plus their commit stamp; events are latency.
  2. A checkpoint is a per-tenant, per-consumer database row under the tenant's binding; never process memory.
  3. The interprocess event carries tenant and stamp, or is treated as a wake-up.
  4. Delivery is at-least-once; consumers are idempotent on (tenant, stamp, collection, typed identity).
  5. Progress is by complete equal-stamp cohort, never by page.
  6. Soft deletes are events; hard deletes and raw writers are outside the spine.
  7. Authority and settings are re-read per operation or per cycle, not invalidated by event.
  8. Replay covers crash-after-commit; the publish covers nothing.
  9. Time-only alarm ticks are separate from the later adopted snapshot-reconciliation schedule; a wake or tick alone establishes no recovery guarantee.
  10. Evaluator and notification state is keyed by tenant, settings version and plugin set, with R50's retention policy.
  11. The contract applies only where the commit-coupled stamp exists; the clock (batch B2) is therefore a prerequisite of the first recovery slice, and the clock is absent from the original anchor 35903069. B2 has since joined it locally; R56 owns the joined baseline and its measured limits.

docs.title: 11. Maintainer acceptance and experiments
docs.text:
The bounded snapshot reconciliation decision selects the initial M5 current-state recovery path. It preserves existing writer contracts and requires explicit row/byte refusal. R73 records bounded functional implementation/native acceptance for the first reference; scan cadence/capacity budgets remain separate measurements. Every-transition and external notification-delivery guarantees retain their own contracts.

The maintainer adopted B7's design direction on 2026-11-06 in the B7 approval chat: proceed with tenant-local durable checkpoints, commit-coupled ordering, at-least-once replay and idempotent consumers, and use experiments to inform scalability and performance. The decision is recorded in the release decisions. This accepts the direction and the executable entry bar, not measured distributed recovery, a performance budget, a provider, milestone promotion or release admission. R73 supplies the functional M5 disposition and recorded instruments. The queue owns broader item state and remaining admission gates; this design document does not make a fresh current-HEAD or production acceptance claim.

What UNMEASURED means. The named behavior has no applicable executed capture on the stated assembled source and workload. It is neither a failure nor a pass. A source reading is a hypothesis; a focused positive and mechanism-specific red control support only the schedules and source actually exercised. Existing clock proofs do not establish distributed consumer or notification recovery.

Correctness experiments before runtime acceptance. Implement the §8 positives and paired breaks in an isolated synthetic producer/consumer slice. Also cut the consumer at each boundary between processing, durable notification handoff and checkpoint persistence: demonstrate no lost accepted durable intent and no second logical request identity for the same retry. Repeated external attempts/effects remain possible after ambiguous acceptance under the adopted retry policy. Provider delivery to a device remains a separate acceptance. Exercise subscription during concurrent commits so startup cannot depend on an uncovered gap between catch-up and listening. Measure an update that overwrites a row, then another update or hard delete before replay: state convergence from current rows is not proof that every intermediate transition can be recovered. Specify which transitions the evaluator must preserve and whether a retained log, outbox or tombstone is required. These are questions for the prototype, not added guarantees.

Performance experiments before capacity claims. Pin the assembled head, hardware, data size and consumer count; compare clock on/off at identical load. Sweep active and idle tenants, write rate per tenant, burst size, bulk cohorts, reconnect backlog and slow consumers. Include one hot tenant beside ordinary tenants on a shared pool. Capture commit-to-view and commit-to-evaluation p50/p95/p99, clock lock wait/hold time, throughput, pool occupancy, CPU/memory, database reads, checkpoint writes, replay lag/catch-up duration and retained bytes. Evaluate idle poll overhead separately: aggregate work depends on tenants and poll frequency, not only incoming writes. Declare workload-specific freshness and recovery targets before judging an operating envelope; do not invent a tenant capacity from a green functional suite.

How results change expectations. Correctness positives with meaningful red controls support bounded recovery claims. A load sweep establishes where freshness and recovery targets hold, and where queues grow. Contention may require shorter transactions or admission limits; aggregate polling cost may require batching or a different provider; lost intermediate transitions may require retained history. Per-tenant ordering avoids a global ordering requirement, but shared pools, CPU, retention and database I/O can still couple tenants. Architecture and provider choices remain revisitable when experiments refute their assumptions.

docs.title: Evaluator, realtime and API communication
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-10 at 4917b2d4a.

Contributor-facing living explanation, 2026-11-07. Mechanisms below are read-derived from cgm-remote-monitor 151de0248a1e4301c85b5c638185eec3ca8c38e6, tree 3bb46431a19e604dc028768f0e72e6ad29616c26. Source file/line anchors were checked against that immutable tree. These are branch implementation mechanisms; pinned source links identify the inspected revision, not a released feature. Recorded reproductions retain their own source in the evidence section. The later c23 native matrix measures bounded tenant-local restart behavior; it does not relabel this inspected tree as the executed source.

This guide explains which process owns each result and which messages cross a boundary. Decisions remain in tenancy decisions, the durable event contract, owner authority and the release decisions. The delivery dashboard owns milestone status; this guide does not promote M6.

docs.title: The two outputs have different owners
docs.text:
Realtime and evaluator each acquire clinical data from PostgreSQL. The evaluator does not send its SQL projection to realtime. Realtime builds the browser's record frames from its own bounded projection and checkpoint. Separately, evaluator consumers can send a durable alarm/notification intent to realtime for browser fanout. That handoff is not a glucose-data replication stream or proof of device notification delivery.

Component Owns Reads or sends API process Current client authority, REST and existing socket write handlers, canonical clinical mutation Tenant-bound PostgreSQL writes; scoped secrets; private socket authorization/mutation receiver Evaluator process Clinical acquisition, plugin cycle and eligibility of its current in-memory output Its own durable input checkpoint/projection; current configuration; independently scheduled durable notification producer/retries Realtime process Browser connections, socket namespace state, independent current-record projection Its own SQL reads/checkpoint; current API authorization; private API mutation forwarding; private alarm receiver Tenant-admin process Current tenant management and owner authority Separate listener and management credential audience; it does not execute clinical socket writes Private restore controller A's suspension, draining and exclusive maintenance claim, committed-data and activation outcome Fixed participants' control endpoints and actual backend identities; per-tenant invalidation

These are application modules wired by explicit preview role configuration. Separate processes/containers can share a private directory containing Unix-domain sockets (UDS): an endpoint is a transport address, not shared JavaScript memory. The adopted separate-process decision retains this deployment boundary. A local EventEmitter does not become a durable cross-process event bus merely because the processes share a host.

docs.title: Clinical acquisition and browser records
docs.text:
The evaluator's acquisition first commits a bounded current-state projection and input checkpoint, then computes the clinical/plugin cycle. Its checkpoint records input acquisition, not completed evaluation or notification delivery. A later failure can therefore leave committed input with no eligible evaluated output. The runtime reports an output revision only from a successful cycle and requires an admitted tenant operation for last(tenant) to expose it. Evaluator acquisition, runtime output and durable snapshot/checkpoint implement these separate stages.

Adopted 2026-11-10, not in the inspected tree. The output revision changes only when the output content changes (time-driven changes included); an identical cycle keeps its revision, and the realtime consumer is woken on real changes only for tenants with a pending alarm. The inspected code bumps the revision on every cycle (read-derived, cited in the decision). Alarm repetition is separate: an active, unacknowledged, unsnoozed alarm repeats on its own clock equal to the single-site heartbeat (same setting, 60 s by default) and on new data, as on a single site. Both are BF-231 / MT-CONSUMER-STALE-RESELECT work. The evaluator only works tenants eligible under the activity policy: while a site is paused or suspended no alarms are computed or delivered.

sequenceDiagram
    participant API as API process
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    participant Eval as Evaluator process
    participant RT as Realtime process
    participant Browser as Browser
    API->>PG: Canonical tenant write + forward tenant clock
    PG-->>API: COMMIT acknowledged
    par Evaluator acquisition schedule
        Eval->>PG: Tenant-bound bounded current snapshot
        Eval->>PG: Persist evaluator input projection/checkpoint
        PG-->>Eval: Snapshot transaction COMMIT
        Eval->>Eval: Compute plugins, publish eligible output revision
    and Realtime recovery/refresh schedule
        RT->>PG: Tenant-bound bounded current snapshot
        RT->>PG: Persist realtime projection/checkpoint
        PG-->>RT: Snapshot transaction COMMIT
        RT->>RT: Build browser frame, recheck current configuration
        RT-->>Browser: dataUpdate, full replacement (delta:false)
    end

The namespaces for evaluator and realtime checkpoints must be distinct. Role composition enforces that ownership boundary. Realtime projection builds a full replacement frame, including absence, so a hard-deleted record is not retained by a delta-only merge. Its runtime rechecks the configuration identity before fanout and exposes no healthy last value after refusal. Realtime refresh supplies these checks.

Public API3 identifier and the storage _id are different identities. A browser SGV frame carries the stored record key in _id and its value in mgdl; an API3 POST acknowledgement names the public identifier. Bind them through the actual stored record when comparing transports, rather than assuming the strings match. The shipping frame loader preserves this distinction.

The current reference uses bounded snapshot reconciliation and polling schedules. It does not implement the full replication-slot/reader-NOTIFY design as a transport between these roles. The durable-event contract owns that longer-term direction; R73's polling/snapshot acceptance does not imply a LISTEN latency guarantee. Time-only evaluator ticks reuse retained successful input; they do not substitute for fresh acquisition or establish recovery after missed writes.

docs.title: Notification intents, retries and alarm handoff
docs.text:
The evaluator's optional realtime consumer is separately scheduled from clinical computation. It reads eligible current output and current configuration, reconciles persisted producer state and suppression acknowledgements, and records durable intents with stable origin/request identity. The producer must still be current after pending reads. The coordinator then selects due requests for retry. Producer and consumer coordinator implement this path; when no consumer is selected, it opens no extra consumer pool, timer or socket.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Eval as Evaluator runtime
    participant Consumer as Evaluator notification consumer
    participant PG as PostgreSQL outbox / suppression
    participant RT as Realtime private alarm receiver
    participant Browser as Authorized browser
    Eval-->>Consumer: Current eligible output + configuration identity
    Consumer->>PG: Reconcile producer state and enqueue stable intents
    PG-->>Consumer: Durable request state committed
    Consumer->>PG: Claim due attempt, commit dispatch token/deadline
    Consumer->>Consumer: Recheck current eligibility and suppression
    Consumer->>RT: POST JSON /alarm over private UDS
    RT->>RT: Current tenant/socket authority checks
    RT-->>Browser: Alarm / clear event for admitted tenant sockets
    RT-->>Consumer: accepted:true (handoff receipt, not device ACK)
    Consumer->>PG: Persist accepted or uncertain attempt outcome
    opt Lost response or restart
        Consumer->>PG: Read durable due/uncertain request
        Consumer->>RT: Retry same stable request identity
    end

The attempt and dispatch state commit before the adapter call; the network wait is not held inside SQL. Deadline, abort or an ambiguous response preserves a durable retryable outcome. Before dispatch, the notifier rechecks configuration eligibility and the current suppression reader, so an old selected cycle is not standing permission to deliver. Notification attempts owns the implementation. Clear requests have their own retirement/suppression handling; this is not a blanket rule to discard every request when an output is unavailable.

The actual alarm adapter sends tenant, request ID, attempt, notification and receipts to /alarm. Acceptance means the realtime handoff completed. It does not mean a browser displayed it, a person acknowledged it, or a provider/device received it. A lost handoff response can repeat the unchanged request: there is no exactly-once delivery promise.

A browser's ack follows the private API mutation route below. API checks current credential/tenant permission and, for linked consumer state, current evaluator configuration inside the acknowledgement admission. It persists original suppression state; the evaluator subsequently reads that state. Private acknowledgement admission is distinct from the transport receipt acknowledging an evaluator-to-realtime handoff.

The diagrams above follow the inspected tree. The 2026-11-10 decisions (evaluator-revision-on-content-change, alarm-repeat-clock, activity-is-pause-suspend) change when the consumer is woken and how an active alarm repeats. Built on lanes 956d0940 and 07981b55, in the batch join that is in acceptance; evidence.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Act as Tenant activity row
    participant Eval as Evaluator runtime
    participant Consumer as Notification consumer
    participant RT as Realtime alarm-delivery
    Eval->>Act: Read the state before each cycle and before publishing
    alt paused or suspended
        Eval->>Eval: No cycle and no output, and the consumer skips the tenant
    else active
        Eval->>Eval: Compute output and its content digest
        alt content changed (new data or time-driven)
            Eval->>Consumer: New revision and a targeted wake
            Consumer->>RT: deliverAlarm for the new or changed request
        else identical content
            Eval->>Eval: Keep the revision, no wake
        end
        loop alarm active, unacknowledged and unsnoozed
            Consumer->>Consumer: Repeat clock: last processing + tenant heartbeat (60 s default)
            Consumer->>RT: deliverAlarm again
        end
    end
    Note over Eval,Consumer: After unpause the evaluator recomputes from current data before publishing

docs.title: Browser authorization and mutations
docs.text:
Socket.IO exposes /, /storage and /alarm. Tenant resolution uses the admitted host/configuration mapping. The root namespace accepts the existing authorize shape; /storage and /alarm use their own subscription/credential contracts. Their credential forms and permissions are not interchangeable. The realtime protocol rechecks current authority across asynchronous acquisition and before fanout; a long-lived connection is not a permanent grant.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser as Browser / existing socket client
    participant RT as Realtime process
    participant API as API private UDS receiver
    participant PG as Tenant-bound PostgreSQL
    Browser->>RT: authorize / subscribe with client credential
    RT->>API: /authorize (host, tenant, namespace, credential)
    API->>PG: Current credential + tenant authority reads
    API-->>RT: Current permissions / selected collections
    RT-->>Browser: Namespace-specific acknowledgement and admitted data
    Browser->>RT: Existing mutation or ack event
    RT->>API: /mutate (host + original tenant/credential/event envelope)
    API->>API: Resolve tenant, authenticate transport AND client authority
    API->>PG: Existing socket write handler / suppression transaction
    PG-->>API: Canonical operation completes
    API-->>RT: Existing callback arguments
    RT-->>Browser: Unchanged callback acknowledgement

Realtime does not replace the user's credential with its database identity. Forwarding preserves the event namespace, arguments and callback shape. Failure or ambiguity produces no synthetic success and no automatic socket mutation retry. The API executor invokes the same socket write handlers/purifier/write intents as the single-tenant socket listener. This is a private HTTP/JSON call over UDS, not a replay of a public REST request. Public REST requests use the real API handlers and shared storage/write-intent ports directly.

The private API independently resolves the host and compares the envelope's tenant, authenticates the owned transport, verifies the current client credential and checks the operation's permission. Private API and namespace credential normalization define these boundaries. A socket-path possession check is not permission to mutate a tenant's records.

docs.title: Wire format and operation lifetimes
docs.text:
The current private transport uses bounded JSON objects in HTTP POSTs over fixed UDS endpoints, with explicit byte/time limits and restrictive same-UID filesystem/socket ownership. It accepts a fixed operation list: /authorize, /mutate, /alarm, /cohort/status and /cohort/invalidate. Application payloads and cohort controls have different handlers; they are not a public administration API. A private directory and fixed manifest are deployment trust inputs, not an authentication substitute for each client's current authority.

A registered tenant operation surrounds actual HTTP response completion, not just entry into a handler. API lifetime middleware waits for response finish/close; private IPC similarly retains its lifetime through response finish. Socket authorization, forwarding, clinical/evaluator acquisition and notification attempts also use the actual operation window. Tenant-scoped lower handles enforce that window when used. These lifetimes let maintenance drain real unfinished work rather than infer quiescence from a callback returning.

docs.title: Disconnect, restart and tenant-local restore
docs.text:
Ordinary process restart reacquires current records and persisted checkpoints. An evaluator's in-memory output is recomputed; a committed input checkpoint is not relabelled as a successful output. Realtime rebuilds its own projection and full browser frame. Durable notification requests survive and retain their retry identity. Current credentials/configuration are checked again; retained process memory does not authorize a new connection.

The logical restore policy requires forward changes and deletion records for known captured/current clinical identities, preserving public IDs and clinical fields. It retains current nonclinical authority, consumer state and the authoritative live clock; physical backup fidelity is a separate operation. Activity retains its existing full-read behavior rather than acquiring a new v3 history contract. IDs purged from both artifact and current retained history remain outside that bounded guarantee. Logical restore source enforces captured/live floor checks.

The controller suspends A durably, drains A operations and holds an actual backend-bound exclusive claim. After definite outer DATA commit, it runs registered commit effects, invalidates the configured roles' tenant caches/sockets/output, then activates A. A's sockets disconnect; fresh readers and evaluator acquisition must obtain the restored current state. B has independent tenant operation keys and counters. Lost COMMIT or invalidation acknowledgement does not authorize blind replay, orphan clearance or expiry-based reopening. Controller contract and participant protocol supply this ordering; participant incarnation changes invalidate an old pin.

docs.title: Independent startup on the inspected candidate
docs.text:
At 151de024, shared schema/ACL checks remain unconditional. Genuine suspension from the actual registered operation gate defers only that tenant's initialization; a lookalike error code, metadata drift, bad binding, transport failure or other application failure is not swallowed as suspension. The full configured tenant roster remains present. A deferred tenant retries through the same gate when work is admitted, with invalidation retiring its cached initialization. Tenant startup implements this provenance distinction; evaluator metadata admission runs READ ONLY, and consumer admission retains unconditional metadata and actual same-datastore checks before tenant-local initialization.

Consequently the source intends a restarted shared API/realtime/evaluator process to serve active B while suspended A remains unavailable, with no stale A output. Realtime startup, API startup and evaluator startup use that mechanism. Aggregate health can remain degraded while B is available: do not omit A from the roster or require A to become active merely to make a process health summary green. The c23 native matrix reproduces this bounded restart criterion on its exact later source; the inspected 151de024 mechanisms above remain read-derived.

docs.text:
Record Actual accepted scope Remaining boundary R73 durable runtime and bounded operations Reproduced functional M5 reference on its recorded source: durable bounded acquisition, current socket authority/compatibility, suppression and stable-request handoff; complete named broad acceptance on that tree Current polling/snapshot reference does not establish provider/device delivery, capacity, multi-node ownership or all later source b029 native operation-window matrix Reproduced all 17 criteria on b029f5d8: actual four CLI roles, forward logical history, B progress, rollback, changed-participant refusal, real COMMIT/invalidation acknowledgement loss and orphan refusal; independent physical closure Not new-source restart-while-A-suspended acceptance, Compose/browser acceptance, released feature or whole M6 c23 native operation-window matrix Reproduced actual fresh shared API/realtime/evaluator startup with B progress while A remained unavailable after the recorded failure cases; unsafe-clock API startup refused; independent physical closure Fixed trusted cooperative participants, private serving credentials and database ingress. Application modules above are real code selected by explicit role configuration. Recording connections, monkey-patched observers, COMMIT-loss proxies, privileged same-PID/different-birth seeds and synthetic fixtures belong to the evidence harnesses. They are not deployed communication services or credential providers. The b029 record distinguishes real backend death from its separate privileged counterfactual. Reproduced handoff or browser protocol equivalence does not imply an Android binary, rig, external provider or device-delivery test ran.

Record

docs.title: 1. What M4 asks for, and what today's evidence is
docs.text:
The roadmap §4 criterion for M4: v1 and v3 uploader/follower shapes exercised on pinned versions; no coordinated app upgrade requirement; tenant-local identity and correct batch/retry/refusal semantics. The dashboard adds: actual client execution distinguished from source-pattern replay, with M4 blocked on M3.

Today's client evidence is source-pinned synthetic replay, not client execution:

  • R40 pins NightscoutKit 4ec9fd12 and LoopFollow 4a74b781 and says "this is extracted client-pattern replay, not execution of Swift binaries". R41 repeats "server contracts and synthetic client patterns, not execution of client applications". The owned runner's README says the same (tools/lab/multitenant-rest-preview/README.md).
  • The CRM test that does it is tests/tenant-rest-client-replay.integration.test.js (opt-in NS_REST_CLIENT_REPLAY_TEST=1), whose fixture tests/fixtures/client-replay-patterns.js:5-8 states "Source-derived synthetic patterns, not execution of either Swift application." Its deployment fixture tests/fixtures/client-replay-http.js:3 boots the shipping multitenant CLI as a child (:98, bin/nightscout.js multitenant api) with two tenants in direct-alias resolution (:45-47) and selects the tenant with an explicit Host header (:136-142).
  • The November 2 draft PR body in this directory (multitenant-draft-pr-body-2026-11-02.md, a peer's file) carries only the M1–M3 "remains open" statements; the client-binary wording lives in R40/R41 and in the CRM READMEs, and in the live #8898 body the maintainer refreshed from R54, which is not in this repository.

So M4's gap is exactly: run real client programs, at their pinned versions, against the preview executable, and classify every difference from single-site Mongo. This packet ranks which clients can be run at all on a Linux lab host, designs the lab for the top three, and names what stays unmeasured afterwards.

docs.title: 2. What credential an unmodified legacy client presents, and what the preview accepts
2.1 Shipping single-site extraction (what every client was written against)
docs.text:
lib/authorization/index.js at 35903069 (shipping, unchanged by the preview):

Carrier Where the server reads it Line Authorization: Bearer <jwt> extractJWTfromRequest :34 ?token=<accessToken> in the query req.query.token :40 ?secret= in the query, else the api-secret header apiSecretFromRequest :76 the admin secret hash as api-secret authorizeAdminSecret :178 a subject access token presented in the api-secret header doesAccessTokenExist(data.api_secret) :201-203

The journey lab catalogues the same dialects per app (tools/review/journey-lab/clients.js:13-19): secret (api-secret header = SHA-1 of the API secret: Loop, Trio, LoopCaregiver, xDrip), jwt (Bearer from the v2 exchange: AAPS v3, nightguard v3), token-query (LoopFollow, Nightscout Reporter), token-path (the exchange request itself), token-header (raw access token in API-SECRET: nightguard v1), socket (AAPS NSClient v1 authorize).

docs.title: 2.2 The preview's extraction and verification
docs.text:
The preview reads credentials through its own extractor and verifies them inside the tenant's secrets boundary; nothing from the single-site enclave is reused.

Rule Source Only the authorization and api-secret headers are read; a duplicated header makes the request invalid lib/authorization/credential-extraction.js:17-22 Authorization: Bearer <token> → carrier bearer (v3 accepts any case of bearer; v1/v2 require exactly Bearer) :32-38 API3 (/api/v3): a token or secret in the query or body makes the request invalid, never anonymous; api-secret header only :40-43; lib/secrets/legacy-credentials.md:96-99 v1/v2: api-secret from req.api_secret, ?secret=, the header, or a body secret; token from Bearer, else ?token= or a body token → carrier legacy :44-59 A presented-but-empty credential is invalid; a supplied invalid credential never becomes anonymous :61-62; legacy-credentials.md:52-54 A legacy-carrier token is first exchanged (secrets.exchangeLegacyCredential, the R26 path) and the issued JWT is then verified; an api-secret goes straight to verifyLegacyCredential (the R25 path) lib/server/tenant-app/data-access.js:108-116 A new-format Ed25519 token (typ: ns-access+jwt, R48) is recognised first and verified locally against operator-provisioned public keys and current PostgreSQL state; no legacy fallback for a recognised new token data-access.js:98-107; lib/tenant-authorization/access-tokens.md:3-6, 44-50, 66-70 Root verification and subject derivation reproduce the shipping enclave.js / authorization/storage.js SHA-1 forms, against the tenant's imported root reference and stable subject IDs legacy-credentials.md:63-69 The v2 exchange GET /api/v2/authorization/request/:accessToken is mounted only when the trusted exchange callback is injected; the path credential is the sole input; root credentials do not exchange; issuance is exactly eight hours lib/server/tenant-app/README.md:152-168, 181-187 Revocation: a request begun after a committed reference/grant removal performs new reads and refuses; no stale-success cache legacy-credentials.md:107-110 Pre-existing single-site JWTs are not assumed portable legacy-credentials.md:77-81 v1 and v2 data routes are composed from the shipping lib/api and lib/api2 factories with tenant-local storage ports (createV1(... { domains, apiEnabled: true }), createV2(... { compatibilityOnly: true })) lib/server/tenant-app/legacy-domains.js:4-5, 23-25 Tenant selection is by the wire Host against configured aliases (direct-alias), or by canonical internal names behind a trusted immediate peer (canonical-internal); no resolved-tenant header selects a tenant lib/tenant-resolution/index.js:58-71, 95, 128; lib/server/serve/preview-config.js:90-109

Finding. An unmodified legacy client that sends the SHA-1 api-secret header (the Loop/Trio/xDrip/oref0/connector dialect) or a Bearer JWT obtained from the v2 exchange (the AAPS v3/nightguard/librelink-up dialect) presents a shape the preview accepts on both v1 and v3. A client that puts its token in the query (LoopFollow, oref0 token mode, Reporter) is accepted on v1/v2 through the legacy-exchange path and refused on v3. The pinned-pattern replay already relies on this split (tests/tenant-rest-client-replay.integration.test.js:24-27: "the pinned uploader hashes its API secret and sends api-secret; the pinned follower sends its subject token in the query"; tests/fixtures/client-replay-patterns.js:66-76 builds the follower path with token in the query for v1 and v2). The intentional multitenant difference is that a supplied invalid credential refuses instead of falling back to anonymous (tenant-app/README.md:252-260). No pinned client emits a new-format Ed25519 token; R48's readers are an addition, not a requirement, and this is consistent with the roadmap's "no coordinated app upgrade" criterion.

What the lab must establish rather than assume: that the v1 legacy domains composed by legacy-domains.js carry the shipping count tolerance (RT-COUNT-COMPAT) and the shipping treatments write validation. Both are inherited by construction and both are UNMEASURED on the preview.
