docs.title: 4. Lab design for the top three (nightscout-connect, oref0, cgmsim-lib)
docs.text: The design borrows from four existing instruments by name: the journey lab (tools/review/journey-lab/: sites per app, scripted fire steps, a fake vendor upstream, secrets kept outside the tree and never printed), the compat pipeline (tools/qc/compat/: two trees, every differing cell explained, a verdict vocabulary), the id-batch-replies lab (tools/lab/id-batch-replies/: real connector module run cycle by cycle, stored rows counted from the database) and the connector-soak lab (tools/lab/connector-soak/: a source site and token/secret sinks through a counting proxy). The CRM-side scaffolding already exists in tests/fixtures/client-replay-http.js.

docs.title: 4.1 Server under test
docs.text:
• The explicit multitenant executable: bin/nightscout.js multitenant api (lib/cli/commands/multitenant.js:3-4, PLAT-SERVE D21; exit codes :6-13), with a preview configuration shaped as tests/multitenant-preview-process.integration.test.js:41-56 builds it: resolution.mode = direct-alias, two tenants A and B, each with one alias, per-tenant Vault encryption/signing keys, operator-applied candidate schemas in separate namespaces, the legacy credential catalogue, and domains covering entries, treatments, devicestatus and profile (the collections the three clients touch).
  • Disposable PostgreSQL and Vault owned by the run, as the owned runner does (tools/lab/multitenant-rest-preview/README.md); never a shared database.
  • Tenant A and B each get an imported root reference and one imported subject with the readable role, provisioned the way the replay fixture provisions them (the root credential a client presents is the SHA-1 of A's root, client-replay-http.js:277).
  • Name resolution is the first setup item. The preview selects the tenant from the wire Host. Real client binaries resolve a hostname themselves, so the lab must make A's and B's aliases reach the loopback listener without editing any client: run each client in its own container with host entries for the two aliases, or run the lab's own resolver. Do not switch to canonical-internal for this: it changes the trust surface (preview-config.js:90-101). The setup control: a plain status read with A's credential and A's alias answers from A, and the same read with an unconfigured alias refuses as an unknown tenant (the M2 criterion) before any client is started.

docs.title: 4.2 Single-site baseline
docs.text: The same head 35903069 booted single-site on a disposable MongoDB (the compat pipeline's and the matrix harness's boot, tools/qc/write-contract-matrix.js:15-19), with AUTH_DEFAULT_ROLES=denied, one API secret and one readable subject. Every client run is executed once against the baseline and once against tenant A of the preview, from the same container image and the same client version, in the same order.

docs.title: 4.3 Per-client runs, positive checks, controls and predictions
docs.text:
Each run records, per request: method, path without query values, status, reply shape (array length, per-item keys), and afterwards the stored rows read through an independent oracle (the lab's own PostgreSQL reader for the preview, as client-replay-http.js reads rows; MongoDB for the baseline). Oracle rows are compared with only the normalisation the compat pipeline already uses (cache/wire and top-level server clock stamps, R41's rule); nothing else is normalised.

Client Positive run on tenant A Predicted outcome (hypothesis) nightscout-connect, forever with the HTTP output pointed at A's alias and A's root secret, reading from the journey lab's fake-share.js as the vendor entries POSTed in arrays per poll; backfill on first poll; later polls send only new readings 200 with one reply object per item; A's oracle shows the readings with device: nightscout-connect; B's oracle is empty. srvModified may advance on a resend; logical rows do not change (R40) nightscout-connect, nightscout source reading tenant A with a pre-issued subject token, writing to the single-site baseline sink exchange at /api/v2/authorization/request/<token> then Bearer GETs with count and find exchange 200 with token,sub,permissionGroups,iat,exp; reads 200; the sink receives A's rows and nothing from B. Without a pre-issued token the connector's subject creation is refused: record the status, do not work around it oref0 ns-upload.sh for entries, treatments and devicestatus, in both credential modes (header and token= query), then ns-get latest-openaps-treatment, then oref0-upload-profile.js v1 POSTs; the treatment lookup with the malformed count=1?...; profile GET/PUT header mode: 200; query-token mode: 200 through the legacy exchange path (data-access.js:108-116); the malformed count answers as RT-COUNT-COMPAT decided on single-site, or differs, and either way the cell is classified; the hashed secret in the URL is a known client defect, so lab logs must apply the same URL redaction as lib/server/log-privacy.js cgmsim-lib driver: upload a synthetic series, read it back with count, read profile.json, read activity with find[created_at][$gte], then the filter DELETE on devicestatus v1 round trip including a filter DELETE reads and uploads 200; the filter DELETE either succeeds as single-site does or is explicitly refused; the preview's documented "no filter DELETE" applies to v3 (tenant-app/README.md:265-266), v1 is UNMEASURED and this cell decides it

Negative controls, run for every client:

Control Mechanism Predicted symptom Same client, same A credential, pointed at B's alias A's root hash does not verify against B's reference; A's subject token exchanges against B's authority and finds no subject refused (401 family); B's oracle unchanged; no row on A either. The exact status per carrier is recorded, not assumed Credential revoked mid-run the operator removes A's subject grant (token clients) or replaces A's root reference (secret clients) between two client cycles the next cycle refuses; rows from the earlier cycle remain; the client's own reaction (connector backoff in lib/backoff.js; oref0 "Unable to upload", exit 2; cgmsim-lib throws) is recorded as a client property Malformed batch an array in which one item is refusable on both stacks (the id-batch-replies scenarios are the model: a Temporary Target with bottom above top under WRITE_VALIDATION=reject; an entry with a non-hex _id) the per-item reply array has the same shape and the same refused index on the preview as on the baseline; the stored-row count is the same. A whole-batch refusal on one stack and per-item on the other is a cell to classify, not a pass Unknown alias a hostname not in the tenant configuration unknown-tenant refusal, no storage effect Absent credential the client run with no secret and no token anonymous denied refuses reads and writes on both stacks

Break-it controls for the lab itself (a check that has never failed is not evidence):

  • Remove the Host entries for the aliases: every positive check must go red with a resolution failure, not a 4xx.
  • Point the oracle at the wrong namespace or database: every stored-outcome assertion must go red with zero rows.
  • Plant one unapproved difference in a captured reply before classification: the classifier must report it as unexplained (the control the compat refresh lane used, roadmap §"RC backwards compatibility").
  • Restore each and re-run; the restored run is the one that counts.

docs.title: 4.4 Differential against single-site Mongo through the compat pipeline
docs.text:
The compat pipeline classifies cells that differ between two matrix runs into named groups with a verdict from Defect | Decided | Bug fix | No value change (releases/cgm-remote-monitor-16.0.0/compat/groups.yaml:10), and refuses to build the page while any cell is unexplained (tools/qc/compat/README.md, step 3). The lab reuses that classification and vocabulary, with one adapter the pipeline does not have today:

  • tools/qc/write-contract-matrix.js boots the server in-process from WC_WORKTREE via lib/server/server.js and reads stored state from MongoDB (:15-19, :23-26, :341-356, :427). It cannot boot multitenant api and cannot read PostgreSQL. So the lab does not run the matrix against the preview; it emits cells in the matrix's cell shape (collection, path, form, reply fields, stored fields) from its own client runs and oracles, and feeds the pair of cell sets to tools/qc/compat/wcdiff.py and classify_compat.py with the existing groups.yaml.
  • A cell that lands in no group stops the run with "unexplained", exactly as the pipeline does for a tree comparison. Differences already documented as intentional (strict invalid-credential refusal; dotted PATCH members refused with 400 on PostgreSQL; JSONB non-representable values refused) need their own group entries with verdict Decided and a decision basis before the run is called green.
  • Nothing in this comparison speaks for old releases: the pipeline's 15.0.9 → dev attribution stays separate, and no old-release-to-PostgreSQL transitivity is claimed.

docs.title: 4.5 Record and gate
docs.text:
• The run is recorded as one dated R entry in the integration record, with the client versions read from the packages that ran, the preview head, the Node/PostgreSQL/Vault versions printed by the runner, every control's exact symptom, and the classified cell table. Logs stay outside the tree; the record carries counts, not URLs.
  • A queue item is needed for this lab (none exists at main for M4 client execution; the nearest are ST-PG and TEN-LAB, whose no-gate notes name client replay as remaining). Its gate must be able to fail, declare its control in queue/gate-controls.yaml, and read the archived head with git show/git archive, never a checkout. The id is allocated when the item is written, not here.

docs.title: 4.6 D23 entry condition 2: the NSClient v1 socket sequence against a forwarding realtime
docs.text:
D23, adopted and amended on 2026-11-06 (execution plan §2.14), makes realtime a reader that forwards every socket write message and the alarm ack unchanged, with the socket's own authorization, to an internal write endpoint on api, which runs the write step with the socket source label and relays the result into the socket acknowledgement. Its entry condition 2 names this packet as the home for the proof, because AndroidAPS 3.4.2.3's NSClient (v1) plugin is the one corpus client whose whole upload path is the socket.

Server under test: the explicit multitenant executable serving api and a forwarding realtime for two tenants, as in §4.1, plus the single-site Mongo baseline of §4.2 on the same head.

Driver: a Node socket.io client replaying the plugin's message sequence as read from the pinned 3.4.2.3 source: authorize, a dbAdd for a treatment and a devicestatus, a dbUpdate by the id returned in the add's acknowledgement, the alarm ack, and a retried dbAdd after the driver withholds its own acknowledgement handling, which is what the plugin does when no ack arrives. The driver is pattern replay (R40's caveat applies: not execution of the plugin) and carries no payload from any real site.

Check Predicted green Exact red symptom each forwarded write is stored once on tenant A with source label socket, and the acknowledgement carries the same id or result string the single-site baseline returns stored rows and ack bodies equal across baseline and preview, per the compat verdict vocabulary a differing ack shape, a missing source label, or a row on tenant B the retried dbAdd after a withheld ack stores no duplicate one row, one ack on the retry two rows for one logical add control: acknowledge before api confirms (patch the forwarder in a scratch copy to reply before the forward resolves, then make the forward fail) the lost-write assertion goes red: an acknowledged add with no stored row if it stays green the assertion is vacuous; restore and rerun control: api unavailable the socket write receives no acknowledgement and the driver's retry fires; nothing is stored until api returns a success reply during the outage control: tenant A's socket credential on tenant B's alias authorize refused; no write reaches api any stored row on B single unchanged the baseline's socket writes go directly to storage as today; no forwarder in the path a forwarded write observed in single-site mode

Hop latency and its effect on the plugin's ack timeout are UNMEASURED and stay so until a quiet-hardware run; the control list above proves correctness of the forward, not its cost.

docs.title: 5. What M4 still leaves unmeasured after this lab
docs.text: Area Why the lab does not reach it Socket transport None of the three clients speaks socket.io. AAPS v3 /storage and /alarm namespaces, LoopFollow's authorize {secret: <token>}, and AAPS v1 dbAdd/dbUpdate (only on the unpinned 3.4.x master) are M5's gate (socket authorization, reconnect, tenant-local rooms), not M4's The NSClient v1 forward path alone is covered by §4.6 under D23; the v3 /storage and /alarm subscribe paths and LoopFollow's socket authorize remain outside this lab. Mobile binaries Every iOS client (Loop/NightscoutKit, Trio, LoopFollow, LoopCaregiver, nightguard, xDrip4iOS, DiaBLE) needs an Apple toolchain; xDrip+ and the AndroidAPS app need an emulator. The journey lab's REAL-APPS.md track is manual, needs HTTPS the phone trusts and a simulated pump, and proves app-side decisions the lab only predicts. Their request shapes remain source-pattern replay Retry semantics under outage R48 measured the server answering 503 with Vault or PostgreSQL paused; the clients' schedulers (NightscoutKit's 24-hour _id cache and completion-handler hang on DELETE error, AAPS WorkManager, xDrip retry-forever) are not executed. The connector's backoff is observable but not under a paused backend at soak scale Subject creation by clients LoopFollow and the connector's source mode create a subject through POST /api/v2/authorization/subjects; the preview's data plane mounts no such route (subject administration is the separate management app, R42). "No coordinated app upgrade" is unproven for any client whose onboarding creates a subject v3 uploader binaries nightscout-librelink-up (rank 4) is the only pinned headless v3 uploader and needs a fake LibreLinkUp upstream that does not exist in the repository; AAPS v3 is Android. The v3 uploader shape stays source-pattern replay plus the CRM's own API3 tests TLS, proxies, canonical-internal The lab uses plain HTTP and direct-alias; clients that insist on HTTPS, TRUST_PROXY behaviour and the trusted-peer mode are untouched The web client under the preview the browser tier runs against single-site boot only nightscout-connect in-process (CONNECT_SOURCE) inside a multitenant serving role the connector's internal output writes through storage ports, not HTTP; a per-tenant composition does not exist at 35903069 New-format Ed25519 tokens no pinned client emits them; R48's acceptance stands on its own synthetic issuer Capacity and latency nothing here is a benchmark

docs.title: 6. What the lab must not claim
docs.text:
• M4 promotion, or any milestone. Promotion is a maintainer decision recorded in the roadmap and dashboard after the criterion list is fully met.
  • Compatibility for any client that was not executed. A green run of three Node/bash clients says nothing about Swift, Kotlin or Java binaries; their rows stay source-pattern replay with the R40/R41 wording.
  • "No coordinated app upgrade requirement" as a general statement. The lab can say it for the credential shapes it exercised (SHA-1 header, query token on v1/v2, Bearer from the exchange) and must say it is unproven for subject-creating onboarding and sockets.
  • Equality of HTTP replies as proof of equal stored outcomes, or the reverse. Both are recorded; the classification is per cell.
  • That single-site behaviour is unchanged. That is the full nonbrowser and browser campaign's job on the batch head, not this lab's.
  • Anything about the vendor drivers beyond "the fake upstream was reached". Real vendor accounts, exports, traces or identifiers never enter the lab; every record is synthetic.
  • Old-release transitivity: the compat pipeline's 15.0.9/dev classification is a separate measurement and is not re-run here.

docs.title: 7. Traps read while preparing this packet
docs.text:
• The externals/nightscout-connect checkout is at 04102f9d, not the lock's b394411a, and its package version is 0.1.1 while the CRM depends on 0.1.0. Quote the version from the package that runs; a result labelled with the lock pin would be mislabelled.
  • The write-contract matrix cannot be pointed at the preview (§4.4); a brief that says "run the matrix against tenant A" is not executable as written.
  • The November 2 draft PR body in this directory is a peer's untracked file and does not contain the client-binary statement; cite R40/R41 and the CRM READMEs instead. It is never staged by anyone else.
  • The connector's scripts/librelinkup-lab.js uses real accounts; it is excluded from any lab under this programme.
  • AndroidAPS at the pinned 7e1d537d has no v1 socket client; a v1-socket result would have to come from the unpinned 3.4.x master and must be labelled as such.
  • The preview refuses a supplied invalid credential where single-site falls back to anonymous (tenant-app/README.md:252-260). A client that probes with a wrong secret and expects anonymous readable behaviour will see a difference that is Decided, not a defect.

docs.title: M5/M6: current decisions and next review
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-10 at 4917b2d4a.

Living contributor-facing decision index, 2026-11-10. Read this before older question packets. Release decisions own adopted policy; the roadmap owns acceptance; the queue/dashboard own claimed work/milestone state. This index records no new application measurement or promotion.

docs.title: Execute now
docs.text:
2026-11-09 restructure. M6 is now M6a identity and owner API, M6b lifecycle and keys, M6c deployment trust (in nightscout-deploy), M6d connector sync, and M7 production readiness (decision). The owner/OIDC native matrix runs through a disposable harness (MT-OIDC-NATIVE); the grant/reservation ceremony is retired. Vault connectivity is a Vault Agent sidecar (DEPLOY-VAULT-AGENT) plus a tokenFile read in core (MT-VAULT-TOKEN-FILE). The umbrella queue items are closed as superseded; one capability item per remaining gap.

The functional M5 reference on one host is accepted in R73. It includes bounded current-state/evaluator recovery, durable alarm/request state and actual reference-role/browser consumers, with accepted final comprehensive verification. Publication and remote CI retain their separate records; production/default admission and live provider/device delivery are not implied.

Reuse the recorded proof gates for source-identical evidence instead of repeating native cases for documentation changes. New source behavior still needs affected checks and an appropriate joined verification. Do not silently add later provider, capacity or multi-node work to the satisfied M5 functional bar.

M6 now includes accepted native tenant-local restore/restart and cold Compose reference evidence. The published ed2 candidate closes that bounded clinical restore capability; restoring or cloning credentials/identity is a separate contract. The owner/OIDC and internal service API work (M6a) and the lifecycle, key-retention, ownership and single-site provisioning work (M6b) have joined acceptance records (M6a, M6b); publication state and the remaining boundaries are in the release contents. The completion schedule owns assignments; the roadmap acceptance families own observable completion. Prefer a minimal working base with explicit later enhancements; that preference grants no production permission or criterion waiver.

docs.title: Settled: do not ask again
docs.text: Topic Canonical home / implementation boundary Supported PostgreSQL writers Exclusive application ownership: declared internal components and admitted maintenance tools cooperate on write/lifecycle contracts; external direct writers are unsupported with undefined behavior. The database ownership map defines command and persistence boundaries. Cooperating replicas remain possible; Kubernetes scale-out acceptance is separate. Current-state recovery Bounded full snapshot reconciliation first; preserve producer deletes/timestamps/replies. Cadence/capacity is measurement work. No every-transition promise. Shared human authentication Shared optional OIDC, provider-backed renewal first, equivalent single/multitenant support; preferred single opt-in ENABLE=oidc. Separate authorization adapters; no implicit root/management grant. OIDC provider outage Existing valid access until existing expiry, with current local authority/session checks, no new login or renewal and unchanged sensitive-action freshness. Equivalent optional single/multitenant behavior; provider-only revocation may remain unknown until expiry/recovery. Local implementation exists; signed native outage acceptance remains UNMEASURED. Alarm suppression scope and restart Tenant-wide group/level suppression, original expiry retained across restart, active-window repeats do not extend it. Per-user/device scope follows separately. Notification retry responsibility Persist request intent before dispatch; retry same identity. Preserve suppression/dedup/single behavior; joined notification-consumer verification required. No exactly-once external delivery claim. Deletion ceremony Explicit request + operator confirmation; cancellable before execution; no mandatory wait. Post-deletion 30-day key/artifact retention remains separate. First-preview ownership changes Operator-assisted; self-service co-owner/transfer follows separately. Last-owner, current authority, audit and secret boundaries remain required. Same-ID restore history Publish ordinary forward updates and deletions, preserving issued history floors and client convergence. Exact physical backup fidelity remains separate. Initial reconciliation covers identities retained live or in the artifact; prior hard purges absent both retain the existing history limitation. Published ed2 cold Compose and client acceptance now cover the bounded forward-history behavior; see the operation-window evidence above. Restore versus cloning Restore original tenant ID; clone establishes new secrets/credentials. Clinical sync does not transfer credential authority. Deleted-tenant keys/artifact Retain 30 days, then operator destroys keys. Destroy/after-window refusal still needs evidence; this does not set a deletion cancellation period. Tenant-local restore and ordering Per-tenant/collection ordering only; pursue tenant-local insertion state. Preserve other tenants' current state and supported client ordering. Standalone native proof retains its early SQL scope; later c23 native and ed2 packaged restore evidence covers the admitted fixed-cohort reference. No global restore pause selected. First-preview owner surface Projected display catalogue, bounded owner thresholds and alarm enables, single-tenant-equivalent credentials, wildcards accepted as single tenant accepts them, under the operator ceiling, tightening applies to both and is a separate proposal, no owner integrations yet. D22 floors stand. Implementation and consuming-runtime tests remain open. First-preview external delivery No live push provider; Nightscout-to-Nightscout sync via nightscout-connect in both directions, outbound first; per-kind operator/owner credential parts; single-tenant constants as first bounds; admission by probes and lab sync. Pushover/Maker deferred. Connector actor and lab sync remain open. M6 human session effects Idle/absolute lifetimes scoped to management sessions only; always-on displays unchanged; local-first logout, provider optional, signal-less providers admitted with disclosure; fenced idempotent renewal; both browser transports, HttpOnly cookie default, headless bearer unchanged. The OIDC native matrix runs in the M6b joined acceptance; real identity-provider interoperability is synthetic only. M6 deployment and trust Peer-list ingress trust, one list for tenant selection and client IP; Vault Transit at every stage, connected through a Vault Agent sidecar with one AppRole per deployment (this replaces the earlier service-login adapter as application work); generic OIDC adapter, Authentik intended reference subject to the Kratos proof; admission by trust record plus live probes. Synthetic Compose edge/TLS Vault is measured at the reference scope; Vault Agent renewal/rotation probes, provider proof and production deployment remain UNMEASURED. Single-site OIDC identity list Each start re-applies the list; list-managed people taken off it are removed; fallback roles for unlisted people. MT-OIDC-SINGLE-PROVISION carries the implementation. Deployment tree home nightscout-deploy holds the Compose tree from the next #8898 batch on; core keeps only the fixture its own tests boot. Refines the 2026-11-09 move. Activity policy Pause and suspend, no third state; owner may pause; deletion request pauses; activity row always provisioned; 423 refusal codes. The admission and activity guide holds mechanism and acceptance; MT-ACTIVITY-ELIGIBILITY carries implementation. Root and admin tools Tenant API_SECRET has single-site parity; root may edit any subject, not the last owner; role edit/delete rules; grant ceiling * by default; admin-role subjects use the admin tools. Owner authority states the rules; MT-ROOT-ADMIN-PARITY carries implementation. Restore census and ownership phase Census admits identities whose grants exclude clinical tables; ownership operations need an active tenant; counter writers are refused too, ownership changes allowed during export. Export removal at key destruction Key destruction removes the export file it knows by digest; no retry of a failed removal. Admin listener address Same address as the public API on a different port is allowed; never every interface; non-loopback still needs the acknowledgement. Internal listener One serve.internal listener per role, Ory-style host/port or socket with a socket default; graceful shutdown with a deadline. MT-ENDPOINT-TRANSPORT carries implementation. Evaluator revision and alarm repeat Revision changes only on content change; targeted consumer wake; active alarms repeat on their own clock equal to the single-site heartbeat. BF-231, MT-CONSUMER-STALE-RESELECT. Legacy authority and management split Reader clamp withdrawn; preserve own-tenant credentials; owner authority governs separate management audience, current authority and adopted lifetimes. Socket writer and recovery direction D23: realtime forwards to API with existing protocol/source; failure gives no acknowledgement. First runtime proof uses separate roles on one machine. No multi-node lease claim.

docs.title: Human policy review
docs.text:
These are bounded topics for a concrete proposal, not blanket implementation stops. A recommendation remains a proposal until recorded in release decisions. Shared OIDC/provider-backed renewal, bounded existing access during provider outage and tenant-wide alarm suppression are adopted. Review remaining session effects and operational parameters while implementation continues. Notification retry responsibility and deletion ceremony policy are settled. Their bounded proofs do not resolve live-provider admission or wider M6 identity/trust. The first-preview owner surface (settings, thresholds, credentials, integrations) is settled. The first-preview external delivery channel (no push provider; Nightscout-to-Nightscout sync) is settled. M6 human session effects (idle scope, logout, renewal, transport) are settled. M6 deployment and trust (ingress peer-list trust, one-provider secrets ladder, generic OIDC adapter with Authentik as intended reference, probe-plus-record admission) are settled. Vault Agent scope is settled: one AppRole per deployment; tenant separation at Vault is not a goal. Evaluator partitioning is settled in direction: member count and ordinal flag with a pool-membership table.

The 2026-11-10 decisions (activity policy, root and admin tools, restore census, export removal, admin listener address, internal listener, evaluator revision and alarm repeat) are rows in the table above. No human-policy topic is open.

The owner lifecycle packet retains source surveys and alternatives; its recommended grace periods, invitation lifetimes and self-service operations are not approved defaults. The earlier open-decision note preserves already answered A questions, not the current backlog.

The counter and restore options analysis separates the tenant-local history clock from internal insertion order. The tenant-local insertion prototype removes cross-tenant allocation state while preserving supported per-tenant order; exact physical and logical backup fidelity retain their separate contracts.

docs.title: From preview to production
docs.text: The production critical path maps these adopted requirements to closing evidence and conditional topology choices. It separates M6 completion, a coherent released candidate and per-deployment production admission. Its proposed one-cohort scope and HA deferrals are not adopted policy.

docs.title: Measure before setting limits
docs.text: Decision 2026-11-09 (row): the envelope is measured first, not declared. MT-BENCH-BASELINE benchmarks the one-host reference at stepped synthetic tenant counts with a hot tenant and publishes p50/p95/p99 latency, socket fanout, evaluator cycle time, pool/lock waits, CPU and memory per role, disk per tenant-day and reconnect recovery. MT-BENCH-CONTRAST runs the same workload against the shapes operators run today (N single-tenant Mongo processes; the per-site process model) and reports the comparison side by side. MT-SCALE-UNBOUND proves each component scales horizontally or vertically as intended and itemises any binding with file:line. Limits, polling cadence and replay horizons are then set from those numbers. Use the experiment contract for oracle and control design. Nothing here is a prerequisite to current correctness work, and no number is invented from functional passes.

docs.title: Reviewing and closing a topic
docs.text: Bring one topic with current code anchors, user/operator effect, compatibility, recommendation, alternatives, reproduced evidence and named unknowns. Record the answer once in release decisions, link it here, and update the acceptance family. Do not add per-commit journals. The coordinator maps each required family to an actual source/command/artifact/verdict and records any explicit deferral before milestone promotion. M5/M6, real-data/identity admission and production/default role enablement remain separate claims.

docs.title: Multitenancy decisions and architectural contracts
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-10 at 4917b2d4a.

Contributor-facing living decision reference. Consolidated 2026-11-06 from the maintainer's D1–D23 decisions and their later amendments. This is a read-derived reorganization, not new implementation acceptance or a new decision. The retained execution journal preserves the original rationale, prototypes, task definitions and measurements.

This document owns the D1–D23 architectural decisions. The owner-authority contract owns the later D17/D22 management and verification amendment; the durable event contract owns B7's consumer/recovery rules. Later release decisions own promotion-bar, compatibility and lifecycle decisions. Their amendments take precedence over earlier journal text. The dashboard owns milestone claims, the queue owns item state and gates, and release contents owns integration/publication status. Read the tenancy guide for the current execution plan; archived “next” instructions are historical.

docs.title: 1. Decisions
docs.text:
Decision Adopted direction and qualifications D1 — targets Multitenant service is the design target; families, clinics and communities are configurations of it. Self-hosted single-tenant remains first-class permanently. D2 — shared storage Shared logical storage with a tenant discriminator, rather than a database per tenant. The retained database experiments own the comparative cost evidence. D3 — isolation PostgreSQL with RLS for multitenancy. Serving connections must not own tables or bypass RLS; trusted tenant binding is transaction-local. A missing binding must not expose other tenants. D4 — MongoDB MongoDB remains permanent for single-tenant sites. The storage seam carries two mature backends; an adapter change must preserve single-tenant behavior. D5 — workload roles One core, with one stateless multitenant api component containing v1/v2/v3 REST adapters, change-driven evaluator, fan-out realtime and connector vcpool; single keeps its server. D21 packages roles under one executable. D6 — feed Replication slot as the durable spine, reader-emitted NOTIFY for latency, bounded aggregate polling as backstop. Never emit notifications from a write trigger. B7 supplies later replay/checkpoint semantics; no direct api → realtime data stream is adopted. D7 — operator plane Platform administration has its own entrypoint/network interface and is secured by unreachability, without a deployment API credential. Tenant administration is authenticated and tenant-bound; D16 gives it a separate listener. D8 — query contract API v3's closed operator set is the initial query contract; v1 is bounded by client/corpus evidence. Use mingo as a differential oracle, with live-backend checks where oracle semantics differ. D9 — original base The September seam work was based on chore/nightscout-modernization. This is its historical base decision, not an instruction to start current work there: the adopted current-dev delivery plan supersedes the old branch sequence. D10 — tenant label Slug is a globally unique host label within one deployment, not a full hostname. Configured trusted resolution maps host to label to stable tenant id; no hardcoded first-label assumption. D11 — devicestatus Generate columns only for the collection's indexed fields; retain the body as JSONB. Decomposition into normalized series is controller-declared and sits above the seam, so single-tenant benefits too. D12 — repositories Alignment holds tooling, evidence, documentation and QC. Shipping code/tests belong in cgm-remote-monitor; findings and experimental scaffolding do not. Harnesses exercise shipping modules by path. D13 — credentials No deployment-wide secret on any multitenant interface. Each tenant retains its own root/legacy credential; root-derived subject tokens must also be tenant-scoped. The operator plane remains credential-free. D14 — token keys Per-tenant signing authority; resolve the tenant before examining a credential. A token for A used on B must fail signature verification, while opaque credential lookup and subjects also remain tenant-bound. Current key/credential state and rotation require their own acceptance. D15 — configuration source single reads the environment. Multitenant per-tenant values come from storage, administered by owners under policy. Deployment-only values remain in each role's environment; D22 clarifies that distinction. D16 — audience listeners Separate data, tenant-owner and private-operator sockets for the deployment, multiplexed by tenant rather than duplicated per tenant. Extract shared tenant resolution/credential verification before adding the owner listener. The adopted initial owner listener is a second bound socket inside api, movable to its own process later. D17 — authentication audiences Devices permanently keep native tenant credentials; Hydra is deferred and D7 is unchanged. External human identity uses the later shared optional single/multitenant OIDC integration, provider-backed renewal first and separate authorization adapters behind Nightscout's own credential exchange. The cohort-wide Kratos pool remains adopted in principle and gated, with cookie scope E and the production conditions below. D18 — registration Well-known declarations describe existing writers without client changes. Controller-owned, dynamic typed declarations support new kinds, states, transitions, initiators, effects and commands. The controller owns lifecycle, composition, synchronization and reconciliation; the hub records and observes, never derives dosing state. Its extensible grammar is specified below. D19 — instances Immutable content-addressed definitions are separate from leased instances. Each channel role declares device or simulated provenance; one device source of record holds a role, with explicit handoff and visible overlap. Definitions survive while data references them. D20 — identities and quirks identifier is client sync identity; _id is the hub storage key. Every legacy surface serves hub-assigned 24-hex _id values on either store; the opaque alternative is withdrawn. Quirks are version-scoped, recorded when applied, and retired only from measured evidence. D21 — executable/profiles One Node executable, bin/nightscout.js: single, multitenant <role>[,<role>…], and operator tools. The namespace is multitenant, not serve; the subcommand selects tenancy and retires TENANCY_MODE as an operator setting. Legacy single-site start paths stay equivalent. Roles/listeners are admitted only by their gates. D22 — policy/secrets Effective settings combine code defaults, operator defaults, permitted owner values and operator pins, under code-enforced project floors. Secrets are a separate encrypted component. The owner-authority amendment governs delegation, sessions and local public-key verification. D23 — socket writes Multitenant realtime is a reader without data-storage write authority. It forwards every socket mutation and alarm ack/snooze unchanged, with the socket's authorization, to an internal api endpoint using the same write step and socket source label. Relay the actual result to the acknowledgement; a failed forward yields no acknowledgement, preserving client no-ack retry. Never synthesize success. No client change; single stays unchanged.

D1–D17 were adopted in September 2026; D18 and its grammar amendment in October, D19/D20 and their walk-through amendments in October, D21 on October 26 with the November 3 namespace amendment, D22 on October 27 with the November 5 owner amendment, and D23 on November 6 with its same-day all-socket-write amendment. The original dated basis for each remains in the journal decision table. D17's human-identity gate is the exception to unconditional adoption.

docs.title: 2. Storage, resolution and profiles
docs.text:
The seam expresses backend-independent storage and write intent, rather than exporting driver semantics. Both supported adapters stay in applicable CI; unavailable backends register pending tests instead of silently disappearing. Query coercion belongs above the seam, generated from the shared schema. MongoDB write validation remains inside its adapter. The initial v3 operators are eq, ne, gt, gte, lt, lte, in, nin, re; v1 admissions and explicit refusals depend on measured client contracts. mingo agreement alone does not establish MongoDB/PostgreSQL agreement for regex or BSON truthiness/order.

One shared write boundary owns identity forms, server dates, soft deletion, resend identity and the logical per-write event. Runtime-derived fields are computed on copies, not persisted as source data. Import uses the admitted write contract and typed-identity rules. Preserve collection/path-specific behavior until a change has its own compatibility decision and consumer replay; the write contract and storage interface own their current admitted contracts.

Tenant resolution precedes authentication. Slug labels use lowercase alphanumerics and -, without leading/trailing -, validated on write and read. A resolver's configured pattern has exactly one capture and no stateful flags; trusted host/header provenance is explicit. Stable ids bind RLS, not reassignable slugs. Socket handshakes resolve by host, not the client-chosen engine path; path-only socket tenancy must refuse unless a reviewed trusted edge supplies the host assertion. Unknown tenants must not allocate an unbounded context cache.

The current target profiles are resident single on MongoDB and multitenant roles on PostgreSQL/RLS. Backend portability does not automatically admit single-tenant PostgreSQL or multitenant MongoDB. SQLite/Celld needs a separate backend/profile decision and compatibility, isolation, migration and operations acceptance. The API v3 headless test launcher is development tooling, outside the operator CLI/image. Resident versus computed execution is a separate axis; its prototype/placement decisions live in the release decisions.

single is dispatched in-process so termination reaches the server directly. Each HTTP role has its own bind; private admin cannot share the consumer address. Unknown commands exit 64 and help names the available commands. Packaging into separate repositories/packages and an all-roles invocation remain separate questions. The original journal's automatic image-healthcheck instruction is historical: the platform plan records no automatic image healthcheck, preserving visible boot-error behavior.

docs.title: Operator, owner and data authority
docs.text:
The operator plane alone provisions, suspends and executes lifecycle deletion. It is cross-tenant by construction, with an explicit reachability/bind contract; code review bounds that authority. Default operator bind is loopback; non-loopback requires explicit acknowledgement (ADMIN_INSECURE_BIND_ACKNOWLEDGED=true) and may never bind every interface. The operator listener may share the consumer listener's address on a different port (2026-11-10), on loopback and non-loopback addresses alike; separation of a shared non-loopback address rests on the port, the acknowledgement and the deployment's network policy. A name used for a loopback bind must resolve only to loopback addresses. Authenticated owner operations remain RLS-scoped. The dashboard's path holds no credential for every tenant, and the operator plane never reveals owner secrets.

Credentials are per-tenant, identity may be per-cohort, authorization is per-tenant. Isolation rests on current authorization and RLS, not the identity provider's tenancy model. D17's native device path remains permanent. Providers handle human password/recovery/MFA/session functions; Nightscout's exchange maps verified (provider, subject_id) to current tenant membership and mints its own tenant-bound credential. Membership keys are text, unique within a tenant, with no foreign key to a Nightscout identity table.

For the gated Kratos direction, scope E is the apex cookie behind a hardened edge. Before real identities: strip Kratos and CSRF cookies before tenant backends; refuse cross-origin writes including WebSocket upgrades; route every API/socket path through that edge; measure the conditions over HTTPS; assign an owner to the compliance question. A different provider still needs its own issuer/audience/cookie and logout/revocation acceptance. External identity alone does not establish current Nightscout grants.

The owner-authority contract is authoritative for explicit ownership, management versus data audiences, permission use versus delegation, proposed-grant transaction fencing, lifetimes and next-operation revocation. Legacy data/root credentials gain no implicit management privilege. Initial headless management credentials are explicitly provisioned; a root bootstrap would need its own explicit exchange ceremony. Last-owner removal must not orphan a tenant. The later compatibility decision drops the optional subject-reader clamping mode; it does not drop proposed-grant writer ceilings or permit breaking existing root/data clients.

As decided on 2026-11-10 (tenant-root-single-site-parity, root-may-edit-owner-subjects, root-grant-ceiling-default-all, admin-role-subjects-use-admin-tools), the three authorities split as drawn below; the decisions amend the "no implicit management privilege" sentence above for subject and role administration only. Built on lane 165c13bf, in the batch join that is in acceptance.

flowchart LR
  Root["Tenant API_SECRET (root)<br/>same as a single site"] --> Data["All tenant data"]
  Root --> Subjects["Subjects and roles, admin tools<br/>grant up to tenant data *<br/>(operator may narrow)"]
  AdminSubject["Subject granted<br/>admin:api:subjects:*<br/>with its own token"] --> Subjects
  Owner["Owner subject<br/>(management audience)"] --> OwnerOps["Settings, export,<br/>deletion request, ownership,<br/>pause / unpause"]
  Operator["Operator<br/>(private admin plane)"] --> OperatorOps["Provision, suspend, execute deletion,<br/>assisted ownership add / transfer / recover,<br/>infrastructure and runtime defaults"]
  Subjects -. "may edit or delete owner subjects;<br/>removing the last usable owner is refused" .-> Owner
  Root -. "never owner or operator authority;<br/>cannot make itself an owner" .-x OwnerOps

docs.title: D22 policy and project floors
docs.text:
Policy per setting has a default, open/bounded/pinned mode and constraint (allowed values, range, floor or host allow-list). Effective order is code default → operator default → permitted owner value → operator pin. Deployment policy may have tenant-specific operator overrides; project floors apply to all. A launch-environment migration sends values an owner can no longer set to a review list rather than dropping them.

Project floor Required behavior in multitenant roles Tenant credentials and API security No API_SECRET/API_SECRET_FILE deployment root; API3 security cannot be disabled. Anonymous authority Default roles limited to denied, readable, status-only; no anonymous writes or TREATMENTS_AUTH=off. Network safety Explicit hop-count/CIDR trust for proxy inputs; public-address webhooks only; driver-defined connector hosts; tenant-derived BASE_URL. App settings privacy Identifier reads require api:settings:admin, as search/history do; strict settings reads always enabled. Data/log safety WRITE_VALIDATION at least log; debug payload logging off; ignore IMPORT_CONFIG; permanent autoprune requires confirmation and an export offered first.

Deployment-only ports, storage URIs, proxy trust, logging and release-driven compatibility switches belong in the consuming role's environment. A role refuses startup when required deployment values are missing and names them. No per-tenant value leaks in from process environment. Operator policy contains tenant-facing defaults/modes/constraints, not deployment infrastructure values.

Changes are versioned with who/when/what, invalidate the tenant cache live, and apply on the next request or background cycle. An owner rollback is refused whole if current operator policy would block any setting, naming every conflict. Alarm settings remain hidden with a plain-language explanation until actual multitenant alarm acceptance; preview/confirmation precedes alarm-policy changes.

Integrations are typed kind-catalogue records with schema-validated settings, credential references, status, and operator-enabled kinds/limits. Several of one kind may coexist. A kind may split credential parts between operator and owner; owners never see the operator part. Existing environment aliases stay in single.

Secrets stay encrypted at rest; only their named consumers decrypt. Reveal is a separate logged permission with recent reauthentication, never an operator-plane operation. The provider remains pluggable: built-in development/small-operator signer, Vault Transit and a cloud key service behind the common interface. Private signing keys stay inside the secrets component. New-format tokens are verified locally with trusted public keys and current PostgreSQL authority; legacy signing/derivation material is retained compatibly until migration is measured. Cache keys, never stale grants; unknown keys and unavailable current authority refuse. The owner-authority contract defines the exact outage/session rules. secrets is a role of the one executable, not an owner-dashboard privilege.

Migration tooling is the adopted Umzug wrapper with explicit operator-run multitenant migrations before serving. PostgreSQL ledger/lock and each migration commit together. MongoDB migrations are safe to rerun with ledger/lease locking; transactional steps use transactions where supported, index creation precedes writes to new collections, listCollections stays outside the transaction, and a repeated body is tolerated. Single-site boot changes retain their own release placement; journal prototype behavior is not an instruction to change defaults.

docs.title: Suspension and lifecycle
docs.text:
Suspend is total blackout, including ingest; pause blocks UI/reads while ingest continues. Delete requires suspend, not pause. On suspension, disconnect sockets and show last data visibly stale using existing staleness vocabulary; silent frozen charts are not sufficient.

Pause and suspend are also the whole operator activity policy (adopted 2026-11-10); there is no third state. Background workers build their work lists from tenants eligible under the current state, not from configured presence. While paused, uploads and connector polling continue and the evaluator stops, so no alarms are computed or delivered while a site is paused; on unpause it recomputes from current data before publishing. While suspended nothing runs for the tenant. Restore and restart preserve the state. An owner may pause their own site; only the operator suspends and deletes. An owner's deletion request pauses the site, cancelling restores the earlier state and execution suspends. Every tenant has an activity row; an unreadable row stops the evaluator for that tenant only. Refused requests return 423 TENANT_SUSPENDED or TENANT_PAUSED. The admission and activity guide explains how this policy stays separate from the claim-bound restore window and current authority.

Destructive lifecycle preconditions, export coverage and key retention are release decisions; after the 30-day window, key destruction also removes the export file. Ownership operations refuse unless the tenant is active. The archived owner-lifecycle packet keeps the alternatives. Do not infer current deletion behavior from the original seam's admin prototype. Shared-role startup follows the adopted tenant-local startup admission decision. The release record owns implementation and acceptance state. Deployment support-contact metadata remains a recommendation, not an adopted schema: its privacy/availability rationale is retained in the journal.

Activity states as decided on 2026-11-10 (activity-is-pause-suspend, owner-may-pause, deletion-request-auto-pauses, suspended-refusal-423, activity-row-always-provisioned); they supersede the open review linked above. Built on lane 07981b55, in the batch join that is in acceptance. Restore and restart preserve the state.

stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  [*] --> Active: provisioning writes the activity row
  Active --> Paused: owner pauses, or requests deletion
  Paused --> Active: owner unpauses, or cancels a deletion request made while active
  Active --> Suspended: operator suspends
  Paused --> Suspended: operator suspends, or executes the deletion
  Suspended --> Active: operator unsuspends
  Suspended --> Paused: operator unsuspends, owner pause kept
  note right of Paused
    Uploads stored; reads and UI refused 423 TENANT_PAUSED
    Evaluator stopped: no alarms computed or delivered
    Sockets disconnected; unpause recomputes before publishing
  end note
  note right of Suspended

docs.title: 4. Typed controllers, provenance and compatibility
docs.text:
The living registration, records, identity and authority specifications own the detailed D18–D20 contracts. The following clauses remain architectural requirements.

  • Unknown grammar fields are must-ignore within a major version: preserve them without interpreting or serving them as data. Controller extensions use owned reverse-DNS namespaces and declared restricted JSON-Schema types. Missing types refuse; missing sensitivity labels withhold. Declarations carry units, ranges, horizon and evidence. The hub derives storage/validation/query, never dosing.
  • Vocabularies stay open through other plus the controller's term. Each kind and extension has its own versions, served/stored selection and optional declared lossless mappings; absent a mapping, never convert. Horizons are cycle, span, effective-dated, definition, aggregate, with cadence/retention; experimental values get no invented well-known mapping or long-term promise.
  • Capability negotiation precedes typed writes; unsupported elements use their declared well-known carrier. Typed 5xx responses retry with backoff until they succeed, never fall back to a carrier after a possibly stored write. Definite 4xx refusal may use the carrier; no arbitrary delivery deadline is adopted.
  • A definition is sha256: of RFC 8785 canonical JSON; many coexist per product. Conflicting meanings for the same kind/version refuse. References to catalogue kinds get the catalogue's native storage/carrier mapping. Retain definitions while stored records depend on them.
  • Instances name definitions and renew capability-defined leases; no hardware identifiers. Identifying fields must be typed and sensitivity-labelled. Labels use reverse-DNS keys, including dev.nightscout/purpose, /build and /migration-group; only device-provenance data enters default therapy views and exports. Labels never substitute for provenance.
  • Source-of-record selection is per channel role among device instances. Refuse a second holder, flag overlap, and hand off by release, lease lapse or owner transfer. Simulated roles never compete with device roles or receive their commands. The hub does not stop, direct or compose dosing.
  • Default read versions obey operator capabilities, owner pins/blocks, then the newest live device instance. Lab/development views select instances explicitly. Legacy readers get declared read-only projections, labelled projected and never stored as sources. Typed/carrier dual-write links by instance and record identity apply only during migration or without a declared carrier mapping.
  • A channel is shared only by the shared-slot catalogue or sameAs. An unlisted slot is product-scoped; equal names across products only produce an observation. Infer a command's product only when exactly one candidate exists; ambiguity refuses. Device command sinks require the product's bound subject or explicit owner transfer. A changed binding drops mismatched sinks immediately except owner-transferred roles; until a new destination exists, commands refuse. Simulated sinks are exempt from that binding rule.
  • A released registration binds its next permitted writer, with binding event and credential kind visible. Migrating an api-secret binding uses the tenant root credential and changes the etag. Loop-status exclusivity remains unspecified until its decomposition is a typed channel. An agent initiator uses the open other/controllerTerm form rather than a new shared agent value.
  • identifier survives retries/devices; resend matches it first and replies return it with the server's _id. Projected legacy ids are assigned at typed write time and remain stable, using hub receipt time rather than record time. Version-scoped quirk mappings are observed, never silent, and move proposed → active → historical → retired only from evidence; “recent” is the declared 365-day measurement parameter. Trio's id observation adds no new mapping. Shared slot candidates remain for controller-author confirmation.

docs.title: 5. Runtime isolation and clinical acceptance
docs.text:
B7's durable event contract owns producer/consumer checkpoints, replay and crash recovery. The per-write logical stamp is the transaction's final clock floor; equal-stamp cohorts commit together. Bound tenant scope is carried in the event; single, settle, MongoDB and clock-off cases retain the contract's null-tenant/null-stamp rules. Provider choice, hard-delete recovery and multi-node failover retain separate decisions.

D23 forwarding must preserve pinned client requests, stored outcomes, retries and acknowledgements. Authorize with the socket's credential, not a role credential; recheck current tenant authority. A failed forward yields no acknowledgement, preserving the client's no-ack retry; never synthesize success. Durable tenant-keyed alarm acknowledgement must survive process/restart changes. Typed role metadata records listener, data-storage authority, feed consumer, egress and forwarding; distinguish a reader's checkpoint bookkeeping from data write authority. B7 leaves provider selection deferred: a slot, polling or both may satisfy the durable contract. When a LISTEN/NOTIFY provider is selected, hold one LISTEN per held/served tenant on a direct connection rather than transaction pooling. The R73 first reference uses polling over consistent tenant snapshots; it establishes no LISTEN handshake or notification-transport latency result. Re-run the socket-writer inventory when client pins change. The retained D23 analysis contains original corpus/rationale and entry-control design.

The evaluator materializes a transient bounded slice rather than resident ddata, while retaining the actual alarm dependencies on treatments, profiles and device status. Device-status bounds must preserve relevant kinds and success conditions, not merely the newest few documents: retained clinical findings explain how crowding can hide alarms. Current acquisition contracts, costs and runtime acceptance remain in their own records; old spike figures are not a capacity guarantee. No single-tenant computed profile is enabled by this design.

Before multitenant alarms/live updates are enabled, require actual A-to-A and not-A-to-B producer delivery, durable ack/snooze, per-tenant exception containment, and health signals for silent evaluation failure. Snooze data-time versus wall-time remains an explicit policy question. Shared mutable locale, levels, plugins, caches and authorization state require tenant-safe lifecycle controls; a source grep is insufficient. Changes to alarm rendering also require a single-tenant regression in a non-English locale. Never hold the synchronous alarm decision waiting for storage; the durability/freshness trade-off needs explicit measured acceptance. The retained alarm-gate analysis contains original failure mechanisms and controls.

docs.title: 6. Retained evidence and current work
docs.text: The archived execution journal retains all original sections: deployment/storage rationale; auth and delegation; registration amendments; query/coercion and write-seam findings; branch-refresh rehearsals; Phase 0–4 task definitions, measurements, controls and limitations; clinical/runtime analysis. Measurements keep their original dates and source heads. The archive is not an instruction to rerun old branch work or a status monitor. Current work follows the dashboard, completion schedule and queue.
