docs.title: 3.1 One tenant service graph, thin version adapters
docs.text:
Recommendation: retain version-specific HTTP handlers over shared, tenant-bound collection ports and shared write-intent rules. Bind a request to stable tenant identity, then obtain a trusted collection/service bundle. Never switch a global ctx, environment, Mongo collection name or "current tenant" between requests.

The source already supplies the hard seams:

  • lib/api3/generic/collection.js:26–44 accepts trusted storage/intentFactory options, while the default still constructs Mongo plus cache. lib/api3/shared/collectionWriteIntent.js:5–8 selects that intent factory. Extend those existing seams where the CRUD lane proves the need.
  • Legacy domain wrappers already share lib/storage/write-intent.js; for example lib/server/entries.js:34–35, treatments 28–29, devicestatus 57–58, profile 34–35, food 20–21, activity 22–23. Their parsers, domain transformations, callbacks and event shaping stay in the wrappers. lib/server/storage-reads.js:34–36 still hardcodes Mongo construction; that, not a new REST framework, is the remaining legacy injection seam.
  • lib/storage/postgres-entries-intent.js:48–89 combines reader/writer with forCollectionResolved, commits through an owned transaction, and emits the intent event after commit. It currently refuses source other than v3; it is not already a legacy adapter. postgres-entries-read.js:85–99 refuses v1 dialect/readOptions and unsorted bounded reads. Do not erase those refusals to make v1 tests green.

Proposed narrow additions, owned by S (§5), defaulting to current behavior:

  1. A trusted logical-collection resolver used by legacy storage-reads.collection, and an injected intent factory in legacy wrapper construction, so each wrapper can use source: 'v1/internal' rules without constructing a raw Mongo handle. Keep callable driver accessors on the single/Mongo path; tenant routers must not receive those accessors.
  2. A small explicit domain registration object per collection: legacy wrapper/router factory, v3 Collection options, schema/readiness requirements, admitted method set. These are trusted code, not user registration or request-supplied SQL identifiers.
  3. An integrator-owned composition point that mounts completed domain routers under all their real prefixes with version-aware admission. An unsupported route is refused before backend lookup, never forwarded to the single application or a catch-all Mongo adapter.

Concretely, the proposed resolver accepts trusted { logical, source } constants and returns the existing storage interface plus an intent factory; tenant identity comes from the bound request scope, not those arguments. Legacy store()/step() closures consume this bundle; API3 consumes the same domain's storage/intentFactory constructor options with source v3. Missing domain capabilities fail closed in tenant mode; absence of the optional injection in single mode preserves today's Mongo construction. S owns the shared resolver contract; each domain owner makes its own wrapper-constructor change against that contract. Test both injected and uninjected construction before expanding mounts.

Share pools and immutable code, not credentials or mutable domain state. Construct tenant settings/authorization views from persisted services; capture tenant-bound bundle references for each handler execution. A bounded cache of router/service bundles may be keyed by stable tenant ID plus configuration generation, with eviction/shutdown; it must not cache permission decisions across protected operations. Request-bound transaction context remains authoritative even if a router bundle is reused.

Why not just mount lib/api with a renamed database? Its handlers capture ctx at construction. Entries uses ctx.ddata for conditional responses and ctx.cache for fast reads (lib/api/entries/index.js:73–98,447–477); writes use ctx.ddata.processRawDataForRuntime and ctx.bus (lib/server/entries.js:167–179). Properties, summary, assistants and notifications capture sandbox/runtime/plugin/egress state. lib/server/bootevent.js:313–335,514–551 constructs this process graph and event subscriptions. A global context clone or Object.assign is not isolation.

For initial legacy data routes, inject tenant-local read snapshots, cache and bus, with the existing normalization functions. Where cache-backed behavior has not been implemented, admit only paths proven storage-only; do not silently return empty ddata or suppress conditional headers. H owns the reusable snapshot/data-loader binding; collection teams can implement and test their storage and version handlers in parallel using an actual tenant snapshot fixture, then join the runtime seam. Expensive sandbox evaluation can later be externalized without changing the REST contract; that is not a prerequisite for collection writes.

docs.title: 3.2 Storage: reuse JSON document machinery, not entries policy
docs.text:
Keep PostgreSQL/RLS as the multitenant target and Mongo as the single compatibility baseline. lib/server/storage-backends.js:21–27 registers only Mongo; tests/support/backends.js:39–63 also marks global PG fixtures unavailable. Do not flip either registry globally to claim every collection works. Add capability-scoped tenant composition and focused real-PG fixtures; promote the global backend only when its advertised fixture/storage contract is genuinely built.

Reuse tenant connection/transaction/scope, typed _id codec, JSON representability checks, filter compiler and common row operations. Proposed storage layout: one RLS-protected table per logical collection, using the existing tenant_id + id_kind + JSON document pattern, with collection-specific generated time/index columns. No per-version tables and no one-off copy of every generic operation. A new collection may use the common row adapter only after its query columns, ordering, identity and write rules are tested.

The entries candidate migrations/candidates/postgres-entries-v1.json is entries-only: typed primary identity, tenant-prefixed indexes, identifier uniqueness and FORCE RLS. Do not rename its table and call the other schemas done. Domain-owned migration candidates must preserve:

collection required semantics to specify and test before admission entries date/sysTime/type, model-specific coercion, fallback identifier and current/history order; existing schema and accepted intent seam are the starting point treatments created_at/eventType/timezone handling, identifier and fallback-key matching, treatment duration/target units, same-time distinct records, array resend and validation outcomes devicestatus created_at/device matching, prediction JSON shape/size rules, stable retry identity and latest read order profile legacy startDate/current profile/list order and pruning; v3 created_at fallback; nested profile JSON, exact identifier/_id rules food quickpick ordering/regular filtering, server-created timestamps versus submitted dates, edit semantics and unknown nested fields activity its own date coercion and v1/internal rules, including absence of automatic server dates where shipping rules omit them; no invented v3 route settings documents generic v3 document/history/strict-read semantics; physically and semantically distinct from versioned tenant-owner settings and secrets

Source detail: lib/storage/write-intent.js:160–171 names collection-specific identity time keys; lib/api3/generic/setup.js:56–115 names v3 fallback dates/dedup fields; lib/server/profile.js:131–177 uses startDate queries/current ordering; lib/server/food.js:136–170 implements quickpick/regular selection. Domain packages inspect their full rules, not just this summary. Missing migration/index/normalization decisions block that collection or path, not every REST team.

Retain unknown representable extension fields without registration. The existing PG codec keeps ObjectId and same-spelling string identity distinct (lib/storage/postgres-identity.js:13–38). JSONB validation and unsupported operations (lib/storage/postgres-entries-write.js:22–79) are deliberate boundaries, not reasons to coerce or discard client fields. A generic JSON schema need not enumerate future controller fields. Use explicit operator migrations/read-only startup checks; never create schema in a gate, route constructor or readiness probe.

docs.title: 3.3 Version-aware parsing, current authority and error contracts
docs.text:
Use the existing permission vocabulary for each collection/action and consult persisted current authority on every protected operation. Host selects a stable tenant ID, not a principal. Keep root explicit; subject mutations require exact current name alongside stable identity. No anonymous writes; invalid presented credentials never degrade to anonymous/default grants. Keep data, service, tenant-owner and private operator authority separate.

Do not reuse v3's credential reader for v1/v2 unchanged: lib/authorization/index.js:30–91 reads bearer, query token, object/first-array-item body token, query secret/header secret and body secret, with its own precedence and removal from the body. API3 security uses its own header flow (lib/api3/security.js:11–39), and the accepted tenant data bridge explicitly refuses legacy carriers. H implements a version-aware extraction bridge that reuses shipping extraction behavior without invoking the process enclave or process subject store. Differentially test valid carrier precedence, empty/duplicate/malformed credentials and body-field consumption. If shipping fallback behavior contradicts the approved tenant invalid-credential rule, preserve single behavior and expose a specific tenant refusal; do not quietly change legacy single semantics or silently accept the fallback.

Preserve middleware order and body limits, not just happy-path documents:

  • lib/api/index.js:40–48,120–145 places experiments before format rewriting and validates counts before data routes. Entries has send-status, raw parser, JSON up to 50 MB, URL encoding, extension rewriting and read permission before action permission (lib/api/entries/index.js:44–59). Other routers have their own ordering/limits.
  • lib/middleware/index.js:23–32 supplies 1 MB JSON/raw/URL-encoded defaults. Treatments and activity override JSON limits. lib/api/notifications-api.js:10–11 also registers parent parsers during router construction; v2 inherits v1 middleware before its extras. Avoid replacing this with one process-wide parser that changes credential consumption.
  • API3 uses its 50 MB JSON parser, parser-error response and extension negotiation (lib/api3/shared/jsonParser.js:6–12, lib/api3/index.js:39–41). Malformed JSON is not automatically the same status in every stack. The accepted tenant v3 mount parses before protection (lib/server/tenant-app/index.js:168); changing order or format admission needs explicit HTTP characterization.

Version responses stay version responses. For example, legacy missing entries ID yields HTTP200 with an empty list; verifyauth returns a boolean/message probe, and API3 addressed mutation/history has distinct statuses, envelopes and headers. Preserve v1 count tolerances, default count/type/sort, deprecation headers, deletion response, batch partial results and optional Nightscout-Write-Results / results=items (lib/api/index.js:76–145, lib/api/shared/batch-reply.js:38–66). Legacy queries carry nested find[...]/sort structures and path models, whereas API3 search parses field/operator parameters, repeated filter_parameters, sort/sort$desc, limit, skip and fields (lib/api3/generic/search/input.js:109–213). Keep those parsers in their version layer and compile their resulting predicates only where representable. Defaults are not uniform: treatments chooses count100 or count1000 when a find is present (lib/api/treatments/index.js:89–103), devicestatus defaults to count10 and may read cache (lib/api/devicestatus/index.js:82–105), while API3 uses its configured maximum/limit and identifier/created_at/date/_id order chain. The PG compiler currently refuses regex, v1 AST, dotted paths and several operand types (lib/storage/postgres-filter.js:11–20,82–96); time/slice pattern support and legacy coercion therefore need real translation work, not an admission-only switch.

The approved tenant mutation policy is narrow: missing current subject name401, actual authority outage503; demonstrably nonrepresentable submitted document400, recognized storage outage503, internal/unclassified error500. It is not a global conversion of legacy exceptions, stored-data faults or TypeError. Preserve shipping API3 read-then-write preconditions, seconds flooring and invalid-date behavior (lib/api3/generic/update/operation.js:67–75, patch 50–58), without claiming atomic CAS. Unsupported PG query/update semantics refuse explicitly, not approximate Mongo behavior. Where a new legacy refusal has no established public mapping, the domain owner brings the exact mechanism and proposed version-specific status to the maintainer; unrelated routes proceed.

docs.title: 3.4 Cross-version writes, histories and notifications
docs.text:
Keep one canonical tenant/collection document store visible to every version. Continue using write-intent's v1/internal versus v3 source rules; they intentionally differ. Reuse its single/array, identifier matching, resend, duplicate-recovery and per-item outcome machinery, plus the legacy batch reply helpers. Do not implement a PG-specific duplicate policy or translate every successful write into an API3 reply.

Preserve srvCreated/srvModified, modifiedBy, validity/tombstones, fallback visibility and lastModified/history after legacy writes, including restart behavior. A v1 create followed by v3 search/history/read is a required test, not an assumption. History is the shipping modified-document synchronization contract, not a newly invented append-only audit log. Physical deletes and configured pruning retain their actual visibility semantics.

lib/storage/write-intent.js:4598,4681–4706 separates resolved write execution from intent event emission. The PG entries wrapper emits after its transaction; legacy wrappers also produce data-update/data-received, and v3 handlers emit storage-socket updates. Keep these layers distinct, tenant-tagged, and non-duplicated. Refused/rolled-back writes must not publish committed changes. A tenant-local in-process invalidation bus suffices for the runnable preview; it must not enable realtime/evaluator roles or imply durable multi-process notification delivery. Durable change-feed/outbox delivery, if needed for later scale, is separately measured.

docs.title: 3.5 Status, discovery and management boundaries
docs.text:
Build an explicit safe env/settings view for each tenant. Never pass process.env, Vault configuration, database configuration, all-tenant maps or process-wide admin notices into a legacy status handler. Preserve legitimate client settings and token exchange behavior, not secret values. v1 status may issue authorization material; mark responses no-store as shipping does (lib/api/status.js:14–18,24–44). v3 status/lastModified must describe only that tenant's admitted, authorized collections, not a configured-but-unimplemented six-collection list.

Keep API3 settings documents separate from owner configuration CAS/rollback APIs. For v2 subject/role administration, the proposed target is a tenant-scoped legacy compatibility facade with its existing admin permissions backed by persisted authority/identity services; data tokens never become owner or platform-operator credentials. Token/name/role changes must invalidate current authorization across workers. That capability needs a concrete authority mutation/import contract; read-only subject fixtures cannot substitute for it.

Runtime target: one consumer API listener for the v1/v2/v3 REST compatibility facade, plus separately authorized owner and private operator listeners. The current headless single api role (lib/server/serve/api.js:3–13,36–40) supplies only v3 and authorization, and is not multitenant merely because of its name; serve/roles.js:14–25 says so. The active CLI lane enables only its explicit API preview; keep that scope and use environment credential references, direct-alias defaults, and per-request immediate-peer checks in opt-in canonical mode. Static operator maps remain configuration, not a durable registry.

docs.title: 4. Policy recommendations, without blocking collection delivery
docs.text:
These are proposed defaults, not new maintainer approvals.

topic recommendation and operator-visible effect trade-off and bounded blocker shared storage vs version forks common collection ports, version-specific frontends; existing client bodies/replies retained a small injection seam is maintained once; rejects unsupported semantics rather than claiming universal Mongo emulation cache/runtime-dependent reads tenant-local snapshots using existing normalizers/loaders; admit storage-only paths earlier preserves conditional/derived behavior; cache-backed legacy paths wait for H's real snapshot seam, not CLI or CRUD unknown helper collection selectors code-owned allowlist; never lookup arbitrary tenant/process services; preserve shipping fallback only when it selects a safe admitted entries port some previously meaningful dynamic contexts may need an explicit new refusal; E must characterize and present any observable change rather than guess v2 subject/role management eventually implement tenant-scoped compatibility facade; keep initial preview excluded avoids breaking existing admin clients long-term; H can deliver status/exchange/discovery now while persisted mutation semantics are resolved notification/assistant endpoints retain explicit exclusion until tenant runtime, receipt ownership and fake-provider egress tests exist preview breadth comes from data clients first; X rows stay incomplete, not "all REST complete" unsupported inputs exact translation where representable, explicit refusal otherwise protects reliability/data fidelity; migration/client footprint and performance are unmeasured, so no parity claim outside tested shapes

Long-term direction and architecture favor one shared domain graph rather than three adapters that duplicate business rules. Backward compatibility is enforced against single/Mongo; forward compatibility retains representable extension fields. Maintenance favors small injected ports over a universal framework. Reliability requires current authority, RLS and honest refusal; performance needs later representative query/index/snapshot measurements, not inferred wins. Only a newly observed policy mismatch blocks the affected path. No new global maintainer decision is required merely to begin domain storage, HTTP and synthetic tests.

docs.title: 5. Executable parallel work packages
docs.text:
Start rule for every implementation brief: confirm the exact clean base commit and that the task is still open; stop and report a mismatch rather than reaching for the nearest working substitute. Do not read another lane's uncommitted changes. Every package owns implementation, its focused tests and red controls together; there is no separate packet prerequisite.

All proposed filenames below are implementation outputs, not assertions that files exist. Default ownership is by domain, across versions. S owns shared-file edits and integrates small exports from domain teams; do not have every agent edit the router, write-intent and census.

package deliverable and owned surfaces real prerequisites / what can start now exclusions and stop condition S — shared seams/integration trusted collection/intent injection in lib/server/storage-reads.js and legacy constructors; reusable PG row helper extracted only from proven common code; tenant domain mount/admission in lib/server/tenant-app/index.js and data-access.js; changes to generic Collection, collectionWriteIntent, shared write-intent, filter compiler, migration catalogue, test tiers/census centrally owned planning/test characterization now; edits touching active entries CRUD/CLI files wait for their accepted join or explicit owner coordination; independent legacy seam tests can start immediately in a clean worktree no new policy/rules, no global backend enablement, no duplicate CRUD/CLI implementation; stop on semantic mismatch or disputed shared-file ownership E — legacy entries + shared query helpers lib/api/entries/index.js, lib/server/entries.js, lib/server/aggregate.js; proposed tenant legacy-entries adapter and tests/tenant-rest-entries.integration.test.js; all legacy entries/helper matrix rows under both versions, formats and conditional reads existing entries schema and accepted POST seam allow query/handler characterization now; production injection uses S; actual CRUD/history consumption uses accepted CRUD join; cache-backed reads use H snapshot seam active API3 CRUD files excluded; no PUT entries invented; count/echo other domains call their exported ports; stop on unsupported dialect/order semantics, not change silently T — treatments across versions lib/api/treatments/index.js, lib/server/treatments.js; proposed tenant treatments adapter, collection migration and tests/tenant-rest-treatments.integration.test.js; all legacy methods + G3 begin migration, normalized fixtures, rule/HTTP differential and adapter implementation now; import S's stable ports at integration; no dependency on profile/food completion no shared write-intent edits without S; preserve duration/target-unit/validation/batch/retry behavior; stop for a new clinical/domain interpretation, duplicate policy or unrepresentable stored semantics D — devicestatus + activity corresponding legacy route/wrapper files; proposed tenant domain adapters/migrations and tests/tenant-rest-device-activity.integration.test.js; G3 devicestatus, legacy devicestatus/activity start independently now with typed JSON and collection rules; depends only on S mount/seam at join no v3 activity or legacy devicestatus PUT; do not couple prediction field registration to admission; stop if normalization loses extension data or requires a new write policy F — profile + food corresponding route/wrapper files; proposed adapters/migrations and tests/tenant-rest-profile-food.integration.test.js; current/plural/quickpick legacy reads, edits and G3 start schemas, nested JSON, order/pruning and cross-version tests now; S injects completed ports no owner-config editing, profile meaning rewrite or universal timestamp policy; stop on ambiguous current-profile ordering/pruning representation H — identity/status/settings/derived reads lib/authorization/endpoints.js/extraction seam with S coordination; lib/api/status.js, verifyauth.js, adminnotifiesapi.js; v2 properties/summary/data endpoints; API3 specific routes; proposed settings document adapter, tenant snapshot service and tests/tenant-rest-context.integration.test.js safe status/exchange/discovery, credential characterization and settings schema begin now; snapshot bridge can be developed against existing normalizers and synthetic collection ports; derived HTTP joins require E/T/F reads; authority mutations wait only for their own persisted mutation contract no active CLI/exchange rewrite, service authority elevation, process env exposure, enabling owner/operator roles; management X rows are separate subdeliverable, not prerequisite for H reads N — notifications/assistant compatibility notifications v1/v2, assistant router adapters, tenant receipt/sandbox/egress ports; proposed tests/tenant-rest-side-effects.integration.test.js fake-provider and tenant runtime characterization can start now; actual admission requires H snapshots and persisted receipt/authority services as applicable no remote production sends or connector role enablement; stop when durable receipts, callback trust or egress provenance lack an approved contract; keep only those rows excluded

The first implementation wave should be S + E/T/D/F, alongside uninterrupted existing CRUD and runnable CLI work, with H's safe status/identity and snapshot work in parallel. N may begin fake-provider characterization but is not on the data-preview critical path. These are bounded packages, not an instruction to launch a workflow or dozens of agents. At each delivery join integrate whichever collection is complete and advertise only its tested routes. A useful preview does not wait for admin/assistant egress.

docs.title: Per-package acceptance: behavior, not document production
docs.text:
Each package must drive its listed actual HTTP methods, both successful and refused, through the composed tenant application with real PG/RLS and persisted current authority. Use single/Mongo shipping handlers as a differential oracle with normalized synthetic time/IDs; normalize only transport nondeterminism, not bodies, ordering, outcome count or status differences. Use two tenants sharing external identifier spellings; inspect stored rows, headers, history, attribution and committed events. Test legacy v2 inheritance, suffixes, HEAD/OPTIONS and unknown routes as well as v1/v3. For every write domain cover:

  • valid create/read/edit/delete routes actually present; single and arrays only where shipping accepts them; default and opted-in item replies; a successful extension-field round trip;
  • same request resent, identifier/_id collision, duplicate race and rollback; mixed failures where legacy batches permit them, without upgrading all batches to atomic transactions;
  • current grant/role/revocation/rename changes after JWT issuance; anonymous reads only when tenant policy permits; denied anonymous writes, invalid credential and exact subject attribution;
  • cross-version read/history/lastModified after legacy writes, tombstones/permanent delete, tenant-local pruning, cache invalidation and restart; data in tenant B remains unchanged;
  • known service outage versus invalid submitted data versus internal fault, using that route's approved status contract; no credential/error payloads in logs or response bodies.

Red controls are part of coding: remove/bypass the newly added admission or intent seam and require an actual HTTP success test to fail; cross-wire the tenant binding in a synthetic owned fixture and require row/cache/event isolation to fail; freeze current authority or drop attribution and require revoke/rename tests to fail. For query support, change the translation of one exercised operator/order and require differential results to fail. For N, wrong-tenant receipt routing must fail a fake-provider assertion; for H, inserting a synthetic sentinel into process-only configuration must fail a non-disclosure assertion. Record exact failure symptoms, restore the source and rerun. A suite that passes because its routes remain refused, fixtures fall back to Mongo, or opt-in suites are skipped proves nothing.

Reuse existing focused instruments rather than rewriting the oracle:

package existing CRM tests to extend/reuse S/E tests/tenant-credential-http.integration.test.js, tests/tenant-entries-http.integration.test.js, tests/api.entries.test.js, tests/api.count-parameter.test.js, tests/api.count-where.test.js, tests/api.v1-read-refusal.test.js, tests/api3.v1-writes-history.test.js T tests/api.treatments.test.js, tests/api.same-time-treatments.test.js, tests/api.treatments.resend-reply.test.js, tests/api.treatments-write-validation.test.js, tests/api.treatments-tt-units.test.js D tests/api.devicestatus.test.js, tests/api.devicestatus.resend-guard.test.js, tests/api.devicestatus.identifier-match.test.js, tests/api.activity.test.js, tests/api.activity-date-coercion.test.js F tests/api.profiles.test.js, tests/api.profiles.resend.test.js, tests/api.food.test.js, tests/api.food.quickpicks.test.js, tests/api3.history-restart.test.js H/N tests/api.status.test.js, tests/api.verifyauth.test.js, tests/api.security.test.js, tests/api3.settings-read-scope.test.js, tests/tenant-jwt-http.integration.test.js, tests/tenant-runtime-vault.integration.test.js, tests/api.alexa.test.js, tests/api.googlehome.test.js

For actual client compatibility, prioritize synthetic uploader/retry/read workflows for entries, treatments, device status and profile. tests/api.aaps-client.test.js and tests/api3.aaps-patterns.test.js are existing client-pattern instruments. Pin the relevant client source revision before extracting another workflow; a source-derived client pattern is a hypothesis until replayed through HTTP. Do not claim real-client acceptance from parser unit tests or assume API3 conventions satisfy a v1 uploader. Replay retained extension fields and retry responses, not private client data/configuration.

docs.title: Execution and integration order
docs.text:
1. Start clean domain worktrees from the accepted cumulative base; pin source and characterize the owned legacy/G3 family against Mongo. Implement domain schemas/adapters and tests while S makes the narrow legacy injection exports. Domain tests may inject completed exported ports, but must later pass through the real integration mount before admission is claimed.
  2. Join existing CRUD and CLI deliveries when accepted. S reconciles their shared surfaces once, preserving their tests; teams rebase/merge only clean accepted commits. Land E/T/D/F independently with scoped capability admission and real-provider HTTP tests. No blanket enabledCollections switch, NS_TEST_BACKEND=postgres availability switch or broad permission wildcard as a shortcut.
  3. Join H's snapshot/credential/status work; expand cache-backed/derived reads only after their cross-tenant tests pass. Implement authority administration and N side effects as their own bounded capabilities. Excluded endpoints remain visibly excluded until delivered.
  4. At coherent delivery joins, run the full established suite and browser/client workflows, then the existing PR check last. Parent records acceptance once; do not manufacture a packet dependency before each collection can code or test.

Representative existing commands, run in the implementation worktree with its owned test environment (not executed for this design):

# Example targeted legacy baseline; substitute the package's existing/new focused files.
node bin/with-env.js ./my.test.env node_modules/mocha/bin/mocha.js \
  --fail-zero --timeout 10000 --require ./tests/hooks.js --exit \
  tests/api.entries.test.js tests/api.count-where.test.js \
  tests/api3.v1-writes-history.test.js

# Existing real-provider HTTP instrument: opt in, never count a skipped suite as a pass.
NS_TENANT_CREDENTIAL_HTTP_DOCKER_TEST=1 node bin/with-env.js ./my.test.env \
  node_modules/mocha/bin/mocha.js --fail-zero --timeout 120000 \
  --require ./tests/hooks.js --exit tests/tenant-credential-http.integration.test.js

# At the coherent integrated join, not after every documentation or isolated adapter change.
npm run test:tiers
npm run test:all
npm run test:browser
# After fetching/merging official/dev and rerunning affected/full tests:
tools/review/prcheck/prcheck.sh

New tenant integration tests must expose explicit opt-ins as the existing instruments do, be assigned in the tier/census registries by S, and report missing providers as skipped/ UNMEASURED, never silently use the dormant lab in place of actual admission. Preserve single/Mongo tests and source controls at every join. Do not install dependencies or run broad tests merely to validate this document.

docs.title: 6. Completion gate for the full REST goal
docs.text:
S adds a focused executable route-matrix regression test in CRM as the implementation evolves: enumerate the actual mounted router graph with its configuration predicates and compare against the families in §2. Exercise each expanded family/method over HTTP for one authorized success and its relevant refusal; distinguish native methods, implicit HEAD/OPTIONS, prefix redirects, inherited v2 and disabled conditional integrations. An unknown collection/method must not acquire permission or storage merely because the generic code exists.

Do not write a constants-only inventory test. Its negative control adds a synthetic mounted route with no matrix case and must fail; remove a mapped mount and require an exercised HTTP case to fail. Turning off provider opt-ins or skipping backend fixtures must make the completeness report incomplete. Existing source fixtures with dormant PATCH routes are not evidence that the real credential bridge admits PATCH.

The full v1–v3 target is complete only when:

  • every unconditional matrix row is tenant-implemented and verified, and every shipping conditional family either has its tenant capability implemented/tested or an explicit approved product disposition; "preview excluded" alone does not close it;
  • Mongo-compatible semantics and explicit tenant differences have actual HTTP evidence for parsing, credentials, response/status/headers, queries, retries, batches, writes and history;
  • persisted authority, PG/RLS, shared identity collisions, tenant snapshots/events and restart controls pass without tenant/process secret leakage or fallback to single/Mongo;
  • the runnable API process advertises and serves that measured breadth, with read-only readiness and owned shutdown; owner/private-operator roles remain separately authorized;
  • the integrated full suite, relevant client/browser workflows and last-step PR check pass, with pending/unmeasured exclusions disclosed rather than counted green.

Production identity/transport provenance, HA, durable registry, activation/owner lifecycle, realtime and connector/evaluator operation retain their own completion criteria. Completing REST does not silently complete those programmes, and a useful partial preview does not require waiting for them.

docs.title: Settings, extensibility, new data, and delegated access: four open questions
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-09-10. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

Contributor-facing. Snapshot — describes 2026-09-10. Status: current as analysis; its auth-related framing predates D13–D17. Current decisions: execution plan §1. §5's delegation requirements are carried as DR1–DR7 in the authority specification §7, which is proposed to supersede the delegation parts of the earlier draft in cgm-remote-monitor's docs/proposals.

Date: 2026-09-10. Fourth in a series with Typed schemas, Extending the document model and devicestatus and profile fidelity.

Nothing here is a proposal to merge, and §5 in particular is a technical sketch, not legal or regulatory advice. Anything acted on from §5 needs review by someone qualified in health-data privacy for the jurisdictions involved.

docs.title: TL;DR — the four questions, answered directly
docs.text:
Question Answer Have we documented all the settings and dosing inputs? Now, mostly. 60 inputs across both algorithm families, each checked against the corpus. What is not documented is the settings surface that never becomes an algorithm input — every user-facing preference in AAPS, Loop and Trio Are they recorded with high fidelity? No, and the gap is symmetric. Loop records its safety limits and none of its algorithm-behaviour switches. oref0 derivatives record their algorithm state and none of their safety limits. Neither family records a complete configuration Is there a roadmap for uniting field names or providing extensibility? There was not. §4 is one, sequenced by measured cost, with the cheapest and least disruptive steps first Does new out-of-band data change anything? Structurally, no — the pattern already exists (activity, type-discriminated). For privacy, yes, categorically, and that is §5's problem more than the schema's Privacy-preserving delegation between agents? Nothing in the ecosystem does this today. Nightscout's read permission is *:*:read — one bit. §5 sets out what would have to exist

The finding worth leading with. Two AID families, two complementary halves of a configuration record, and no site has both:

Safety limits Algorithm behaviour Loop recorded (loopSettings.maximumBolus, maximumBasalRatePerHour, minimumBGGuard) absent — 8 switches, including one that scales every automatic dose AAPS absent — maxIob, maxBasal are preferences, uploaded nowhere partly recorded (sensitivityConfiguration, apsConfiguration, smoothing) Trio absent — its uploader writes no limits recorded (the openaps.* determination)

automaticBolusApplicationFactor is the sharpest single example. It is the fraction of a recommended bolus Loop actually delivers, it defaults to 0.4, and it is recorded nowhere. Two sites with identical therapy settings and identical glucose will dose differently, and nothing in Nightscout says why.

docs.title: 1. What is now documented
docs.text:
specs/nsschema/dosing-input-sources.yaml covers 60 dosing inputs across two algorithms, each mapped to the Nightscout paths that could carry it and each claim checked against the census by make schema-dosing. All 60 currently hold.

Inputs recorded derivable partial absent oref0 (AAPS, Trio, OpenAPS) 40 20 9 3 8 Loop 20 4 7 1 8

The two sets come from different kinds of evidence, and the difference matters:

  • oref0's is capture-derived — the union of input.* paths across the 385 replay vectors in conformance/, from real AAPS and Loop phone runs.
  • Loop's is source-derived, from AlgorithmInput in externals/LoopAlgorithm/Sources/LoopAlgorithm/AlgorithmInput.swift. No vector set in this repo carries Loop's native inputs: the files under conformance/loop/vectors/ are Loop data replayed through the oref0 harness for cross-validation, so they describe oref0's input shape. An earlier reading of this document's series treated them as Loop's, which would have missed every finding in §2.

docs.title: 1.1 What is still not documented
docs.text:
• The settings surface that is not an algorithm input. Alarm thresholds, display preferences, connection settings, pump-specific configuration. AAPS's overviewConfiguration alone carries ~25 of these. A dosing replay does not need them; a support conversation, a bug report or an incident review often does.
  • Loop's override presets as configuration. overridePresets is recorded (10 sites, 100% of profile documents) but is a list of things the user might do, not a record of settings in force; the active override is elsewhere.
  • Pump-side limits. Every pump enforces its own maxima independently of the controller. None of it reaches Nightscout.
  • Anything from AndroidAPS, from data. The corpus has no AAPS closed-loop site; all AAPS statements here are read from its wire models.

docs.title: 2. The configuration gap is symmetric, and that is the interesting part
docs.text:
If this were one vendor being careless it would be a bug report. It is two mature projects each recording the half the other omits, which means it is a missing shared expectation rather than a missing feature.

Loop's absent eight are all algorithm-behaviour switches: automaticBolusApplicationFactor, carbAbsorptionModel, recommendationInsulinModel, useIntegralRetrospectiveCorrection, includePositiveVelocityAndRC, useMidAbsorptionISF, maxActiveInsulinMultiplier, gradualTransitionsThreshold. Several change the delivered dose directly.

oref0's absent eight are run state and one limit: microBolusAllowed, flatBGsDetected, the unannounced-meal detection slopes, bolus-snooze IOB, and maxIob.

Neither is hard to fix in principle — both are small, stable, and already serialized somewhere on the device. The obstacle is that nothing says they should be recorded, which is what OBS-PROF-004 in specs/conformance/observability-profile.yaml now says, and what §4 phase 4 sequences.

docs.title: 3. Naming: what actually diverges
docs.text:
Before proposing unification it is worth being precise about how much divergence there is, because the answer is "less than it feels like, but in load-bearing places". From the quirks registry and the vendor surfaces:

Kind Example Scope Same concept, different name Loop bolusVolume vs Nocturne's expected bolus; tempBasalAdjustment vs tempBasal 4 paths, 10 sites, drops the dosing decision Same concept, different word order Suspend Pump (Nightscout, corpus) vs Pump Suspend (Nocturne's V4 map) 22 documents unroutable Same concept, different shape flat pump.bolusing vs nested pump.status.bolusing 85.1% vs 10.5% of device statuses Same concept, different vocabulary mg/dl, mg/dL, mmol, mmol/L across three of our own specs and the data every profile document Same name, different concept activity = insulin activity (dU/min, a dosing input) and physical activity (a collection) ecosystem-wide Same concept, different case Normal vs normal 130,257 documents

The last two are the dangerous ones. A case mismatch fails loudly. A name collision between insulin activity and physical activity fails silently, in a generated type, in a clinical context.

docs.title: 4. A roadmap, sequenced by measured cost
docs.text: Each phase states what it costs, from the measurements rather than from estimation, and phases are ordered so that nothing later depends on a decision that has not been made.

docs.title: Phase 0 — done, and it was the precondition
docs.text: Census, spec correction to 2025.2.0, the quirks registry, the generated artifacts. Strict validation went from rejecting 93.5%/63.4%/100%/100% of live documents to 6.4%/15.2%/10.5%/0.0% without any client changing anything. Documenting a field is strictly cheaper than relocating it, and that is the measured basis for everything below.

docs.title: Phase 1 — alias, do not rename. Cost: zero for writers
docs.text:
Nothing in §3 needs a writer to change. Every divergence there can be resolved by declaring both forms and naming one canonical:

  • declare the alias pairs in the spec (bolusVolume ↔ bolus, tempBasalAdjustment ↔ tempBasal, flat ↔ nested pump status)
  • extend enums to the union, as 2025.2.0 already did for direction, eventType, type and units
  • add a reader-facing normalization table — the quirks registry's reader_guidance is already this, for 17 deviations

A rename breaks every existing reader. An alias breaks nobody, and a generated normalizer makes the canonical form available to anyone who wants it. Renaming should be reserved for the one case where both names cannot coexist — and §3 contains no such case.

docs.title: Phase 2 — fix the two mismatches that lose data. Cost: two small patches
docs.text: Pump Suspend/Suspend Pump in Nocturne's V4 event map, and bolus/tempBasal in LoopAutomaticDoseRecommendation. Both are upstream one-liners; both currently discard real dosing records. Neither needs a convention to be agreed first.

docs.title: Phase 3 — extension points where the data actually is. Cost: measured at 6.4–15.2%
docs.text:
x-aid-extensions as documentation costs nothing and should be adopted now. As an enforced layout it costs 6.4%/15.2%/10.5%/0.0% of live documents per collection — that is the migration, and it is now a number rather than a fear.

The structural finding is more important than the convention: an extension bag at a document's root does not protect a tree. devicestatus loses 56 of 166 paths to a typed model because [JsonExtensionData] sits on DeviceStatus and on none of its nested classes. Either every level gets an extension point, or devicestatus is composed from separately-typed resources. The second is what activity already does.

docs.title: Phase 4 — record the configuration. Cost: new fields, no migration
docs.text:
The §2 gap. Concretely:

  1. Agree a vendor-neutral location. profile.loopSettings is the existing precedent and the wrong name for a shared one.
  2. Loop adds its eight behaviour switches; AAPS adds maxIob and maxBasal; Trio adds both halves.
  3. Declare it in the spec, so it is a contract rather than another flattened subtree.

This is additive: no existing reader breaks, and the fields already exist on every device.

docs.title: Phase 5 — new collections follow the activity pattern
docs.text: One collection, a type discriminator, per-type payload fields, an extension bag on the model. Shipped and working (§5.1 of the fidelity report). Our own aid-heartrate-2025.yaml proposes a conflicting separate /heartrate collection and should be reconciled to the shipped pattern.

docs.title: What should not be on this roadmap
docs.text: Tenant-registered custom resource definitions, on current evidence. The long tail this corpus shows is five leaf fields and one misspelling — thin justification for a per-tenant schema store, per-tenant validators, and a schema-migration story. Revisit if a controller maintainer names a new kind of record with its own lifecycle.

docs.title: 5. New data, and delegation between agents
5.1 Structurally, new data changes little
docs.text:
Adding heart rate, steps, sleep, menstrual cycle or geolocation needs no new architecture. The activity collection is already a polymorphic, type-discriminated resource with an extension bag, and cgm-remote-monitor already has the collection and the api:activity:create permission.

Three practical consequences, none architectural:

  • Rate and retention differ by orders of magnitude. CGM is one reading per five minutes. Heart rate from a watch can be per-second. The dbsize and retention machinery assumes the former.
  • The activity name collision (§3) must be resolved before generated types make it permanent.
  • aid-heartrate-2025.yaml conflicts with the shipped pattern and should be reconciled rather than implemented.

docs.title: 5.2 For privacy, new data changes the category
docs.text:
This is where the answer stops being "no". Glucose and insulin are sensitive. Menstrual-cycle data, precise geolocation and calendar contents are sensitive in different ways: they identify, they reveal things about people who never consented (a calendar names other people), and several carry specific legal regimes that vary sharply by jurisdiction.

Combining them is the point — predicting dinners from a calendar, or correlating sensitivity with cycle phase, is real clinical value — and combination is also exactly what makes a dataset re-identifying. This work's own experience is the small version of that: field names were safe to publish, and it took five successive rules before field values were, with each rule added because the previous set demonstrably leaked.

docs.title: 5.3 What exists today
docs.text:
Capability Status Read permission granularity One bit. The readable role is *:*:read; there is no per-collection, per-field or per-time-range read scope Write permission granularity Per collection (api:treatments:create, api:activity:create) Identity enteredBy, a free-text nickname, unverified Delegation grants Designed in docs/10-domain/authority-model.md — scopes, constraints, expiry, time windows — and not implemented Time-bounded access Concept exists in nightscout-roles-gateway (scheduled_policies, connection_policies) Purpose limitation Nothing anywhere Audit of reads Nothing. srvCreated/srvModified track writes only

ADR-003 is a real constraint on any design here, and a deliberate one: Nightscout does not implement credentials, on liability grounds, and treats access as consent-granted rather than credential-proven. So delegation has to ride on an external identity provider — which is what the roles gateway's Mode B does — and cannot become a bespoke auth system.

[Decided since for the hosted target (D13, D17 — plan §2.8–§2.9): each tenant holds its own root credential and devices keep a native per-tenant credential permanently; an external identity provider for human identity (one cohort-wide Ory Kratos pool) is direction of travel, held pending T30-ORY-PROOF; Hydra is deferred.]

docs.title: 5.4 What a delegation design would have to provide
docs.text:
Carried as requirements DR1–DR7 in the authority specification §7.

Stated as requirements rather than a solution, because this is the part that needs qualified review:

  1. Scoped reads, enforced in storage. Today a delegated reader gets everything. The multitenancy work measured Postgres RLS at 0.3–0.6 ms overhead and showed it is fail-closed — an unbound connection returns zero rows, not everything. A read scope that is a storage predicate rather than an application filter is the only kind that survives a forgotten WHERE.
  2. Bounded queries. §6.5 of the multitenancy discussion found $regex reaching MongoDB with no pattern guard, no index requirement and no maxTimeMS. A read grant is a denial-of-service grant today, before any privacy question is reached. Query profiles are a prerequisite for delegation, not a parallel workstream.
  3. Purpose and expiry as first-class, not documentation. A grant for "meal prediction" should not read cycle data, and should stop working on a date. authority-model.md already models constraints and expiry for writes; reads need the same shape.
  4. Answers rather than data, where it suffices. An agent predicting dinner needs carb patterns by time of day, not the treatment log. A derived-value grant is a smaller disclosure than a raw-read grant, and for AI agents in particular the difference is the whole risk.
  5. Read audit. Delegation without a record of what was read is indistinguishable from a copy.
  6. Revocation that is real. Once an agent has read raw data, revocation cannot un-read it. This argues for narrow, short-lived, derived grants over broad standing ones — and it is the single strongest argument for (4).
  7. Minimization at the boundary. The de-identification machinery built here (tools/nsschema/redact.py, scan_pii.py) is a working precedent: a name denylist, a cardinality cap, value-shape rejection, suffix rules and cross-site corroboration, each added because the previous set leaked. Anything exporting to an agent needs an equivalent, and should expect to need several iterations.

docs.title: 5.5 What this evidence base can and cannot say
docs.text: It can say that the read-permission model is one bit, that query cost is unbounded, and that combining collections is what makes data identifying — all measured or read from code. It cannot say what a correct consent model looks like for cycle data in any given jurisdiction; that is a question for counsel and for the people whose data it is, and this document should not be read as having answered it.

docs.title: 6. What is not measured
docs.text:
• The full settings surface of any controller — §1.1. Only inputs that reach the dosing algorithm are inventoried.
  • Whether the absent configuration fields are stable enough to record. A switch that changes between builds may need a version alongside it.
  • Anything about delegation in practice. No implementation exists to measure; §5 is requirements, not results.
  • Rate and volume for physiological data. §5.1's claim that retention assumptions break is reasoning from the collection interval, not a measurement.
  • AndroidAPS from data, still.

docs.title: The earlier control-plane draft and the specifications proposed to supersede it
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-09-11. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

What this is: a supersession map (contributor-facing). Read after the platform specifications; leads to integration questionnaire defaults. Snapshot — describes the earlier draft at cgm-remote-monitor a8888f0d and this repository's specifications at main df93608c (2026-10-18). Status: current; no decision rests on it. Current decisions: execution plan §1. The 2026-09-11 analysis of the same draft is in git: full text at 85c645c8.

The earlier draft in cgm-remote-monitor's docs/proposals came from earlier versions of this repository and was added there in cgm-remote-monitor 12c90cfc (2026-01-19). This repository's platform specifications are proposed to supersede it. Each row below names the rule that now carries an idea of the draft and what changes. The specifications share one premise: the hub routes and records, never composes intents, never judges whether a change is safe and never doses; validation and enactment stay the controller's (D18).

docs.title: 1. The earlier draft
docs.text:
Read at cgm-remote-monitor a8888f0d; none of the five files has changed since db32bdc6 (2026-01-18).

file what it proposes proposed to be superseded by agent-control-plane-rfc.md an event envelope; configuration, runtime, computed, delivery and capability objects; ten collections and an event stream; bridge mode; authority, scopes, delegation and audit records, registration, state and intent, commands, sync transport, authority bridge-rules.md synthesising those objects from today's devicestatus, treatments and profile registration §2–§3 (well-known registrations), records R1–R2, state and intent S6–S7 conflict-resolution.md an authority hierarchy, five conflict scenarios, optimistic locking, a global event cursor, delegation grants, safety invariants state and intent S1, A7–A9, sync transport T8–T9, authority §7 oidc-actor-identity-proposal.md verified actor identity through OpenID Connect, an actors collection, delegation claims, a migration away from enteredBy authority AU1–AU4, authority §8 integration-questionnaire.md 16 questions to Loop, AAPS, Trio and OpenAPS implementers integration questionnaire defaults: a default answer per controller, read from source

The hub reports each product's instances, ends one by another only as the controller declares (supersedes, overlay), and marks overlap without resolving it (A9) Flip-flop prevention: rate limits per issuer, a cooldown, confirmation after N activations commands §9 (proposal volume, UCA-PROP-002) Open: nothing limits the open proposals one instance holds on a channel Optimistic locking on srvModified; a global eventCursors counter registration §5.4; sync transport T3, T8, T9 Registration resources use etags and If-Match. No global counter document Identity model: human and caregiver by OAuth, controller by a device-bound key, agent by OAuth with a delegation token authority AU1–AU4 By audience: devices and uploaders hold a native per-tenant credential; owners and caregivers are to sign in through one Ory Kratos pool on hosted sites (adopted in principle, gated); third-party delegated access is deferred. docs.title: 3. Measured findings the specifications carry
docs.text: Measured over the corpus in reports/schema-census/ (snapshots dated 2026-04-01 and 2026-04-26; 11 sites, 9 of them Loop; one site carries openaps.*, and it is Trio's; no AndroidAPS closed-loop site and no oref0 rig). Counts are docs_present across both snapshots, which overlap, so they bound distinct documents from above; §3.4 counts distinct documents.

docs.title: 3.1 Fields already on the wire
docs.text: what the draft proposes on the wire today where the specifications use it an idempotency key treatments.syncIdentifier, 306,741 (83%, 10 sites) the client's identifier (identity I1, I5) a human or automation flag treatments.automatic, boolean, 300,228 (81%, 10 sites) Bolus.Automatic (records §3); a wire value can stand for an initiator through wireProxy (state and intent S8) controller version loop.version 597,335 (85%, 10 sites); openaps.version 73,898 (1 site) the product and version a settings snapshot carries (records R5) override state override.active 597,335 (85%, 10 sites) Loop's applied override carrier (state and intent S7)

docs.title: 3.2 Trio and AndroidAPS both write openaps
docs.text: No corpus document has a top-level trio key, and Trio's wire model declares openaps, suggested and enacted (Trio/Sources/Models/NightscoutStatus.swift). The well-known Trio and AndroidAPS registrations use the same structural discriminator, {path: openaps, test: is-object} (specs/sync/registrations/trio.yaml:18-20), so the two cannot be told apart by a top-level key, and cgm-remote-monitor's readers cannot either (lib/plugins/openaps.js:82). In the specifications a registered controller's records are attributed to its instance and definition (registration §11), and a controller-published registration takes precedence over a structurally inferred one (registration §2).

docs.title: 3.3 Instance identity and the device string
docs.text: devicestatus.device is on every devicestatus document and is free text: one site's device strings read like a controller while its treatments show no automated dosing. An instance id is a random UUID v4 the controller supplies, never derived from a device name, model, serial number or devicestatus.device (identity §2); the hub may keep the string as an observed alias, labelled {level: identifying, category: device} and withheld by default (registration §8).

docs.title: 3.4 Overrides with a name and no effect
docs.text:
Of the 55,938 distinct devicestatus documents with an active override:

count share effect and name both present 42,799 76.5% effect only 2,176 3.9% name only, no effect 10,892 19.5% neither 71 0.1%

Of 2,865 temporary effects in treatments, 399 carry a label and no effect. A reader that synthesises an override's effect from these records gets none for one in five. In the specifications the hub never computes a composed result from them (state and intent S1); a kind declares the fields it does not publish (unpublishedFields, S6); and a setting a controller does not publish is recorded as not published, never filled with a default (records R6). The draft therapy-effect schema separates an effect from why it was asked for (state and intent §5).

docs.title: 3.5 Suggested, requested and confirmed
docs.text:
state Loop oref0 family (Trio, AAPS) suggested, manual bolus loop.recommendedBolus, 597,143 (85%, 10 sites) openaps.recommendedBolus, 41,474 (1 site) suggested, automatic dose loop.automaticDoseRecommendation, 183,049 (26%, 10 sites) openaps.suggested, 73,898 (1 site) requested not published not published confirmed loop.enacted with received, 405,228 (58%, 10 sites) openaps.enacted with received, 73,834 (1 site)

Loop's writer sets loop.enacted.received to true whenever there is a recommendation and no error, so it is not a pump acknowledgement; Trio sets received from the pump call's result (questionnaire defaults C7). Loop's only failure text is loop.failureReason, a string on 16,550 documents (2.4%). The suggestions decompose into ApsSnapshot's RecommendedBolus and Enacted (records §3); a request recorded apart from its effect is the requested carrier (state and intent S7); for a command, handed over and not yet acknowledged is the sent or fetched state (commands §4).

docs.title: 3.6 Safety limits
docs.text: Loop records its limits in profile.loopSettings (200 profile documents, 10 sites). The corpus holds no max_iob from any oref0 derivative, so a replay of corpus data has to assume it. oref0's own rig uploads its preferences file, max_iob included, as devicestatus.preferences (oref0 d219baf9 bin/ns-status.js:40-49,175-177); Trio and AndroidAPS write a cap only into reason text when it binds. Of the dosing inputs each family declares, Nightscout records 20% for Loop and 50% for the oref0 family (55% and 72% counting derivable inputs). The specifications carry this as the settings snapshot and the declared replay inputs (records R5, R6, R8, §5).

docs.title: 3.7 Sync cost of typed collections
docs.text: API v3 gives a client one delta read per collection, so a client that uses it as designed reads each collection separately, and every typed collection added adds a read. One read and one write across collections make the cost independent of the number of collections (sync transport §3, T5, T7). The change list is the replay-fidelity proposal §1.

docs.title: 4.1 An override proposed, approved, requested and applied
docs.text:
An agent instance proposes an exercise override; a person approves it; Loop, as a registered controller holding the override channel's command-sink, enacts it. Each step is a typed record. Identifiers are shortened, and the payload is illustrative, because no definition yet declares a command payload's shape (commands §9 item 3).

# 1. Proposal (commands CM11). The agent's own instance holds a propose role (CM12).
proposal:
  proposalId: p-41
  instanceId: 9b2f…            # the agent's instance (registration §8)
  channel: override
  payload: {preset: Exercise, durationMinutes: 60}
  payloadHash: sha256:7c1e…
  basedOn: sha256:a90d…        # Loop's state version the agent read (state and intent A12)
  expiresAt: 2026-10-18T15:10:00Z
  state: open

# 2. The approval names the hash (CM13, CM14). The hub creates one command (CM1).
approval: {proposalId: p-41, payloadHash: sha256:7c1e…}
command:
  commandId: c-118
  proposalId: p-41
  payloadHash: sha256:7c1e…
  initiator: {value: other, controllerTerm: agent}   # state and intent S8
  state: pending

# 3. Loop fetches it (CM18), checks the hash, the expiry and its own limits (CM10),
#    enacts it, and reports the record that shows the effect (CM7).
outcome: {commandId: c-118, state: succeeded, payloadHash: sha256:7c1e…, record: {identifier: 5d3a…}}

# 4. Loop's records give the two layers the hub reports (state and intent S7, A10):
#    treatments   `Temporary Override`, duration in minutes      -> the requested instance
#    devicestatus `override`, duration in seconds remaining      -> the applied layer

docs.title: 4.2 An approval bound to a payload hash
docs.text: The proposal's payload hashes to sha256:7c1e…. An approval naming sha256:7c1e… creates a command whose payload is the proposal's, byte for byte. An approval naming any other hash is refused 409 hash-mismatch, and the proposal stays open. An approval after Loop's records have changed the state version is refused 409 state-changed (CM15); one after the override channel's command-sink has moved to another Loop instance is refused 409 destination-changed (CM13). The state version is the hub's record of what Loop reported, so state-changed tells the approver that the record changed, never that Loop's own state is unchanged.

docs.title: Design — how ordering crosses the storage seam
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-06 at 773c8bc59.

Contributor-facing. Snapshot, written 2026-09-15. Current: the only statement of how ordering crosses the storage seam. Proposal, for whoever owns the adapter. Written against seam/t1-2-storage-interface (externals/work/crm-seam @ 81a1f6ce); not implemented beyond what §5 marks done. Decisions it assumes: D3, D4, D8 — execution plan §1. Evidence: ordering and pagination · tools/qc/order-arm.js

The filter got an AST. Ordering did not, and T2.5 landed a PostgreSQL backend without one — it has an orderBy in lib/api3/storage/pgCollection/sql.js that solves one of the three sub-problems correctly and records a second as a known difference. This is the missing design: what the three sub-problems are, what is already settled, and what remains a decision.

Scope. This is about ordering, not pagination strategy. Keyset pagination is a better answer than skip/limit for both backends and is out of scope here — though §4 notes that the tiebreak below is its precondition.

docs.title: 1. The interface change
docs.text:
findFiltered(col, ast, { sort, … }) currently takes sort as a MongoDB sort document and hands it to cursor.sort(). That is a driver object crossing an interface whose stated purpose is that driver objects do not cross it.

Ordering should become an AST the same way filters did:

// lib/storage/order.js — sibling of lib/storage/filter.js
{ terms: [ { field: 'date', direction: -1 }, … ] }
toMongoSort(order)  -> { date: -1, _id: -1 }
toOrderBy(order, { columns, jsonbColumn })  -> ' ORDER BY "date" DESC NULLS LAST, id DESC'

Two adapters, one normaliser, and the same differential-test treatment the filter AST got. The normaliser is where §4's tiebreak lives, so that neither backend can forget it.

docs.title: 2. Sub-problem A — null and missing placement · settled, and already implemented
docs.text:
MongoDB sorts missing and null together, first ascending. PostgreSQL defaults to NULLS LAST, and a missing jsonb path is SQL NULL.

Emit NULLS FIRST ascending and NULLS LAST descending. T2.5's orderBy already does exactly this, with the reasoning in a comment. Nothing further is needed.

docs.title: 3. Sub-problem B — cross-type ordering · open, and harder than it looks
docs.text:
Ten documents, one field holding one value each, ascending, measured against mongod 7 and PostgreSQL 16:

BSON  asc:  null | -5 | 0 | [1] | 1000 | "120" | "a" | {a:1} | false | true
jsonb asc:  null | "120" | "a" | -5 | 0 | 1000 | false | true | [1] | {a:1}

Three distinct disagreements, not one:

  1. Number and String are transposed. BSON: Null < Number < String. jsonb: Null < String < Number.
  2. Boolean moves. BSON puts Boolean after Object; jsonb puts it before Array and Object.
  3. MongoDB does not give arrays a type rank at all. [1] sorted between 0 and 1000 — an array is compared by its minimum contained element ascending. jsonb ranks arrays as a type, above every scalar.

The third one is why "write a bson_type_rank() function" is not a complete answer. A rank function reproduces 1 and 2 for scalars and cannot reproduce 3 for arrays without jsonb_array_elements and an aggregate — per row, per sort term.

docs.title: 3.1 Three options
docs.text: what it does cost what it gives up O1 type-bucketed key leading bson_type_rank(doc#>'{f}') term, then the typed value an IMMUTABLE function and a composite expression index per sortable field still wrong for arrays unless the element-minimum rule is also implemented O2 declare sortable fields single-typed restrict ?sort= to schema-declared single-typed fields; HTTP 400 otherwise a schema annotation and a validation branch clients sorting on an undeclared field O3 accept and document what T2.5 did none silent divergence when a sort key is mixed-typed

docs.title: 3.1b The strategy T2.5 built: a type-guarded generated column
docs.text:
order-arm.js measured four translations and none matched. T2.5 built a fifth that was not in that set. From the emitted DDL:

"sgv" numeric GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
  CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(doc #> '{sgv}') = 'number'
       THEN (doc #>> '{sgv}')::numeric END) STORED

orderBy sorts on that column whenever one exists. Measured against mongod 7 with tools/qc/typeguard-arm.js:

On single-typed data it matches mongod exactly, ascending and descending. That is the first translation of the five to do so, and the guard is what earns it — without it a mixed column raises 22P02 (divergence class D).

On mixed-typed data it does not merely differ, it inverts. The guard rejects a wrong-typed value to SQL NULL, which is indistinguishable from an absent key and from an explicit JSON null, so under NULLS FIRST it sorts to the front — where MongoDB sorts it after every number:

sort {sgv: 1}
  mongod                   null | ABSENT | 40 | 100 | 400 | "120" | "high" | true
  pg, typed column (T2.5)  "120" | "high" | null | ABSENT | true | 40 | 100 | 400

A string sgv moves from last to first. The emitted DDL already warns that a column built from ->> cannot distinguish an absent key from an explicit null, and directs $exists to read doc #> '{path}' instead. The same warning applies to ORDER BY and is written down nowhere — and unlike $exists, ordering has no alternative expression that would be correct, because the jsonb path diverges too (it carries jsonb's type order, not BSON's).

This is measured, not derived: the harness reports matches on a single-typed corpus in both directions, so a DIFFERS is a fact about the data rather than about the harness.

docs.title: 3.2 Recommendation, and the measurement that decides it
docs.text:
O2, falling back to O1 only if the corpus shows a mixed-typed sort key in real data.

§3.1b turns this from a preference into a measurement: the translation T2.5 already ships is exactly correct under O2's condition and inverted without it. So O2 is not a restriction bolted onto the adapter — it is the precondition the adapter is already assuming. Enforcing it makes an existing assumption checkable; declining to enforce it leaves a silent inversion behind a 200.

O2 is cheap, it is enforceable, and it converts a silent wrong answer into a loud rejection — which is the trade this project has made everywhere else (BF-04's allowlist, v3's parseLimit). O1 is real work and buys nothing if no deployment stores a mixed-typed sort key.

T2.5's orderBy comment asserts the favourable case:

Every sort this code path issues is on a field that is one type in practice (date, srvModified, identifier, created_at), so it does not bite today.

That claim was measured against the 11-site corpus (1,968,464 documents, two snapshots) in sort-key typing: confirmed for the four named fields (single-typed wherever present), and every entries path is single-typed. But on the client-reachable set it is false at 11 of 11 sites — treatments.carbs and treatments.insulin hold null and number everywhere; that pair does not reorder, which is a property of those two types, not of the field being one type. Two things follow:

  • The claim is about the fields this code path issues. API v3 lets the client choose the sort key via ?sort=/?sort$desc=, so the enforceable set is not the same as the observed set. O2 is what closes that gap; without it the comment describes today's callers, not tomorrow's requests.
  • The clean result supports O2. It does not support O3, because O3 leaves the client free to sort on a field nobody measured.

docs.title: 4. Sub-problem C — ties and total order · settled; one line, both backends
docs.text:
ORDER BY is not a total order unless the terms uniquely identify a row, and neither engine promises stability among equal keys. BF-13 is this defect on MongoDB: when v3's whole tiebreak chain ties, skip/limit paging lost 7 of 12 documents and duplicated two, deterministically (reproduced). Its MongoDB-path fix is merged to dev via PR #8738 (2026-09-18) and is not released. Sized against the corpus it is concentrated in devicestatus — median 23.46 expected straddles per paginated sweep, against 0.01 for entries.

The normaliser appends _id (ascending or matching the last term's direction) as a final term, always, for every backend. _id is present and unique by construction, so the order becomes total and both engines become deterministic.

T2.5's orderBy emits only the caller's terms, so BF-13 reappears on PostgreSQL unless this lands in the shared normaliser rather than in either adapter.

This is also the precondition for keyset pagination later: a total order is what makes WHERE (k, _id) > (:last_k, :last_id) well defined.

docs.title: 5. What this leaves for the adapter owner
docs.text: status null/missing placement done in T2.5 _id tiebreak in a shared normaliser not done — one line; closes the BF-13 class on both backends at the seam sort as an AST rather than a driver object not done typed generated column + guard done in T2.5, and correct under single-typed data cross-type ordering decide O1/O2/O3 — see §3.1b and the corpus measurement

docs.title: 6. Limits
docs.text:
• §3.1b tested one field, one numeric column, one sort term. sgv with eight values. Text columns, compound sorts and descending-with-NULLS LAST on a text column were not measured, and a compound sort could interact with the guard in ways a single term cannot show.
  • O1 is described, not prototyped. No bson_type_rank() has been written or benchmarked, and the index cost of a composite expression sort key is unmeasured.
  • The array rule is established for one shape. [1] versus scalars, ascending. Descending uses the array's maximum, which follows from the documented rule but was not measured here. Nested arrays and arrays of mixed type were not tested at all.
  • Collation is untouched. Both engines were compared with default collation and ASCII values. MongoDB's default is binary; PostgreSQL's depends on the database's LC_COLLATE, so string ordering can diverge between two PostgreSQL deployments before either is compared to MongoDB. Nothing here measures that, and it should be measured before any string field is declared sortable under O2.

docs.title: T1.1 — the storage seam: interface definition and call-site classification
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-09-14. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

Contributor-facing living interface definition. Sections 1–10 retain their dated historical census and implementation captures; §11 records current admitted ports. Task T1.1 of the execution plan; decisions it rests on: D3, D4, D8, D9 — plan §1. §1–§7 were measured 2026-09-14 against origin/chore/nightscout-modernization @ 0a4109f6; §8–§10 describe what was built on the seam/* branch chain (tip seam/t1-2-storage-interface @ 81a1f6ce, externals/work/crm-seam), which is unpublished. That base has since moved (to b1bdaca0 on 2026-09-21, a merge of dev); the seam is 68 behind it and trial-merges with 19 conflicting paths — queue item SEAM-REFRESH. Those branch/status observations describe that historical capture, not current dev or preview; see §11.

Deliverables: this document, plus reports/storage-seam/t1-1-call-site-classification.tsv (every site, classified) and the two scripts that produce it, so the count can be re-derived rather than trusted.

docs.title: 1. The count: 85 call sites
docs.text:
Method matters because two plausible greps undercount:

count method why it is wrong "~30 call sites" {M} §2.5, by inspection an estimate, never enumerated 68 grep excluding .find( dodging Array.find also dropped every col.find(filter) — the most common read in the codebase 82 grep excluding .find(<identifier>) the same exclusion still swallowed col.find(filter) 85 exclude only jQuery selectors and Array.find callbacks, then remove one verified DOM false positive —

85 storage call sites across 20 files. lib/plugins/pluginbase.js:45 (container.find(pillName), jQuery over majorPills) is the removed false positive.

docs.title: 2. The finding that changes the task: a third of it is already done
docs.text:
The sites are not 85 pieces of equivalent work. They stratify:

tier sites what it is T0 · interface consumers 15 lib/api3/generic/* and mongoCachedCollection already call col.storage.* / baseStorage.*. They never touch the driver. T1 · the interface + its Mongo adapter 14 mongoCollection/{index,find,modify}.js — this is a storage interface plus its MongoDB implementation, already written T2 · v1 domain modules 40 lib/server/{entries,treatments,devicestatus,profile,food,activity,aggregate}.js, lib/authorization/storage.js, lib/api/entries — raw driver T3 · socket write path 15 lib/server/websocket.js — raw driver (§5) T3 · factory 1 lib/storage/mongo-storage.js:216, createIndex

API v3 is roughly three-quarters of a seam that already exists. MongoCollection (lib/api3/storage/mongoCollection/index.js) exposes findOne, findOneFilter, findMany, insertOne, replaceOne, updateOne, deleteOne, deleteManyOr, version, getLastModified and identifyingFilter — a real interface, with a real decorator (mongoCachedCollection) already layered over it.

So T1.2 is not "design an abstraction and apply it to 85 sites". It is "finish the abstraction that api3 already has, then bring v1 to it". That is a materially smaller and lower-risk task, and it sets the sequencing in §7.

docs.title: 3. Classification
docs.text:
Full table in reports/storage-seam/t1-1-call-site-classification.tsv.

class sites meaning fits 39 maps onto the existing interface with no semantic loss needs-escape-hatch 27 works, but needs a capability the interface must name explicitly must-change 19 leaks driver semantics the caller must stop depending on fits escape-hatch must-change T0 consumer 15 — — T1 interface 5 — 1 T1 adapter 2 5 1 T2 v1 domain 6 21 13 T3 socket 11 — 4 T3 factory — 1 —

docs.title: 3.1 The 19 must-change sites are four root causes, not nineteen problems
docs.text:
root cause sites fix query_for(opts) returns a Mongo filter document 9 entries 44/52, treatments 251/276, devicestatus 129/138, profile 110, activity 120, authorization 88 $set / $unset partial updates 4 modify.js 49, websocket 358/411/578 Literal Mongo filters in domain code 2 food 146 ($and), treatments 114 ($in) ObjectId construction by the caller 2 entries 179, authorization 100 Raw collection/cursor handles 2 websocket 749 (ctx.store.collection()), mongoCollection/index 65 (self.col.find())

Nearly half of the must-change work is one root cause, and it is a root cause three other planned tasks already converge on — see §4.2.

docs.title: 3.2 The 27 escape hatches, grouped
docs.text: capability sites Postgres equivalent explicit upsert 7 INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE batch upsert (bulkWrite) 5 INSERT … ON CONFLICT, multi-row bare find → findMany 5 — (caller shape only) delete by filter 2 DELETE … WHERE cursor chaining .sort().limit() 2 findMany args batch insert (insertMany) 2 multi-row INSERT aggregation pipeline 2 GROUP BY — but see §4.3 projection 1 column list createIndex 1 migrations

docs.title: 4.1 Shape
docs.text:
Extends MongoCollection's existing surface; additions marked NEW, and each exists because §3.2 counted sites that need it.

// ---- reads
findOne(identifier, projection?, options?)
findOneFilter(filter, projection?, options?)
findMany({ filter, sort, limit, skip, projection, options })
count(filter)                                   // NEW — and §4.3 shows it is the ONLY one
getLastModified(fieldName)

// ---- writes
insertOne(doc, options?)
insertMany(docs, options?)                      // NEW — 2 sites
replaceOne(identifier, doc, { upsert })         // upsert becomes explicit — 7 sites
updateOne(identifier, patch)                    // patch is a plain object, NOT {$set: …}
deleteOne(identifier)
deleteMany(filter)                              // NEW — supersedes deleteManyOr
bulkUpsert(docs, { matchOn })                   // NEW — 5 sites

// ---- the only aggregation that actually occurs (§4.3)
//      `aggregate(pipeline)` is deliberately absent

// ---- lifecycle
ensureSchema(collectionSpec)                    // replaces createIndex
version()

Three rules that make it a seam rather than a façade, each aimed at a specific leak the classification found:

  1. No member returns or accepts a driver object. self.col becomes private; getLastModified goes through findMany. (T1 must-change ×2.)
  2. identifier is opaque. The caller never constructs an ObjectId; identifyingFilter moves inside the adapter, where it may keep its current Mongo-specific fallback logic. (T2 must-change ×2.)
  3. updateOne takes a plain patch object. The adapter decides $set versus jsonb_set. $unset becomes an explicit null-or-sentinel convention in the patch — the socket path's dbUpdateUnset is the only caller and it needs a deliberate decision, not a translation.

docs.title: 4.2 The filter representation — the one decision that matters
docs.text:
Nine of nineteen must-change sites are query_for(opts) handing a Mongo query document to the driver. So the filter language is the seam, and there is a convergence worth taking:

D8 already chose the vocabulary. API v3 declares exactly nine operators — eq ne gt gte lt lte in nin re (lib/api3/generic/search/input.js:111). Make that the seam's filter AST. query_for becomes filterFor, emitting {op, field, value} nodes with and/or grouping, in v3's vocabulary.

That single change resolves four planned work items at once:

item how it lands T1.1/T1.2 9 of 19 must-change sites T0.5 (type coercion) the AST is where the schema-driven coercion table applies T2.3 (v3's nine operators in SQL) the AST is v3's nine operators T2.4 (v1 allowlist) an AST that cannot express an unlisted operator is the allowlist — {M} §6.5's security fix falls out structurally rather than being bolted on
