Recommendation: do the filter AST first, as its own change, before converting any call site. It is the highest-leverage piece and everything else gets easier behind it.

docs.title: 4.3 Aggregation — investigated, and it is one operation
docs.text:
lib/server/aggregate.js builds [{$match: query}].concat(conf.pipeline).concat(opts.pipeline).concat(template()), and every extension point is empty in production:

  • conf.pipeline has no supplier — the factory is constructed in exactly three places (entries.js:223, devicestatus.js:162, treatments.js:439), all with {}.
  • opts.pipeline is rejected with HTTP 400 before reaching storage (lib/api/entries/index.js:452-457), closed deliberately in commit 479a6a4d.
  • template() is a literal: [{$group: {_id: null, count: {$sum: 1}}}], with _id hardcoded to null — there is no code path that sets a grouping key.

So there is exactly one shape: count(collection, filter) → integer, over {entries, treatments, devicestatus}. No groupBy, no distinct. The [{_id: null, count: N}] envelope is a MongoDB artifact the API leaks and the route layer can reconstruct.

aggregate(spec) therefore comes out of the proposed interface in §4.1 — count(filter) is sufficient and complete. If a general aggregate is kept in the Mongo adapter for future use, it must stay off the neutral interface or the seam leaks.

Two constraints on doing it: tests/count-pipeline-boundary.test.js pins the response shape and the exact 400 message; tests/mongo-query-javascript.test.js:75-94 constructs the helper directly and passes opts.pipeline, so it depends on that parameter existing even though no production caller supplies it.

docs.title: 4.3.1 The count path's date bound (BF-01)
docs.text:
aggregate.js:21 calls find_options(opts) with one argument, so the collection's queryOpts never reach it and lib/server/query.js falls back to its defaults — dateField: 'date', no useEpoch. The consequence, run directly:

list  path (useEpoch:true):  {"date":{"$gte":1789099222823}}       <- number
count path (defaults)     :  {"date":{"$gte":"2026-09-11T04:00:22.824Z"}}   <- ISO string

entries.date is declared number in specs/nsschema/entries.model.json, and MongoDB orders BSON types before comparing values, so a numeric field never matches a string bound. GET /api/v1/count/entries/where with no explicit date filter silently matches nothing — the injected two-day window excludes every document rather than bounding it.

This is the same class as T0.5's under-coercion finding: a string where a number belongs, returning 200 and an empty result. Filed as BF-01 (reproduced); the fix routes count and list through the same query_for and is merged to dev via PR #8738 (2026-09-18), not released.

docs.title: 4.4 Dedup across the three write paths — investigated, and they are not equivalent
docs.text:
The §5 recommendation — convert the socket path last, file unification separately — holds. The three paths disagree on match key, match scope, post-match write semantics, and which collections dedup at all:

socket dbAdd API v3 API v1 treatments NSCLIENT_ID, else created_at+eventType, plus a ±2 s fuzzy window on amount fields UUIDv5 of device_date_eventType; fallback created_at+eventType identifier → _id → created_at+eventType entries no dedup identifier; fallback date+type sysTime+type, device-blind devicestatus NSCLIENT_ID, else created_at (device-blind) created_at+device no dedup profile startDate → full replace created_at no dedup on a match, writes treatments: only $sets created_at, keeps the stored body; devicestatus: nothing full replace treatments: replace; entries: $set merge permission on a match create rights api:<col>:update create rights

Divergences that would change behaviour if unified — the load-bearing ones:

  1. Only the socket path matches fuzzily (±2 s plus amount fields, websocket.js:535-568). Removing it duplicates AAPS/NSClient treatments; adding it elsewhere silently swallows legitimate rapid boluses.
  2. NSCLIENT_ID is a socket-only key; v1 and v3 treat it as opaque payload.
  3. v3's fallback clause carries identifier: {$exists: false} (utils.js:159), which the others lack. A unified rule would make v3 start matching identifier-bearing documents by created_at+eventType — a real loosening.
  4. created_at normalisation differs: v1 normalises through moment to ISO-UTC and lets eventTime override it (treatments.js:449-450, 473-479); the socket path uses the raw client string. Identical payloads produce different keys.
  5. Entries get three different answers for the same SGV, and devicestatus/profile each dedup in some paths and not others.

Also worth recording: the socket write API is not browser-only. It is attached to the same HTTP server and uses the same credential model as REST (websocket.js:81-84, :115-131), so dbAdd/dbUpdate/dbRemove are reachable by any client that can reach the site. Anonymous writes are denied by default, but a deployment adding careportal to AUTH_DEFAULT_ROLES opens them — exactly as it would for REST.

Unsettled: whether the socket similarity branch's use of truthiness (if (data.data.insulin)) rather than presence is intentional. A falsy value is skipped as a match key, and no test covers it. Register BF-09 (queue BFQ-09, unsettled) carries the corpus measurement of which fields this actually affects.

docs.title: 5. A third write path, not previously named
docs.text:
lib/server/websocket.js is 15 sites — the largest single concentration — because it implements a complete CRUD API over Socket.IO: dbAdd (:449), dbUpdate (:332), dbUpdateUnset (:395), dbRemove (:734). It carries its own deduplication logic (exact-match then similar-match, :528/:572) parallel to — not shared with — v1's and v3's.

Consequences:

  • The seam covers three API surfaces, not two — v1, v3 and the socket path.
  • Dedup semantics exist in three places and are not obviously identical. Unifying them is a behaviour change and must not ride along inside a "no behaviour change" refactor.
  • 11 of its 15 sites classify as fits — it is mostly findOne/insertOne/replaceOne, so the conversion itself is routine. It is the dedup question that needs a decision.

Recommendation: convert websocket.js last, and file the dedup unification as its own task with its own tests.

docs.title: 6. What this does not cover
docs.text:
• lib/server/query.js itself is not in the inventory — it builds filters, it does not execute them. It is nonetheless the largest single item of work implied here (§4.2).
  • Read paths that bypass storage entirely — ctx.cache (lib/server/cache.js) serves /api/v1/entries from memory with no driver call ({R} §12.2), so it does not appear as a call site while very much being part of the read path.
  • lib/storage/mongo-storage.js's connection/pool/index management — one createIndex site is listed, but connection lifecycle, pool configuration and ensureIndexes are a separate concern from the per-collection interface and need their own design.
  • Transactions. Nothing in the shipping code uses them; RLS binding under D3 is per-transaction ({DB} §8.2), so the interface needs a transaction scope. That scope is §9.

docs.title: 8. The filter AST — built and validated
docs.text: tools/seam/filter-ast.js, validated by tools/seam/{validate,coverage}.js.

docs.title: 8.1 It is not a new design — v3 already had it
docs.text:
lib/api3/generic/search/input.js produces [{field, operator, value}] with a top-level logicalOperator, and parseFilter() in mongoCollection/utils.js is already its MongoDB adapter. So the work is v3's existing model plus the smallest extensions that let v1's real output be expressed, plus a second adapter.

Two extensions, each because a measured v1 shape needs it:

  1. Nested groups. v3's AST is flat — one logicalOperator joins every clause — and v1 emits top-level $or with clause objects. This is the only structural change.
  2. exists. v1 passes $exists through and it is not among v3's nine. Added deliberately, because the alternative is that v1 queries using it silently stop working.

Everything else maps unchanged: implicit equality → eq; {$gte, $lte} on one field → two clauses under and; dotted paths → field names containing dots.

parseFilter's non-array pass-through (if (!Array.isArray(filterDef)) return filterDef) closes for free. Its only callers are create/patch/update, all passing identifyingFilter — a raw Mongo {$or:[…]}. §4.1 rule 2 already moves identifier handling inside the adapter, so the escape hatch that stops the AST being total disappears with it.

docs.title: 8.2 What it deliberately cannot express is the feature
docs.text: There is no $where, no $expr, no pipeline, no operator escape hatch. Structural validation runs before either adapter. An AST that cannot represent an unlisted operator is the allowlist {M} §6.5 says does not exist today — so T2.4's security fix is structural rather than a check somebody has to remember to write. Regex patterns are length-bounded (RE_MAX_LEN), which is the ReDoS mitigation, also structural.

docs.title: 8.3 Differential validation: 3,000 randomised filters, both backends
docs.text:
Same AST → toMongo → mingo, and → toSql → real PostgreSQL 16, over 300 fixture documents built to be hostile: every field independently present-or-absent, explicit JSON nulls distinct from missing keys, empty strings, mixed types.

run agreement all operators except re 3000/3000 (100 %) with re on plain patterns 1500/1500 (100 %)

Non-vacuity: the differential caught two adapter defects during construction — reverting either fix reproduces the disagreement (332 for nin, all one direction):

  1. nin and missing fields. MongoDB's $nin matches a document where the field is absent; NULL NOT IN (…) is NULL in SQL and matches nothing. Fixed as (x IS NULL OR x NOT IN (…)), the same three-valued-logic gap ne needed.
  2. exists cannot read a generated column. MongoDB's $exists is key presence, and a generated column is built with ->>, which returns SQL NULL for both an absent key and an explicit JSON null — it cannot tell them apart. doc #> '{path}' can: jsonb null for the first, SQL NULL for the second. Verified directly, then fixed so exists always reads the document even when a column exists for that field.

The second is a trap in the §6.3 storage shape rather than in this AST: generated columns are not a faithful projection of the document. Anything that needs to distinguish absent from null must read the jsonb.

docs.title: 8.4 Coverage against real v1 output
docs.text:
coverage.js takes the shapes lib/server/query.js actually emits (captured by running it) and checks each is expressible and semantically identical, compared through mingo rather than by string equality:

10/10 v1 filter shapes expressible AND semantically identical

implicit equality · injected date bound · range on one field · two fields · top-level $or · dotted path · $ne null · $in · $exists · $regex.

The two _id shapes are not filters — they are identifier lookups, resolved by §4.1 rule 2's identifier opacity rather than by the AST.

docs.title: 8.5 Limits
docs.text:
• mingo is a reimplementation of MongoDB's query language, not MongoDB. A three-arm comparison (mingo / live mongod / live PostgreSQL) in {3A} agrees 3000/3000 on same-type values. Cross-type values gave mongod-vs-postgres 96.15 % in four nameable classes before the type guard of §8.6; with it, 100 % (§8.6.2).
  • The regex result covers a deliberately plain subset — literals, anchors, character classes. Mongo's $regex is PCRE-flavoured and Postgres ~ is POSIX; they diverge on lazy quantifiers, lookaround and \d-style shorthands. The measured 100 % describes the subset we would allow, not the whole language, and the allowed subset needs to be written down. RE_MAX_LEN is a length bound, not a work bound (T2.3, plan Phase 2).
  • 300 documents, one collection shape. Sort, limit, skip and projection are not covered — only the filter.
  • No tenant predicate is in these filters. Under D3 the tenant bound comes from RLS, not from the AST, which is the point — but it means this validation says nothing about isolation.

docs.title: 8.6 The cross-type break is also inside the adapter — found by T2.1
docs.text:
The cross-type disagreement is not only a coercion problem above the seam. Building the T2.1 DDL forced a decision about generated columns, and measuring it produced this on live PostgreSQL 16 over four rows (sgv: 120, sgv: "120", sgv: null, key absent):

predicate rows WHERE "sgv" >= 100 — the guarded generated column 1 WHERE (doc #>> '{sgv}')::numeric >= 100 — toSql's fallback 2

Both are toSql emitting gte sgv 100. Which one it emits depends only on whether that field happens to appear in the column manifest. So whether a field has an index accelerator can change a query's answer — and the accelerator is supposed to be exactly the thing that cannot. The emitted DDL says so in every file header ("dropping every generated column must not change an answer"); today, dropping one would.

The guarded column is the correct arm: MongoDB orders BSON types before values, so sgv: "120" does not match {sgv: {$gte: 100}}, and the column agrees while the fallback does not. Two further consequences of the same mismatch: a dirty value makes the fallback raise 22P02 at query time where the column is merely NULL, and a numeric field given an ISO-string bound raises where MongoDB silently matches nothing — BF-01's live defect arriving as an error instead of an empty page. Louder, still a behaviour difference.

Fixed on the seam branch 2026-09-15 (d75c1154, unpublished): the jsonb path carries the same CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(…) = '<type>' THEN … END the emitted DDL builds its columns with, so the two agree by construction rather than by review. CASE and not AND jsonb_typeof(…) = t, because SQL does not promise to evaluate conjuncts in order — a planner free to try the cast first turns one dirty value into a 22P02 for the whole query.

Three things came with it, each a defect in its own right:

  • A generated column is typed, so columns is now a map of name → JSON type. Comparing a string against a numeric column emitted numeric = text and raised 22P02 at query time — a 500 where MongoDB simply matches nothing. With names alone the type is unknown, so every comparison takes the (correct, unaccelerated) jsonb path; specs/generated/postgres/index.json now carries columnTypes, and passing it is what turns the accelerator on.
  • Mixed-type in/nin lists get one arm per type. {$in: [1, 'a']} is two questions; a single cast has to pick one and silently loses every value of the other.
  • A null operand is its own type bracket. Measured against mongod 7.0.43 over {null, missing, 0, 'a', false}: $eq, $lte and $gte against null all match null and missing, while $lt and $gt match nothing — there is no value above or below null inside its own bracket. Without this handling the ordering operators emit the literal string undefined into the SQL (114 of 3000 three-arm fixtures fail).

docs.title: 8.6.1 Non-vacuity of the cross-type differential
docs.text:
Without cross-type fixtures the differential cannot see the guard: every fixture mkDocs builds stores each field's own type, so removing the guard changes no result. With --cross-type (both halves: a document of the wrong type, and a query of the wrong type, which are opposite sides of the bracket):

mismatches over 5000 guard removed 398 unclassified, plus hard cast errors — readings like mongo 0 / sql 140 guard in place 0

A generated column declared with a bare cast fails at insert: one document holding sgv as the string "120" kills the INSERT with 22P02. That is exactly the argument postgres_emit.py makes for emitting a CASE guard — on a real deployment it is an ingest outage caused by a data-quality problem.

docs.title: 8.6.2 The seam now matches real MongoDB, and the oracle is what is wrong
docs.text:
tools/qc/three-arm.js against a live mongod 7.0.43, 3000 fixtures, cross-type injection on, regex arm on:

comparison result mongod vs postgres 3000/3000 — 100 % mingo vs mongod 2977/3000 — 23 disagreements mingo vs postgres 2977/3000 — 23 disagreements

(Without the §8.6 guard, {3A} measured mongod-vs-postgres at 96.15 % on cross-type values.) The seam's claim holds exactly against the database self-hosters actually run.

Every remaining disagreement is the oracle's, and the defect is pinned to one construct: mingo's $lte/$gte against a null operand does not match a missing field; mongod's does. mingo agrees with mongod on $eq, $ne, $lt and $gt null. With T2.3's re finding (where the oracle masked a real divergence; here it manufactures one) the conclusion is the same: mingo ≡ postgres is a claim about the AST, never about MongoDB. validate.js now declares these fixtures oracle-declined at the point of use, the way it already declares the x flag, rather than counting them against the adapter.

docs.title: 8.7 Two capability gaps T2.1 surfaced
docs.text:
• Multikey is not expressible as a generated column. treatments.boluscalc.foods is an array and the live query is ?find[boluscalc.foods._id]=… (lib/report/reportclient.js:294). doc #>> '{boluscalc,foods,_id}' is NULL on an array, so no column can reproduce MongoDB's multikey semantics. T2.1 emitted nothing rather than an approximation that would have looked right and answered wrong. This is why the emitted index count is 30 secondary + 4 primary = 34, not {M} §6.7's 41: 6 of the difference is food and activity, which have no model yet (T2.2), and the remaining 1 is this. §6.7 counts six collections; T2.1 had four models.
  • Seven indexed field paths no model declares: NSCLIENT_ID (treatments, devicestatus, profile), date (treatments, devicestatus), created_at (entries), plus the multikey one. They get no column and appear in the index as a jsonb expression carrying an inline UNDECLARED note, so the index stays faithful to the Mongo declaration and the gap stays visible. NSCLIENT_ID is a real field the websocket write path uses (lib/server/websocket.js:538) — a T2.2 input, not a T2.1 defect.

docs.title: 8.8 Date-like columns are text, and cannot be anything else
docs.text: created_at, startDate, sysTime and dateString are declared string + date-time. Range predicates on them are therefore lexicographic, which is chronological only while every writer emits a UTC-normalised ISO string of constant width. timestamptz would fix the ordering and break eq — and its cast is not immutable, so it cannot be a generated column at all. Left as text and flagged rather than quietly made wrong.

docs.title: 9. The transaction scope
docs.text:
{S} §6 flagged that the interface had none and that D3's RLS binding is per-transaction. Confirmed: set_config('app.current_tenant_id', …, is_local => true) is transaction-scoped, so every tenant-bound operation must run inside a transaction that has been bound.

store.withTenant(tenantId, async (tx) => { … })   // NEW

Three findings that make this more than a signature change:

  1. The safety property differs by backend, and only one of them fails closed. On Postgres an unbound transaction returns 0 rows ({DB} §8.2) — forgetting the scope is visible and harmless. On MongoDB there is no equivalent: an unbound context queries without a tenant predicate and returns everything ({DB} §7.1). The MongoDB adapter must therefore assert an explicit binding and throw, to reproduce by hand what RLS gives Postgres for free.
  2. MongoDB transactions require a replica set. A standalone mongod — which many self-hosters run — does not support them, and grep confirms the codebase uses none today. Under D4 the Mongo adapter must therefore degrade to "no transaction, assert the binding", and the interface cannot promise atomicity across operations on both backends.
  3. Single-tenant has no tenant. Under D4 withTenant must have a legitimate single-tenant mode rather than a fake tenant id, or {M} §11's "never a degraded mode" is violated on the first line of the adapter.

docs.title: 9.1 As built — 2026-09-14
docs.text:
Built after T1.2, which had left one choke point — the MongoCollection delegations — so the change touched three files.

lib/storage/tenant-scope.js, with withTenant exposed on the store (lib/storage/mongo-storage.js) and requireTenant asserted in lib/api3/storage/mongoCollection/index.js. All three findings are implemented rather than deferred:

  1. The assertion. Every document-touching delegation calls requireTenant(<collection>.<op>) first. Non-vacuity checked: removing the call makes the unbound-multitenant test fail with the query reaching the driver — which is the whole exposure, one tenant's query returning another's documents.
  2. No transaction on MongoDB. withTenant binds and does not open one. The interface therefore does not promise atomicity across operations, and that is stated at the method, not left to be discovered from a partial write.
  3. SINGLE_TENANT is a Symbol, not a reserved string. A Symbol cannot compare equal to a tenant id, be serialised into a log line, or be concatenated into a query — so the single-tenant binding cannot leak into a multitenant code path by accident. Binding a tenant id under 'single' is refused, and SINGLE_TENANT under 'multi' is refused.

AsyncLocalStorage, not a threaded handle, and the failure mode is the argument rather than the diff size. If the async chain breaks and the scope is lost, the caller has no binding — which throws here and returns zero rows under RLS. A lost scope cannot silently become a different tenant's binding, because there is nothing to fall back to. It fails closed in both directions. Rebinding a different tenant inside an existing scope is refused outright: crossing a tenant boundary is an admin-plane operation and belongs on its own request.

What this is not. The only caller of setTenancyMode('multi') is T3.1's fromEnv under TENANCY_MODE=multi, on the same unpublished branch chain, so the assertion is inert in every deployment that exists. It is the scope T2.5 needed; it is not tenancy.

14 tests; the suite is 2229 passing, 1 pending, 0 failing, lint clean.

docs.title: 7. Sequencing
docs.text:
The tiering in §2 sets the order. Status as of the seam tip 81a1f6ce; the queue is authoritative for item state.

  1. The filter AST — built and validated (§8). Owed: write down the allowed regex subset.
  2. The transaction scope — built (§9.1).
  3. Close T1's two leaks — getLastModified now routes through findMany (§10.1); whether self.col is private on the seam tip is not recorded here and should be checked there.
  4. Convert T2's 40 v1 sites behind the finished interface — done in T1.2 except profile.list_query (§10.6).
  5. Aggregation (§4.3) — resolved as count(ast).
  6. Convert T3's socket path — converted; dedup unification filed separately (§4.4).

T0's 15 sites need no work at all, and T1's 14 are mostly already correct — which is the practical headline: the conversion is ~55 sites, not 85.

docs.title: 10. As built — what T1.2 actually delivered, and where it diverged from §4.1
docs.text: The delivered interface differs from §4.1 in four places. §4.1 is kept as proposed so the reason for each deviation stays readable.

docs.title: 10.1 The delivered surface
docs.text:
// ---- reads
findOne(identifier, projection?, options?)
findOneFilter(filter, projection?, options?)
findMany({ filter, sort, limit, skip, projection, options })
findFiltered(ast, { sort, limit, skip, projection, readOptions, options })   // NEW
count(ast)                                                                   // NEW
getLastModified(fieldName)                    // now routed through findMany

// ---- writes
insertOne(doc, options?)
insertMany(docs, options?)                                                   // NEW
replaceOne(identifier, doc)
updateOne(identifier, setFields)
updateMany(ast, { set, unset })                                              // NEW
replaceFiltered(ast, doc)                     // NEW — replace in place, NO upsert
deleteOne(identifier)
deleteMany(ast)                                                              // NEW
deleteManyOr(filterDef)                       // v3's existing OR-of-clauses form, kept
bulkUpsert(ops, { mode, ordered })                                           // NEW

aggregate() is absent, as §4.3 argued it should be.

docs.title: 10.2 Deviation 1 — bulkUpsert(ops, {mode}), not bulkUpsert(docs, {matchOn})
docs.text: §4.1 assumed one match rule for a batch. The call sites do not share one: each operation carries its own filter, and more importantly entries upserts with $set (stored fields absent from the incoming document survive) while treatments, food and activity replace wholesale. That is a real semantic difference on a write path, so mode: 'merge' | 'replace' is explicit and has no safe default — defaulting it away would silently change behaviour for whichever group lost.

docs.title: 10.3 Deviation 2 — updateMany(ast, {set, unset}), not a null-sentinel patch
docs.text:
§4.1 rule 3 proposed that $unset become "an explicit null-or-sentinel convention in the patch". Rejected once the caller was read: a sentinel makes "set this field to null" and "remove this field" the same wire shape, and websocket.js genuinely does both. Two named maps cost nothing and cannot be confused.

The method also validates field names, refusing any that begins with $. On the socket path those names arrive straight off the wire and go into $set/$unset, which is precisely where a field name becomes an update operator. MongoDB rejects most of these itself; making it structural is the same argument as the AST's operator allowlist.

docs.title: 10.4 Deviation 3 — deleteMany returns three fields, and the wire is shaped elsewhere
docs.text:
It returns { deleted, deletedCount, acknowledged }. deleted matches deleteManyOr's existing contract; deletedCount and acknowledged are what the v1 delete endpoints put on the wire, because normalizeDeleteStatus copies the whole object into the response body.

Three modules independently re-synthesised acknowledged: true before this was centralised — which would misreport an unacknowledged write. The driver's value is passed through instead, and the internal deleted alias is stripped in normalizeDeleteStatus, the single choke point for all four v1 delete endpoints.

docs.title: 10.5 One change to the AST itself: re carries options
docs.text:
A fromMongo that reads clauses with Object.keys loses a native RegExp silently — Object.keys(/x/i) is [], so the clause produces no nodes and vanishes. lib/server/query.js's parseRegEx returns a native RegExp for the treatments notes/eventType/enteredBy filters, so on the seam branch before this change a request for boluses returned every treatment.

Flags now live on the node ({op: 're', field, value, options: 'i'}) rather than inline in the pattern. Two reasons, and the second is the one that matters for Phase 2:

  1. flags must not consume the RE_MAX_LEN budget, which is the ReDoS bound;
  2. the adapters spell them differently — MongoDB has $options, while PostgreSQL has a case-insensitive operator (~*) and no inline i at all. A flag smuggled into the pattern string would have made the SQL adapter's job incorrect rather than merely awkward.

Only the flags MongoDB honours (imsx) are kept; g/y/u say nothing about whether a single document matches, and the driver drops them too. Verified against live MongoDB 7 that /Bolus/i, /Bolus/gi and /change/ims select the same documents through the seam as they do natively.

docs.title: 10.6 What is still on the raw collection
docs.text:
site reason profile.list_query accepts $expr today, with a test asserting it. A query-surface decision (D8/T2.4), not a conversion detail. The T2.4 census found no client in the corpus sends $expr, so rejecting it is a security fix rather than a compatibility break — but it is still a deliberate behaviour change and belongs with the allowlist. each module's api() / collection accessor bootevent still needs raw collections for ensureIndexes. Removing these is the last step, once index creation moves behind ensureSchema. lib/server/bootevent.js:145-146 a hardcoded require('../storage/mongo-storage') under a //TODO assume mongo for now comment — no way to choose a backend. Replaced on the seam branch by T2.0 (lib/server/storage-backends.js, selection by URI scheme); see the plan's Phase 1.

websocket.js is converted. Its dedup logic remains knowingly inconsistent with lib/server/treatments.js (§4.4) — the storage calls moved, the logic did not, and unifying it is filed separately as a behaviour change.

docs.title: 10.7 Deviation 4 — replaceFiltered, found by converting the socket path
docs.text:
Not in the proposal at all. The socket path's profile dedup is a replace-in-place that must not insert, and every route §4.1 offered was an upsert: replaceOne matches on a v3 identifier and upserts, and bulkUpsert is upsert by definition. Either would resurrect a profile deleted between the lookup and the write — a user removes a profile, a queued socket message recreates it.

It returns matchedCount so a caller can distinguish "replaced" from "was already gone". That distinction is the reason the method exists, so it is tested directly rather than inferred.

docs.title: 11. Current admitted ports and independent scopes (2026-11-05)
docs.text:
Current-source amendment at local CRM d4570e585d0e12e46386ed26772790b269b2b736, based on dev 4a482627 and R41. The archived port instrument runs the committed parameterized corpus against real MongoDB and PostgreSQL. The interface is a set of explicit capabilities, not a promise that every backend implements historical §4.1. Historical counts and measurements above are unchanged.

Actual object Contract and admitted boundary api3/storage/mongoCollection Driver-backed reads/writes/results, strict/v1 AST and broader BSON. Tenant assertion does not filter a shared collection or add a transaction. postgres-entries-read / postgres-entries-write Typed string/ObjectId identity, JSON-safe representation, strict query/sort/projection subset, real persistence outcomes and partial duplicate-key batches. Unsupported shapes refuse. postgres-entries-intent Shared v3 intent rules, a fresh owned transaction and logical post-commit events. An existing caller transaction refuses. postgres-collection-intent Trusted logical collection/source composition; bounded legacy predicate translation and top-level projection helpers. Its projection capabilities differ from the lower reader. storage-reads.resolve / API3 Collection injection Trusted capability acquisition by logical collection/source. Partial ports refuse; default single constructs Mongo when no replacement is supplied.

Measured distinctions a future backend must preserve or explicitly refuse:

  • Raw ObjectId and same-spelling string IDs remain distinct. Identifying reads prefer an explicit identifier, then ObjectId, then string. Normalized shown documents supply the stored ID when identifier is falsy; raw absent/null/false/ zero identifiers remain distinguishable.
  • Mongo's driver generates an ObjectId for submitted _id: null; Mongo admits numeric/boolean IDs. PG refuses those submitted identity kinds. Silent stored- kind coercion is not a supported adaptation.
  • Lower PG admits dotted inclusion projections but refuses exclusion and _id: 0; preview projection admits top-level 0/1 and refuses dotted projection. There is no single universal projection capability yet.
  • Supported null/missing AST comparisons, existence and false/zero/string-zero operands retain their characterized distinctions. Bounded unsorted PG reads and unsupported query/representation shapes refuse. Natural order requires its ordinal/schema/import capability; these tests do not prove imports.
  • PG acquires the current UUID at operation time, uses RLS inside a transaction, reuses only the same scope and rejects cross-tenant rebinding. Mongo scope leaves the explicitly selected collection handle unchanged; its composition must supply physical isolation. Caller failure does not roll back an already completed standalone Mongo write.
  • Persistence counts describe real writes. Duplicate-key batches retain their successful ordered prefix or unordered continuation; PG savepoints leave the outer transaction usable. Representation validation may refuse before a batch.

The corpus distinguishes logical intent events from backend instrumentation and checks PG commit failure without false publication. It does not measure durable delivery/restart, every renderer/collection, event collapse, lost-reply retry ambiguity or arbitrary Mongo emulation. Domain/write policy remains in the write-contract current amendment and linked platform specifications. Executable details live in CRM lib/storage/PORT-CONTRACT.md and tests/storage-port-contract.integration.test.js; the architecture execution plan owns consolidation sequencing. New adapters consume measured capabilities, rather than inherit unsupported methods from the historical proposal.

docs.title: Tenant owner authority and token verification
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-10 at 4917b2d4a.

Contributor-facing living contract. Adopted by the maintainer in the owner-authority chat, 2026-11-05; current with the release decisions of 2026-11-10. Supplement to execution-plan D17/D22; this is the home of the owner authority and local-verification amendment. Implementation acceptance is separate. Queue homes: MT-OIDC-NATIVE and MT-M6A-JOIN (M6a), MT-OWNERSHIP-OPS (M6b), MT-OIDC-SINGLE-PROVISION, MT-ROOT-ADMIN-PARITY; the earlier MT-CONFIG-MIN, MT-SECRETS-CONTRACT, T30-WIRING and MT-IDENTITY-PLAN are closed as superseded.

docs.title: Authority and storage boundaries
docs.text:
PostgreSQL is authoritative for tenant status, identities/access grants, subject and role assignments, sessions, credential status/generations, operator ceilings and accepted signing-key generations. It already carries current data permissions; local signature verification removes a cryptographic service dependency, rather than moving an existing permission database out of Vault.

The secrets component protects recoverable credentials and private signing keys. For a new asymmetric token, its private key creates the signature; a public key checks the signature without permitting token creation. A JWT is the signed credential presented by a client, not its signing key. Existing NS-style HS256 uses a shared secret for signing and verification, rather than this key pair. MongoDB single-tenant subject/role/credential records are distinct from signing keys.

Value Storage and use New first-party API/machine credential PostgreSQL credential metadata plus one-way verifier for sufficiently random credentials where compatibility permits; plaintext issued once. Existing legacy hash/header forms can themselves be bearer credentials and must not be exposed as harmless hashes. Access JWT Presented by client; current session/credential state in PostgreSQL. Do not store a recoverable copy merely to authorize it. New claims use stable subject/session IDs, not the legacy raw accessToken. Refresh/session credential PostgreSQL session record and one-way verifier; rotation/reuse detection or provider-supported session equivalent. Existing tenant root/legacy derivation material Preserve encrypted recoverable form while legacy derivation or reissuance requires it; migrate only after measuring client compatibility. PostgreSQL ciphertext/reference, protected by secrets component. Private token-signing key Non-exportable inside Vault/production secrets provider; never in serving-worker memory or plaintext application tables. Public verification key and trusted tenant/purpose/version binding may be cached. Vendor-cloud credentials, nightscout-connect credentials, APNs private keys, push/webhook credentials Recoverable by explicitly authorized consumers. Existing Transit design stores tenant-bound ciphertext/references in PostgreSQL and encryption keys in Vault. Vault Transit is not a KV store for the submitted application values. A separate Vault KV choice is not implied.

Single-tenant MongoDB and legacy token behavior remain supported. New multitenant token semantics do not silently change legacy issuance or refuse existing clients. Management credentials are a distinct audience/purpose from data credentials.

docs.title: Owner permissions and ceilings
docs.text:
Owner is an explicit tenant relationship, separate from legacy data wildcards. Initial capabilities cover reading effective configuration/provenance, changing permitted settings, managing uploader/follower credentials and grants, configuring enabled integrations, export and deletion requests. Operator provisioning, suspension, policy changes and execution of lifecycle deletion remain on the private operator plane. The preview deletion ceremony requires an explicit request/operator confirmation, permits cancellation before execution starts and imposes no mandatory waiting period. Current authority and verified artifact/recovery prerequisites still apply. Controller commands require their own reviewed authority.

Secret reveal is a separate permission with recent reauthentication. Ownership transfer and adding co-owners are sensitive explicit operations; last-owner removal must not orphan the tenant. Transactional transfer/recovery details require a bounded implementation contract, not automatic operator access to owner secrets. For the first preview, ownership changes are operator-assisted. Self-service co-owner addition and transfer are later enhancements; last-owner protection, current authority and audit remain required for the operator path.

A grant must fit all three: project delegable catalogue, operator tenant ceiling, and actor's explicit delegation authority. Possessing a permission does not grant the right to delegate it. For the first preview the owner defines roles from any permission string single tenant accepts, wildcards included, under the ceiling (decision); a stricter permission model is a separate proposal for both modes. Unknown roles refuse. An upgrade must not silently add new capabilities to an existing delegated role. Role edits have the same ceiling checks as direct assignments. Tightening current policy bounds effective authority even when an old stored assignment remains.

Management authorization must inspect proposed roles/grants, the actor's current delegation authority and current policy together inside the mutation transaction. The existing operation/target-only callback is insufficient for this ceiling. Permission spellings and complete role catalogue remain design outputs; the adopted capability groups do not pretend those implementation details are complete.

docs.title: Selected current proposed-grant wiring (R53)
docs.text:
Accepted native17f9a457 explicitly selects ownerPolicy on the existing subject store transaction. Proposed grants must fit reviewed catalogue ∩ locked operator ceiling ∩ current matching management actor delegation, with current actor and authority row fencing before subject/credential mutation and audit commit. This implements only the selected REST37 operation subset. DELETE refuses and managementAuth remains injected; human issuer/refresh, full wildcard/default catalogue, existing-grant clamping and production owner listener remain unimplemented. R48 data-token readers are unchanged.

Bounded native acceptance and parent semantic controls are recorded in R53. This selected transaction does not make an operation/target-only management callback sufficient for general proposed-grant enforcement.

docs.title: Shared OIDC integration
docs.text:
The shared OIDC decision adopts one optional integration for single-tenant and multitenant Nightscout, provider-backed renewal first, and separate authorization adapters. Human login, renewal and logout support should be equivalent for comparable capabilities in both modes; storage and tenant-resolution differences remain explicit. The intended single-tenant opt-in is ENABLE=oidc, or an equivalent explicit flag if integration measurement refutes that spelling. Default-off behavior preserves current startup, web/data authentication and unattended clients. No OIDC feature is implemented or enabled merely by setting that value today. The identity provider decision adopts a generic adapter with Authentik as the intended reference, subject to the Kratos proof, and Kratos as the measured fallback.

Share the provider-facing protocol and session integration. Single-tenant maps verified provider/subject to local current authority; multitenant resolves the selected tenant and maps it to current membership, session and grants under RLS. A provider identity or ID token is not automatically an accepted Nightscout data credential, root grant or management credential. Human data access and management access can share login plumbing while retaining explicit permissions/audiences. Keep native API_SECRET, subject/device tokens and machine renewal compatible.

The existing single application supplies the single-tenant HTTP boundary. Multitenant owner operations use tenant-admin on its own listener, initially co-locatable with api; DATA api, realtime and the private operator admin retain their existing responsibilities. Login/callback/exchange/renewal routes are not yet implemented or placed by this direction. Prefer composing the common adapter into the applicable existing boundary over requiring a new process. No first-party browser UI is required by this integration decision.

Provider-backed renewal obtains new short-lived Nightscout management access from valid provider authentication and current Nightscout authority. It does not require Nightscout-owned rotating refresh credentials initially. The provider's login cookie/session, any Nightscout browser-session cookie, the current server-side Nightscout session and access bearer token are distinct. The adopted session contracts scope idle/absolute lifetimes to management sessions, order logout local-first with an optional provider call, fence concurrent renewal and default browsers to an HttpOnly cookie with direct-token mode retained. The adopted provider-outage policy allows existing valid access only until existing expiry under current local checks, with no new login/renewal or relaxed freshness. Adopted lifetimes below remain; provider activity alone cannot bypass current Nightscout authority.

Acceptance must exercise the same synthetic provider/login/renewal contract on both supported modes, enabled and disabled. Cover missing/wrong issuer/audience, invalid signatures, identity-to-permission mapping, revocation/expiry, logout, provider outage and ordinary legacy data-client compatibility. Multitenant adds foreign-tenant/selector refusal and isolated current authority; single-tenant must not require multitenant PostgreSQL, a cohort identity service or extra role listeners. Record unsupported provider capabilities rather than silently weakening guarantees. Both browser transports are adopted, cookie default; each needs its own acceptance.

docs.title: Management authentication and lifetime policy
docs.text:
The owner listener stays separate from data/private-operator listeners. Human authentication uses an interchangeable identity provider; Nightscout maps verified provider/subject to current tenant access and exchanges it for a tenant-bound management token. No custom password/recovery system. Provider sessions alone do not certify current Nightscout grants; provider logout/revocation propagation must be part of the eventual session integration contract.

Initial headless management uses explicitly provisioned management credentials from the private operator plane. A tenant's root secret (API_SECRET) has single-site parity: all data, subjects, roles and the admin tools, never owner or operator authority. It may edit any subject except removing the last usable owner, and cannot grant itself ownership. In multitenant mode every subject write goes through the owner-aware writer that enforces that guard. Through the admin tools root may edit a role's permissions, not rename it, and may not delete a role a subject holds; it may grant any tenant data permission (*) unless the operator narrows the list, never owner or operator permissions. A subject whose roles grant admin:api:subjects:* uses the admin tools with its own token under the same guard. Implementation is MT-ROOT-ADMIN-PARITY. An owner may revoke subjects and may pause their own site; only the operator suspends and deletes. Unattended uploaders use revocable machine credentials whose renewal does not require a human login.

Adopted initial limits, subject to measured implementation acceptance:

Policy Initial value Human management access token 10 minutes Human management session idle / absolute lifetime 30 minutes / 12 hours Authentication freshness for reveal, ownership changes, privileged credential issuance Within 5 minutes Existing device/client exchange JWT Preserve 8 hours initially

Owners may narrow permitted lifetimes; they cannot exceed operator/project bounds. Idle/absolute expiry requires current server-side session enforcement. Token expiry is not revocation. Removing a grant or revoking a credential/session takes effect on the next protected operation across workers, including protected stream delivery. Already-authorized in-flight work may finish. No stale permission window is adopted.

docs.title: Vault verification amendment
docs.text:
For new-format tokens, private signing keys remain in the secrets component; serving workers verify asymmetrically signed tokens locally with provisioned public keys. This supersedes D22's requirement to send every verification to the secrets component. It does not export private/HMAC keys or weaken current authorization. Prototype algorithm: Ed25519; production JOSE/library/provider interoperability is an acceptance requirement before selecting/enabling the production format.

Verification pins algorithm, issuer, audience, tenant, purpose and key binding; validates issued/not-before/expiry/lifetime; and rejects unknown keys. Key discovery never follows a request-supplied URL/JWK. Cache public keys, not stale grants. Current accepted-key state prevents cached public keys bypassing retirement.

Each protected operation obtains one current authority snapshot covering tenant, principal/session/credential status, key acceptance, grants and applicable policy. Evaluate required permissions from that operation's snapshot. Use primary or equivalently consistent reads; asynchronous replicas/worker-local TTL grants cannot satisfy next-operation revocation. Management writes additionally fence policy and grant changes transactionally. RLS and trusted tenant binding remain mandatory.

Bound pools across workers, batch required checks into the snapshot, and apply pre-verification throttling. A logical snapshot may still require transaction and tenant-binding round trips; one snapshot is not a claim of one wire request.

docs.title: Dependency failures and acceptance
docs.text:
With a trusted cached public key and available current PostgreSQL authority, existing new-format tokens continue ordinary data operations during a Vault outage. New issuance, reveal and secret consumption that requires Vault refuse. Unknown keys refuse rather than fall back. PostgreSQL authority outages refuse protected reads and writes even when the token signature verifies. The OIDC provider-outage decision allows existing human access only within its adopted lifetime and current Nightscout authority during an identity-provider outage. Provider-dependent renewal refuses. Local logout/revocation takes effect on the next protected operation across workers; unavailable current authority refuses even with an unexpired token. No grace extension or Nightscout-owned refresh system is added. Provider logout propagation, qualifying idle activity, concurrent renewal and browser transport have adopted contracts. Upstream logout cannot take immediate local effect until it is known locally. Human login/session implementation is on draft #8898 with joined acceptance records (M6a, M6b); real identity-provider interoperability is synthetic only.

The lab compares the actual current credential component/authority adapter with local verification and a bounded combined snapshot. Required controls cover signatures/audience/tenant, committed revocation across pools, expired sessions, key retirement and stopped dependencies. Performance results are synthetic authorization-pipeline measurements, not API-handler throughput, production capacity, full owner-ceiling acceptance or milestone promotion.

The November 5 measurement records the reproduced prototype results and their controls. The R48 application acceptance tracks the local branch that wires new-format verification through the actual API preview. Legacy issuance migration, complete management/session flows and production deployment acceptance remain separately scoped; local wiring is not a claim that published operators or all existing clients use the new format.

docs.title: Transactional PostgreSQL tenant clock: proof plan
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-06 at 773c8bc59.

Current-use guide, 2026-11-06: R60 accepts the joined clock with bounded correctness evidence. R65 descriptive HTTP workload adds four small fresh cohorts; no performance budget or acceptance follows. Earlier corpus benchmark-pending captures remain unchanged. This page retains the original proof plan and invariants. Use the current dashboard and R60 disposition for implementation acceptance.

Contributor-facing design/proof plan, 2026-11-06. The maintainer selects this proof direction; implementation and performance acceptance remain UNMEASURED. This is an additive lane proposal for central reconciliation, not a change to queue state, release admission or the verification schedule.

docs.title: Adopted direction
docs.text:
Prove a transactional PostgreSQL tenant clock first, preserving existing numeric history cursors and single/Mongo behavior. Measure contention and fresh-ingestion latency once the coordinator assigns a verification slot. Preserve the adopted separate-role single-machine reference deployment and later multi-machine proof.

The motivating parent reproduction is the REST replica history record. Source for that reproduction is CRM 2a6eaf738382ef62b8b3bfd0c76dbd005abb8480; the later corrected-control/cleanup candidate is 714f6c8b229fbea171db4e75cbf8179edd7d2d57. No production clock change is contained in either head. Preserve the reproduction independently of any remedy.

docs.title: Proposed invariant
docs.text:
Uniqueness alone is insufficient. For the same tenant, a reader must not observe a later committed history watermark and then have an earlier watermark become visible behind that cursor. Allocation, record mutation and ownership of the ordering fence must therefore be coordinated through the actual commit boundary. Transaction rollback must not leave an acknowledged write or prematurely release an ordering guarantee. Existing HTTP history shape and server-owned date fields remain compatible; do not silently reinterpret milliseconds as sequence IDs.

A candidate design uses a durable tenant clock row locked/advanced in the same transaction as the relevant data write, retaining the lock until commit or rollback. Different tenants should use independent clock rows. Exact schema, privileges, initialization, timeout and batch behavior are engineering proposals to test, not accepted implementation choices. Do not substitute a separate sequence call, process mutex, leased timestamp range or wall-clock timestamp for the commit-order proof.

docs.title: Scope to characterize before implementation
docs.text:
• Locate every relevant stamping call and its actual write transaction, including API3, legacy REST and independently admitted in-process writers. Unadmitted socket/connector paths remain explicit; no full-surface claim from one route.
  • Preserve the default single/Mongo allocator and behavior. An adapter-specific capability must not make shared synchronous stamp helpers silently perform detached asynchronous allocation or fall back to a process clock on failure.
  • Initialize above existing persisted numeric watermarks, including imported or future-dated values, without rewinding issued cursors. Restore/migration and concurrent startup must not allocate overlapping ranges.
  • Keep tenant RLS, app-role grants, transaction ownership and nested/savepoint behavior explicit. Use an append-only candidate migration; no boot-time DDL.
  • Define no-op, resend, multi-item write, partial batch failure, update, soft delete and hard-delete behavior against existing supported contracts.

docs.title: Required positive and semantic controls
docs.text:
Proof Expected positive Break-it control / required symptom Two actual API processes, equal allocator time Later committed write appears after the earlier exclusive history cursor Remove shared coordination; reproduce equal stamps and missed later row Stalled first writer and competing second writer No later visible cursor overtakes an earlier still-committable write Release fence before commit; demonstrate a later cursor followed by a late lower-stamped commit Rollback and crash before commit No acknowledged/visible partial write; subsequent writer progresses correctly Separate allocation/fence lifetime from transaction and detect broken visibility/recovery invariant Same-tenant concurrent batch/write sources Supported rows retain compatible dates and history visibility Bypass coordination in one admitted write path; actual HTTP/persisted-state assertion must fail Other tenant under contention Its allowed writes remain isolated and progress within measured limits Cross-bind clock state or use a global fence; detect isolation failure or serialized cross-tenant schedule Restart, stored high watermark and migration No rewind; current persisted state restored under safe schema Omit initialization/readiness or corrupt ledger; detect lost history or unsafe listener bind Compatibility Existing single/Mongo results and cursor/date shapes remain unchanged Deliberately route single through the new PG capability; existing behavior checks must detect it

Controls must fail semantically. Setup errors, zero tests, timeout without a confirmed scheduling barrier and a failed unrelated route are not evidence. Restore the original source and rerun positives on the immutable candidate head. A standalone ordering sequence cannot be accepted without data-commit proof.

docs.title: Performance and operational measurements
docs.text:
Record reproducible synthetic workloads and actual environment versions. Compare a single writer, same-tenant competing writers, independent tenants, batches and fresh ingestion during bounded import/rebuild contention. Measure end-to-end ingestion latency distributions, completed throughput, clock-lock wait, database load, errors/retries and any timestamp lead over wall time. Separate cold/restart from steady-state measurements. No numeric threshold is selected before evidence.

Keep lock-held work short; characterize rather than assume how much work runs between acquiring the fence and COMMIT. Never hold the ordering fence across external provider calls without explicit justification and measurement. Preserve explicit retryable refusal, bounded per-tenant work and fresh-ingestion priority.

docs.title: Ownership and next steps
docs.text:
Central coordinator owns source reservations, serial verification slots and queue/release/dashboard/map reconciliation. This lane retains the reproduced replica fixture and standalone evidence. A separate read-only investigation of clock/fencing options must be reconciled before product implementation; do not have two agents edit shared storage/date helpers independently.

Capacity has recovered following separately authorized cleanup, but other lanes retain the current verification slots. Do not self-start DB/full/browser runs on seeing free disk. Static planning may proceed. Once source ownership and slot are assigned: implement a narrow candidate, reproduce concurrency/rollback controls, measure performance, run affected/full/browser checks and final prcheck, then return additive source/evidence commits. No agent push.

docs.title: From multitenant preview to production
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-12 at e0765ac4a.

Living contributor-facing production guide, reconciled 2026-11-12 against the release decisions at alignment 8ae6f4a3729548de0c88cc0ee5b3c0aede9aba61. This is read-derived sequencing and explanation, not an application measurement. Release decisions own adopted policy; the queue owns claimed work state; release contents and linked reports own executed acceptance, source heads and publication. Use those records for the current candidate and blockers.

Production means a particular deployment is admitted for a stated workload and failure/recovery envelope. It is a stronger claim than implementing a component, passing a functional preview or running a capacity experiment. This guide explains how those pieces join without making every later production feature a prerequisite to testing an independently ready capability.

docs.title: The proposed first production boundary
docs.text:
Qualify a bounded deployment of the reusable API, evaluator, realtime, admin and supporting roles. The runtime topology explains their contracts and scale profiles; the deployment binding guide explains placement, transport and public access. Colocating roles and scaling them independently are different configurations of capabilities that still need their own deployment proof. A role diagram is not a required number of Pods or nodes.

Recommendation for review: start with the smallest topology that meets the chosen workload and outage objectives. A single application host is an option only when its outage and operator-led recovery are acceptable. Multiple application nodes, a replicated database or an external secrets service are not automatic proofs of availability. Specify which dependency or failure domain may be lost, what continues serving, and what recovery must establish before service resumes.

The capacity campaign's tenant levels are experimental points. The adopted capacity gate defines its current milestone and stretch target; it does not select a production node type or an ultimate fleet size. Small-group efficiency and a larger fleet's bounded growth must be evaluated separately. Multiple independently admitted deployments are a fleet option, not an adopted cell architecture or implemented tenant-migration service.

docs.title: Dependency map
docs.text:
There are two boundaries: learn from a scoped-ready capability, then admit a coherent deployment. Independent experiments can run before full acceptance; their results keep their exact scope and cannot substitute for final acceptance.

flowchart TD
  C["Completed capability and explicit question"] --> D["Focused diagnostic on pinned inputs"]
  D --> R["Repair concrete failures and join"]
  R --> F["Freeze coherent candidate"]
  F --> A["Full applicable functional acceptance"]
  A --> M["Matched capacity and recovery measurements"]
  M --> P["Select deployment profile and operating limits"]
  P --> Q["Deployment trust and recovery qualification"]
  Q --> O["Reviewed release and explicit operator admission"]
  X["Selected candidate’s applicable identity/lifecycle/client scope"] --> F

This is a dependency explanation, not a new serial reservation process. The completion schedule owns integration practice. Ready diagnostics may run in parallel with isolated state and an aggregate resource budget. Production scope work on separate branches must not silently change a frozen experiment or delay its agreed deliverable. A failed level with correct measurement is useful capacity evidence; it is not permission to admit that workload to production.

docs.title: What blocks the path, and what closes it
docs.text:
These are enduring closure criteria, not a second live task list. Identify each remaining implementation change in the queue and its exact failing or missing criterion in the release record. Existing measurements are evidence inputs, not blanket admission for a changed source or topology. A skipped criterion remains UNMEASURED.

Boundary Design question Closing evidence and canonical home Workload and resource envelope How much useful work fits, including interference and recovery? Matched synthetic measurements with stored-write, authority and evaluator/consumer outcomes; latency/freshness tails, CPU, memory, pool/lock waits and recovery. Follow M7 measurement policy and the capacity gate. The latter closes the separate single-site contrast requirement. Historical counts or node density are assumptions until reproduced on comparable inputs. Human identity and owner authority Does the selected identity provider preserve current tenant authority throughout sessions and streams? Actual provider/HTTPS login, renewal, logout, revocation and outage behavior, owner settings consumed by roles, legacy-client compatibility and strict audience separation. Owner authority, M6a criteria in the roadmap. Provisioning, ingress and secrets Are storage, authority and keys ready before serving; are private controls actually private? Operator provisioning and recoverable partial failures; current grants/RLS; TLS/host/selector/client-IP/socket probes; service credential renewal, expiry, revocation and outage/recovery, CA verification/rotation and recoverable Vault unseal custody. A disposable lab bootstrap is not an operator provisioner. Existing Agent proofs retain their scope; the selected deployment needs a trust record and probes. Lifecycle, keys and recovery Can supported operations finish or stop safely, and can an operator recover? Provision/pause/suspend/export/delete/ownership, retained-key destruction, production key-custodian responsibilities and artifact fidelity; interrupted restore/upgrade, lost acknowledgement, participant death and dependency/host replacement. Verify the affected tenant and an independent tenant's progress. Use M6 acceptance families and the recovery boundaries. Safe refusal is distinct from eventual recovery. Connectors and supported clients Which actual journeys work through the selected ingress and credentials? Declared collection coverage, independent stored/history outcomes, cadence/retry/revocation and supported credential renewal; required Android and pinned client journeys. Source-pattern replay is distinct from executing a client binary. Roadmap and current release evidence own the supported scope; do not infer an all-client claim or treat an old entries-only run as the latest result. Shared-fault and operating behavior What happens when bursts or outages affect many tenants together? Hot tenant, reconnect flood, large history, active-alarm work, backlog, slow/down dependencies, restores/upgrades and storage/backup growth. Measure other-tenant progress and authorized effects while queues fill and recover. Experiment contract. Release and deployment admission Are the actual source, configuration, image and operational procedure qualified together? Applicable full/browser/enabled-corpus/native/client acceptance, named pending cases, final prcheck, deployment trust and recovery rehearsal, rollback and explicit operator admission. Release contents, deployment admission decision.

Do not reopen completed capability work merely because this guide names its production criterion. Conversely, ancestry or an old green report does not prove new inputs. Reuse evidence through an explicit affected-input assessment and keep its original source/instrument attribution.

The supported application cohort follows the exclusive application ownership contract. External direct SQL writers are outside that contract. Every supported participant still follows its authority, write and lifecycle rules; current connections alone do not prove complete membership or credential custody. A load-balanced address is not a census of actual role instances.

docs.title: Multi-host and HA work that can wait
docs.text:
Deferral depends on the declared deployment profile and recovery objectives, not on the application being unable to reuse its components at another scale.

Capability Can wait when Required before enabling it Dynamic API membership A fixed roster meets workload and outage needs Admission/removal serialized with maintenance; all-instance drain/invalidation and incarnation-aware replacement. Request replicas are not evaluator owners. Additional evaluator/realtime workers The qualified worker set meets its measured budget Explicit tenant assignments, complete participant coverage, checkpoint/effect continuity and safe moves. Additional workers distribute ownership; they are not automatically standby failover replicas. Cross-host placement The selected local transport and fixed roster meet the profile Qualified private reachability, lifetime/uncertainty behavior, complete direct instance control and partition/late-join refusal. The application owns these semantics; the platform supplies placement/network primitives. Automatic failover Operator-led recovery meets the outage/data-loss objectives Old-owner exclusion, uncertain commits, dependency/key recovery and measured cutover. Backups and rehearsed restoration remain necessary with or without HA. Fleet placement and tenant migration Independently provisioned deployments suffice Durable tenant-to-deployment mapping, compatible target initialization, credential/data/checkpoint handling and a controlled routing cutover. This is a separate design proposal, not a replica-count flag. Transaction-pooling proxy Direct connection budgets suffice Re-prove backend identity, RLS/transaction binding, operation lifetimes and recovery. Do not add a proxy to hide multiplied pools without qualifying its semantics. Broker, cache or alternate CDC transport Current signalling and authoritative-state recovery meet measured needs A named missing capability or measured cost/lag bottleneck, publication/replay/idempotency and authority contracts, bounded failure/recovery, and a comparative experiment. No product is selected merely by a tenant-count target.

Live external providers, self-service ownership transfer, first-party owner UI and richer sharing schedules retain their own adopted scope and decision boundaries. The public-name contract explains authentication, group policy and native credential preservation.

docs.title: Prior art from the existing projects
docs.text:
Initialize durable resources before serving. Separate public names from stable tenant identity. Make ownership, deletion, consent and partial provisioning explicit. Preserve data and keys independently of compute. Existing per-tenant process designs do not establish shared-role resource or failure limits.

The retained November source assessment contains commit-pinned node-multienv, roles-gateway and WWW mechanisms, their original hypotheses and re-proof boundaries. Those source readings are not measurements of deployed services or security/production approval of those projects.

docs.title: Where provider experience changes the decisions
docs.text:
Use aggregate or synthetic descriptions to define representative work and failure scenarios. Keep private organization names, adoption estimates, real identifiers, credentials and clinical traces out of public plans and metric labels.

Input Design or measurement it informs Active/quiet mix, histories, viewers, uploads, enabled plugins and alarms Workload families, fixed/marginal resource cost and interference; tenant count alone is insufficient. Common-mode outages and available operator response Failure domains, redundancy, spare capacity, recovery time and acceptable loss. Restores, key loss, credential expiry and upgrades Custody, retention, rotation, rehearsal and uncertain-state stop conditions. Alias changes, tenant movement and partial provisioning Stable identity, routing publication and recoverable reconciliation. Sharing, revocation and support journeys Current-owner/session proof and separately scoped delegation requirements.

Publish deployment recommendations only after connecting these requirements to measurements on named resources. Fewer nodes are an economic hypothesis: include all application and dependency resources, storage/backups/network and operational cost, plus capacity surviving the declared failure. Neither a stress rig nor a single successful run supplies that recipe.

docs.title: Retained planning baseline
docs.text: The November 8–10 assessment preserves the original gap table, topology/HA proposals and source survey from alignment 8ae6f4a3729548de0c88cc0ee5b3c0aede9aba61. Its present-tense statuses belong to that capture. Use this guide for sequencing, runtime topology for architecture, and the release/queue/report homes for current state and evidence.

docs.title: Realtime sharding, composition and recovery
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-10 at ac7d19f80.

Contributor-facing living proposal, 2026-11-10. Read-derived from joined application dc795bd1515f11808a8d0732f2be9925cb2ffcd1; no sharding implementation, capacity or failover acceptance is claimed. Queue home: MT-REALTIME-SHARDING. The runtime topology owns current composition; this page owns the proposed realtime scaling/recovery contract. Existing captured joined acceptance retains its original single-realtime scope.

docs.title: Recommendation and boundary
docs.text:
Start with tenant-sharded realtime: every tenant has one admitted realtime owner for connections, projection refresh and notification handoff. A stable logical shard contains tenants; worker placement is a separate versioned mapping. The evaluator's assignment is independent. Do not equate adding Socket.IO processes behind a load balancer with complete notification delivery.

Review dimension Proposed direction Long-term direction Stable logical shards with controlled ownership changes; retain a separately scoped connection-fanout option for tenants larger than one worker. Architecture Separate evaluation and realtime responsibilities; allow co-location. Edge routes consumer connections; a direct application adapter routes alarm handoff using the same admitted placement generation. Backward/forward compatibility Preserve polling/WebSocket clients, namespaces, credential/write/ACK behavior and full current-state recovery. Specify coordinated changes to internal contracts; no silent new frame/epoch requirement on old clients. Maintenance One placement contract, explicit owner/incarnation and route generation, existing platform/config inputs and per-instance maintenance census. No new discovery/consensus product or mandatory gateway. Reliability Warm before owner admission, drain/terminate or effectively fence the old owner before replacement, and refuse unknown ownership rather than claiming transparent failover. Separate current-state recovery from alarm replay. Performance Bound assigned tenant refresh work, viewer count, frames/bytes and authority fanout. Measure hot-tenant and reconnect load; CPU/memory capacity is not established by this plan.

This is a proposal to evaluate, not an adopted shard count, hash algorithm, automatic failover policy, schema or new product dependency.

docs.title: Evaluator and realtime: logical components versus deployment
docs.text:
Evaluator schedules acquisition/time-based computation and owns evaluated output and notification intent. Realtime owns consumer protocol, subscriptions, current state frames and per-recipient delivery. Computation should continue without viewers; a connection flood should not consume the clinical scheduler's budget. Those are useful logical boundaries, not proof that every role needs a separate deployment or network hop.

The current role launcher accepts composed roles (evaluator,realtime) and keeps their contexts distinct. It requires different owned checkpoint namespaces. That source capability does not qualify combined-process CPU/event-loop isolation or a colocated sharding/failover profile.

Deployment profile Benefit Required qualification Same host/Pod, separate processes Local UDS/TCP calls and shared placement can reduce operational overhead while keeping event loops separate. Resource budgets and shared host/Pod failure remain explicit; scaling the Pod must not accidentally duplicate evaluator ownership. Same process, separate modules Can use an explicit in-process contract adapter and share selected immutable inputs. Measure computation stalls, connection load, shutdown/drain and failure coupling. Preserve separate lifecycle and output ownership; source composition alone is not acceptance. Independently placed pools Scale scheduled work and viewer delivery for different demand. Independent assignment maps, direct service contracts and complete maintenance coverage.

Recommendation: preserve the logical boundary and permit co-location. Do not require a distributed deployment for a small installation, or force both pools to have identical counts merely to remove an inexpensive local call.

There is shared machinery to inspect before creating another service: tenant-projection-evaluator.js materializes/evaluates clinical views; realtime projection.js separately reconciles a durable input projection and builds a snapshot/frame using shared read-context code. Realtime does not currently consume a durable evaluator-produced frame contract. Combining processes will not automatically remove those separate acquisitions/checkpoints. Measure the duplicate input/view work and define any reusable immutable output boundary before claiming a merger or new materialized-output API improves it.

docs.title: Placement and routing contract
docs.text:
The first prototype uses an explicit fixed worker roster and controlled map revisions. It consumes configuration/platform placement, not a new membership service. Freeze these source-owned facts together:

Fact Rule Tenant key Stable tenant UUID; never public alias, session ID or user-supplied destination. Alias-to-tenant resolution retains existing trust rules. Logical assignment Versioned deterministic hash/encoding and deployment-selected logical shard count. Keep that count fixed when merely adding/removing workers; changing it is an explicit repartition operation. Owner placement Each shard maps to a declared worker identity plus actual boot incarnation and placement generation. One worker may own multiple shards; a reusable ordinal/hostname is not a process incarnation. Consumer route Trusted edge resolves tenant to the admitted owner. Polling session IDs, upgrades and all namespaces remain on the same actual process for a connection lifetime. Alarm route The direct notification adapter resolves the same tenant/shard/owner mapping. Preserve logical consumer, request and attempt identity when an endpoint moves. Route publication Owner readiness and mapping generation are explicit. Stale edge or sender views must not make a wrong owner accept work; no arbitrary healthy-backend fallback or generic HTTP redirect.

The edge can consume a rendered map or an existing application's routing decision projected into response headers, as in the roles gateway. It need not ask an authentication service for every frame, and internal application calls need not traverse that edge. Deployment chooses UDS or private TCP/HTTP. No authentication redesign, new bearer protocol or custom proxy belongs to this capability.

A backend verifies current tenant assignment before admitting new connections, refresh work and alarm handoff. The routing map does not grant client authority: current permissions, tenant bindings, exact writes/ACKs and operation lifetimes remain enforced. If placement generation/owner admission becomes a wire field, change the exact schemas/versioning deliberately; current alarm messages do not already carry an ownership epoch.

The prototype must specify freshness/admission of its fixed map. A local cache or Kubernetes readiness observation alone is not an exclusive owner fence. Unknown or inconsistent placement refuses new admission until resolved.

docs.title: Projection and checkpoint ownership
docs.text:
Warm only assigned active tenants before routing them to a worker; report genuine suspended tenants separately so healthy B remains routable. Process liveness, owner readiness and tenant readiness are distinct. Operational inspection stays available when application work is blocked.

Preserve a stable durable realtime consumer/checkpoint identity across worker incarnation changes. Current code has one process-wide consumer, freezes tenant configuration at boot and rejects another consumer in a tenant's checkpoint namespace. Sharding therefore needs explicit parser/admission/assignment-update changes; it cannot be implemented by starting the same configuration twice. Do not derive durable identity from a Pod UID or reset checkpoints to hide a collision. If a shard-specific identity is selected, specify legacy migration and multi-shard ownership explicitly.

Owner admission protects checkpoint/projection work as well as socket delivery. The new owner reconstructs current state, validates its source/tenant binding and only then becomes routable. Independent physical-row/checkpoint inspection must prove continuity; a plausible first browser frame is insufficient evidence.

Logical shards may be empty and a worker may initially own no active tenants. Define an inspection-only idle state with no consumer route or synthetic jobs; do not invent a tenant to satisfy the current nonempty runtime constructor. Control-plane liveness, readiness to accept an assignment and readiness to serve an assigned tenant are different signals. All-suspended assignments remain inspectable without fabricating healthy clinical progress or blocking unrelated owners. Empty-to-active and tenant-roster changes need explicit admitted startup and coverage transitions; the current frozen boot configuration is not dynamic tenant admission.

docs.title: Controlled moves and failure behavior
docs.text:
Initial scope is controlled fixed-roster moves and restart recovery, not automatic takeover under an ambiguous partition. Planned sequence per affected shard:

  1. Serialize the move against tenant maintenance and freeze the source/target assignment generation. Do not change a pinned restore cohort underneath it.
  2. Stop new admission to the old owner, including new alarm attempts; retain accounting for existing connections, requests and responses.
  3. Quiesce assigned work, finish or record uncertain in-flight handoffs, close connections and stop/terminate or effectively fence the old owner. Merely removing its route or observing lease expiry does not prove it stopped emitting.
  4. Confirm old-owner exclusion, transfer the admitted generation, warm the target from durable state, then publish its route/readiness.
  5. Clients establish new sessions, reauthorize and obtain current state. A live TCP/Socket.IO session is not migrated between processes. Stagger reconnects within measured bounds; prove healthy-tenant progress.

Resynchronization is namespace-specific. The main namespace can provide a current full frame; a storage subscription acknowledgement is not a collection/history reload, and an alarm subscription is not replay of earlier alarms. Qualify actual API3 client reload/subscription ordering, concurrent changes and deletions rather than assuming every namespace has the main browser's snapshot behavior.
