docs.title: Lifecycle control boundary
docs.text:
Read-derived control diagram. The participant group means every declared instance, including replicas. A load-balanced endpoint reaching just one instance cannot replace this control boundary. Controller orchestration belongs to the private operator worker; the receiving instances host participation hooks, not restoration engines. The restore sequence below gives ordering and uncertainty rules, not administrative activity-policy transitions.

flowchart LR
  LC["Private operator controller<br/>CLI / job / worker"] -->|"pin / drain / invalidate each instance"| Roles["Participant hooks<br/>API / realtime / evaluator / tenant-admin"]

Application APIs preserve existing client payloads, authority and reply behavior. Ambiguous mutation completion must preserve the existing no-acknowledgement/error contract rather than trigger a transparent new retry. Database-backed transaction and idempotency semantics remain explicit. The communication guide owns actual runtime sequences; no RPC consolidation has been benchmarked here.

docs.title: Kubernetes scalability smell test
docs.text:
Yes, as an architecture smell test: a replaceable request-serving instance with durable authority outside the process is a natural candidate for a Kubernetes Deployment. Exclusive application database ownership permits multiple cooperating replicas; it does not mean a single API process. An internal API boundary helps separate those replicas from consumers, but does not itself make either end stateless.

Component Scale-out implication Required boundary before claiming it works Static UI serving Replaceable replica candidate. Consistent assets/configuration and edge behavior. Unified v1/v2/v3 REST/API and management modules Stateless request-serving replica candidates when local state is reconstructible and durable authority/transactions remain shared; versions are adapters within the same component. Current authority/config consistency, safe concurrent writes, graceful drain, bounded aggregate pools and actual participation of every replica in restore. Existing canonical serialization still bounds same-tenant write throughput. Realtime Connection-owning service with retained frames and subscriptions. Admitted session routing, cross-instance fanout and reconnect/recovery; a load-balanced alarm call does not reach every viewer by itself. Evaluator / notification producer One current workload owner with durable recovery; partitioning is deferred. Preserve current producer/checkpoint identity, eligibility and durable retry under restart/replacement. No new scheduler or replicated evaluator is required for API scaling; future disjoint assignments need their own contract. Lifecycle controller / migrations Controlled operations with exclusive authority. Maintenance claims, every participant's incarnation and uncertain-outcome handling; Kubernetes placement or Job completion cannot substitute for application ownership.

The current fixed cohort needs a declared roster containing every serving replica. A load-balanced API endpoint can route an ordinary command to any equivalent admitted API, whereas restore control must address every instance. Dynamic HPA membership and Kubernetes-specific bindings are deferred. Selectable private network transport and fixed-roster API serving have their own queued native acceptance. Reuse platform/configuration inventory and identities as application inputs; no parallel membership product or evaluator scheduler is selected. Deployments can overlap old/new Pods during rolling updates, so replica count is not an exclusion guarantee. A StatefulSet's stable identity/storage does not supply the application's producer or restore protocol either. See the deployment binding and replica assessment for endpoint semantics and acceptance cases. Kubernetes is an architectural frame; cluster proof and Jsonnet are deferred. Throughput, failover and any later actual binding retain their own acceptance; no new runtime measurement follows here.

docs.title: Tables and their ownership
docs.text:
Every selected namespace has its own schema_migrations(name,checksum,applied_at) ledger. Tenant tables carry tenant_id; ledgers describe a whole namespace and are not tenant records. Domain documents use JSONB with typed identity metadata and generated/indexed projections where the candidate declares them. SQL columns and indexes support the existing document interfaces rather than introducing a new client record identity. See the entries candidate and lifecycle catalogue inventory for exact definitions.

Family Tables / durable responsibility Relationship and restore treatment Clinical/document domains entries, treatments, devicestatus, profile, food, activity, settings in their selected namespaces. Tenant-bound documents. The first five have insertion counters. settings is the existing document collection, distinct from owner presentation tenant_settings. Logical restore reconciles these selected domains. Insertion state tenant_insertion_ordinal(tenant_id,last_ordinal) in each ordered domain namespace. One row per tenant/collection; allocation trigger and unique tenant/ordinal index. The document relation and counter share a binding, not a declared foreign key. History state tenant_write_clock(tenant_id,last_stamp). Tenant-wide history floor across admitted stamped writes; current floor is retained and advanced during logical restore. Projection state tenant_consumer_checkpoint(tenant_id,consumer,checkpoint,projection,contract_digest). Per-consumer recovery position/materialization. Preview realtime and evaluator select separate checkpoint namespaces. Retained current during logical clinical restore; actual invalidation and fresh acquisition reconcile output. Authentication / authorization tenant_authorization_*, owner policy/actor tables and audit; access_tenants, access_credentials, access_sessions, access_keys; legacy_credential_*; secret_records, secret_audit. Current authority, credential generations, sessions and encryption/signing references remain current during clinical restore. Access credentials/keys reference tenant rows; sessions reference their credential/subject tuple. Provider key material is outside tenant artifact handling. Owner / operator policy subject_policy, subject_policy_audit, tenant_operator_policy, tenant_settings, tenant_settings_history, tenant_owner_configuration_authority, when selected. Policy and management state, not a clinical snapshot to rewind. The owner settings history is independent of the clinical settings collection. Notification delivery tenant_notification_state, tenant_notification_heads, tenant_notification_requests. Durable producer state, deduplication heads and attempts/receipts. Retained current; invalidation retires retained output/intents through the actual consumer protocol. No general exactly-once external effect follows from these tables. Alarm acknowledgement tenant_alarm_suppression(tenant_id,alarm_group,alarm_level,acked_at,expires_at). Current suppression state is retained; fresh eligibility reads remain tenant-bound. Restore control tenant_lifecycle_windows, tenant_lifecycle_operations, tenant_lifecycle_restore_authority, tenant_lifecycle_restore_audit. Durable phase/generation/claim, unfinished operations, authorized maintenance roles and audit. Operations, authority and audit reference window tenant rows. These are control authority, not clinical restore payload. Deletion ceremony tenant_lifecycle_requests, tenant_lifecycle_ceremony. Separate requested/confirmed/cancelled/executing/executed deletion workflow; ceremony references request plus tenant. A restore claim does not itself authorize deletion. Tenant activity tenant_activity(tenant_id,version,paused,suspended,deletion_request_id,paused_before_deletion), tenant_activity_audit. Control namespace, migration 0007_tenant_activity. One row per tenant, referencing its window row; audit rows reference the activity row. Operator/owner policy, not clinical payload: a restore neither rewinds nor clears it. Key retention tenant_lifecycle_key_retention with artifact_removal, artifact_removal_code. Control namespace, migrations 0005 and 0006. One record per deletion request: retained → destroying → destroyed, or restored. The destroyed row records the export-file removal outcome.

The preview lifecycle mapping explicitly extends the reviewed catalogue with both checkpoint namespaces, outbox and suppression. The generic lifecycle module has its own admitted inventory; an arbitrary relation found in PostgreSQL is not automatically exported, restored or deleted. Exact outbox, suppression and control DDL lives in the notification candidate, suppression candidate and lifecycle candidate.

docs.title: Binding, forced RLS and privileges
docs.text:
The lower connection transaction acquires the selected window lease before starting SQL, binds the tenant with transaction-local app.current_tenant_id, then verifies current window admission. Tenant policies compare tenant_id with that setting for both reads and writes. Reviewed tables use ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. An application identity must be a nonowner without superuser/bypass authority. A tenant binding is trusted service context; RLS does not authenticate the end user or constrain a compromised worker that holds all tenants' credentials.

Readiness examines effective grants and ownership, including inherited rights; a reassuring role name is insufficient. The insertion readiness oracle distinguishes:

  • serving roles: clinical read/update/delete, input-column INSERT excluding insertion_ordinal, allocator execution and bounded counter read/insert/update;
  • readers: clinical/counter SELECT, without mutation or allocator execution;
  • restore roles: separately checked explicit-ordinal and counter maintenance rights for the admitted restore protocol.

The actual trigger is SECURITY INVOKER, with fixed pg_catalog search path. It neither grants a writer extra authority nor requires a service with elevated function privileges. The structural oracle checks the current function body, trigger enablement/binding, exact counter shape, ownership, RLS, constraints and absence of a native identity default. A ledger check alone cannot prove these physical invariants.

The reserved metadata tenant binding is a separate lower-connection path that requires a database-confirmed read-only transaction. It permits shared schema/ACL checks while normal tenants are suspended; it is not permission to read a paused tenant's documents. The source uses it for the consumer advisory-lock same-database challenge and unconditional metadata checks. The c23 native matrix measures its stated actual startup cases; other guard controls retain their own source/protocol scope. Consumer startup source

docs.title: History clock and insertion counter serve different contracts
docs.text:
State Meaning Client-visible implication last_stamp The clock decorator locks the tenant row through the outer data transaction, allocates strictly increasing numeric server stamps and updates the durable floor. Preserves the existing srvModified / history cursor protocol. Clinical timestamps and public IDs retain their own meanings. Serialization is tenant-local; a sequence value alone would not prevent a reader advancing past an earlier uncommitted write. last_ordinal The insertion trigger allocates within one tenant/collection in the same transaction as the row. Missing/invalid state refuses; updates cannot change tenant/ordinal identity. Reproduces supported natural/first-match ordering. The read path selects id_kind,doc and orders by the private ordinal; the ordinal is not a public ID or history cursor.

There is no required cross-tenant total order. Separate insertion state also works without opting into the history-clock decorator. Counter-row contention serializes same-tenant inserts for that collection; history-clock composition serializes admitted stamped writes across that tenant's domains. Pools, storage, CPU and DDL locks remain shared resources. The adopted insertion semantics and history-forward restore policy own compatibility decisions; the counter analysis retains alternatives and comparisons with database revision/change-stream designs.

docs.title: Upgrade and readiness sequence
docs.text:
The catalogue validator accepts an explicit ordered JSON catalogue, checks SQL checksums and validates the exact reviewed typed conversion/correction plans. It does not discover arbitrary executable migrations. The runner's ledger inspection requires applied migrations to be an exact checksum-matching prefix, refusing unknown entries, gaps and drift.

The operator runner uses one direct client for the namespace advisory lock, DDL and ledger writes. Each migration and its ledger entry commit atomically; the catalogue as a whole can span several transactions. status and check use a read-only inspection transaction; stale check refuses. There is no migration-down operation. Serving boot checks; it does not run migrations or provision grants.

Deployment backup restore has a stricter order: prepare fresh target namespaces with the artifact's exact catalogue, verify exact ledgers and restore raw state, then upgrade. A longer current ledger is not interchangeable with the artifact's schema. The physical restore module validates before effects, recreates selected ACLs and verifies restored counts/digests before COMMIT; it does not fabricate migration ledger entries.

The insertion conversion takes an ordinary access-exclusive DDL lock, validates existing identity rows, seeds counter maxima by tenant, removes the table-wide identity and installs the tenant trigger/index. That one-time upgrade exclusion is distinct from a recurring tenant restore pause. Its original catalogue bytes remain immutable; the binding SQLSTATE correction is an appended checksummed operation. An upgraded binary must still verify the current physical trigger/function, grants and tenant floors before admission.

Read-derived upgrade/readiness sequence:

sequenceDiagram
  participant Operator
  participant Runner as Direct migration client
  participant DB as Selected namespace
  participant Role as API / RT / evaluator / admin
  Operator->>Runner: Explicit catalogue and namespace
  Runner->>Runner: Validate checksums and typed SQL
  Runner->>DB: Acquire namespace advisory lock
  Runner->>DB: Inspect exact applied prefix
  loop Pending migrations
    Runner->>DB: BEGIN, reviewed DDL/data conversion
    Runner->>DB: INSERT schema_migrations row, COMMIT
  end
  Runner->>DB: Release lock, close client
  Role->>DB: Read-only catalogue and physical metadata checks
  Role->>DB: Check effective ACL / RLS / datastore / binding
  loop Every configured tenant remains in roster
    Role->>DB: Actual tenant-window admission
    alt Active tenant
      Role->>DB: Floors, provisioning and tenant warmup
    else Genuine suspension
      Role->>Role: Defer tenant warmup, keep tenant unavailable
    end
  end
  Note over Role: Shared readiness errors still refuse process startup

The startup helper defers only actual-window suspension errors, not arbitrary errors with a matching string. Lazy initialization runs under the actual later tenant admission; invalidation rejects stale initializer completion. A suspended A therefore need not prevent B startup in the new source. The startup decision requires fresh-process native proof. The c23 native matrix reproduces the bounded shared-role restart criterion on its exact later source; this guide retains the inspected source attribution above.

docs.title: Write transaction and restore transaction boundaries
docs.text:
For ordinary admitted writes, the upper HTTP/IPC/socket lifetime and the lower SQL transaction have different lengths. The operation window records unfinished work until the outer callback/response/acknowledgement ends; ending a SQL transaction alone does not prove that work drained. Within SQL, the tenant clock, document changes and insertion counter changes commit or roll back together. Post-commit publication runs only after the outer transaction acknowledges COMMIT.

Logical tenant restore uses the private maintenance controller, not an arbitrary quiesced: true assertion. It pins actual fixed participants, checks current operator authority, commits durable suspension/generation/claim, drains unfinished operations, then obtains the tenant's exclusive advisory lock. The bound claim is revalidated on the same operator transaction. Unknown actors and changed participant incarnations refuse; a restarted process cannot inherit an earlier pin's authority.

Read-derived tenant A restore sequence; B has its own admission window:

sequenceDiagram
  participant Op as Trusted maintenance operator
  participant Control as Durable control tables / tenant lock
  participant Cohort as Fixed separate service processes
  participant Data as A clinical rows / clock / counters
  Op->>Cohort: Pin current incarnations and actual datastore identities
  Op->>Control: Verify authority, COMMIT suspension and claim
  Op->>Control: Drain unfinished operations, acquire A exclusive lock
  Op->>Cohort: Exact actor census and pinned status checks
  Op->>Data: BEGIN DATA, lock live history floor
  Op->>Data: Plan current plus captured identities
  Op->>Data: Rebuild A rows with forward history and tenant-local allocation
  Op->>Data: Verify rows, floors and held claim, COMMIT DATA
  Op->>Op: Publish acknowledged post-commit effects
  Op->>Cohort: Fresh A invalidation request, await every pinned ACK
  Op->>Control: Recheck authority / claim / audit, COMMIT activation
  Note over Control,Cohort: Before activation, failure retains suspension
  Note over Op,Control: Activation ACK loss may leave active state, inspect, do not auto-retry

The logical planner preserves public/typed identities and sorts captured ordered rows using BigInt ordinals. It replays them through ordinary allocation, preserving relative order without preserving private numeric ordinal values. Unchanged documents keep current server metadata. Changed/restored history documents receive stamps above the live issued floor; current records absent from the artifact become isValid:false deletion records. Activity has no v3 history protocol and uses snapshot replacement plus invalidation. Exact physical/raw backup import has a separate fidelity contract in tenant operations; it must not be substituted for client history reconciliation.

The restore implementation retains current nonclinical catalogues, including selected authority, sessions, secrets, policies, checkpoints, outbox and suppression. It retains the live history floor and advances it through the clock decorator. It does not replay old control claims/audit as clinical data. The identity guarantee covers records retained in the current tenant or artifact; identities hard-purged from both retain the existing history-retention limit.

A DATA COMMIT whose acknowledgement is lost has an uncertain outcome. Retrying or reopening automatically could publish contradictory history or reuse stale cache state. A committed suspension, unresolved unfinished operation, missing invalidation acknowledgement or uncertain activation requires verification and operator recovery. If the activation COMMIT acknowledgement is lost, the stored window may already be active and its audit activated; the uncertain response does not prove continued suspension. Inspect the committed state rather than automatically replaying activation. The controller commit handling preserves those distinctions. This preview provides no automatic orphan clearance or supported suspended-restore resume command. Operator-verified recovery remains separate work; no deterministic recovery-time bound follows from the refusal/restart evidence.

docs.title: Activity, retention and the admin identity at 16a1fc2d
docs.text: Read-derived from the 16a1fc2d source. The four mechanisms below joined

docs.title: 8898 in the 2026-11-10 batch. Each anchor is pinned to that head.
Tenant activity: pause and suspend
docs.text:
Migration 0007_tenant_activity in the lifecycle control catalogue creates tenant_activity (primary key tenant_id, referencing tenant_lifecycle_windows; a positive version; paused and suspended booleans; a deletion_request_id/paused_before_deletion pair that is set or null together) and an append-only tenant_activity_audit whose verb is one of provision, pause, unpause, suspend, unsuspend, deletion-request, deletion-cancel or deletion-execute, with authority owner or operator. Both tables use enabled and forced RLS on app.current_tenant_id, and PUBLIC has no rights.

A row for every tenant. The same migration backfills one active row (version 1, both flags false) for every existing window row, with a provision audit row attributed to principal migration, consumer backfill-0007. It lifts FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on tenant_lifecycle_windows for the two backfill statements and restores it before the migration commits; migration and ledger entry are one transaction (see upgrade and readiness). New tenants get their row from provisionInTransaction, which the Compose bootstrap calls in the same transaction that inserts the window row (activity-row-always-provisioned).

Two flags, three states. The policy module defines active, paused and suspended, with suspended taking precedence. Paused admits uploads and connector polling and stops the evaluator, so alarms are not computed or delivered; suspended admits nothing. The column grants enforce who sets which flag (grant set): the owner identity may update version and paused only, the operator identity version, paused and suspended, and the deletion-ceremony identity also the deletion pair. The ceremony effects pause on a deletion request, restore the earlier pause state on cancel, and suspend on execution, each inside the ceremony's transaction (deletion-request-auto-pauses).

Where it is read. Each consumer reads the row afresh through a reader store, after a check of the control catalogue ledger:

Consumer Effect Anchor API (HTTP) Write methods, OPTIONS and the v2 credential exchange count as uploads; everything else is a read. Refusals are 423 TENANT_PAUSED / TENANT_SUSPENDED; an unreadable row is 503 TENANT_ACTIVITY_UNAVAILABLE. serving gate, API wiring, status map Realtime Every current-state read checks eligibility; an ineligible tenant reads as disabled and its sockets are invalidated. realtime gate Evaluator Work lists are built from tenants eligible now; an unreadable or missing row makes that tenant ineligible with its own code (ACTIVITY_UNAVAILABLE, ACTIVITY_NOT_PROVISIONED). eligibility, evaluator wiring

The activity block is optional in each role's configuration; without it the role does not consult the table. The in-tree Compose plan at 16a1fc2d provisions rows but grants no role the activity tables (deployment grants contain no tenant_activity grant), so its roles run without activity admission.

docs.title: Key retention and export-file removal
docs.text:
Migration 0005_tenant_lifecycle_key_retention keeps one record per deletion request: the export artifact's 64-hex digest, the retained key names and a phase of retained, restored, destroying or destroyed. Migration 0006_tenant_lifecycle_artifact_removal adds artifact_removal (removed, absent or failed) and artifact_removal_code, with a CHECK that a removal outcome is present exactly when the phase is destroyed and a code is present exactly when the outcome is failed.

destroyRetainedKeys refuses LIFECYCLE_ARTIFACT_REMOVER_REQUIRED before any state change when no remover is composed. It commits destroying, has the key custodian delete and confirm the absence of every key, then removes the export file by digest and records the outcome in the same row update that commits destroyed. A missing or unremovable file never blocks key destruction; a repeat call on a destroyed record reports the recorded outcome without retrying. The filesystem remover builds the path only from the configured private directory and the recorded digest (tenant-artifact-<digest>), and refuses a symlink or non-directory at that name. Copies outside that directory are the operator's responsibility (key-destruction-removes-export, export-removal-no-retry).

docs.title: Restore census and non-clinical identities
docs.text: The actor census in assertComplete reads every other client backend in the database whose identity holds any privilege, direct, inherited or by ownership, in the protected namespaces. A backend matching a pinned participant's PID, birth and role passes. Any other backend is exempt only when its identity holds no privilege on any clinical table (entries, treatments, devicestatus, profile, food, settings, activity) and no write privilege on tenant_insertion_ordinal or tenant_write_clock; otherwise the census refuses RESTORE_COHORT_UNKNOWN_BACKEND. Grants read from the catalogue in the census statement decide; role names and application_name do not. Read-only identities and the admin role's ownership_operator are therefore accepted while connected (restore-census-and-ownership-phase, restore-census-counter-writers). The exemption is a configuration check of connected identities, not a check of live writes. The disposable-PostgreSQL integration test admin-lifecycle-fit exercises the admin role beside a restore, including granting it a clinical table to make the census refuse.

docs.title: The ownership_operator identity
docs.text: The deployment plan declares a separate <prefix>_ownership_operator database identity for the admin role's ownership operations. In the authorization namespace it may read and row-lock tenant_authorization_config and tenant_owner_policy through UPDATE(owner_fence), insert and update active, can_update and delegable on tenant_owner_actors, read tenant_authorization_subjects and insert into tenant_subject_admin_audit. In the control namespace it gets only SELECT on the window, request and ceremony tables (phase grants). It holds no clinical grant and no counter grant, so the census above accepts it. Each ownership change reads the tenant phase under the shared window lock before any ownership row lock and refuses OWNERSHIP_TENANT_INACTIVE unless the tenant is active (ownership check). The admin role is not a lifecycle cohort participant.

docs.title: Shared resources and remaining fences
docs.text:
The fixed cohort uses private same-UID sockets and trusted credential custody. It compares actual backend PID, birth, role and datastore identity; application names are not membership. The actor census refreshes PostgreSQL's statistics snapshot on the same operator client before reading actors; at 16a1fc2d it also accepts non-clinical identities. It remains a diagnostic/refusal check, not a physical database fence against a newly opened raw client with already-authorized DATA credentials. Such external writers are unsupported under the application ownership contract; arbitrary-writer exclusion is not a supported-topology admission gate. A trusted all-tenant worker or DBA remains within the deployment trust boundary. See the deployment/trust decision.

Tenant-local state removes cross-tenant counter maintenance during restore; it does not partition database capacity or remove shared service failure. Restarts, full membership availability and operator recovery remain distinct from running B continuity. Realtime aggregate readiness remains strict while additive live and per-tenant fields describe partial tenant availability. The exact startup, health and fixed-cohort boundaries live in the application cohort guide. The ed2 cold measurement adds the packaged ordinary-restore/UI/B-continuity scope. HA, multihost membership, capacity and whole M6 retain separate admission criteria. The current acceptance family owns the distinct browser, cold Compose, client, regression and corpus verdicts.

docs.title: Tenant admission, activity and recovery
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-10 at 4917b2d4a.

Contributor-facing living guide, current with the release decisions of 2026-11-10. Activity policy adopted 2026-11-10: pause and suspend are the operator activity policy (decision), with the rows listed under adopted activity policy. Implementation is MT-ACTIVITY-ELIGIBILITY (fixed on its lane, not joined to #8898; the queue owns its state and the lane record its measurements). The REST component direction below is recorded in the release decisions. Mechanism assessment in the first three sections is read-derived from application ed2ced00c80bd0a6a7d75f834d2c6e2af8c71364; later acceptance stays attributed to its actual heads in the operation-window acceptance family. The tenancy decisions own the pause/suspend meanings and owner authority the owner and root boundaries.

docs.title: One logical API does not require one listener or process
docs.text:
Architecture direction: REST APIs (v1/v2/v3) are one stateless request-serving component. Version-specific routers/adapters live inside that component; API version numbers do not select separate processes, services or scaling groups. Each replica serves the same configured, admitted route set. Compose service instances and a Kubernetes Deployment are alternative placement/lifecycle mechanisms for that component; neither is a new route-acceptance claim or a requirement to demonstrate Kubernetes now.

“Stateless” means no replica owns authoritative tenant data or an exclusive clinical evaluation workload. Durable authority, clinical state and operation records remain in their backing stores. Each replica still owns connections, in-flight responses, pools and reconstructible startup/cache state, so it must participate in maintenance drain and invalidation. Do not require client affinity or introduce per-version deployment boundaries as part of API scale-out.

The source already composes configured API3 and legacy routers in one API role: preview-api.js:110, tenant-app/index.js:187, :217. These read-derived mechanisms support the component boundary; the acceptance family still owns exactly which routes/clients were exercised. Internal v1/v2/v3 adapters retain their reply, authentication and compatibility rules.

The business REST surface groups data, authorization and owner-management capabilities. Owner operations retain their separate audience/listener and privileges, even when their module is colocated with request-serving API. A logical component describes responsibility. A listener describes who can reach which interface and with which audience. A process describes placement, resource custody and failure coupling. Grouping REST business APIs does not merge their credentials, privileges or trust boundaries, and it does not put every worker or maintenance engine inside HTTP request handling.

The current CLI can compose selected roles in one process, with role-owned contexts and separately resolved listeners: serve/index.js:42, :85. That includes the available api and tenant-admin roles under their explicit configurations; it does not authorize a public operator listener. The current DATA API intentionally excludes owner/operator routes: preview-api.js:110. Whether the selected deployment combines those listeners or separates their processes remains distinct from their logical grouping. This clarification adopts no process-count, ingress or deployment-layout change.

Responsibility Current mechanism and placement boundary What this means for the logical API Data REST and credential authorization api owns request-serving DATA behavior and canonical clinical writes. Current tenant/client authority and RLS still apply. A business API responsibility; it may have explicitly declared replicas. It does not gain operator restoration credentials. Owner REST tenant-admin has its own configuration, listener and owner-management audience. roles.js:88 Part of the logical business surface while preserving owner versus DATA authority. Logical grouping does not imply one permission set. Restore orchestration A private operator CLI/tool constructs the maintenance controller and invokes logical restoration: deploy/multitenant/restore.js:97. It is not an API replica's normal request handler. The API participates in safe maintenance; it does not host the restore engine. A future control-plane request may initiate a separately authorized operator job, but that API/job contract is not selected here. Evaluator Headless runtime, with one active owner of the current tenant set; it computes clinical output and participates in durable notification/recovery contracts. roles.js:59 A worker responsibility, not a REST route or API replica. Tenant eligibility and producer ownership remain separate checks. Connector vcpool Declared role metadata has no start/multitenant runtime: roles.js:81. CLI rejects unavailable roles: serve/index.js:31. Future connector workers perform external acquisition and send canonical writes through the admitted API/write boundary. The descriptor is not proof of an implemented worker or permission for a new direct-write path. Exact deployment and activity policy remain open. Realtime Owns connected sockets, projections and private API forwarding; it is a reader and forwards writes to api. roles.js:68 Retained connection state makes it a different runtime responsibility from request-serving REST, even when composition shares a process.

The endpoint/API-scaling plan separates transport, service discovery, per-instance restore inventory and producer ownership. It does not add evaluator replication or a custom scheduler. Platform scheduling/inventory may supply placement and assignment; application eligibility and actual operation lifetime still have to be enforced.

docs.title: Why every API instance is restore-aware
docs.text:
An API need not perform restoration to conflict with it. It can hold a request or response open, prepare tenant-specific startup/floor state, read a frame, or commit a write while another component replaces that tenant's clinical state. Restoration must therefore exclude new conflicting operations, drain actual in-flight work and invalidate each instance's retained state before reopening the maintenance gate.

The operation window:77 checks the tenant's current lifecycle phase under its lease; a non-active phase refuses. The cohort contract:24 keeps an outer operation unfinished through callback, HTTP/private response or socket acknowledgement completion, not merely SQL completion. The API's tenant invalidator:129 resets local startup/readiness floors; request frames are acquired fresh.

The controller pins every actual participant, suspends the maintenance window, drains, restores, awaits actual invalidation and only then attempts maintenance activation: maintenance-window.js:133, :177. Missing/replaced peers or uncertain acknowledgement retain the affected tenant's protected state. A load-balanced API service address does not establish that all actual API instances drained or invalidated. None of this requires exposing a restore endpoint on every API.

docs.title: Maintenance safety is not an activity policy
docs.text:
Several existing mechanisms use an active/disabled concept, but their meanings and consumers differ. Do not collapse them into one status flag.

Existing mechanism What source establishes What it does not establish Maintenance phase The exact lifecycle schema admits active and suspended, with claim/digest consistency constraints: operation-window-readiness.js:24. Restore owns the claim-bound transition and later clears its own maintenance claim. A general operator activity enum, read-only mode, connector scheduling policy, account disablement or deletion policy. Reusing its columns would mix safety recovery with business intent. Current access authority The signed-token adapter reads tenant, credential, session and key activity and current grants: access-postgres.js:39, :71. Proof that every legacy/anonymous/owner route and background worker consumes one tenant-wide activity/resource policy. A token-authority bit alone is not a complete workload-admission contract. Evaluator current-config refusal A missing current configuration discards its local component and output: evaluator-runtime.js:43. Maintenance-window refusal also discards state. Proof of no scheduled work for an inactive tenant. The runtime retains configured tenant states, iterates all configured tenants at line 101, and installs acquisition/time timers at line 152. Refusing the attempted cycle is not the same as removing it from eligible background work. MT-ACTIVITY-ELIGIBILITY replaces this with an eligible work list (lane record above). Restore preserves live authority Same-ID clinical restoration retains current authority, credentials, secrets, checkpoints and live clock: logical-restore.js:3. A new general operator activity policy, or proof that future policy is preserved until it has its own persistence, transition and consumer contract.

Recovery provides exclusion, drain, invalidation and uncertainty mechanisms to reuse; it does not by itself stop a paused or suspended tenant consuming background resources. Configured presence is not workload eligibility: a configured tenant stays discoverable to operators and recovery while it is ineligible for clinical evaluation or connector polling.

docs.title: Adopted activity policy
docs.text:
Pause and suspend are the operator activity policy; there is no third state and no separate "inactive" flag. Each fact keeps its own owner and its own reported reason:

Fact Owner and use Boundary Activity state (active, paused, suspended) Durable per-tenant row, written by authorized owner (pause only) or operator action with audit. Every tenant has one: a migration backfills existing tenants as active and provisioning writes the row in the same transaction. Neither a successful restore nor a process restart changes it. An unreadable row stops the evaluator for that tenant only, with a per-tenant health code. Maintenance/recovery state The existing operation-window/controller owns exclusion, claims, uncertainty and safe maintenance completion. Finishing restore clears only its own maintenance claim; it never clears pause or suspend. Unknown maintenance outcome is not success. Current authority Tenant/client/session/key/grants and owner/operator policy decide whether the actor may perform the operation. Unpausing grants no permission, revives no revoked key or session and overrides no RLS. Clinical restoration does not rewind current authority. Worker assignment Configuration (and later evaluator partitioning) names which worker may own a tenant's task. Assignment does not make a paused or suspended tenant eligible. Observed health/readiness Runtime reports dependencies, last acquisition, freshness and refusal reasons. A green probe cannot override pause, suspend or recovery refusal; an outage is never reported as an intentional state.

Effective admission for an operation is the intersection of activity state, maintenance safety and current authority; a background task also needs its assignment. Dependency health may refuse work and never expands permission.

Decision (2026-11-10) What it fixes Pause and suspend are the activity policy Workers build work lists from eligible tenants. Paused: uploads and connector polling continue, the evaluator stops, and on unpause it recomputes from current data before publishing. Suspended: nothing runs. Restore and restart preserve the state. Adopted semantics in full Suspend refuses ingest and reads and disconnects sockets; pause blocks UI and reads while uploads continue. Owner may pause Owner-API pause/unpause with audit. Only the operator suspends and deletes (delete requires suspend). Single-site behaviour is unchanged. Deletion request pauses Request pauses; cancel restores the earlier state; operator execution suspends. An owner may pause or unpause during a pending ceremony; ownership changes still refuse. Refusal status Suspended: every refused request, uploads included, returns 423 TENANT_SUSPENDED. Paused reads return 423 TENANT_PAUSED. Uploaders are not invited to retry. Activity row always provisioned A missing row is a provisioning defect, not an operating state.

What operators and owners notice. No alarms are computed or delivered while a site is paused, including the pause that starts with a deletion request. The pause control and the deletion confirmation say so in plain language. Some uploaders treat a 4xx as final and drop data sent during a suspension; that cost was accepted with the 423 choice.

An activity transition makes prohibited work ineligible before clinical acquisition, provider polling or notification production, drains or invalidates running work under an explicit race contract, and releases retained tenant-specific resources when safe. A small amount of shared eligibility and recovery observation remains; "no unnecessary background work" is not a measured promise of zero shared overhead. Operators keep separately authenticated inspection and recovery controls. Connector workers do not yet exist as a multitenant runtime (roles.js:81); they adopt the same eligibility when built.

docs.title: Focused future acceptance
docs.text:
The criteria below are the acceptance bar for the adopted policy. The activity-eligibility lane record holds what its two passes measured and with which controls; the queue item MT-ACTIVITY-ELIGIBILITY lists what is still open (deploy wiring and grants, full API/realtime role runs with activity selected, per-request read cost, and isolation of one tenant's unreadable row). A criterion counts as met only on the joined candidate that carries it. Use synthetic tenants A and B, actual serving/worker consumers and independent stored-state/work/resource oracles.

Criterion Positive experiment and independent oracle Planned semantic negative control Pause/suspend survives restore Pause or suspend A through the authorized activity transition while a restore is in progress. Complete permitted maintenance or retain refusal under the settled transition protocol. The state stays paused/suspended; prohibited requests/work remain blocked after maintenance activation. B continues actual operations. Make restore activation overwrite the activity state: the post-restore state/operation oracle detects unintended reactivation. Confirm that exact control, then restore and rerun. Restart and replacement preserve intent Start fresh API/realtime/evaluator processes with A paused or suspended and B active. A's state persists; B becomes ready; no component derives reactivation from boot or cleared maintenance. Treat lifecycle active, process restart or absent local cache as reactivation: A executes prohibited work and the effect/work counter assertion fails. Eligibility differs from configuration Keep A in configuration and recovery inventory but make its clinical evaluation/connector workload ineligible. Exercise actual timer/poll/notification triggers; observe no prohibited acquisition/provider work, bounded retained resources and continued B work. Measure any required eligibility-check overhead separately. Schedule from configured tenant presence alone: the independent workload/egress oracle detects A's unnecessary work even if the request eventually refuses. In-flight transition and invalidation Hold an actual A callback/HTTP response or evaluator/connector cycle open during pause or suspend. Apply the drain/cancel contract; late generations cannot publish output, acknowledgements or newly disallowed effects. Current local contexts are invalidated. Complete at SQL commit/transport abort only, skip an invalidator or accept a late generation: the callback barrier or stored/output oracle detects premature completion/stale publication. Current authority remains independent Change the activity state without reviving revoked session/key/grants; restore an older clinical snapshot and confirm current authority and the activity state survive. Exercise supported legacy/anonymous/owner paths explicitly. Permit an unpause or old artifact to replace current authority: revoked access/effect assertion fails. A signed-token-only check cannot count as all-path coverage. Policy is operation-specific and visible Execute the adopted matrix for reads, ingest, evaluation, notifications and connectors in active, paused and suspended states, including the 423 codes. UI/health exposes the state separately from maintenance, dependency failure and data freshness. Substitute a generic active flag or UI-only gate: an operation outside its policy runs, or an outage is reported as intentional inactivity. Exact path/reason assertions must detect it. Safe reactivation After an authorized unpause or unsuspend, reacquire current settings, authority and clinical inputs before eligible publication/work. Preserve uncertainty and do not resume suspended restore/orphan work automatically. Reuse stale output/credentials or clear uncertainty to become ready: source-attributed refusal/freshness/effect oracle fails. Isolation and shared failure behavior A's pause/suspend, or an unreadable A activity row, does not block B's HTTP, realtime and evaluator progress. Shared schema/privilege/datastore/trust failures still refuse where required rather than being treated as an A-only state. Broadly defer a shared failure or globally stop healthy tenants: unsafe startup or lost B progress triggers its intended assertion.

Before implementation, confirm the current head and queue openness; stop and report mismatches rather than choosing the nearest behavior that passes. Record actual source/instrument/role/topology and confirmed semantic reds. Focused checks run during development; the coherent joined candidate owns the full, default-browser, enabled-corpus and final prcheck campaign.

docs.title: Tenant configuration schema for hosted Nightscout (T30-SCHEMA-CONFIG)
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-10-27. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

Current-use note, 2026-11-05: retain this bounded schema design and its pinned lab evidence. Owner authority owns the later management/delegation, session-lifetime and local-verification decisions. Open-question rows below must be checked against that contract; this candidate is not the deployed schema or a claim that the application token path already uses the new verifier.

Contributor-facing. Draft of 2026-10-27, for the maintainer's review. Queue item T30-SCHEMA-CONFIG. It builds on D22 (execution plan §2.13), the census re-measured on dev (§3a), and the configuration-surface document (§A, §A.3, §B.3, §C, §E, §F.1). The schema runs in tools/lab/tenant-config-schema/, which holds 59 tests and 77 controls. Nothing here decides a question those documents leave open: such questions are listed in §11.

Revised the same day after three maintainer answers: class D values live in each role's environment; tenant_members names a person by provider and subject; and rollback against a changed policy is refused whole (Q3, now decided). The first round's migrations 0002 to 0007 are now 0003 to 0008.

Marks: [M] means measured by the lab, in the run recorded in its results.json (PostgreSQL 16.15). [R] means read or reasoned, not measured. Test ids (ISO-…, FLOOR-…) name the lab's tests.

docs.title: 1. What this is
docs.text:
Under TENANCY_MODE=multi, a tenant's configuration decides what a person's site shows, who may read it, what it connects to and, once multi-mode alarms pass the gate in §7a, when an alarm fires. D22 gives that configuration three layers:

  1. project floors, which are fixed in code;
  2. the operator's policy, written on the operator plane;
  3. the owner's values, written on the tenant-owner listener.

D22 also says that integrations are typed records, that credentials live in a separate secrets component, and that every change is versioned and can be rolled back.

This document gives those decisions a PostgreSQL schema. It has three design goals:

  • a wrong value fails loudly at the moment it is written, and is never stored and then silently rewritten;
  • a forgotten tenant filter returns nothing (D3);
  • no table holds secret material.

docs.title: 2. The tables, and why each exists
docs.text:
Two tables already exist on the seam branch (81a1f6ce:lib/admin/platform.sql):

  • tenants has no RLS, because it is read before a tenant context exists. This schema leaves it unchanged.
  • tenant_members has RLS. Migration 0002 changes it as the maintainer decided on 2026-10-27: a person is identified by identity provider and subject, both text, unique together, with no foreign key to any identity table of Nightscout's, so a Kratos, Clerk or any OIDC subject fits (D17 as amended).
  • The lab makes the pair unique within a tenant, as (tenant_id, provider, subject_id), so that one person can be a member of two tenants.
  • The column keeps the seam's name, subject_id, so seam code still reads it.
  • 0002 refuses to run while the table holds rows, because nothing records which provider issued them.

MEMBER-identity and MEMBER-migration-refuses-rows cover this, with three controls. [M]

The lab's migration 0001 is that file byte for byte. [M]

table tenant-scoped written by why it exists config_setting no migrations only The catalogue of setting names hosted configuration may carry. It records each setting's type, whether the owner may set it, whether it is an alarm setting, whether it needs a deletion confirmation, and its project floor. A name missing from here cannot appear in any policy or owner row, because foreign keys forbid it. That absence is how the "not offered" floors reach the database. integration_kind no migrations only The driver catalogue. For each kind: the schema its settings must satisfy, the hosts a driver may call, and the names of the credential parts the owner and the operator each supply. deployment_policy no operator D22's one deployment policy of tenant-facing settings: per setting, a default, a mode (open, bounded or pinned), a constraint and a pin. Deployment-level (class D) values are not here: they are environment variables of the role that reads them (maintainer, 2026-10-27). tenant_policy_override yes operator, with the tenant bound D22's operator overrides for individual tenants. A row replaces the deployment row for that tenant and setting. tenant_setting_value yes tenant-owner listener The owner's values, accepted only within the governing policy row and the floor. tenant_alarm_thresholds yes nobody yet (see §5) The owner's four glucose thresholds, as typed NOT NULL integer columns in mg/dL. It exists so the §A.3 hazard cannot be expressed. See §6. tenant_config_version yes tenant-owner listener (insert only) One numbered, append-only row per change. It records the plane, the identity provider (required for an owner) and its subject, the time, the kind (change, rollback, bootstrap, import) and the full owner-scope state after the change. deployment_integration no operator The operator's part of a kind's credential (for example a push service's application token), held as a reference. tenant_integration yes tenant-owner listener One record per connector, webhook or push target. Each has a kind, settings validated by the kind's schema, a reference to the owner's credential, and an enabled flag. tenant_integration_status yes consumer and connector roles The last success and last error. They are kept apart so that a connector's polling never creates a configuration version.

Three functions carry the write path. All are SECURITY INVOKER, so RLS and table grants apply to everything they do:

  • cfg_apply(tenant, changes, plane, subject, …) is the single write path for owner-scope state.
  • cfg_rollback(tenant, version, …) restores an earlier version.
  • cfg_policy_for(tenant, key) returns the governing policy row: the override, else the deployment row, else the catalogue default.

docs.title: 2.1 Roles
docs.text:
The lab's roles are cfg_owner, ns_operator, ns_tenant_admin and ns_api.

  • cfg_owner runs the migrations and owns every table. It is NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS.
  • The other three own nothing. They map to D7's operator plane, D16's tenant-owner listener, and D5/D21's consumer, evaluator and connector roles.

The grants are in 0008_grants.up.sql.

Measured, and in tension with a claim in the seam's code (§10, M7): the tables are owned by a role that is not the application role. RLS is still active for every application role, with row_security_active() true on all seven tenant tables (ISO-roles, ISO-<table>). [M]

docs.title: 3. The merge rule, and where it runs
docs.text:
Rule (D22). For each setting, the effective value is:

  1. the code default;
  2. replaced by the operator default, if the governing row has one;
  3. replaced by the owner value, if:
  4. the catalogue marks the setting owner-settable,
  5. the value is well typed,
  6. it satisfies the floor,
  7. the mode is not pinned,
  8. and, where the mode is bounded, the constraint accepts it;
  9. replaced by the operator pin, if the mode is pinned.

An owner value that fails step 3 is not used, and it is reported in ignoredOwnerValues with the reason (MERGE-override-narrows, MERGE-pin-beats-owner). [M]

A floor is checked once more on the effective value. For example, with no operator row, WRITE_VALIDATION falls back to the code default off, which breaks the floor. The merge reports this so that the process refuses to serve (MERGE-floor-on-effective). [M]

The thresholds are merged as a set:

  • the owner's row if one exists;
  • otherwise the effective BG_* values, key by key.

A set that is out of order is reported. It is never nudged, unlike dev's verifyThresholds (lib/settings.js:311-334 on db3b9e4e, BF-67) (MERGE-thresholds-refused-not-rewritten). [M]

Where it runs. The merge runs in application code (lib/merge.js in the lab). The write-time checks run in the database, as triggers. There are four reasons. [R]

  1. The code defaults live in the code (lib/settings.js, lib/server/env.js). A merge in SQL would need them passed in, or copied into the database, and a second copy can drift.
  2. The process environment is visible only to code. D22 says floors are "enforced in code under multi", and several of them are process-level (§4).
  3. D22's "saving invalidates the tenant's cached settings" implies that the merged result is cached in the process. The merge is computed on a cache miss, and the result is what the evaluator and the API use.
  4. An operator or owner can write rows through a path other than the intended code. A wrong row must not be storable at all, so acceptance (type, floor, mode, constraint) is checked by triggers on every write.

Two spellings of one rule can drift. The lab therefore runs a differential test: 30 cases go through the JavaScript acceptance rule and the SQL one, and the test requires agreement. Its control plants an off-by-one in the JavaScript ordinal minimum, and the test goes red (MERGE-differential). [M] A release should generate both rules from one source, or keep this differential in CI. [R]

docs.title: 4. Project floors: the database or the application
docs.text:
D22 lists five floor groups.

The execution plan's §2.13 now says five as well. It said "four groups" when this document was first drafted (M1, fixed on main in 2222116ea).

group floor where test no deployment secrets API_SECRET, API_SECRET_FILE refused at start application: only code sees the environment FLOOR-app-process [M] neither name can be a setting database: absent from config_setting, so a foreign key refuses any row naming them FLOOR-not-offered [M] no credential-like name can enter the catalogue, even through a migration database: config_setting_no_secret_names CHECK FLOOR-catalogue-no-secret-names [M] API3_SECURITY_ENABLE=false refused at start application FLOOR-app-process [M] no anonymous writes default roles only from denied, readable and status-only database: the catalogue floor checks owner values even when the policy is open, and checks operator defaults, pins and allowed lists FLOOR-anon-roles-owner, FLOOR-anon-roles-policy [M] TREATMENTS_AUTH not offered database: absent from the catalogue FLOOR-not-offered [M] network safety TRUST_PROXY a hop count or CIDR, never empty application: a listener property of the process (census row 5: never a tenant row) FLOOR-app-process [M] webhooks to public addresses only both. The database refuses non-https URLs, URLs with user-info, literal private, loopback, link-local, shared or multicast IPs, and local-only names. The application must check the resolved address at send time, which the database cannot see (DNS) FLOOR-webhook-public [M]; send-time check [R], not built connector endpoints only on driver-defined hosts database: a URL field marked hosts: driver accepts only the kind's driver_hosts FLOOR-connector-driver-hosts [M] BASE_URL derived from the slug database: absent from the catalogue. The derivation itself is application code (D10). FLOOR-not-offered [M] app settings stay private reading an app's settings record by identifier needs api:settings:admin application: a route check, with API3_SETTINGS_STRICT_READ_ENABLED absent from the catalogue FLOOR-app-settings-private, FLOOR-not-offered [M] data and log safety WRITE_VALIDATION at least log database (owner values, operator defaults, pins) and application (on the effective value, when no operator row exists) FLOOR-write-validation, MERGE-floor-on-effective [M] DEBUG_LOGGING off application: process-level; absent from the catalogue FLOOR-app-process, FLOOR-not-offered [M] IMPORT_CONFIG ignored, with a warning application FLOOR-app-process [M] permanent autoprune needs an explicit confirmation, with an export offered first both. The database refuses an API3_AUTOPRUNE_* value without confirmed_at and export_offered_at. The application must actually offer the export; the database can only see that one was recorded. FLOOR-autoprune-confirmation [M] (D22, alarm decision) alarm settings hidden until §7a's gate database: the owner listener has no write grant on tenant_alarm_thresholds, alarm keys are not owner-settable, and a CHECK forbids making them so FLOOR-alarms-hidden [M]

The rule behind the split [R]:

  • A floor goes in the database when it is a property of a row, so that no tool, script or future endpoint can store a row that breaks it. Each such check is in a trigger or CHECK that the application roles cannot alter: FLOOR-catalogue-readonly shows the catalogue is read-only to all three. [M]
  • A floor goes in the application when its input is something the database cannot see:
  • the process environment;
  • a DNS answer at send time;
  • whether the person was actually shown an export offer;
  • the merged value when no row exists.

docs.title: 5. Census §3a, row by row
docs.text:
# settings how the schema expresses it evidence 1 AUTH_DEFAULT_ROLES, TREATMENTS_AUTH AUTH_DEFAULT_ROLES is a role_list with floor {"allowed": ["denied","readable","status-only"]}. The catalogue ships it bounded within the floor. The operator may narrow it per deployment or per tenant. TREATMENTS_AUTH is absent. FLOOR-anon-roles-*, POLICY-bounded, POLICY-per-tenant-override [M] 2 API_SECRET, API_SECRET_FILE absent from the catalogue; refused at start FLOOR-not-offered, FLOOR-app-process [M] 3 IMPORT_CONFIG absent; warned and ignored at start same [M] 4 outbound endpoints Not scalar settings. They become tenant_integration records of kind webhook or cgm-connector (driver hosts only). The operator's switches are policy rows: INTEGRATION_MAX:<kind> (0 disables a kind; otherwise the per-tenant count) and the optional webhook allow-list INTEGRATION_HOSTS:webhook. BASE_URL is absent. FLOOR-webhook-public, FLOOR-connector-driver-hosts, INTEGRATION-kind-limits, POLICY-webhook-allowlist [M] 5 TRUST_PROXY absent from the catalogue; refused at start unless it is a hop count or CIDR FLOOR-app-process [M] 6 WRITE_VALIDATION an ordinal (off < log < reject) with floor {"min": "log"}. The catalogue ships bounded {"min": "log"}; an operator may raise the minimum, and the owner may tighten above it. FLOOR-write-validation, MERGE-floor-on-effective [M] 7 API3_SETTINGS_STRICT_READ_ENABLED absent; always on under multi, in code FLOOR-app-settings-private [M] 8 API3_SECURITY_ENABLE absent; refused at start if false FLOOR-app-process [M] 9 API3_AUTOPRUNE_* (six names, lib/server/env.js:286-293) Integers in days, floor {"min": 1}, needs_confirmation. The catalogue ships them pinned with no pin, so they are off until the operator writes a policy. The operator's minimum retention is the bounded constraint's min. Turning one on needs a fresh confirmation, also on rollback. FLOOR-autoprune-confirmation, POLICY-bounded, VERSION-rollback-needs-fresh-confirmation [M] 10 alarm thresholds and enables Hidden (see §4). BG_HIGH, BG_TARGET_TOP, BG_TARGET_BOTTOM and BG_LOW are operator-only integers in mg/dL, with floor {"min": 20, "max": 600}. ALARM_URGENT_HIGH, ALARM_HIGH, ALARM_LOW and ALARM_URGENT_LOW are operator-only booleans. The owner's own thresholds go in tenant_alarm_thresholds (§6) once the gate passes. FLOOR-alarms-hidden, MMOL-* [M] 11 plugin credentials Never in a settings row. Each kind names its credential parts. The owner's parts are referenced from tenant_integration.owner_secret_ref, and the operator's from deployment_integration.operator_secret_ref. The owner listener can see that the operator's part exists, not its reference. SECRETS-*, INTEGRATION-credential-parts [M] 12 DEBUG_LOGGING, DBSIZE_* absent; DEBUG_LOGGING refused at start FLOOR-not-offered, FLOOR-app-process [M]

Class D values (decided 2026-10-27). Deployment-level values live in each role's environment. This covers TRUST_PROXY, DEBUG_LOGGING, ports, storage URIs and the release-driven compatibility switches. None is in the catalogue, so the database refuses each of them as a deployment policy row or a per-tenant override. The lab's deploymentValues(env) reads them from the role's own environment, so two roles can differ. CLASSD-environment covers both halves. Its two controls add API_V3_DATA_WARNINGS to the catalogue, and make the roles ignore their environment. [M]

The eight names new on dev:

  • API_V3_DATA_WARNINGS, API_V1_COUNT_LEADING_NUMBER and API_V1_COUNT_ZERO_WINDOW are class D: environment variables of the role that reads them (CLASSD-environment). [M]
  • SHOW_SECONDS is open to the owner. [M]
  • The two CUSTOMCONNSTR_* spellings are absent. [R]

The lab's catalogue (0004) covers these rows plus SHOW_SECONDS and DISPLAY_UNITS. It does not cover the remaining class-T names. A release would generate the catalogue from the census (J7). [R]

docs.title: 6. Alarm thresholds and the §A.3 hazard
docs.text:
§A.2 drafted the thresholds as keys inside a JSON settings object, guarded by one CHECK. §A.3 predicted, from PostgreSQL's documentation, that a partial mmol override would pass that CHECK on SQL NULL. The lab applied §A.2's tenant_settings verbatim (old-shape/) and measured it (MMOL-old-shape-profile). [M]

input §A.2 draft this schema partial {"bgHigh": 14} accepted refused: all four are written together (and the columns are NOT NULL) complete mmol {3.1, 4.5, 10, 14} refused (23514) refused: not a whole mg/dL value; convert mmol/L at the write boundary integer mmol-looking {3, 5, 10, 14} refused refused: tenant_alarm_thresholds_plausible_mgdl misordered {80, 55, 180, 260} refused refused: tenant_alarm_thresholds_ordered. It is not rewritten (contrast BF-67). string {"x", 80, 180, 260} refused, 23514 (the read-derived cast error did not reproduce on this input) refused: must be a number valid {56, 81, 180, 252} accepted accepted, stored exactly

The draft's CHECK works when all four keys are present. It fails only on the NULL path. In this schema the NULL path does not exist, because each threshold is its own NOT NULL column. MMOL-stored-safely is green on the new shape. It goes red on the old shape, and red again when the new shape's range CHECK is dropped and the columns are made nullable. [M]

The write boundary is the application's. It converts mmol/L with dev's factor 18.01559 (lib/constants.json:10), stores mg/dL, keeps entered_units, and echoes the stored numbers back (§A.3 defence 2). The lab's thresholdsForStorage turns 3.1/4.5/10/14 mmol/L into 56/81/180/252. Its control skips the conversion, and the database then refuses the write (MMOL-converted-and-echoed). [M]

Refusing partial input follows J11's recommendation, and J11 is still open. A nullable-per-column variant would also refuse a lone mmol bgHigh on range. Its ordering could then only be checked after the merge, in code. [R]

docs.title: 7. Versions and rollback
docs.text:
Recording. cfg_apply takes a per-tenant transaction advisory lock, applies the changes, and appends version N+1 with the state after the change.

  • Two owner sessions saving at once get consecutive versions. Without the lock, the second fails with a duplicate version (VERSION-concurrent-writers). [M]
  • A deferred constraint trigger requires, at commit, that the tenant's live owner-scope state equals its newest version's state. A direct UPDATE, INSERT or DELETE that skips cfg_apply cannot commit (VERSION-unversioned-write-refused). [M]
  • Limit: this guard compares the live state with the version through the same cfg_current_state function. If that function were wrong, the guard would not notice; the test did (VERSION-numbered, control). [M]
  • Versions are append-only:
  • the owner listener has no UPDATE or DELETE grant;
  • a trigger refuses both, even to the owning migration role (VERSION-append-only);
  • the one exception is the cascade from deleting the tenant. [M]

Rollback. cfg_rollback(tenant, N) computes the changes that make the live state equal version N. It applies them through cfg_apply as a new version, with kind rollback and rollback_of N. Values, thresholds and integrations are all restored (VERSION-rollback-restores). [M]

Rollback against a policy that has changed since version N. Every restored row passes the same checks as a fresh write, against the current policy and floors.

  • Decided (maintainer, 2026-10-27; Q3). An owner's rollback to an earlier version is refused whole when the operator has since pinned or narrowed a setting that version used. The error names each blocked setting and the operator rule behind it. Nothing changes, and no version is written.
  • cfg_rollback pre-checks every value it would restore with the same function the write trigger uses (cfg_owner_value_error), and raises one error listing all of them.
  • Measured message, with one deployment pin and one per-tenant narrowing: rollback to version 1 refused; 2 setting(s) blocked: policy: AUTH_DEFAULT_ROLES = ["readable"] is outside the operator's constraint (override rule: bounded {"allowed": ["denied"]}); policy: SHOW_SECONDS is pinned by the operator (deployment rule: pinned to false).
  • The test is VERSION-rollback-vs-new-policy. Its two controls remove the checks, and report only the first blocked setting. [M]
  • The first round's lab stopped at the first blocked setting. That did not meet the decision, and is fixed.
  • Integration records restored by a rollback are still checked one at a time by their trigger, so a blocked integration is reported alone (Q13). [R]
  • A rollback to a version with permanent deletion turned on needs a fresh confirmation. The old confirmation is not part of the version state and is not carried forward (VERSION-rollback-needs-fresh-confirmation). [M]

What is versioned. Owner-scope state is versioned: owner values, thresholds and integration records. Integration status is not. Operator policy changes are not versioned here, so whether they need history is open (Q5). Saving a new version should invalidate the tenant's cached merge; how the hosted processes learn of that (D6's feed, or a version-number check) is not built here. [R]

docs.title: 8. Integrations and secret references
docs.text:
tenant_integration has these guarantees:

  • Settings are validated against the kind's schema: required fields, no unknown fields, enums, types, lengths and host rules (INTEGRATION-settings-schema). [M]
  • The operator controls which kinds are enabled and how many each tenant may have (INTEGRATION-kind-limits). [M]
  • A kind's owner credential parts require a reference. A kind with an operator part is refused until the operator has configured that part (INTEGRATION-credential-parts). [M]

No plaintext secret column anywhere (SECRETS-schema-scan). [M] The test scans information_schema and requires:

  • no column named like a credential, except *_ref and *_parts;
  • no bytea column;
  • that every *_ref column is guarded by the reference-format CHECK.

Three controls each add an offending column, and the test goes red each time. Two more checks close the gaps around the scan:

  • Settings cannot smuggle a credential. An unknown field such as password is refused, and no kind's schema may declare a credential-like field (SECRETS-not-in-settings). [M]
  • A pasted plaintext value in a reference column is refused by the format check (SECRETS-reference-format). [M]

The reference format sref:v1:<backend>:<opaque id> is a lab placeholder. The format CHECK catches accidents only: a plaintext value shaped like a reference would pass it. Whether a reference belongs to the tenant can only be checked by the secrets component, which holds the keys (D22: keys never leave it). [R]

docs.title: 9. RLS on every tenant-scoped table
docs.text:
Every tenant-scoped table has RLS enabled and forced, with the seam's predicate copied character for character: tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.current_tenant_id', true), '')::uuid, in both USING and WITH CHECK.

ISO-complete discovers tables by their tenant_id column, as the seam's tenantScopedTables does, and requires all three properties. Its control adds an unprotected table, and the test goes red. [M]

For each of the seven tables, the role bound to tenant A:

  • reads only A's rows;
  • reads nothing when unbound;
  • updates none of B's rows;
  • is refused (42501) when inserting a row for B.
table reader in the test cross-tenant insert attempted by tenant_members ns_api ns_tenant_admin tenant_policy_override ns_api ns_operator tenant_setting_value ns_api ns_tenant_admin tenant_alarm_thresholds ns_api ns_tenant_admin (with the post-gate grant) tenant_config_version ns_api ns_tenant_admin tenant_integration ns_api ns_tenant_admin tenant_integration_status ns_api ns_api

Each table has two controls, RLS disabled and the same reads done as the container superuser. All 14 go red. [M]

The operator writes per-tenant overrides with the tenant bound, which is J12's option 1 shape applied to a new table. J12 is still open. [R]

docs.title: 10. single mode
docs.text: Nothing changes. single reads the process environment, as today (D15, D1). It does not create or read these tables, does not run these migrations, and does not apply the floors above. The floors are multi-only (D22). The environment names keep their meaning, including CONNECT_*, BRIDGE_*, WEBHOOK_* and PUSHOVER_* as aliases (D22). The lab's settingsReadByIdPermission keeps dev's behaviour for single, and FLOOR-app-settings-private checks it. [M]

docs.title: 10a. Comparison with Nocturne
docs.text:
Nocturne at 42275c812 was read for comparison. [R]

  • Generic settings are rows keyed by tenant and key, with a value (SettingsEntity).
  • Thresholds are alert rules with JSON parameters (AlertRuleEntity.condition_params).
  • TenantAlertSettingsEntity holds a do-not-disturb schedule, not thresholds.
  • Connector configuration keeps its secret properties encrypted in a secrets JSON column on the same row (ConnectorConfigurationEntity.SecretsJson, AES-256-GCM per its comment).
  • Migrations are EF Core migrations, run at start under a dedicated migrator role, separate from the application role (DatabaseInitializationExtensions.cs:80-113).

The two designs agree in several places:

  • a generic key/value layer;
  • typed side-tables where constraints matter;
  • a migrator role separate from the application role.

They differ in one place. D22 moves secret material into a separate component, so this schema holds references only, where Nocturne keeps ciphertext beside the configuration it belongs to. That difference follows from D22's keys-stay decision. It is not a judgement on Nocturne's choice. [R]

docs.title: 10b. Mismatches found (stop-and-report)
docs.text:
These are inconsistencies between decisions, documents and code. None was resolved by this work. M1, M2, M4 and M5 were settled on 2026-10-27, as each entry says.

  • M1. (Fixed on main in 2222116ea.) The execution plan's §2.13 listed five floor groups but introduced them as "Decided as four groups". [R]
  • M2. (Settled 2026-10-27: provider and subject, both text, unique together, no foreign key. Migration 0002.) D17 as amended makes the identity provider interchangeable and tenant_members.subject_id the provider's subject, with no foreign key. Two places do not fit that:
  • On the seam (81a1f6ce), the column is uuid NOT NULL. A provider whose subjects are not UUIDs cannot be stored.
  • On seam/t30-schema-cred (65ce54b9), the column became text with a composite foreign key to tenant_subject, against "no foreign key".

The first round left tenant_members unchanged. [R] - M3. tenant_secret stores material bytea in the platform schema. It is drafted in config-surface §A.2 and §C.5 (J4) and built on 65ce54b9. D22's later decisions say keys never leave the secrets component. They do not say where the built-in signer keeps its encrypted keys. This schema holds references only, and SECRETS-schema-scan forbids bytea in it. If the built-in signer's store is to live in the same schema, that check needs a defined scope. [R] - M4. (Settled 2026-10-27: class D values live in the environment, so neither is a policy row.) Census §3a row 5 says TRUST_PROXY is "never a tenant row", and row 12 gives DEBUG_LOGGING no policy. The call-path lab's lib/policy.js models both as per-tenant pinned policy rows. That lab is evidence for the call path, not for the setting model, but the two disagree. [R] - M5. (Settled 2026-10-27: each role's environment; deployment_policy holds only tenant-facing defaults, modes and constraints; D15 reads as "no per-tenant configuration from the environment". The scope column and the deployment-scope row were removed.) Config-surface §B.3 says class D settings are read from process.env under multi, "as today". D22 and census §3a describe release-driven D names as "deployment values the operator pins", which is a policy row. D15 says env-sourced configuration must not reach the multi path. Where D values live under multi is therefore not stated consistently. The first round supported pinned deployment rows (scope = 'deployment'), and the process-level floors read the environment. [R] - M6. Config-surface §A.3 cites settings.js:290-296 and a bgHigh < 50 heuristic. Dev at db3b9e4e converts each threshold on its own when it is below 30 (lib/settings.js:292-305). The silent rewriter BF-67 is still present (lib/settings.js:311-334). The citations are stale, and the hazard remains. [R] - M7. The seam's comments say the connecting role must own the tables, or "a setup step run as a superuser would leave the policy quietly unenforced" (81a1f6ce:lib/storage/postgres-storage.js:290-293, lib/storage/ack-store.js:199-203). Measured here: with the tables owned by a separate non-superuser migration role, RLS is active for every non-owner application role (ISO-roles). FORCE matters only for the owner. [M] The danger the comment names is real only if the application itself connects as a superuser. This bears on who runs migrations (plan §4). - M8. The queue item's note says Nocturne's TenantAlertSettingsEntity is a typed side-table "where constraints matter". At 42275c812 it holds a do-not-disturb schedule; Nocturne's thresholds are JSON parameters on alert rules (§10a). [R]

docs.title: 11. Open questions for the maintainer
docs.text:
The lab made a working choice for each question below, so that it could run. Rows marked decided were answered by the maintainer on 2026-10-27. For the others, the working choice is not a decision.

# question lab's working choice Q1 Does an operator override replace the deployment row whole, or field by field? decided (2026-10-29): whole row. A later deployment change does not leak into overridden tenants Q2 When the operator has written no row, what applies? Is there a project-shipped default policy? the catalogue's shipped mode and constraint. Autoprune and alarm keys are pinned off, ordinary T settings open, contested rows bounded within the floor Q3 Rollback against a changed policy: refuse it whole, apply it partly with a report, or restore values the merge then ignores? decided: refused whole, naming each blocked setting and the operator rule behind it (§7) Q4 When an operator narrows or pins a setting, owners' stored values fall outside it. Who tells the owner, and how? D22's "review list, never dropped silently" covers migration only. the merge ignores and reports them; nothing tells the owner Q5 Are operator policy changes, at deployment and per tenant, versioned or audited? How do they invalidate tenants' caches? direction (2026-10-29): audited, by whichever of audit, invalidation and versioning each need calls for, but through one audit approach shared across the code base, not a second incompatible one. An inventory of the existing audit and history mechanisms comes first (see the note under this table); the lab's working shape is AFTER triggers writing append-only audit rows with the operator's identity from SET LOCAL, a policy generation number and pg_notify Q6 J11: refuse partial threshold input, or allow it per key with nullable typed columns? refuse partial (J11's recommendation) Q7 Threshold bounds: §A.2 uses 20 to 600 mg/dL. Dev now treats values below 30 as mmol/L. Which bounds, after clinical review? decided (maintainer, 2026-10-29): lower bound 30 mg/dL, aligned with dev's below-30-is-mmol/L rule. The maintainer's reasoning: 30 is far below Dexcom's mandatory urgent low of 55, Dexcom sensors report nothing below 40, and values below 39 are error and algorithm state codes. Upper bound 600 unchanged (not discussed) Q8 The secret-reference format, and how a reference is bound to its tenant. direction (2026-10-29): the secrets component enforces ownership (it stores each secret under tenant and id, and refuses to resolve a reference outside the calling tenant); the format and any database-side tenant check are decided with the secrets component design Q9 Where does the built-in signer keep encrypted keys: in this database (separate schema and role) or outside it? (M3) decided (2026-10-29): outside the database by default; an operator may keep them in the same database in a separate schema owned by a separate role no application role can read, documented as weaker, since every dump then carries the encrypted key material Q10 tenant_members.subject_id type and foreign key under D17 as amended (M2; J1, I.2) decided: provider and subject, both text, unique together, no foreign key (0002) Q11 Under multi, do class D values live in the environment or as pinned deployment rows? (M5) decided: each role's environment Q12 Export and deletion: which configuration tables are "tenant data" for tenantScopedTables and NOT_TENANT_DATA? Owner values, versions and integrations are the owner's.
