docs.title: Owner authority local-verification prototype
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-05 at f814f967c.

Contributor-facing synthetic lab for the adopted owner authority contract. The current lab imports the application's lib/tenant-authorization/access-token.js; local-token.js is a loader, not a second verifier implementation. The original prototype remains retrievable at the instrument commit in the immutable November 5 measurement. Application integration acceptance is recorded separately in the release integration record; no single-tenant default or legacy token changes are implied by this lab.

docs.title: Run and predicted outcome
docs.text:
Requires Docker, Node, and an existing CRM worktree with locked dependencies. Set CRM_WORKTREE to that worktree's absolute path. The source must still include the application access-token module, real secrets component/Transit adapter, PostgreSQL secrets/legacy/authority adapters and migration runner; missing or changed boundaries fail, never substitute. All dependencies/keys/data are synthetic, loopback-only and owned by the harness. Do not point this lab at an existing Vault or database. It creates/removes only its own randomly named disposable containers and prints no credentials or key bytes.

CRM_WORKTREE=/absolute/path/to/crm-worktree \
OWNER_AUTH_OUT=/tmp/owner-authority-results.json \
node tools/lab/owner-authority/harness.js

CRM_WORKTREE=/absolute/path/to/crm-worktree \
OWNER_AUTH_CONTROLS_OUT=/tmp/owner-authority-controls.json \
node tools/lab/owner-authority/controls.js

OWNER_AUTH_SAMPLES optionally changes samples per case (default 120). Two repeats reverse arm order; each measures read/write authorization at concurrency 1 and 8 using two independently pooled workers. Warmups are excluded. Request durations include pool wait, crypto, metadata and synchronous audit where used. This is authorization-pipeline throughput, not HTTP/data-write throughput.

Arm Measured operation current Actual verifyLegacyCredential with an HS256 JWT: current legacy metadata, root decrypt and Transit verify with real PostgreSQL synchronous audit. Actual shipping authorize; write also reads subjectSnapshot as data-access does. local-shipping-authority New-format local Ed25519 verifier, then the same actual shipping authority calls. Isolates authentication-path removal; this diagnostic arm lacks the combined candidate's session/key policy. local-combined Local verifier and one current tenant-bound SQL snapshot joining fixed provisioned roles, stable subject and candidate session/tenant/key/generation state. Includes write attribution.

Predicted call counts per operation: current has two Transit calls, two durable secret-audit insertions, two legacy metadata reads and one authority snapshot for read/two for write; local-shipping has no Transit/secret-audit/metadata calls and the same authority snapshots; local-combined has no Transit/secret-audit/metadata calls and one combined snapshot. These are instrumented logical calls, not wire round trips: the existing tenant transaction foundation uses BEGIN, set_config, SELECT and COMMIT. Management mutation/audit remains outside this benchmark.

docs.title: Owner subject-policy evidence instrument
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-06 at 9ae6381b7.

This additive lab archives an exact cgm-remote-monitor commit and runs its actual subject-policy tests. It never checks out or mutates another worktree. Source, dependencies and a writable scratch root must be explicit. Use a scratch root on a filesystem with capacity; this lab does not assume /tmp is available.

node tools/lab/owner-subject-policy/archive.js \
  --repository "$CRM_REPOSITORY" --dependencies "$CRM_DEPENDENCIES" \
  --ref "$CRM_COMMIT" --scratch-root "$OWNER_SCRATCH"

The default runs the pure catalogue/Shiro tests without services. Add --database only after the shared test coordinator grants capacity. The database suite creates its own synthetic PostgreSQL service, records its returned container and volume identities, uses private roles, removes that exact service and its volumes, and checks cleanup. It covers the selected existing subject-management update path; it does not implement an owner login, issuer, listener or complete role platform.

--control universe replaces closed-universe membership with the prior literal shape check in scratch and selects the namespace-prefix rejection test. Predicted result: one missing expected TypeError. A successful instrument control exits zero only after verifying the underlying test failed for its intended assertion.

With --database, --control catalogue, ceiling, delegation or actor removes one source guard only in scratch and selects its independently bounded HTTP test. Predicted result: one assertion sees an unauthorized HTTP 200 instead of 403. The instrument accepts a control only for that semantic failure. A timeout, hook failure, service setup error, pending test or unrelated assertion is invalid. The original guard must pass again on a fresh restored archive.

The reviewed permission universe bounds the current REST surface. Shiro literals still imply descendants outside it. Adding new authorization operations requires reviewing the universe and implication tests; this lab does not prove arbitrary wildcard/default semantics, complete owner management, throughput or deployment readiness. docs.title: Optional nested-container audit
docs.text:
docker-audit.js can be symlinked as docker in a private per-campaign PATH folder. Set NS_OWNER_DOCKER_REAL to the absolute real Docker executable and NS_OWNER_DOCKER_AUDIT to a fresh private 0700 directory. The helper stores only returned full container IDs, volume names and cleanup state in 0600 files, before subsequent inspections can fail. It augments supported top-level rm calls only when every current target ID is in that campaign's records, then removes by those immutable IDs. A reused container name cannot redirect augmented removal.

Unsupported commands/flags and unknown/mixed targets pass through unchanged. This is scoped test instrumentation, not a general Docker permission boundary. The extra --volumes flag removes anonymous volumes; Docker preserves named volumes (Docker CLI contract). It never issues a direct volume delete or global prune. Recorded removal success is not proof of volume absence; the campaign must inspect the recorded IDs after cleanup. Nonzero create/run outcomes without a returned ID cannot establish ownership and are not claimed leak-free. Detached successful test services are the supported creation path. A failed audit triggers exact-ID compensation; failed compensation retains and reports the returned ID for private recovery.

Pure/fake-process checks run with node docker-audit.test.js; child-process execution must be permitted. Fake checks do not start Docker or establish real Docker behavior. Runtime smoke must wait for the coordinator's explicit slot.

docs.title: Capability boundary reproduced
docs.text:
The actual lib/import/entries.js API importer accepts only nonempty textual _id values. A raw ObjectId is IMPORT_DOCUMENT_INVALID; ObjectId/string twins exposed as the same API string produce IMPORT_ID_COLLISION before the first page write. This is fail-closed behavior, not typed import fidelity. The lower-port lib/storage/postgres-identity.js codec preserves kind outside JSONB, and its actual encode/decode functions distinguish the twins across JSON serialization.

Therefore an API JSON export/import cannot be assumed to preserve a complete typed Mongo snapshot. Do not flatten IDs, rewrite the importer or claim typed restore from its string-only success. The existing importer is a bounded, one-time live baseline plus best-effort history pass, not a snapshot: moving offset boundaries and permanent deletions remain explicit limitations. Each target page has its own transaction; a failed later page does not imply rollback of earlier pages. Rerun starts at the beginning; no durable cursor is implemented.

The migration runner provides catalogue validation, checksums and transactional ledger foundations. Its Mongo primary-restart test is same-server recovery; it has no exported-volume restore. The older execution-plan reference to lib/admin/platform-store.js is absent from the frozen CRM tree used here; that historical export path must be located and reconciled before using it as an instrument for current implementation acceptance. It has no import counterpart in the execution plan. No replacement export service is invented here.

docs.title: Current-dev PostgreSQL transaction-pool proof
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-02 at f214b7dab.

Run from the alignment repository with Docker available and the local externals/work/crm-multitenant-20261102 dependencies installed:

node tools/lab/postgres-foundation/harness.js

WORKTREE can select another owned integration worktree relative to the alignment root. The lab uses the actual postgres-connection.js, the committed generated entries DDL, pinned local images, synthetic documents and a random isolated Docker network. It publishes only dynamic loopback ports. Credentials are generated into a private temporary directory, never printed, and removed with only the lab's own containers/network on completion.

Two independent application clients share exactly one PgBouncer backend in transaction mode, without automatic per-transaction session reset. Checks cover reads/writes, rollback, binding cleanup and generated-column handling of dirty/missing/null fields. Controls disable RLS, grant BYPASSRLS and mutate the actual connection module's binding to session-local in memory (no source-file edits). The latter must leak a tenant to an unbound second client.

Nonzero exit means failure. Successful JSON is sanitized evidence, not production acceptance. This exercises the existing DDL but does not refresh its historical index catalogue, build the migration runner or implement the entries adapter. The generated DDL still needs current v3/history/identifier-index reconciliation.

The same run also exercises the opt-in typed-key candidate generated with:

python -m tools.nsschema.emit.postgres_emit --collection entries --identity-kinds \
  --out tools/lab/postgres-foundation/generated

Four identityChecks use the actual integration worktree's identity codec. id_kind is separate storage metadata; it never becomes a client field. The key is (tenant_id, id_kind, _id), so ObjectId, lower/upper-case strings and custom string ids remain distinguishable. A kind-scoped delete preserves the other kind and the other tenant. Invalid kinds/encodings refuse; mutating the codec to flatten kinds recreates the key collision. This is not a complete adapter or import/round-trip proof for arbitrary BSON values.

The report's adapterBlockers are unsatisfied M1 properties, not passing adapter acceptance. The probe demonstrates that normal JSON serialization collapses an ObjectId and the same-spelling string into one primary key; raw Extended JSON fails the generated string-only _id constraint instead. It also checks the actual emitted index inventory for missing current v3/identifier requirements. These findings require a lossless identity representation and operator-managed migrations before adapter promotion. The typed candidate discharges the narrow identity representation proof, not those broader gates.

docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-02 at 79cbc140c.

Measures how Nightscout (cgm-remote-monitor) resolves the client address (lib/server/client-ip.js / getRemoteIP) and how the failed-login delay (lib/authorization/delaylist.js) behaves, behind real proxy software and real sockets, under each TRUST_PROXY setting. Built for PR nightscout/cgm-remote-monitor#8754 (branch bf2/auth-hardening).

All numbers here were reproduced live on 2026-09-24 against:

tree branch SHA dev baseline dev f1591069 PR (TRUST_PROXY) bf2/auth-hardening 81623f9b (PR head 280eccbe is this + a dev merge; lib/server/client-ip.js is byte-identical) delay-order revert (O4b; O2 across all header families) bf2/auth-delay-dev-order f6f361b1 (lib/server/client-ip.js identical to 81623f9b and unchanged at 607d51b0)

docs.title: What TRUST_PROXY does (from the code under test)
docs.text:
lib/server/client-ip.js compiles TRUST_PROXY into how the address is resolved:

  • unset / empty (default = compatibility): address comes from the forwarded-for npm package exactly as dev does today. It reads several header families and takes the left-most entry. This is header-derived with no proxy trust boundary.
  • false: socket peer only (ignores all forwarding headers).
  • integer n: Express hop count — trust the n proxies closest to Nightscout; the address is the entry the n-th proxy saw.
  • IP / CIDR list: proxy-addr, trusting only those proxy addresses.
  • true: Express trust-all — the left-most entry.

The failed-auth delay keys on the resolved address and on a salted hash of the credential (AUTH_FAIL_DELAY ms, default 5000). It is therefore only as good as the address, which is only as good as TRUST_PROXY.

docs.title: proxy-trust lab: auth_request chain (AR) topologies
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-02 at 79cbc140c.

Add-on to this lab (lab.sh, run_matrix.sh). It does not modify either file. It covers a shape the F/TLS/L-B topologies do not: a multi-tenant hosted platform where nginx picks the next hop for each request from an auth_request subrequest, several times in a row. The shape looks like this:

client ─► L4 LB ──PROXY protocol──► GATEWAY ──► ROUTER ──► TENANT ROUTER ──► Nightscout
          (TCP)                     auth_request auth_request auth_request
                                    name→origin  name→tenant  tenant→host:port

This add-on follows the disclosure rule in README.md: mechanism, not recipe.

docs.title: Why this shape needs its own cells
docs.text:
• The hop count changes with the route. The gateway's authorizer returns the upstream origin, so one gateway can send one public name through a second router (3 HTTP hops to Nightscout) and another name straight to the tenant router (2 hops). A single TRUST_PROXY value has to be right for every route that reaches the same Nightscout.
  • The edge overwrites X-Forwarded-For. It does not append. The gateway sets X-Forwarded-For $proxy_protocol_addr and does not use real_ip. Every other lab topology appends.
  • The last hop does not set X-Forwarded-Proto. The tenant router leaves it out, so the scheme Nightscout sees is whatever the first HTTP hop wrote.
  • The backend comes from a variable. It is a header from the subrequest (proxy_pass $tenant$request_uri), so the routing itself is part of what is being tested.

docs.title: proxy-trust lab: socket.io (WebSocket) cells on the AR chain
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-02 at 79cbc140c.

This is an add-on to ar_chain.sh. The only change to existing lab files is a source guard in ar_chain.sh (AR_SOURCED=1), so this runner can reuse the AR containers and ar_up.

It fills a gap listed under "Not covered" in README-ar-chain.md: WebSocket upgrades.

This add-on follows the disclosure rule in README.md: mechanism, not recipe.

docs.title: Why sockets need their own cells
docs.text:
Nightscout's socket server resolves the client address of socket.request, the socket.io handshake request. It uses the same helper as HTTP: forwarded-for on 15.0.x and dev, and lib/server/client-ip.js on #8754. A socket authorize event with a wrong secret goes through authorization.resolve(). That makes it subject to the same failed-auth delay as HTTP, and it produces the same admin-notify that the lab reads back. Three things could still differ from HTTP:

  • The handshake request depends on the transport.
  • With polling then websocket (socket.io's default, used by native clients), it is the first long-poll GET.
  • The Nightscout web client never upgrades. lib/client/index.js connects both the main and the /alarm namespaces with transports: ["polling"] (15.0.5 through dev 7000eb18). So every browser socket, including alarm acks, is a series of HTTP long-polls through every hop. The polling cells in W1, W2 and W3 are the browser's case.
  • With websocket alone, it is the Upgrade request.
  • A hop can pass HTTP but break the upgrade. It might drop Upgrade or Connection, or not speak HTTP/1.1 upstream. When that happens, the client quietly stays on polling. Any "the socket path is fine" result then describes polling, not WebSocket.
  • Upgraded and long-poll connections stay open. Hop timeouts that are harmless for REST requests can cut them off.

docs.title: rc-soak: A/B soak harness for a Nightscout release candidate
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-09-27 at 7081a144c.

Contributor-facing. Synthetic data only: never point this at a real site. Nothing here is medical advice.

The harness runs two copies of Nightscout (cgm-remote-monitor) side by side, arm A and arm B, each with its own server process and its own MongoDB container, and sends both the same synthetic traffic at the same moment. It then checks that both arms stayed up, answered the same way (except where the release notes say they should differ), stored the same records, and did not grow in memory or slow down. The usual pairing is A = the shipping release, B = the release candidate.

file what it does lab.sh starts and stops everything, runs a proof or a long soak, records every PID it starts traffic.js the synthetic household: CGM uploader, Loop / Trio, AndroidAPS (API v3), followers, a web page over socket.io, edits and deletes sampler.js every 10 s (60 s real-time): is each server alive, answering, and serving the newest reading; RSS, open files, document counts from MongoDB preload.js loaded into each server with NODE_OPTIONS=--require (the build is not modified): heap, RSS, event-loop delay every 10 s proxy.js fault injection only: a proxy that silently drops a fraction of devicestatus uploads fake-apns.js a local stand-in for Apple's push service, one per arm, counting the HTTP/2 sessions each server leaves open analyze.js turns a run directory into a verdict: PASS, FAIL (findings) or INVALID probe-deleted-entry.js a one-shot check against one server: is a reading deleted by _id still returned by GET /api/v1/entries.json?count=10? probe-v3-late-mills.js BF-146: boots a tree's server on its own test database; do a bolus, carbs and a device status written through API v3 with a time in the past count in IOB and COB and take their place in GET /api/v1/devicestatus.json, as v1 writes do? expected-diffs.json the differences 15.0.9 makes on purpose, each tied to a release-notes section; thresholds

traffic.js, sampler.js, proxy.js and analyze.js adapt the connector soak lab (tools/lab/connector-soak/: writer, sampler, proxy, analyser, disturbances). The request shapes follow the client surveys in tools/lab/object-id/probes.js and reports/consumer-impact-15.0.9/lab-results.md.

docs.title: What this run adds over run 022
docs.text:
Run 022 (proof-2026-10-07-run022.md) proved official/dev at 43289dde. Since then the 15.0.9 release head has advanced by one merge to fade2299 = 43289dde + PR #8807 (BF-168, the context-chart brush-extent fix). git diff 43289dde fade2299 is exactly three files, all client/test, zero server/API code:

  • lib/client/chart.js (+8): the d3 brushX now declares an explicit .extent() (the context chart's own width and height), instead of letting d3 read the <svg> element's own size, which is the browser default 300×150 when the chart is drawn before layout settles; and chart.update() re-reads the extent and rebinds the brush overlay so the context window can still be dragged back to "now" after a resize.
  • tests/dependency-d3.test.js (+23): two new it cases, parametrised over mouse and touch, drags the context window back to now after the chart was drawn before layout, using <input>.
  • tests/fixtures/d3-chart.js (+17/−4): the fixture gains an optional layout argument; with layout undefined it behaves exactly as before.

package.json and package-lock.json are byte-identical between the two heads (package.json sha256 c0b31562…, package-lock.json sha256 9a5f616c…), so dependencies and audit do not change. git diff 43289dde fade2299 -- lib/ app.js server.js bin is only lib/client/chart.js; with that path excluded the server-side diff is empty — the server tree is byte-identical to 43289dde on every non-chart path. The A/B soak is API-level traffic and cannot reach client chart code.

lib/client/chart.js is required by lib/client/index.js, the client webpack entry, so the served browser bundle differs from run 022 (not claimed byte-identical). The server-side mocha suite requires lib/client/chart.js directly through tests/fixtures/d3-chart.js (line 33), so bundle state does not affect the suite result.

docs.title: 8807 changes only lib/client/chart.js and its tests; it is client-only, so the A/B soak
docs.text:
cannot reach it and the A/B verdict is unchanged from run 022. The fix is covered where it lives:

  • On any head before #8807 (15.0.8 and 43289dde included), d3's brushX with no explicit .extent() reads the context <svg>'s own width and height. When the chart is first drawn before the browser has laid the page out, that size is the SVG default 300×150, so the brush's draggable area is clamped to the stale 300-pixel width and the context window cannot be dragged all the way back to "now" after the chart is later resized. #8807 declares the extent from the chart's own scale and height, and has chart.update() re-read it and rebind the overlay, so the window drags to now regardless of draw order. This is a display-only fix in the secondary-display chart; it does not change any stored data or any API reply.
  • It is live on 15.0.8 too, so this file states the mechanism only, not a reproduction recipe.
  • It is covered by the two new tests/dependency-d3.test.js cases (mouse and touch), green in every suite cell: the fixture draws the chart before layout and the test asserts the dragged window reaches now — red without #8807's change, green with it.
  • The gate section above records that lib/client/chart.js has entered the browser hand-check surface, so a chart-drag hand check at fade2299 is owed.

docs.title: record-identity lab
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-18 at 0e70c2a81.

What each cgm-remote-monitor path does with a client-sent _id and identifier: v1 POST, PUT, GET and DELETE, API v3 POST, GET, PUT and DELETE, and the socket's dbAdd, dbUpdate and dbRemove, for entries, treatments, devicestatus, profile and food, against several refs side by side. It records the HTTP status, the reply's _id, and what is stored, read from mongo (how many copies, and whether _id is an ObjectId or a string). Built for the record identity reference (queue item DOCS-RECORD-IDENTITY). Same harness as v3-identifier-immutable.

Contributor-facing. Synthetic data only: the lab writes its own records and must never be pointed at a real site.

Latest results: results/record-identity-2026-10-18.md.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
tools/lab/record-identity/lab.sh up     # mongo:7 in docker on 127.0.0.1:27184; archive and start each ref
tools/lab/record-identity/lab.sh run    # probes.js against each build, then one table
tools/lab/record-identity/lab.sh down   # stop the builds, remove the container
variable default meaning RID_BUILDS 1508=15.0.8:3983 dev=fade2299:3984 NAME=REF:PORT, space separated RID_REPO externals/cgm-remote-monitor-official the clone each ref is git archived from (read only) RID_NM_<NAME> unset a node_modules installed from the same package-lock.json, symlinked instead of npm ci RID_STATE $TMPDIR/record-identity archived builds, server logs, per-build JSON, the generated API secret RID_MONGO_PORT 27184 host port for the lab's mongod RID_MONGO_IMAGE mongo:7 RID_NODE node the Node binary that runs the servers and probes

The API secret is generated per lab into $RID_STATE/secret; nothing secret lives in this directory. Each build gets its own database, ridlab_<NAME>, dropped by up. Every case uses fresh ids and its own minute, so run can be repeated without up. The probes need mongodb, uuid and socket.io-client from the build's own node_modules.

build what head /api/v3/version 1508 15.0.8, the shipping release 92d08342 15.0.8, apiVersion 3.0.5 dev official/dev fade2299 15.0.9 (package version on dev), apiVersion 3.0.5

MongoDB: dedicated container ridlab-mongo, mongo:7, server version read back 7.0.43. Node 22.23.2. UUID_HANDLING unset (default on). v1 calls carry the api-secret hash, v3 calls a JWT for an admin subject the probe creates, the socket authorizes with the hash. The probes were run four times (three against one pair of servers, one after a fresh up); every cell was the same each time, except the order of two records in one cell, which the probe now sorts, and the treatments GET row, whose case-sensitivity probes were corrected before the fourth run.

How to read a cell: HTTP status (and the MongoDB cause when the reply body names one), then what is stored, read from mongo: n= copies, each with _id:oid (an ObjectId) or _id:string, =sent / ≠sent against the _id the client sent, and identifier=X when it equals the value the case sent as identifier (or as _id, for the cases that test UUID_HANDLING). reply says whether the reply item's _id is the one sent, the one stored, both, or absent. Times are one minute apart per case, 1 to 2 days back.

docs.title: stpa-diagrams — which tools can draw STPA control structures
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-16 at 16a87d452.

Contributor-facing. A feasibility lab: the same three generic structures drawn by every candidate tool and measured, so the choice of diagram tool for the STPA, hub-and-spoke and governance views rests on measured layouts rather than on reading each tool's documentation.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• inputs/*.yaml: three tool-neutral structures, all generic:
  • aid-loop: an AID control loop (person, controller app, pump, CGM, the body, disturbances).
  • hub-spoke: a Nightscout hub with uploaders, followers and remote commands down a push path.
  • governance: a two-column (development / operations) sociotechnical control structure, from open-source projects through a shared commons and companies to regulators and governments.

Each input gives every node a level (0 = top) and a column (left-to-right lane), and every edge a kind (control, feedback, data, disturbance). Its mutation is one extra feedback edge, used to measure how far the layout moves when the diagram changes. - gen.py emits, per input, one source per variant, using the layout hints each tool offers:

variant tool hints used dot-spline, dot-ortho Graphviz dot rank=same per level, invisible edges for column order, dir=back for upward edges, compass ports to put control left and feedback right d2-dagre, d2-elk D2 declaration order, containers for groups (no rank or port hints exist) d2-grid D2 grid layout one cell per (level, column); containers dropped mermaid-dagre, mermaid-elk Mermaid flowchart declaration order, subgraphs for groups plantuml PlantUML (on Graphviz) -down->/-up-> arrows, hidden right links for column order, packages for groups control-grid none (positive control) every node at its exact (column, level); loop pairs offset left/right control-random none (negative control) seeded random positions, straight edges, one forced node overlap - lab.sh renders every variant for the base and mutated inputs. Mermaid is rendered by mermaid-render.js inside Chrome, as the docs site renders it, with the ELK layout registered. - measure.js loads each SVG in Chrome, reads node boxes and sampled edge paths in screen coordinates, and scores them against the model (report.py builds results/metrics.md; the column meanings are at its top). A variant whose nodes or edges cannot all be identified is reported as not scored rather than scored on partial geometry. - sheet.js writes the contact sheets in results/sheets/. 
PYTHON=/path/to/python-with-pyyaml ./lab.sh     # render + measure, prints results/metrics.md
NODE_PATH=.tools/node/node_modules node sheet.js results/build "$(command -v google-chrome)" results/sheets

docs.title: stpa-grid-style — drawing control structures in Leveson's style
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-17 at 7ac473fce.

Contributor-facing. A styling lab, dated 2026-10-17. The published control-structure drawings (tools/structure-diagrams/render.py, Graphviz dot with splines) were judged "lots of elbows crossing each other, and hard to follow". This lab asks which way of drawing the same YAML inputs gets closest to the classic STPA control-structure figures, and measures the answer. It changes the visual form only: every candidate draws the same nodes, edges and labels from the same inputs. Nothing here replaces render.py or the published SVGs; the integrating session decides that.

docs.title: The conventions being aimed at
docs.text:
These are the visual conventions of the control-structure figures in Nancy Leveson's Engineering a Safer World (2011) and the STPA Handbook (Leveson and Thomas, 2018), described from memory in our own words. No figure is reproduced.

Confident (they define the notation and recur across the published figures):

  1. Vertical axis means authority. Controllers sit above what they control. Control actions are drawn going down, feedback going up. Position on the page carries meaning.
  2. One loop, two lines. A controller and its controlled process are joined by a pair of arrows: control action down on the left, feedback up on the right, as two separate parallel lines rather than one double-headed line.
  3. Straight, orthogonal lines. Lines are vertical or horizontal, with right-angle corners where a corner is needed. Curves are not used.
  4. Labels beside the line, not on it. The text naming a control action or feedback sits next to its arrow (control text on the outer left side, feedback text on the outer right side of a pair) and does not cut through any line.
  5. Plain rectangles, plain text. Boxes are simple rectangles with short names. Colour carries no meaning in the originals (the colours in this repo's drawings are a local addition).
  6. The two-column sociotechnical form. The generic safety control structure has system development on the left and system operations on the right, each a column of levels from legislatures down through regulators, company management and project or operations management, to the operating process at the bottom, with a few links between the columns.

Inferred (consistent with the figures as remembered, but not a stated rule we can cite):

  1. Grid alignment. Boxes on one level share a baseline, and boxes in one column share a centre line, so most connections are single straight verticals.
  2. Horizontal bands between levels. The sociotechnical figures read as layers (government, regulators, companies, operations, physical process), which suggests horizontal boundaries for legal, organisational and technical regions. The originals separate levels by placement; whether they draw explicit bands or rules is not something we can confirm from memory. Here bands are an optional extra (bands: below), off unless an input asks for them.
  3. Few bends, and crossings avoided or made deliberate. Long links between distant boxes run round the outside rather than through the middle; where a crossing is unavoidable it is a plain right-angle crossing, not an oblique tangle.

The measurements below are chosen to test exactly these: bends, the axis-aligned share of line length, crossings, label text over lines, loop pairs drawn straight and parallel, and grid alignment of node centres.

docs.title: Focused tenant backup/upgrade PostgreSQL proof
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-06 at fbf184322.

This lab runs the application's explicit five-case PostgreSQL suite against an owned disposable PostgreSQL 16 fixture, then semantic mutants and restorations. It archives the selected committed application source into scratch and uses an explicit private dependency copy whose recorded source lock must match.

A coordinator runtime grant is required. --grant records its reference; it does not obtain a slot. No serving listeners, Vault, MongoDB, full suite, browser or corpus campaign runs here. Representative entries/clock evidence does not establish full Batch C inventory, durable backup storage or provider-key recovery.

python tools/lab/tenant-backup-upgrade/run.py \
  --worktree "$CRM_WORKTREE" --deps "$PRIVATE_NODE_MODULES" \
  --out "$NEW_CAPTURE_DIRECTORY" --grant "$COORDINATOR_GRANT"

Before running, copy the exact source package-lock.json into private node_modules as .codex-source-package-lock.json. No dependency install or application pool is used. The local postgres:16 image must already exist; pulling is disabled. Fixture credentials are random, passed through the child environment and never recorded.

Every invocation captures a JSON reporter result, stderr, resource audit, source archive and semantic patch metadata. Exact owned containers and their observed anonymous volumes must be physically absent; the independent Docker inventory must return to baseline. Emergency cleanup is restricted to a recorded exact container ID and invalidates acceptance. No unrelated resource is removed.

Predictions: initial five cases green; four semantic mutations each produce one assertion failure (not an SQL/setup/timeout error), then the corresponding restored test passes. Final five-case restoration must be green with zero pending.

Control Required red symptom Disable artifact file-digest check Damaged artifact loses the prewrite RESTORE_DIGEST_MISMATCH refusal Disable restored-row comparison Lying successful insert no longer raises RESTORE_ORACLE_MISMATCH Substitute COMMIT for ROLLBACK Interrupted restore leaves rows visible to independent raw SQL Suppress independent comparison differences Self-consistent lost tenant-B entries are no longer named

--stages initial, --stages controls or --stages restored limits an invocation to an explicitly selected stage after a stopped run or focused repair. Existing capture directories are refused. Unexpected outcomes stop the campaign and retain raw failed history; repairs require a new committed source head and new capture. manifest.json and sha256.json freeze attribution and artifact hashes. No disabled suite, registered case or fake-client result counts as native evidence.

docs.title: Recovery scope
docs.text: The representative native proof records the executed entries/clock boundary. Apply the restore identity and cloning decision: this laboratory exercises original-tenant recovery. Cloning implementation/native acceptance, the full selected catalogue and durable backup storage remain unmeasured.

docs.title: Tenant cell + SQLite lab
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-02 at 3d6d68bb0.

Synthetic data only. Runs real celld v0.6.3, not an actor mock or an in-memory SQLite substitute. Each authenticated fixture tenant is routed to a Durable Object with its own SQLite database. SQLite is the sole record authority: no MongoDB/PostgreSQL record copy or cross-system commit is involved.

This is a storage feasibility experiment, not a Nightscout storage adapter, API, deployment recipe, authentication system or third supported backend. The tiny /lab/ protocol intentionally differs from NS and must not serve real records. The shared-cell flag exists only to make the isolation test fail.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
Requires Linux, Node 22+ and the pinned celld binary. No npm dependencies, bundler, Docker, credentials or cloud bucket are needed. Download and verify celld using the project's release attestation:

mkdir -p /tmp/ns-celld-063
gh release download v0.6.3 --repo denoland/celld \
  --pattern celld-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.gz --dir /tmp/ns-celld-063
gh attestation verify /tmp/ns-celld-063/celld-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.gz \
  --repo denoland/celld
gzip -dk /tmp/ns-celld-063/celld-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.gz
chmod u+x /tmp/ns-celld-063/celld-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
CELLD_BIN=/tmp/ns-celld-063/celld-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu \
  node tools/lab/tenant-cell-sqlite/run.mjs

Use a new empty download directory if that path already exists. The measured compressed asset SHA-256 is 5084a083472cf036551a7eac63fa24d22bb9a56323c517f63205724c12783047; the executable and source hashes are in results/local.json.

The runner creates uniquely named .runs/ projects with generated synthetic principal bindings. Public and operator listeners bind to loopback. It waits for HTTP readiness, stops its own process trees, and retains local state and logs for diagnosis. .runs/ is ignored; the compact measured report is tracked as results/local.json and overwritten on the next run. Do not copy real dotenv files into a fixture project. Do not run celld dev directly on this directory: bindings are supplied by the runner, not the template config.

docs.title: Tenant-configuration call-path lab
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-06 at 773c8bc59.

Contributor-facing. Lab approved by the maintainer on 2026-10-27 to inform the open question in execution plan §2.13 (D22, "Not decided"): how does a hosted owner dashboard reach the tenant-owner listener? The lab informs that decision. It does not make it. Synthetic tenants, owners and credentials only.

Marks: [M] means the lab measured it, in the run recorded in results.json. [R] means it is reasoned from the code or the design documents and was not measured.

docs.title: What it compares
docs.text:
A tenant is one Nightscout site on a shared host. Its owner is the person whose site it is. The operator runs the host.

design how an owner's edit travels A, owner token end to end The dashboard logs the owner in at the identity provider, then trades that login for an owner token: a short-lived token signed with that tenant's own key (D14). Nightscout mints it after checking the login (D17). The dashboard sends the edit straight to the tenant-owner listener (ns-tenant-admin, D16) with that token. B0, trusted orchestrator, no identity The dashboard forwards the owner's login to an internal orchestrator. The orchestrator checks ownership itself, then writes the tenant's configuration through an internal API. Internal calls carry no identity and name the site in the URL. B1, trusted orchestrator, service tokens As B0, but every internal call carries a service token (a credential that names a component, not a person): dashboard to orchestrator, operator console to orchestrator, orchestrator to listener and to the secrets service. C, split by audience Owner edits travel as in A. Provisioning and suspension go through an orchestrator that lives only on the operator plane (D7) and that the dashboard cannot reach. AK, A with keys kept in the secrets service ("A-keys-stay", added 2026-10-27) As A, but tenant signing keys never leave the secrets service. The token exchange asks the secrets service to sign; the listener asks it to verify each token. The secrets service takes the tenant from the address, sets the claims and the token lifetime itself, and refuses to hand a signing key to anyone.

docs.title: Tenant configuration schema lab (T30-SCHEMA-CONFIG)
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-27 at 1670247de.

Contributor-facing. Built 2026-10-27 to support the tenant configuration schema spec (queue T30-SCHEMA-CONFIG) and the migration-tooling plan. It uses synthetic tenants, hosts and credential references only. No real data and no real credentials are involved.

Marks: [M] means this lab measured it, in the run recorded in results.json. [R] means it is read or reasoned, not measured.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The lab has three parts:

  • The schema, as eight ordered migrations in migrations/, each with a .down.sql.
  • 0001 is the seam's lib/admin/platform.sql from cgm-remote-monitor 81a1f6ce, byte-identical below a three-line header. It has the same sha256, b50efaf0…, as git show 81a1f6ce:lib/admin/platform.sql.
  • 0002 changes tenant_members so that a person is identified by identity provider and subject, as text, unique together within a tenant, with no foreign key (maintainer, 2026-10-27). It refuses to run while the table holds rows, because nothing records which provider issued them.
  • 0003 to 0008 add the configuration tables without altering tenants. They were 0002 to 0007 in the first run, renumbered before anything shipped.
  • A runner, lib/migrator.js, which drives the migrations through umzug 3.8.3. It adds the three things umzug leaves to its caller: one transaction per migration and its ledger row, an advisory lock, and a checksum drift check.
  • A harness, harness.js, with 59 tests. Each test runs twice on a fresh database cloned from a migrated template:
  • the pass run must be green;
  • each control removes the protection under test, and the same test must then go red.

A control that stays green is reported as VACUOUS?, and the harness exits non-zero. A control whose setup fails is reported as a setup error and never counted red. (Run 3 of this lab found one such control, whose SQL still named a dropped column. Raw tests, which set up inside run, are not covered by that guard; their assertions match specific messages instead.) - A tool comparison, compare.js, which measures umzug against node-pg-migrate on PostgreSQL, and umzug (with a project ledger and lease lock, lib/mongo-migrator.js) against migrate-mongo on MongoDB, for the same five properties. Results are in compare-results.json; the side-by-side table is in the migration-tooling plan §3. - MIG-VV, mig-vv.js, which repeats the MongoDB rows on four servers: - MongoDB 8.0 standalone and as a three-member replica set; - MongoDB 5.0.32 (dev's floor) standalone and as a replica set.

It adds a primary step-down during a migration, and the adapter running a migration and its ledger record in one transaction (--txn 1). Results are in mig-vv-results.json; the table is in the plan's MIG-VV section. Each replica set is one container running three mongod processes on the host network, bound to 127.0.0.1 (mongo-rs/start-rs.sh).

docs.title: Tenant export/import fidelity and deletion: early Batch C proof
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-11-06 at fbf184322.

Contributor-facing research instrument, 2026-11-06. This is the Batch C early proof the completion plan names in its "Populated restore/import and contention" row and the roadmap's M6 packet row C8. It builds beside, not inside, the source-only populated recovery preflight and R62's schema-level pg_dump/pg_restore laboratory (tests/fixtures/populated-recovery/lab.js in the application tree): those answer whether a whole-schema dump restores; this one answers whether one tenant can be exported, re-imported and deleted with typed identity, tenant binding and ciphertext/key references intact.

The artifact this lab writes is a research artifact format, not an adopted backup format. No backup tool, retention rule, numeric bound or owner capability is selected here; see the DECISION lines below and in the module README.

docs.title: What it measures
docs.text:
The application-side primitives are the dormant, opt-in module lib/tenant-lifecycle/ on the CRM branch codex/tenant-export-delete-20261106 (README.md there describes the operations and refusals). The lab requires them by worktree path, provisions its own disposable PostgreSQL 16 and Vault dev server, and decides every fidelity claim with an independent admin-side oracle (SELECT * per admitted table and tenant, canonical JSON, multiset comparison) that shares no code with the module.

df -h /home   # rule 3: stop under 10 GB free; the runner refuses below the floor
node tools/lab/tenant-export-delete/run.js --worktree "$CRM_WORKTREE"
# optional: --stages positive,controls,restored   --out results/<date>

One invocation runs eight isolated stages (own schemas, roles and Vault keys each): the positive stage, six controls, then the positive stage again (restored). It records the PostgreSQL and Vault version strings, every count, each control's exact red text, and cleanup verification (docker inspect must say "No such" for every container and volume the run created).

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The claim reproduces, at both refs, for all three collections. A v3 POST with an identifier that is already stored and a different date, device or eventType is answered 400 with "Field <name> cannot be modified by the client", and the stored record is unchanged: one copy, first values kept. Nothing is stored twice. PUT /api/v3/<col>/<identifier> with a changed date gives the same 400. The identical re-send (control) is 200 with the identifier, so the probe tells the two apart.

Why POST reaches the check: lib/api3/generic/create/operation.js:43-56 (15.0.8) looks the identifier up and, on a match, calls replace(..., { isDeduplication: true }); replace runs update/validate.js, whose loop skips only identifier under deduplication (update/validate.js:21-43 at 15.0.8, :71-91 at fade2299).

case treatments entries devicestatus e. identical re-send (control) 201 → 200, n=1 201 → 200, n=1 201 → 200, n=1 a. same id, date +60 s 201 → 400 date, n=1 201 → 400 date, n=1 201 → 400 date, n=1 b. same id, other device, date +1.5 s 201 → 400 date, n=1 201 → 400 date, n=1 201 → 400 date, n=1 b2. same id, other device, same date 201 → 400 device, n=1 201 → 400 device, n=1 201 → 400 device, n=1 c. same id, other eventType 201 → 400 eventType, n=1 — — d. PUT by id, date +60 s 201 → 400 date, n=1 201 → 400 date, n=1 201 → 400 date, n=1

Every cell above is the same at 15.0.8 and fade2299. In b, date is the first immutable field the loop meets, so the message names date; b2 shows device alone is enough.

docs.title: Where the two refs differ: a record first written through v1
docs.text:
case 15.0.8 92d08342 dev fade2299 f. v1 POST (identifier, created_at, no device), then v3 POST same identifier + device, same time 200 → 400 date; stored record has no date, no device 200 → 200; stored record now has date = created_at and the device f2. as f, v3 time +60 s 200 → 400 date 200 → 400 date

On dev, isSameAsStored (update/validate.js:28-55 at fade2299) accepts a first device or app on a record that has none and a date equal to the record's created_at; a different time is still 400.

docs.title: v1, for contrast
docs.text:
case 15.0.8 dev fade2299 v1 treatments: same identifier, created_at +60 s 200 → 200, n=1, created_at moved to the second value same v1 entries: same identifier, date +60 s 200 → 200, n=2 (v1 entries match on sysTime + type, not identifier) same

So on the same server a time change under one identifier is an update on v1 treatments, a second record on v1 entries, and a 400 on API v3.
